### [1] [ChestPheNoT: Deployable, Auditable Label-Status-Evidence Extraction from Radiology Reports](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31629)
*Kai Yu,Chenyu Zhu,Zaifu Zhan,Meijia Song,Min Zeng,Xiaoyi Chen,Mingquan Lin,Rui Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CHESTPHENOT is a small, locally deployable language model that extracts chest radiology findings, their status, and supporting text spans from reports, achieving competitive or superior performance to larger or conventional systems, with auditable evidence and without needing external APIs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical applications such as cohort building, quality auditing, and analytics need structured phenotypes from radiology reports. Existing labelers provide labels and assertion status but not explicit textual evidence, and many powerful LLMs require cloud APIs that are unsuitable when protected clinical text cannot leave the institution. There is a need for compact models that can run locally, produce auditable predictions with supporting evidence, and work well despite limited expert annotations.

Method: The authors develop CHESTPHENOT, a family of compact 0.5–3B-parameter language models trained to jointly output: (1) radiology finding labels, (2) 3-way status (present/absent/uncertain), and (3) verbatim supporting evidence spans from the report. Training uses a hybrid silver supervision signal combining CheXbert labels and outputs from a 72B LLM, followed by supervised fine-tuning and lightweight GRPO (a reinforcement-style preference optimization) refinement. The model is evaluated on three human-annotated gold datasets that test in-distribution performance, cross-taxonomy generalization, and cross-institution robustness, and is compared against CheXbert and larger prompted LLM baselines (e.g., Qwen2.5 models).

Result: The 3B CHESTPHENOT model underperforms its CheXbert silver teacher on in-distribution data but becomes competitive or better under distribution shift, achieving a +2.0 F1 gain over CheXbert in cross-institution detection. It matches or exceeds substantially larger prompted LLMs on most detection and status prediction metrics. For evidence-grounded extraction, more than 99% of predicted evidence spans are present in the source report, and the 3B model reaches 47.5 auditable-F1, outperforming Qwen2.5-7B one-shot prompting by 7.6 F1 points and approaching the performance of Qwen2.5-72B.

Conclusion: CHESTPHENOT shows that small, locally deployable language models can perform competitive, evidence-grounded extraction of chest radiology phenotypes, supporting auditable clinical NLP workflows without sending text to external API-based LLMs. This enables privacy-preserving, transparent deployment for applications like cohort construction and quality auditing, with performance that rivals or surpasses larger general-purpose models under many conditions.

Abstract: Structured phenotype extraction from radiology reports supports cohort construction, quality auditing, and clinical analytics, but practical deployment requires local inference and auditable predictions, while expert annotations remain scarce. Conventional labelers provide structured findings and assertion states but no supporting evidence, while API-hosted large language models may be unsuitable when clinical text cannot leave institutional infrastructure. We present CHESTPHENOT, a compact 0.5-3B language model that jointly extracts finding labels, three-class status (present/absent/uncertain), and verbatim supporting evidence spans. CHESTPHENOT is trained using hybrid CheXbert+72B silver supervision followed by supervised fine-tuning and lightweight GRPO refinement. Across three human-annotated gold sets spanning in-distribution, cross-taxonomy, and cross-institution evaluation, the 3B model remains below its CheXbert silver teacher in distribution but is competitive under distribution shift, significantly surpassing CheXbert on cross-institution detection (+2.0 F1). Task-specific training also enables the 3B model to match or exceed substantially larger prompted models on most detection and status comparisons. For evidence-grounded extraction, over 99% of final evidence spans are locatable in the source report, and the 3B model achieves 47.5 auditable-F1, outperforming Qwen2.5-7B one-shot prompting by 7.6 points and approaching Qwen2.5-72B. These results demonstrate that locally deployable models can provide competitive and directly auditable radiology-report extraction without relying on external inference APIs. Code and the full extraction/judge prompts will be made available at https://github.com/yukkai/ChestPheNoT.

</details>


### [2] [A literature-guided descriptor-based framework for filtering composition search spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31650)
*Lei Zhang,Markus Stricker*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They use word embeddings trained on scientific literature to pick meaningful descriptors and build Pareto filters that rapidly shrink materials composition search spaces while still keeping the best-performing candidates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific literature encodes rich, implicit knowledge about how materials compositions relate to properties, but that knowledge is spread across words and associations rather than explicit rules. In materials discovery, composition spaces are huge, so we need automated, data-driven ways to narrow down candidates without losing top performers. The authors want to exploit the latent structure in large text corpora to guide this filtering in a quantitative and reproducible way.

Method: They train a word embedding model on a large corpus of materials-science literature and construct a filtered vocabulary of candidate descriptors (terms that capture relevant materials concepts). For a given target performance metric, they automatically select two descriptors from this vocabulary, using their positions in the embedding space. These two descriptors are then used to define a two-dimensional descriptor space for candidate compositions. In this space they build a Pareto-based filter that retains compositions lying on or near the Pareto front with respect to the chosen descriptors, discarding the rest. They benchmark this framework over multiple performance metrics and composition search spaces, and compare against filters using expert-chosen descriptors and random descriptors.

Result: Across all tested performance metrics and composition spaces, their framework removes on average 74.27% of candidate compositions while keeping the best-performing ones nearly intact, with an average error of only 1.93% between the best retained composition and the true experimental best. Their literature-guided, performance-metric-dependent descriptors outperform both expert-selected and randomly chosen descriptors, achieving a more favorable trade-off between how many candidates are retained and how close the retained best is to the true best.

Conclusion: Latent knowledge captured in literature-trained word embeddings can be turned into practical tools for materials discovery. By automatically selecting descriptors from embeddings and using them in a Pareto-based filtering scheme, one can drastically shrink composition search spaces yet still preserve high-performing candidates. This provides an intuitive, reproducible, and scalable approach for literature-guided screening in materials design.

Abstract: Scientific literature contains latent knowledge about materials behavior, but much of this knowledge is expressed through words, contexts, and recurring associations rather than explicit design principles. This raises a central question: how can large-scale scientific corpora be used for practical problems in materials discovery? Here, we present a literature-guided descriptor-based filtering framework for reducing composition search spaces. For a given performance metric, the framework selects two descriptors from a filtered vocabulary in a literature-trained word embedding model and uses the selected descriptors to construct a Pareto-based filter for candidate compositions. Across the evaluated performance metrics and composition search spaces, the framework filters out an average of 74.27\% of the candidate compositions, with an average best-value error of 1.93\% relative to experimental measurements. Compared with expert-chosen and random descriptors, our performance metric-dependent descriptors provide a more controlled balance between retained fraction and best-value error. These results show that literature-derived embeddings can support intuitive and reproducible filters for narrowing candidate composition spaces while preserving high-performing compositions.

</details>


### [3] [Distributional sentiment modeling and anomaly detection for consumer complaint assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31653)
*Peiheng Gao,Chen Yang,Shimin Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They analyze consumer complaint texts by modeling negative sentiment as a continuous distribution (Beta) and use divergence measures to detect complaints whose textual severity is inconsistent with monetary relief and company response.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most sentiment analysis in finance/risk uses coarse labels or a single feature and ignores how sentiment intensity varies across texts. The authors want a richer, distributional view of sentiment to better understand and monitor consumer complaints and operational risk.

Method: They score each complaint narrative with a transformer-based sentiment classifier, treating the resulting negative sentiment scores as continuous in [0,1]. For meritorious vs non-meritorious complaints they fit Beta distributions to these scores and compare the distributions using Kullback–Leibler divergence and squared Hellinger distance. They then combine these fitted distributions with monetary amounts and company response categories to build anomaly diagnostics that flag complaints where the severity implied by the text does not align with the recorded relief.

Result: The distributions of negative sentiment for meritorious and non-meritorious complaints overlap substantially, so sentiment alone cannot sharply classify outcomes. However, when sentiment distributions are combined with dollar amounts and company response types, the method highlights unusually severe complaints relative to the relief given, providing useful operational risk signals.

Conclusion: Modeling sentiment as a bounded continuous distribution rather than discrete labels allows a unified framework that connects sentiment extraction, Beta response modeling, and anomaly detection. This distributional approach yields practical diagnostics for identifying anomalously severe consumer complaints for risk monitoring, even though sentiment by itself is not a strong classifier of complaint outcomes.

Abstract: Sentiment analysis is a common tool for converting unstructured text into quantitative signals in finance and risk management. Yet most applications reduce the output to a discrete polarity label or a single predictive feature, overlooking the distributional structure of sentiment intensity in consumer complaint narratives. In this paper we treat negative sentiment in consumer complaints as a bounded continuous variable and study its full distribution rather than a single label. We score each narrative with a transformer classifier, model the scores with Beta distributions, and compare the fitted distributions of meritorious and non-meritorious complaints through the Kullback Leibler divergence and the squared Hellinger distance. The fitted distributions are then linked with dollar amounts and company response outcomes to construct anomaly diagnostics that flag complaints whose textual severity is inconsistent with the recorded relief. We find that the two groups have strongly overlapping distributions, so negative sentiment intensity is not a sharp classifier of outcomes on its own; combined with monetary and categorical attributes, it isolates unusually severe complaints for operational risk monitoring. Treating sentiment analysis as continuous distributional measurement, this study links sentiment extraction, bounded response modeling, and anomaly detection in a unified framework for consumer complaint assessment.

</details>


### [4] [Parser, Chunking, and Embedding Interactions in Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Indian Government Regulatory Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31660)
*Shubham Kumar Singh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper systematically studies how different combinations of parsers, chunking strategies, and embedding models affect RAG retrieval performance on regulatory documents, finding strong interactions between components and no universally best configuration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG systems are usually built by independently picking a parser, chunking strategy, and embedding model, but these choices are rarely evaluated jointly or at scale. Existing evaluations often focus on a single corpus and lack rigorous statistical analysis, leaving practitioners without clear guidance on how component interactions affect retrieval quality, especially for complex, structured documents like regulations.

Method: The authors conduct a controlled factorial experiment combining 3 document parsers, 3 chunking strategies, and 5 dense embedding models plus a BM25 baseline across four structurally distinct Indian central-government regulatory documents. They create 800 questions with associated evidence strings, automatically verify evidence against source text, and manually review a 10% sample. They then compute retrieval outcomes for all 54 retriever configurations (yielding 72,000 rows), fit linear mixed-effects models with document-query-level random intercepts, perform Holm-corrected paired comparisons between dense and sparse setups, and use clustered bootstrap methods to estimate confidence intervals. They also run ablations on embedding dimension and chunk size/overlap and perform an efficiency–quality Pareto analysis.

Result: No single retriever family consistently outperforms others across the different documents. Retrieval performance is strongly affected by interactions between parser and chunker choice. The MPNet-base embedding model consistently underperforms and fails badly on table-based questions. The corpus achieves an evidence-preservation ceiling above 98%, implying that most relevant information survives ingestion and that observed performance differences mainly stem from ranking quality instead of information loss. Detailed metrics and CIs are reported for all 54 retriever configurations, alongside ablation and Pareto analyses.

Conclusion: RAG retrieval quality is highly dependent on the joint configuration of parser, chunking strategy, and embedding model, and these components cannot be optimized in isolation. For regulatory-style corpora, attention to parser–chunker interactions and robustness to structured content like tables is crucial, as some popular embedding models (e.g., MPNet-base) can exhibit severe failure modes. Since evidence preservation is nearly saturated, future improvements should focus on better ranking and model choices rather than ingestion. The authors provide their evaluation harness, corpus manifest, and 800-question benchmark to support reproducible, component-level RAG research and practical tuning.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines are typically assembled from independently-chosen components -- a document parser, a chunking strategy, and an embedding model -- yet these choices are rarely evaluated jointly, and evaluations that do combine them are usually run on a single document or corpus. We present a controlled factorial study of 3 parsers, 3 chunking strategies, and 5 dense embedding models, together with a sparse BM25 baseline, evaluated against 800 question instances, each with one or more required evidence strings, with evidence strings automatically validated against source text and a 10% random sample manually reviewed, across four structurally distinct Indian central-government regulatory documents. We fit linear mixed-effects models with document-query-level random intercepts to the resulting 72,000-row result set, run Holm-corrected paired comparisons between matched dense and sparse configurations, and report clustered bootstrap confidence intervals for all 54 unique retriever configurations. We find that no single retriever family dominates across documents; parser and chunker choice interact significantly; MPNet-base is a consistent underperformer with a severe failure mode on table-derived questions; and the corpus exhibits a near-saturated evidence-preservation ceiling above 98%, indicating that retrieval differences are driven primarily by ranking quality rather than information loss during ingestion. We additionally report embedding-dimension and chunk-size/overlap ablations and an efficiency/quality Pareto analysis. We release our full evaluation harness, corpus manifest, and 800-question benchmark.

</details>


### [5] [LLM-Guided Ontology-Driven Knowledge Graph Construction from Unstructured Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31663)
*Abdelhadi Belfadel,Maxence Gagnant,Joseph Kattan,Sana Tmar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes and evaluates an ontology-learning pipeline that uses compact open-source LLMs, reusable prompts, and open knowledge bases to convert unstructured industrial incident reports into ontology-based knowledge graphs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial domains lack annotated data and have complex, domain-specific ontologies, making it difficult to build high-quality knowledge graphs from text, especially when data is private and models must be locally deployable. The authors aim to lower the barrier to constructing and enriching ontologies and knowledge graphs from such text using practical, resource-efficient methods.

Method: They design an ontology learning pipeline that: (1) uses open-source LLMs (7B–32B parameters) with schema-guided prompting to extract entities and relations from industrial text; (2) converts the extracted information into RDF triples; (3) derives and refines an OWL ontology; (4) enriches the ontology with external open knowledge bases; and (5) evaluates ontology quality and builds a populated knowledge graph. The approach is tested on a private French corpus of power-grid incident reports, including experiments with quantized models to study the performance–cost trade-off.

Result: On 80 manually annotated incident reports, schema-guided prompting yields a notable improvement in extraction quality compared to non-schema-guided approaches, and quantized open-source LLMs maintain good performance while reducing computational requirements. The pipeline successfully produces coherent RDF triples, an OWL ontology, and a populated knowledge graph from the unstructured reports.

Conclusion: The study shows that it is feasible to transform domain-specific industrial text into ontology-based knowledge graphs using locally deployed open-source LLMs. Reusable, schema-guided prompting strategies generalize the extraction process and, combined with model quantization, offer a practical and cost-effective solution for ontology learning and knowledge graph construction in specialized industrial contexts.

Abstract: Ontology-driven knowledge graph construction from industrial text remains challenging due to the domain specificity of documents, the scarcity of annotated resources, and the complexity of ontology engineering workflows. This paper presents and investigates the applicability of an ontology learning pipeline that combines compact open-source Large Language Models (LLMs), reusable prompting strategies, and open knowledge bases to support the extraction, structuring, enrichment, and evaluation of knowledge from textual corpora. The approach is tested and evaluated on a private French corpus of power-grid incident reports, using locally deployable open-source LLMs ranging from 7B to 32B parameters. Starting from unstructured reports, the approach extracts entities and relations, generates RDF triples, constructs related OWL ontology, enriches it using external knowledge sources, assesses the quality of the ontology, and subsequently constructs a populated knowledge graph grounded in the resulting ontology schema. Experiments on 80 manually annotated private reports show that schema-guided prompting significantly improves extraction quality, while quantized models provide an effective trade-off between performance and computational cost. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transforming domain-specific industrial text into ontology-based knowledge graphs using locally deployed open-source LLMs, while supporting the generalization of the extraction process through reusable prompting strategies.

</details>


### [6] [What Drives Dialectal Jailbreaks? An Ablation of Surface Form, Cultural Framing, and Strategy Banks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31664)
*Qingyang Xu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper finds that high jailbreak success comes from powerful strategy banks and optimization, not from using dialects or obscure language forms themselves.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work showed that using obscure or dialectal language (like classical Chinese) can weaken safety refusals in large language models, especially with black-box prompt optimization. It was unclear whether the core cause was the dialectal surface form, cultural framing, or the use of large expressive strategy banks plus optimization. The authors want to disentangle these factors to correctly understand why such attacks work and how to defend against them.

Method: They extend an existing classical-Chinese red-teaming framework to two Chinese dialects (Shanghainese and Cantonese), and design a 36-cell ablation study. The factors are: (1) surface form (English, Mandarin, dialects and their naive translations), (2) different versions of a strategy bank (including a culture-neutral generic one), (3) presence or absence of black-box optimization, and (4) two different target LLMs. They measure attack success rates, query efficiency, response severity, and perform qualitative coding of attack conversations to identify recurring mechanisms like semantic glossing and procedural scaffolding. They also check how results depend on safety-judge calibration and limitations in distinguishing one-shot from iterative strategies.

Result: They find that just using dialectal or obscure surface forms is neither necessary nor sufficient for high attack success. Non-optimized prompts in English, Mandarin, or naive dialect translations all have low attack success (<8%). In contrast, any condition that preserves an optimizer-driven, expressive strategy bank reaches 98–100% attack success, even with a culture-neutral, generic bank, and does so with near single-query cost. Dialect choice still influences how many queries are needed and how severe the model’s unsafe responses are. Qualitative analysis reveals common attack mechanisms such as semantic glossing (rephrasing unsafe content) and procedural scaffolding (step-by-step guidance). They also show that the apparent ceiling-level success is sensitive to how the safety judge is calibrated and acknowledge design limitations in isolating one-shot from iterative optimization effects.

Conclusion: The dominant driver of jailbreak success in these settings is the expressive, optimizer-controlled strategy bank, not dialectal, obscure, or culturally specific language per se. Dialects modulate efficiency and severity but are not the core vulnerability. This corrects prior interpretations that emphasized cultural or surface-form factors and suggests that defenses should focus on limiting or hardening against powerful strategy-bank-based optimization attacks and improving safety-judge calibration, rather than treating dialectal prompts as uniquely dangerous on their own.

Abstract: Recent work suggests that obscure language registers can weaken large language model refusal behavior, especially when paired with black-box prompt optimization. It remains unclear whether failures stem from non-standard surface form, culturally grounded framing, or optimization over an expressive prompt-strategy space. We study Chinese registers by extending a classical-Chinese red-teaming framework to Shanghainese and Cantonese and running a 36-cell ablation across surface forms, strategy-bank variants, and two target models. The main finding is corrective: dialectal surface form is neither necessary nor sufficient for high attack success. Non-optimized English, Mandarin, and naive dialect translations remain below 8\% attack success rate, whereas all conditions that retain an optimizer-controlled strategy bank reach 98--100\%. A culture-neutral generic strategy bank reaches the same ceiling at near-single-query cost, further indicating that strategy-bank expressiveness, rather than dialectal or cultural content, accounts for most of the observed effect. Dialect choice still affects query efficiency and response severity, and qualitative coding identifies recurring high-level mechanisms such as semantic glossing and procedural scaffolding. We qualify the absolute ceiling-level attack success rate by showing sensitivity to judge calibration and noting that the design does not fully separate one-shot strategy construction from iterative search.

</details>


### [7] [Age-Adaptive Handwriting Reconstruction from an IMU-Based Digital Pen through Shared Representations and Domain-Specific Heads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31666)
*Florent Imbert,Yann Soullard,Eric Anquetil,Hui Han*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a cross-domain neural model based on a Temporal Convolutional Network with multiple prediction heads to robustly reconstruct handwriting traces from IMU-equipped digital pens across both children and adults.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: IMU-equipped digital pens can be used on any surface and are promising for large-scale handwriting acquisition in classrooms, but handwriting reconstruction from sensor data is difficult because sensor signals differ significantly between adults and children due to differences in writing dynamics, motor control, pen grip, and confidence. High variability in children’s handwriting makes collecting enough in-domain data impractical at school scale, and models trained on one population (adults or children) do not generalize well to the other, necessitating a unified, robust model that works across age groups without user-specific adaptation and can be deployed on-pen.

Method: The authors propose a cross-domain learning approach using a novel neural network architecture built on a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) with multiple prediction heads. The architecture is designed to learn shared representations from IMU signals that capture common structure between adult and child handwriting, while separate or specialized heads handle domain-specific variations related to graphomotor development. This setup allows the model to leverage data from both adults and children simultaneously to improve handwriting trace reconstruction.

Result: The abstract indicates that the proposed TCN-based multi-head model improves robustness of handwriting trace reconstruction across age groups, with each domain benefiting from the presence of data from the other. Though specific metrics are not given, the implication is that performance degradation in cross-population scenarios is reduced compared to single-domain models trained only on adults or only on children.

Conclusion: A unified, cross-domain neural model based on a TCN with multiple prediction heads can better handle the variability between adult and child handwriting in IMU pen signals, enabling more reliable handwriting trace reconstruction from a single model deployable directly on the pen. This approach mitigates the need for large, population-specific datasets collected in constrained environments and shows that leveraging shared features across domains improves generalization and robustness.

Abstract: Digital pens are widely used to capture handwriting on digital devices, enabling precise trace recording and enhancing human-computer interaction. However, most are bundled with tablets and lack cross-brand compatibility. Recent digital pens equipped with kinematic sensors have emerged, designed for use on any surface. This especially opens significant potential for supporting handwriting acquisition in classrooms.  Handwriting reconstruction from such an IMU-equipped pen poses a challenge due to the significant variability in sensor signals between adults and children. Even when producing visually similar traces, variations in writing dynamics, motor control, pen holding, and user confidence introduce substantial discrepancies in the captured signals. Additionally, the high variability in children's handwriting requires collecting large amounts of data, which is not feasible to implement in a school environment at scale. Furthermore, models trained exclusively on adult data fail to generalize to children's handwriting, and conversely, models trained on children's data perform poorly on adult writers. This crosspopulation degradation highlights the need for a unified model that can be deployed directly on the pen, without any user-specific adaptation. To address this issue, we propose a cross-domain learning, using an original neural network architecture based on a Temporal Convolutional Network and multiple prediction heads. The model is designed to be robust across age groups by leveraging shared features while effectively handling variability induced by differences in graphomotor development. This approach aims to improve handwriting trace reconstruction from sensor data, where each domain benefits from additional data provided by the other domain.

</details>


### [8] [An Evaluation of AI-Supported Evidence-Based Learning for Public Speaking Skill Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31676)
*Sashini Hettiarachchi,Shahbaz Siddeeq,Mika Saari,Pekka Abrahamsson*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents and pilots an AI system that gives context-aware feedback and generates model speeches (text + audio) to help students improve public speaking and reduce anxiety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public speaking is critical in academic and professional settings but frequently triggers anxiety. Existing AI speech coaching tools mostly provide generic, context-agnostic feedback and do not supply high-quality example/model speeches for learners to emulate. There is a need for tools that can tailor feedback to the specific content and goals of a speech and that can also show learners improved versions of their own speeches to facilitate example-based learning and confidence building.

Method: The authors designed an AI-based public speaking coaching system that: (1) incorporates the context of a speech into its evaluation criteria to deliver more tailored feedback, and (2) generates improved, model versions of users’ speeches in both text and audio forms. They ran a small pilot study with seven undergraduate students over one to three weeks. Each participant repeatedly used the system to practice the same speech at least three times, receiving context-aware feedback and model speeches in each iteration. The study measured changes in filler word usage, self-reported anxiety, and users’ subjective perceptions of usefulness and confidence.

Result: Across all seven participants, public speaking performance improved over repeated system use. Specifically, filler word usage decreased, and self-reported anxiety levels dropped between 15.3% and 34.4%. Qualitative feedback indicated that participants considered the context-aware feedback and generated revised speeches helpful and confidence-enhancing.

Conclusion: Integrating speech context into evaluation criteria and providing AI-generated model speeches (text and audio) appear effective for improving public speaking skills and reducing anxiety. Even in a small pilot, all participants showed measurable gains and reported positive experiences. The work suggests that context-aware, example-based AI coaching can be a promising direction for public speaking training. The authors propose future research on extending the system with video-based analysis to assess and coach physical delivery aspects such as gestures and posture.

Abstract: Public speaking is an essential skill in academic and professional contexts, but it often causes anxiety. Although several AI-based speech coaching tools exist, they typically provide generic feedback and lack model speeches for learning. This study addresses these gaps by developing a system that incorporates speech context into evaluation criteria, enabling more tailored feedback. It also generates improved model speeches in both text and audio formats to support example-based learning. The system was evaluated in a pilot study with seven undergraduate students over one to three weeks. Participants used the system repeatedly and practiced the same speech at least three times. Results showed improvements in public speaking performance for all participants. Filler word usage decreased, and anxiety levels dropped by 15.3% to 34.4%. Participants found the context-aware feedback and revised speeches useful and confidence-building. These findings suggest that context-aware feedback and model speeches can enhance public speaking skills and reduce anxiety. Future studies could explore video-based analysis of physical behavior during speeches.

</details>


### [9] [The Temporal Tug-of-War: Visualizing and Detecting RAG Conflicts in Diffusion Models via Trajectory Variance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31684)
*Sravan Karthick T,Pranav Darshan,Pranav A,Minal Moharir,Ivan P. Yamshchikov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies and measures conflicts between retrieved context and model’s own knowledge in diffusion-based RAG systems using a simple trajectory-variance metric.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In Retrieval-Augmented Generation with discrete diffusion language models, retrieved documents can contradict the model’s internal (parametric) knowledge. This creates a unique, temporally extended conflict during iterative denoising that can visibly affect generation but is hard to diagnose and detect automatically. The authors want a reliable, lightweight way to detect when such knowledge conflicts occur, to better understand and control RAG behavior in diffusion architectures.

Method: They study the denoising trajectories of discrete diffusion LMs under RAG when the retrieved context conflicts with the model’s parametric knowledge. They define temporal semantic divergence as the evolving difference in meaning of intermediate answers over time and across stochastic runs. To quantify this, they introduce the Trajectory Variance Score (TVS), which computes the mean pairwise cosine distance between embeddings of answers generated along multiple independent denoising trajectories. This metric is then used as a feature in simple classifiers, mainly Logistic Regression, and compared against more complex sequential models, to predict whether a knowledge conflict is present. They evaluate across four datasets (Synthetic, SciQ, PopQA, CounterFact) and on two architectures (LLaDA and Dream 7B), varying the number of trajectories (e.g., 2 vs. 5) to test computation–performance trade-offs.

Result: TVS is computationally cheap, requiring as few as two parallel inference trajectories, yet captures the tug of war between parametric and contextual knowledge. A Logistic Regression classifier using only TVS achieves 70.10% accuracy and 0.7647 AUROC on LLaDA across four datasets. On Dream 7B, using TVS with five trajectories improves accuracy from 63.91% (with two trajectories) to 69.62%. More sophisticated sequential models that attempt to leverage richer temporal patterns offer only marginal gains over the simple linear classifier based on TVS. The conflict-induced trajectory dynamics detected by TVS appear consistent across different diffusion architectures, as demonstrated on LLaDA and Dream 7B.

Conclusion: Temporal semantic divergence in diffusion trajectories is a robust and architecture-transferable signal of conflicts between retrieved context and parametric knowledge in RAG setups. The proposed Trajectory Variance Score offers a simple, interpretable, and efficient way to detect these conflicts, often making complex modeling unnecessary. This work suggests that examining the geometry of multiple denoising trajectories can reveal internal knowledge tensions and may guide future methods for monitoring, diagnosing, and potentially resolving RAG conflicts in diffusion-based language models.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) introduces a specific failure mode in discrete diffusion language models: when retrieved context contradicts parametric knowledge, the iterative denoising process becomes a visible battleground between competing knowledge sources. We identify temporal semantic divergence as an observable for detecting these conflicts and introduce the Trajectory Variance Score (TVS), a simple and interpretable measure of this divergence. TVS computes the mean pairwise cosine distance of answer embeddings across independent stochastic denoising trajectories, capturing the temporal tug of war between parametric and contextual attractors. Requiring as few as two parallel inference runs, TVS is computationally lightweight. Across four diverse datasets (Synthetic, SciQ, PopQA, and CounterFact), a simple Logistic Regression classifier using TVS achieves $70.10\%$ accuracy and $0.7647$ AUROC on LLaDA. On Dream 7B, increasing the number of trajectories from two to five improves accuracy from $63.91\%$ to $69.62\%$. More complex sequential models provide only marginal improvements over the linear classifier. Evaluation across LLaDA and Dream 7B demonstrates that conflict-induced trajectory dynamics and their key properties transfer across distinct diffusion architectures.

</details>


### [10] [Verification of PETSc with CIVL using LLM-generated ACSL contracts and deterministic driver generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31687)
*Hansol Suh,Jan Hückelheim,Stephen Siegel*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a semi-automated pipeline using LLMs plus a deterministic verification toolchain to generate checkable specifications and drivers for formally verifying numerical library functions, demonstrated on PETSc, where it also uncovers a long-standing bug.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Parallel numerical libraries like PETSc are widely used in critical scientific and engineering computations, where silent numerical errors can be very costly. Yet such libraries are rarely formally verified due to the effort and expertise required: writing precise formal specifications, building verification harnesses/drivers, and using verification tools, all of which can introduce new bugs and mis-specifications. With advances in LLMs, there is an opportunity to automate some of this work, but naive code or harness generation is brittle and just shifts the verification burden. The authors are motivated to find a way to safely leverage LLMs to reduce specification effort while keeping a high-assurance, auditable verification process.

Method: The authors design a constrained pipeline in which an LLM is used only in a narrow, auditable role: generating small ACSL (ANSI/ISO C Specification Language) contracts from existing human documentation of library functions. They then employ a deterministic verification toolchain that supports a restricted subset of ACSL to ensure predictability. This toolchain automatically generates a driver that connects the implementation under test with the contract and, when available, an existing reference model, and uses the CIVL verifier to check for correctness. The process is applied end-to-end to three PETSc matrix operations—MatAXPY (with an existing reference model), MatAYPX (without a reference model), and a non-compressing mode of MatFilter (without a reference model but with conditional behavior)—thereby testing the approach across different levels of oracle availability and behavioral complexity.

Result: The pipeline successfully generates certifiable ACSL contracts and corresponding verification drivers that can be used with CIVL to check PETSc functions. In the MatAXPY case, the implementation is verified against both the contract and the existing reference model, validating the approach when a trusted oracle exists. For MatAYPX, even without a reference model, the contract alone enables the detection of a previously unknown bug in PETSc that had persisted since 1997. For the more complex non-compressing MatFilter behavior, the approach still supports verification against the synthesized contract, demonstrating its applicability to more conditional logic.

Conclusion: The study shows that LLMs can be productively and safely integrated into formal verification workflows if they are restricted to generating small, human-certifiable specifications rather than full verification harnesses or implementations. Coupled with a deterministic toolchain and a restricted ACSL profile, this approach avoids introducing large amounts of unaudited code while still reducing human effort. The successful application to PETSc, including the discovery of a decades-old bug, suggests that such pipelines can make formal verification of numerical libraries more practical and valuable in real-world scientific and engineering software.

Abstract: Parallel numerical libraries such as PETSc are widely used in science and engineering applications where wrong results can have costly consequences. Despite this, numerical libraries are rarely formally verified. One of the challenges is the need for an expert to hand-write a specification and manually apply a verification tool, often requiring the development of a harness or driver, all of which can contain additional bugs that lead to false positives or false negatives during verification. With recent advancements in large language models (LLMs), it is tempting to generate such drivers and reference models automatically, but one-shot generation based on a simple prompt is brittle and leads to additional unverified code that needs to be audited. In this paper, we present an approach to use LLMs in a limited setting to generate a small, human-certifiable ACSL contract from the function's documentation, combined with a deterministic toolchain that supports a restricted ACSL profile and generates a driver that uses the CIVL verifier to check the implementation against the contract and, when available, an existing reference model. We demonstrate the pipeline end-to-end on three PETSc functions: MatAXPY (reference model already exists), MatAYPX (no reference model, so the certified contract is the sole oracle), and the non-compressing mode of MatFilter (no reference model, with more complex, conditional behavior). With this pipeline, we were able to discover a bug in PETSc's MatAYPX function that was previously undiscovered and had been present in the code since 1997.

</details>


### [11] [Don't Repeat Yourself: Self-Supervised Fine-Tuning for Coverage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31688)
*Eric Fithian,Kirill Skobelev,X. Y. Han*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces DRY-SFT, a post-training method that increases the diversity of solutions produced by large language models in verifiable domains like coding and math, boosting the chance that at least one of many attempts is correct.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In tasks where solutions are verifiable, such as programming benchmarks, what really matters is whether at least one correct solution appears among multiple samples (pass@k), not just the accuracy of single attempts (pass@1). However, standard post-training tends to make models mode-collapsed—concentrating probability mass on a few stereotyped outputs—so simply sampling more or turning up temperature often yields many similar, redundant attempts. The authors aim to systematically increase the diversity and structural variety of generated solutions, thereby improving coverage of the solution space and increasing the probability of a correct answer with multiple attempts, without relying on reward models, verifiers, or correctness labels.

Method: The authors propose DRY-SFT (Don't Repeat Yourself Supervised Fine-Tuning), a two-stage post-training procedure. Stage 1 (data generation): For each problem, the model is prompted to sequentially generate K different solutions. Each new attempt is conditioned on the problem plus all prior attempts, with instructions to produce a different solution, thereby collecting a diverse set of candidate solutions per problem. Stage 2 (fine-tuning): These K attempts are then used as independent training examples, but when fine-tuning, each attempt is presented with only the original problem in context, not the prior attempts. This avoids baking the multi-attempt prompt pattern into the model while encouraging it to map a single problem to many distinct valid solution patterns. The training uses standard supervised learning; there is no ranking, reward modeling, verifier feedback, or filtering by correctness.

Result: On coding benchmarks HumanEval+, MBPP+, and DS-1000, applying DRY-SFT to open-weight models substantially improves pass@100: +10.8, +12.5, and +12.4 percentage points, respectively, compared to the base models, with only a small reduction in pass@1. Structural diversity among successful programs, quantified via abstract syntax tree (AST) edit distance between passing solutions, increases markedly on all three datasets. DRY-SFT enables the model to solve 244 of 600 problems that the base model fails to solve under the same 200-sample evaluation budget. Experiments across nine open-weight models show that those with lower initial structural diversity benefit most, with base-model diversity strongly predicting DRY-SFT gains.

Conclusion: DRY-SFT is an effective, implementation-simple post-training strategy for increasing output diversity and solution-space coverage in verifiable domains like code generation, without requiring correctness labels or external reward signals. By training on multiple, explicitly different solutions per problem, models become less mode-collapsed and more structurally diverse in their generations, leading to significantly higher pass@k scores at modest cost to single-sample accuracy. The method is particularly impactful for models that are initially highly mode-collapsed, suggesting a broadly applicable way to improve multi-sample performance of existing open-weight LLMs.

Abstract: In verifiable domains such as math and coding, finding one correct solution among many attempts can matter more than the pass rate of each attempt. Post-training can concentrate large language model outputs around a few modes, while increasing sampling temperature has limited effectiveness. We introduce Don't Repeat Yourself Supervised Fine-Tuning (DRY-SFT), a post-training method that increases output diversity and coverage: the probability of at least one correct solution among many attempts. DRY-SFT has two stages. First, for each problem, sequentially generate K solutions, showing the model all prior attempts and asking for a different solution. Second, fine-tune on each attempt independently, removing prior attempts from the context. The process uses no reward, verifier, or correctness filter. On HumanEval+, MBPP+, and DS-1000, DRY-SFT raises pass@100 by 10.8, 12.5, and 12.4 percentage points, respectively, at a small cost to pass@1. Structural diversity, measured by abstract syntax tree edit distance among passing solutions, rises significantly on all three benchmarks. DRY-SFT also solves 244 of 600 problems that the base model did not solve in the same 200 attempts. Across nine open-weight models, lower structural diversity of the base model significantly predicts larger DRY-SFT gains, indicating that the method is especially effective on more mode-collapsed models.

</details>


### [12] [The Ongiini-Eval-OW Benchmark: A Concept Paper for the Planned Benchmarking of Machine Translation and Large Language Models on Oshindonga and Oshikwanyama](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31727)
*Sebastian Küpers*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes Ongiini-Eval-OW, the first machine translation evaluation benchmark for Oshiwambo (Oshindonga and Oshikwanyama), detailing its planned design, coverage, and release timeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Oshiwambo, despite being widely spoken and representing about half of Namibian households, lacks any published MT evaluation benchmark and is not covered by major commercial or open multilingual MT systems. This gap hinders progress on MT and NLP for these languages and limits systematic comparison of systems. The authors aim to fill this empirical coverage gap and provide infrastructure for future research and system evaluation.

Method: The authors design Ongiini-Eval-OW as a 600-item benchmark for English↔Oshindonga and English↔Oshikwanyama, with references from two independent native translators. They include a 30-item inter-translator agreement subset, stratify data using 11 linguistic/phenomenon tags with at least 30 items per tag, and define a deterministic 30% blind split for fair evaluation. They specify a reproducible scoring protocol using chrF++, BLEU, and COMET-22, plus a 50-item human evaluation component. They also plan a public leaderboard with a model matrix spanning major commercial and open-weight systems, and publish data and code under CC-BY-4.0 and MIT licenses.

Result: As a concept paper, there are no experimental MT accuracy results yet. Instead, the paper delivers: (1) a detailed benchmark design; (2) documentation of the current lack of Oshindonga/Oshikwanyama coverage in mainstream MT systems and open models; (3) a concrete data collection and annotation pipeline with quality controls; and (4) a planned leaderboard setup and participation framework. The main outcome is the specification of the forthcoming Ongiini-Eval-OW benchmark rather than empirical model comparisons.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that there is a significant and currently unaddressed gap in MT evaluation resources for Oshiwambo, which impedes both academic and commercial progress. Ongiini-Eval-OW is proposed as the first standardized benchmark for Oshindonga and Oshikwanyama, with careful design to enable reproducible, fine-grained evaluation and community participation. They commit to releasing data and code under permissive licenses by Q4 2026 and invite contributions from MT developers and researchers to populate the initial leaderboard and to help extend the benchmark over time.

Abstract: Oshiwambo -- a cluster of mutually intelligible Bantu languages spoken by over a million people across northern Namibia and southern Angola, and the home language of roughly half of Namibian households -- has, to our knowledge, no published machine-translation evaluation benchmark. Major commercial services (Google Translate, DeepL, Microsoft Translator), open multilingual MT models (NLLB-200, MADLAD-400), and the open Masakhane checkpoint collection all lack coverage of either standardised dialect, Oshindonga or Oshikwanyama. We announce Ongiini-Eval-OW, a planned 600-item English-Oshindonga and English-Oshikwanyama benchmark with native-speaker references from two independent translators, a 30-item inter-translator agreement set, an 11-tag phenomenon-tagged stratification (at least 30 items per tag), a deterministic 30% blind split, and a reproducible scoring protocol over chrF++, BLEU, and COMET-22, supplemented by a 50-item human-evaluation round. We document the empirical coverage gap, the dataset composition, the launch-leaderboard model matrix across American, European, and Chinese frontier and open-weight systems, and the contribution pipeline. The dataset is targeted for first public release in Q4 2026; this v1.0 concept paper announces the design and the call for participation. Data and code will be released under CC-BY-4.0 and MIT respectively.

</details>


### [13] [Omni-IO Skills: Harnessing Your Agent Omni-Native](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31847)
*Yanlin Li,Mingyang Hao,Shengqiong Wu,Hao Fei,Mong-Li Lee,Wynne Hsu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Omni-IO Skills, an agent harness that makes existing language agents natively multimodal across many artifact types by coordinating tools and models via a standardized execution interface and asset registry.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current general-purpose agents have fragmented capabilities across different modalities (text, images, audio, video, documents, 3D assets, code). Extending base foundation models to support new modalities is expensive and slow, while assembling many specialist models and tools creates coordination problems for multi-step, multi-asset workflows (tracking dependencies, reusing intermediate artifacts, managing cross-turn edits). The authors aim to provide a scalable, modular way to compose multimodal capabilities without retraining or modifying the core reasoning model.

Method: The authors design Omni-IO Skills, a plug-and-play "Agent Harness" that wraps existing agents. It introduces (1) hierarchical Skills that encapsulate multimodal tasks, (2) a standardized multimodal execution interface, (3) dependency-aware orchestration, and (4) a persistent Asset Registry. Workflows are encoded as Declare Execution Graphs that express tasks, dependencies, and parallelizable operations. These graphs schedule independent steps concurrently and automatically register their outputs for downstream reuse, across interchangeable execution backends (e.g., different tools or models for the same skill). The harness is instantiated with 27 skills covering 38 tasks across seven artifact modalities and four capability types (understanding, generation, reasoning, retrieval). Performance is evaluated on the UniM-90 benchmark with different host agents (GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5).

Result: Using Omni-IO Skills, the authors raise the input-support rate of GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5 on UniM-90 from ~40% to 100%, meaning the agents can now handle all task input formats. The relative Semantic–Quality Coupled Score (a joint measure of semantic correctness and output quality) increases from 26.99 to 74.94 for GPT-5.6 Sol and from 27.82 to 77.78 for Claude Sonnet 5. The Strict Structure Score (measuring adherence to required output structure) reaches 100.00 and 99.78, respectively. These metrics indicate substantial improvements in both breadth and reliability of multimodal task handling without changing the core models.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that capability composition at the harness level—via Omni-IO Skills—provides a practical, scalable path to building omni-modal systems. By standardizing multimodal execution, managing dependencies, and enabling persistent asset reuse, the harness transforms existing agents into omni-native ones while keeping their reasoning core untouched. The strong gains on UniM-90 demonstrate that broad, evolvable multimodal competence can be achieved through modular orchestration of skills and tools rather than continual foundation-model retraining.

Abstract: General-purpose agents can plan, reason, and act over long horizons, yet their production capabilities remain fragmented across text, images, audio, video, documents, 3D assets, and code. Extending a foundation model to additional modalities ties capability growth to costly model updates, while assembling specialist models and tools leaves unresolved how procedures, dependencies, intermediate assets, and cross-turn revisions should be coordinated. We present Omni-IO Skills, a plug-and-play Agent Harness that makes existing agents omni-native through hierarchical Skills, a standardized multimodal execution interface, dependency-aware orchestration, and a persistent Asset Registry. Multi-asset workflows are represented as Declare Execution Graphs, which schedule independent operations concurrently and register successful outputs for downstream and cross-turn reuse across replaceable execution backends. Its 27 Skills cover 38 representative tasks spanning seven artifact modalities and four capability families: understanding, generation, reasoning, and retrieval. On UniM-90, the harness raises the input-support rates of GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5 from 40.00% and 38.89% to 100%, while increasing relative Semantic--Quality Coupled Score from 26.99 to 74.94 and from 27.82 to 77.78, respectively; Strict Structure Score reaches 100.00 and 99.78. These results establish harness-level capability composition as a practical route to broad, evolvable Omni systems without changing the host agent's reasoning core.

</details>


### [14] [Agents Can Use Base Models to Evade AI Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31876)
*Bhuwan Dhingra,Danish Pruthi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a coding-agent-based attack that stitches together text from a base language model, producing high‑quality responses that substantially evade current AI-text detectors and watermarking schemes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI-generated text detectors and watermarking methods are increasingly used for provenance and misuse detection, but base language models can already evade some detectors. Prior humanization methods typically paraphrase model outputs iteratively, causing semantic drift and hurting task performance. The authors are motivated to find a more effective, controllable way to generate detector‑evading text that preserves task accuracy and to stress‑test current detection defenses.

Method: The authors equip a coding-style orchestrator agent (Claude Opus 5 within a Claude Code environment) to call a local 32B OLMo-2 base language model and assemble final responses by stitching together selected samples from the base model. Rather than paraphrasing, the agent decomposes the task, queries the base LM for candidate continuations, and programmatically selects and concatenates segments to form a coherent answer. They evaluate this pipeline across multiple benchmarks (creative writing, factual grounding, health QA, instruction following) and test its impact on both post‑hoc detectors (e.g., Pangram v4) and soft watermarking schemes, while also measuring token usage and cost overhead.

Result: The stitched-output system maintains nearly the same task performance as a standard Claude Opus 5 agent while using up to 90% of the tokens from the local base OLMo-2 model. It sharply reduces post‑hoc detector effectiveness, with Pangram v4’s detection rate dropping from 77% to 24%. It also significantly weakens soft watermarking, with simulated detection falling to about 10% at low false positive rates. However, this evasion becomes much more expensive in practice, with token counts and estimated query costs rising by as much as 30x compared to straightforward API usage.

Conclusion: Coding agents that orchestrate and stitch base-model samples constitute a powerful new adversarial technique against AI text detection and watermarking, enabling high‑quality, task‑accurate yet detector‑evading outputs. Although the attack is computationally and financially costly, it demonstrates a realistic threat model and highlights that current detectors trained mainly on assistant-style outputs are insufficient. The authors recommend that post‑hoc detection providers incorporate base‑model style generations into training data and reconsider threat assumptions in light of such orchestrated attacks.

Abstract: We show that coding agents equipped with a base language model can successfully assemble responses from its samples to evade detection. Base models have been shown to evade commercial detectors, however, prior "humanization" techniques rely on using these models to paraphrase AI outputs over several iterations, which invariably results in semantic drift. In contrast, equipping coding agents to directly orchestrate the writing process by stitching text samples from a base model allows it to produce outputs that are coherent, task-specific and generally high quality. We find that Claude Opus 5 operating in a Claude Code harness effectively orchestrates a local 32B parameter OLMo-2 base LM and sacrifices little task accuracy across benchmarks spanning creative writing, factual grounding, health QA and instruction following, while using up to 90% base LM tokens. Responses constructed in this manner reduce the effectiveness of both post-hoc detectors (Pangram v4 detection rate drops from 77% to 24%) and soft watermarking applied a priori to the agent's generations (down to a simulated 10% detection at low FPR). While effective, this evasion requires a significantly larger number of input and output tokens from the agent, increasing the dollar cost per query up to 30x at API-pricing. Overall, this work demonstrates the effectiveness of a new class of adversarial attacks against AI text detection, and urges post-hoc detection providers to include outputs of base models in their training.

</details>


### [15] [Transformer MLP Gate Thresholds Are Couplings to a Carried Reference Direction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31956)
*Olli Tuomi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that the corpus-mean direction in a transformer’s residual stream is not just nuisance variance: it acts as a functional reference level that sets MLP gate thresholds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Researchers often subtract the mean residual direction before analysis assuming it is uninformative, but this practice may discard mechanistically important structure if that mean plays a role in how neurons/gates are activated.

Method: They analytically decompose MLP gate pre-activations in Phi-2 to separate contributions from explicit biases and from coupling to the residual stream’s mean direction, then run causal interventions: removing or perturbing the projection onto this direction, adding noise, and comparing with random-direction and random-initialized controls. They replicate these analyses across multiple transformer families with different nonlinearities and bias designs.

Result: In mid-stack layers of Phi-2, over 99.9% of gates’ resting inhibition largely comes from coupling to the mean residual direction, contributing 48–56× more than the explicit bias terms. This coupling is highly direction-specific: ordering gates by their coupling to the true mean direction yields a Spearman ρ ≈ 0.95 for firing rates, versus ≤ 0.09 for random directions. Removing the projection on this direction increases above-threshold firing about 9×, far larger than norm-matched controls, and noise along this direction is 8–42× more disruptive than the same energy along random directions. Similar patterns appear in other models using GELU/SiLU, but not in OPT, where LayerNorm biases cancel the effect.

Conclusion: The residual-stream mean direction acts as a learned constant reference that MLP gates use to implement thresholds, with explicit bias parameters playing only a minor role. Architectures differ in whether this reference is implemented in the residual stream or in learned biases, implying that standard mean-centering procedures can remove a core part of the network’s gating mechanism.

Abstract: The corpus-mean direction of a transformer's residual stream is a component shared across all inputs, and is commonly removed by mean-centering before representational analysis. We present evidence that it is a functional component: the reference against which the MLP gate population sets its operating point. In Phi-2, an exact decomposition of resting gate pre-activations shows that at mid-stack layers the resting inhibition of >99.9% of gates is carried by the coupling $w \cdot b_L$ to the carried mean direction, at 48-56$\times$ the explicit bias parameter, and the coupling is direction-specific: a random direction at matched norm orders the population's firing rates at Spearman $ρ\leq 0.09$ where the reference reaches 0.95. (That 0.95 is near-tautological on its own; the paper derives its null.) Causally, removing the stream's projection on the reference multiplies above-threshold firing by about 9$\times$, dose-monotonically, at 23-59$\times$ a norm-matched control; a random-initialised twin is flat, and replacement tests show that the direction carries the function and the magnitude does not. A direction-matched control makes the same point: noise injected along the reference costs 8-42$\times$ the same energy along a random direction. The decomposition replicates on four further families spanning both gate types (GELU with an explicit gate bias, bias-free SwiGLU), and the dose-response on two of them. Across an eight-model scan the mechanism is present in every GELU and SiLU family and absent only in OPT, where an opposing LayerNorm bias cancels the carried reference. Gate thresholds are implemented as couplings to a constant the network builds for the distribution it is reading, with the bias parameters contributing little; how much of that constant is carried in the stream and how much in parameters depends on the architecture.

</details>


### [16] [IndicFDB: Benchmarking Full-Duplex Voice Agents across Indian Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31967)
*Rajarshi Roy,Shobhit Banga,Jonathan Raiman,Supriya Paul,Bhaskar Singh,Manmeet Kaur,Sagar Jain,Hanuman Sidh,Pranav Sharma,Aditya Singh,Aaditya Pareek,Manas Dhir,Adi Margolin,Niket Agarwal,Bryan Catanzaro*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: IndicFDB extends Full-Duplex-Bench to 10 Indian languages with a much larger multilingual corpus and a cross-lingual evaluation pipeline for full-duplex voice agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Full-Duplex-Bench for evaluating real-time conversational behaviors of voice agents is limited to English and depends on word-level ASR timestamps and an English-prompted LLM judge, which do not transfer well to Indian languages. There is a need for a scalable, language-agnostic way to evaluate full-duplex behaviors (pauses, turn-taking, backchannels, interruptions) for multilingual settings, especially for Indian languages.

Method: The authors build IndicFDB by (1) mining pause handling, turn taking, and backchanneling events from ~50,000 hours of channel-separated multilingual conversations using language-independent voice activity detection (VAD); (2) constructing synthetic but human-validated user interruption samples; (3) evaluating timing with VAD-based heuristics instead of word-level alignment; and (4) using an open-weight transcription+translation pipeline to convert agent responses into English so that an LLM (prompted in English) can rate relevance and quality. They then benchmark seven voice agents (commercial APIs and monolingual open models) on this dataset.

Result: IndicFDB consists of 12,350 samples across ten Indian languages, ~17x larger than the original English Full-Duplex-Bench. Experiments show that commercial APIs behave surprisingly consistently across languages but exhibit a key tradeoff: agents are either fast or robust to pauses, not both. Monolingual open full-duplex models reveal additional tradeoffs across backchannel behavior, response quality, and latency.

Conclusion: It is feasible to extend full-duplex evaluation from English to multiple Indian languages without language-specific annotations by using VAD-based event extraction and cross-lingual LLM judging via transcription+translation. IndicFDB exposes important speed–robustness and quality–latency tradeoffs in existing voice agents and provides a broader benchmark for developing and comparing multilingual full-duplex systems.

Abstract: Full-duplex voice agents must handle pauses, take turns, backchannel, and respond to user interruptions in real time. Full-Duplex-Bench evaluates these behaviors, but its English-only corpus and reliance on word-timestamped ASR and an English-prompted LLM judge make it difficult to extend to Indian languages. We introduce IndicFDB, which extends it to ten languages spoken in India with 12,350 samples, nearly 17 times as many as the original. We address three challenges: finding conversational events in multilingual speech, evaluating their timing without reliable word-level alignment, and judging responses across languages. We mine pause handling, turn taking, and backchanneling samples from roughly 50,000 hours of channel-separated conversations using voice activity detection (VAD), and construct human-validated synthetic user interruption samples. Language-independent VAD heuristics evaluate timing, while an open-weight transcription and translation pipeline converts responses to English for LLM ratings of relevance and quality. Across seven voice agents, commercial APIs show unexpectedly consistent behavior across languages but are either fast or robust to pauses, never both, while monolingual open full-duplex models expose further tradeoffs among backchanneling, response quality, and latency.

</details>


### [17] [Extraction of clinical findings from mammography and breast ultrasound reports: a comparison between specialists and Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31974)
*Lorenzo Farias,Hanna Reckziegel,Daniela Duarte da Silva Bagatini,Daniel Schulz,Gabriela de Andrade Monteiro,Letícia Zanatta,Ana Laura Brill Thum,Priscila Schmidt Lora,Débora Oliveira da Silva,Ana Paula Wernz da Cunha Müller,Cristiane Drebes Pedron*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates whether a large language model (Gemini 2.5 Flash) can automatically extract clinical findings from Brazilian Portuguese mammography and breast ultrasound reports, showing that it matches or surpasses human researchers’ manual extraction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related death among Brazilian women. Timely interpretation and reporting of mammography results are crucial for early diagnosis and improving adherence to screening programs. Manual extraction of clinical findings from imaging reports is slow, labor-intensive, and prone to omissions or errors, especially at scale. There is a need for faster, reliable methods to process large volumes of unstructured radiology text in Portuguese so that critical findings are identified and acted upon quickly.

Method: The authors frame the task as Named Entity Recognition (NER) on free-text mammography and breast ultrasound reports written in Brazilian Portuguese. They use Prompt Engineering with a few-shot strategy to instruct a Large Language Model, specifically the Gemini 2.5 Flash model, to identify and extract relevant clinical entities from these reports. Gemini 2.5 Flash was chosen after exploratory comparisons with four candidate models. Its performance is compared against manual extraction performed by trained health researchers, using standard NER evaluation metrics (Macro and Micro F1) and a subjective validation step with experts rating extraction quality via a Likert scale on a sample of 29 exams of varied formats.

Result: The Gemini 2.5 Flash model achieves a Macro F1 score of 0.91 and a Micro F1 score of 0.98 on the NER task. In a subjective expert evaluation of 29 diverse reports, the model’s outputs reach an agreement index of 93.1% with health researchers’ ratings. Overall, the model surpasses human manual extraction in Macro F1 (0.91 vs. 0.72). In four cases, the LLM correctly captured findings that human annotators had either omitted or misrecorded, indicating both high sensitivity and error-correction potential relative to manual review.

Conclusion: LLMs, when carefully instructed via Prompt Engineering and few-shot examples, can perform clinical information extraction from Brazilian Portuguese breast imaging reports at a level comparable to or better than trained health professionals. The evaluated Gemini 2.5 Flash model not only accelerates the extraction process but can also serve as a complementary verification tool, catching omissions or errors in manual review. This suggests a strong potential role for LLM-based NER systems in scaling and enhancing breast cancer screening workflows in Brazil, thereby supporting earlier diagnosis.

Abstract: Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related death among women in Brazil, and the time between the request and the release of mammography reports directly influences adherence to screening, making the agility in processing these reports a critical factor for early diagnosis. In this context, this study compares the performance of a Large Language Model (LLM) with manual extraction performed by a team of health researchers in identifying clinical findings from mammography and breast ultrasound reports written in Brazilian Portuguese. Named Entity Recognition (NER) was applied through Prompt Engineering using a few-shot strategy, employing the Gemini 2.5 Flash model, selected from preliminary exploratory tests with four candidate models. The Gemini 2.5 Flash model demonstrated the best performance, achieving a Macro F1 of 0.91 and a Micro F1 of 0.98. The subjective validation, in which 29 exams of different formats were evaluated by health researchers using a Likert scale, yielded an agreement index of 93.1%. The model outperformed human extraction in overall Macro F1 (0.91 vs. 0.72), as in four reports the model correctly identified information that had been omitted or incorrectly recorded during manual extraction, demonstrating its potential as a complementary verification tool alongside specialists. The results confirm the hypothesis that LLMs, when instructed through Prompt Engineering, can achieve performance comparable to or superior to manual extraction by health professionals.

</details>


### [18] [Toward Embedding-Based Psychometrics: Structural Modeling of Assessment-Item Semantics With Contextual Scores](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31976)
*Jinsong Chen,Shi-Ting Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether contextual semantic scores for TIMSS math items reflect meaningful latent structures and how they compare with traditional diagnostic and unidimensional IRT models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand if text-derived contextual scores (similarities of items to reference words in a large corpus) can serve as a valid, structured representation of item content and support diagnostic interpretation in large-scale assessments like TIMSS.

Method: The authors analyze 40 TIMSS math scored units using a partially specified two-step factor analysis procedure on contextual scores. They explore multiple factor solutions to identify stable group structures and assess a general factor vs group factors. They then compare alternative Q-matrix (attribute) constructions and their Hull-PVAF-based revisions within higher-order and saturated diagnostic classification models, benchmarking them against a unidimensional 2PL IRT model using BIC and AIC criteria.

Result: They find a robust seven-group structure in the contextual scores with a strong general factor, though specific group assignments vary with modeling choices. Anchoring item representation to reference words improves over a single-factor solution but does not minimize BIC compared to more flexible models. In the diagnostic modeling comparison, BIC prefers the official TIMSS content framework and AIC prefers its four-factor extension, yet a simple unidimensional 2PL model outperforms all diagnostic specifications on both BIC and AIC.

Conclusion: Contextual semantic scores provide a meaningful but limited conditional representation of item content: they capture general and grouped structure but are not sufficient for strong diagnostic claims and are statistically outperformed by a unidimensional IRT model. The authors recommend using such semantic representations cautiously, and point to future applications in learned, text-assisted calibration that will require larger calibrated item banks and independent validation.

Abstract: Contextual scores represent assessment items through their similarities to reference words in an external corpus. We examine the semantic structure of scores for 40 TIMSS mathematics scored units using a partially specified two-step factor procedure. A search across factor counts identifies a persistent seven-group structure under the featured construction. Subsequent comparisons consistently favor a general dimension alongside group associations, although individual group memberships remain sensitive to some specification choices. Item examples distinguish recurring, cross-domain, sensitive, and imposed associations. Simpler and unrestricted references clarify the contribution and limits of the anchored representation: it improves on a single factor but does not achieve the lowest working Bayesian information criterion (BIC). A separate response benchmark compares three initial Q constructions and their Hull-PVAF revisions under higher-order and saturated attribute distributions. Among these diagnostic models, BIC favors the official content framework and the Akaike information criterion (AIC) favors its direct four-factor augmentation, but a matched unidimensional two-parameter logistic model has lower AIC and BIC than all twelve conditions. These findings support a conditional semantic representation while limiting direct diagnostic interpretation. We discuss learned text-assisted response calibration as a prospective application requiring a larger calibrated item bank and independent evaluation.

</details>


### [19] [Communication between Frozen Large Language Models via Prompt Optimization in a Referential Game](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31989)
*Vivek Anand,Muthu Chandrasekaran,Shiva Chaitanya*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper explores how two frozen large language models (from different providers and with different tokenizers) can learn to communicate about objects via prompt optimization alone, without updating model weights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether and how fixed, black-box LLMs can develop a shared communication protocol—analogous to a language or code—using only prompt engineering and interaction feedback, despite architectural and tokenizer differences and tight communication bottlenecks.

Method: The authors set up referential games where a sender LLM must describe a given object using a short, fixed-length message over a constrained alphabet, and a receiver LLM must identify the correct object from a set of candidates. Each LLM is wrapped by a separate prompt optimizer, which uses a reflection model to analyze that agent's past scored interactions and iteratively rewrite its prompt. They study two main settings: (1) a positional setting where each message position can carry an independently optimized symbol, enabling a positional code; (2) a more constrained setting where independent per-letter blocks no longer fit, but an overall place-value code over the entire message could work.
