They test variations such as removing memory windows, adding penalties for sender collisions (same message for different objects), retaining successful interactions, and performing sequential optimization, while measuring performance against a no-codebook baseline and across different reflection models and random seeds.

Result: In the positional setting, the optimized prompts converge on a shared coding scheme that generalizes to unseen objects and outperforms a baseline without an emergent codebook, even when the reflection models do not have access to a memory window. In the constrained setting, the basic system does not naturally develop a reliable protocol: the sender fails to maintain an injective mapping from objects to messages, and the receiver lacks sufficient validated examples to infer the code. However, when the authors introduce a sender collision penalty, preserve successful interaction traces, and use sequential optimization, some runs successfully discover a robust place-value communication scheme. Performance and stability depend strongly on random initialization and the specific reflection models used.

Conclusion: Frozen, API-accessed LLMs with different tokenizers can nonetheless be induced—via prompt-level optimization and interaction feedback—to develop shared, auditably explicit communication protocols for referential games, at least in relatively favorable positional settings and, more fragilely, in more constrained place-value settings. The success is highly sensitive to optimization details and run conditions, but when it works, the resulting protocol becomes explicitly encoded in the optimized prompts, making the emergent code interpretable and auditable by humans.

Abstract: We study communication between two frozen large language models from different providers, with different tokenizers, accessed through their API endpoints. The two play a referential game: one sees an object and describes it in a short fixed-length message over a small alphabet; the other must pick that object out of a candidate set. Neither model's weights are updated. Each agent's prompt is rewritten by an isolated prompt optimizer whose reflection model reads that agent's scored interactions. In the positional setting, optimized prompts carry a shared code that generalizes to held-out objects above a measured no-codebook baseline, including when the memory window is removed. In a second setting, independent per-letter blocks no longer fit within the message, although a whole-object place value code does. The base system fails to establish reliable communication: the sender struggles to retain an injective rule, and the receiver has too few confirmed examples in view. A sender collision penalty, retention of successful interactions, and sequential optimization enable successful place value communication in some runs. Outcomes vary across runs and reflection models. In successful runs, the protocol is written into the optimized prompts, where it can be read and audited directly.

</details>


### [20] [Before the Rollout Ends: Early Terminal Reward Prediction for Long-horizon Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31995)
*Jihan Yao,Sihan Zeng,Shangbin Feng,Zhiyuan Fan,Banghua Zhu,Yulia Tsvetkov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes Contextual Early Reward (CER), a method to give dense, early, and interpretable rewards to long-horizon coding agents by predicting final task success from partial trajectories, significantly improving efficiency and performance over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon coding agents only receive verifiable rewards after completing long, expensive sequences of tool calls. This leads to high inference cost, amplification of early mistakes, sparse terminal rewards, and unstable reinforcement learning. The authors want a way to evaluate progress earlier and more frequently, in a way that is accurate, task-aware, and efficient, to stabilize training and improve test-time performance.

Method: CER introduces a learned mechanism that predicts terminal reward from behavioral evidence in partial trajectories (trajectory prefixes). It builds contextual, adaptive rubrics for evaluation that are specific to the current task and stage, based on experiences distilled from related historical tasks. In practice, CER observes the ongoing interaction (e.g., code edits, tool outputs), matches it against summarized patterns from similar past tasks, and outputs an early reward signal estimating whether the final outcome will be successful, serving as a dense reward or test-time scoring function.

Result: On the SWE-bench Verified benchmark, in test-time scaling experiments, CER improves RM@8 over the strongest baseline by 4.2 percentage points on Nemotron 3 Ultra and 2.0 percentage points on Qwen 3.6 27B. Moreover, on Nemotron, CER reaches the best baseline performance using only 15.3% of the tokens, demonstrating large efficiency gains. In reinforcement learning training, using CER as the evaluation signal outperforms full-rollout TMax by 1.9 percentage points while consuming 52.7% fewer online tokens for policy and judge calls.

Conclusion: CER is an effective approach to provide early, dense, and interpretable reward signals for long-horizon coding agents. By leveraging contextual rubrics derived from related historical tasks, it can reliably predict terminal rewards from partial trajectories, reducing token usage and improving performance in both test-time scaling and RL training. This suggests that early, context-aware reward modeling is a promising direction for building more efficient and stable long-horizon coding systems.

Abstract: Long-horizon coding agents receive verifiable rewards only after completing expensive sequences of tool calls. This increases inference cost, amplifies early wrong hypotheses, and can lead to sparse terminal reward and unstable training. We introduce Contextual Early Reward (CER), which predicts terminal reward through behavioral evidence in a trajectory prefix. CER synthesizes adaptive rubrics specific to the current task and stage through experiences summarized from related historical tasks. In test-time scaling on SWE-bench Verified, CER improves RM@8 over the strongest baseline by 4.2 percentage points (pp) on Nemotron 3 Ultra and 2.0 pp on Qwen 3.6 27B; on Nemotron, it takes only 15.3% tokens to match the best baseline performance. In RL training experiments, CER exceeds full-rollout TMax by 1.9 pp while using 52.7% fewer online policy-and-judge tokens. Together, CER provides an interpretable, efficient, and dense evaluation method for long-horizon coding agents.

</details>


### [21] [Quantization Thresholds Replicate, Failure Modes Do Not: A Three-Model Study of Agentic Tool Use in Polish from 8-bit to 2-bit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32042)
*Jakub Prejzner*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Study of how GGUF quantization impacts tool-using LLMs in Polish, using a new benchmark PolAgentBench across multiple models and bit-precisions, finding a sharp performance collapse from 3-bit to 2-bit and heterogeneous failure modes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantization is widely used to compress LLMs, but its impact on complex agentic tool use, especially in non-English languages like Polish, is underexplored. Existing evaluations tend to use English-only benchmarks and generic QA or reasoning tasks, which may miss failures that emerge in multilingual tool-calling scenarios. The authors want to understand whether quantization-induced degradation patterns are consistent across model families and sizes, and to provide a rigorous, deterministic benchmark to study these effects and their failure modes.

Method: They construct PolAgentBench, a deterministic benchmark with Polish natural-language prompts and English tool schemas. It consists of a 67-task main suite (including 15 adversarial probes and 52 hard tasks) and a 46-task arithmetic isolation ladder to analyze tool-use vs raw reasoning. They evaluate three models representing two axes of variation: (a) Bielik-11B-v3.0 vs its pruned/distilled variant Bielik-Minitron-7B-v3.0 to isolate compression effects; and (b) Llama-PLLuM-8B to introduce a different pretraining family. For each model they generate GGUF quantizations at six precision levels from Q8_0 down to Q2_K and run them on the benchmark. They analyze performance scores, failure patterns (e.g., long tool-chains vs immediate hallucinated answers vs content errors), token lengths, and tool-call parsing rates. They also include controlled arithmetic subtasks with scaffolding/no-tool conditions and interpret results both under strict original evaluation criteria and corrected criteria that account for identified artifacts.

Result: 1) All three models show a sharp performance drop between 3-bit and 2-bit quantization, with scores collapsing dramatically (e.g., for the 11B model from 0.716 to 0.045) and this effect is statistically significant (McNemar p < 0.001) and consistent across models and capability levels. 2) Despite the shared collapse threshold, the detailed failure modes differ: at 2-bit, the 7B model tends to produce long multi-step trajectories before failing, the 11B usually fails immediately with confidently confabulated answers, and PLLuM mainly exhibits content errors while still producing mostly parseable tool calls. 3) On the arithmetic ladder, the unscaffolded tasks act as a performance floor that persists even when the no-tool rule is clarified; explicit tool calls substantially improve performance for 8-bit models, but the apparent gains are exploratory and do not remain significant after correcting for multiple comparisons. The special order-trap condition strongly separates the two Bielik models at 8-bit (11B perfect, 7B always failing). 4) Performance gaps between Polish and English appear tied either to quantization-induced degradation or to particular task families. They identify four evaluation artifacts—rounding-sensitive gold answers, overly strict answer typing, an implicit no-tool constraint, and priority-ordered failure labeling—that influenced results; they re-report affected metrics under both strict and corrected scoring. They also release the benchmark, trajectories, and versioned artifacts.

Conclusion: GGUF quantization has a robust, cross-model collapse point for agentic tool use in Polish between 3-bit and 2-bit precision, but the resulting failure behaviors are model-specific rather than universal. Tool-using competence, particularly with multilingual prompts and English tool schemas, is sensitive to low-bit quantization in ways that simple accuracy metrics don’t fully capture. Careful benchmark design, explicit instructions about tool use, and transparent accounting for evaluation artifacts are necessary for reliable measurement. PolAgentBench, together with the released trajectories and artifacts, provides a foundation for systematically studying quantization effects, model compression, and multilingual agent behavior in future work.

Abstract: We ask how GGUF quantization affects agentic tool use in Polish and whether the effects generalize across models. We introduce PolAgentBench, a deterministic benchmark with Polish prompts and English tool schemas: a 67-task main suite (15 adversarial probes, 52 hard-tier tasks) and a 46-task arithmetic isolation ladder. Three models span two axes of variation: Bielik-11B-v3.0 and its pruned, distilled child Bielik-Minitron-7B-v3.0 isolate model compression, and Llama-PLLuM-8B adds a change of pretraining family. Each is measured at six precisions, Q8_0 to Q2_K. Only the collapse threshold replicates. (1) All three models fall off a cliff between 3-bit and 2-bit (11B 0.716 to 0.045, 7B 0.463 to 0.149, PLLuM 0.224 to 0.015; paired McNemar p < 0.001 in each), across a fourfold capability spread and both axes. (2) Failure modes do not replicate: at 2-bit the 7B fails long (median 9.1k tokens, 4 steps) while the 11B mostly answers at the first step with a confabulated final answer (37 of 64 failures); PLLuM fails on content across precisions (71.8-92.0% of steps parse). (3) On the arithmetic ladder the unscaffolded rung is a floor, left standing by a rerun that states the no-tool rule; four explicit calls lift the 8-bit 11B from 1/10 to 9/10 and the 7B from 0/10 to 7/10 after format-only failures with the gold value are forgiven, an exploratory effect with eight distinct baseline inputs that does not survive multiplicity correction, while the order-trap arm separates the models at 8-bit (11B 6/6, 7B 0/6). (4) The Polish-versus-English gap is associated with degradation or with task family. We document four artifacts that shaped our conclusions (rounding-hostile gold values, strict answer typing, a no-tool rule the prompt never stated, priority-ordered failure labels), report affected results in strict and corrected form, and release the benchmark, trajectories and commit-stamped artifacts.

</details>


### [22] [mu-bench: A Multilingual Utterance Transcription Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32082)
*Andrea Li,Soham Ray*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build a multilingual, real-call benchmark and a semantic error metric (UER) for evaluating ASR on voice agents, showing it aligns much better with humans than traditional WER and revealing provider and language differences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ASR evaluation is misaligned with real-world voice-agent use: it focuses on read, mostly English speech and uses word error rate, which punishes surface mismatches instead of true meaning errors. For transactional phone agents (like banking), what matters is whether critical fields—names, emails, codes—are captured correctly across multiple languages. There was no realistic, multilingual benchmark or semantically-aware metric tailored to this setting.

Method: They collect mu-bench, a dataset of 4,270 utterances from 250 real banking calls in five languages, focusing on form-field content. They design Utterance Error Rate (UER), where a large language model judges whether an ASR transcript preserves the user’s intended meaning, and they calibrate this judge against human ratings. They also build an LLM-based normalizer so that WER becomes comparable across ASR vendors with different formatting conventions. They then evaluate six commercial ASR providers using these metrics and compare scores, including human agreement levels.

Result: On 1,847 utterances with human annotations, the LLM-based UER metric achieves high agreement with human judgments (Cohen’s kappa 0.78), clearly outperforming WER computed on normalized text (kappa 0.53). Across six commercial ASR systems, the best system attains 11.9% UER. All systems show worse performance on Mandarin than on the other languages, indicating consistent difficulty for that language in this real-world setting.

Conclusion: UER, a semantics-based LLM judge, is substantially better aligned with human perceptions of ASR correctness than traditional WER, especially for high-stakes, field-oriented utterances. The mu-bench dataset and leaderboard provide a realistic multilingual benchmark for phone-based banking agents, revealing significant variation across vendors and highlighting Mandarin as a particularly challenging language. These resources should guide both ASR development and evaluation toward meaning preservation rather than surface word matching.

Abstract: Voice agents depend on accurate automatic speech recognition (ASR) to act on what callers say, yet ASR is evaluated on read, English-centric speech with word error rate (WER), which penalizes surface rather than semantic differences. We introduce mu-bench, a dataset of 4,270 caller utterances from 250 phone calls to an AI banking agent in English, Spanish, Turkish, Vietnamese, and Mandarin, centered on form-field inputs such as names, email addresses, and confirmation codes. We release Utterance Error Rate (UER), an LLM judge of whether a transcript preserves meaning, calibrated against human raters, together with an LLM normalizer that makes WER comparable across providers' output formats. On 1,847 human-rated transcripts, UER agrees with annotators at $κ$ = 0.78, versus 0.53 for exact-match WER on normalized text. We rank six commercial providers on a public leaderboard; the best reaches 11.9% UER, and Mandarin is hardest for all six.

</details>


### [23] [Using LMs to Model the Effects of Context and Coreference during Sentence Comprehension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32119)
*Kohei Kajikawa,Lin Ai,Tatsuki Kuribayashi,Ethan Gotlieb Wilcox*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how the size of a language model’s context window affects how well its surprisal predicts human reading times, finding that both very short and very long contexts matter, with best fit at long ranges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Psycholinguistics often uses language models as proxies for human prediction during reading. Prior work improved model–human alignment by forcibly limiting context, assuming human working memory is short-range. But this may ignore humans’ use of long-distance discourse structure (e.g., coreference and coherence) during comprehension. The authors want to disentangle the contributions of short-term memory limits and long-range discourse representations to model–human alignment.

Method: They systematically vary GPT-2’s effective context window over a wide range of sizes and evaluate model surprisal against human reading times in four large-scale, naturalistic English eye-tracking / reading datasets. They then run a counterfactual inference experiment where they selectively disrupt long-range discourse structure—specifically, cross-sentential entity chains—by replacing repeated mentions of entities with pronouns, thereby weakening coreference links, and measure how this manipulation impacts model–human fit at different context sizes.

Result: They find a U-shaped pattern: shrinking GPT-2’s context window to fewer than about 20 tokens captures local memory constraints and yields better fit than unrestricted or moderately sized contexts, but allowing much larger contexts (roughly 500–1,000 tokens) produces the best overall psycholinguistic fit. When they break cross-sentence entity chains by pronominalization, the predictive advantage of large context windows drops substantially (by around 20–40%), showing that long-range coreference tracking is a major driver of the long-context benefit.

Conclusion: Human-like language processing appears to rely on both short-range memory constraints and long-range discourse representations. While restricting context can mimic human working-memory limits, truly human-like predictions require models to exploit extended context for tracking entities across sentences. The extent of performance loss when disrupting coreference suggests that global discourse relations play a sizable, quantifiable role in real-time human language comprehension, and that psycholinguistic modeling with LMs should account for both local and global factors rather than only enforcing strict memory decay.

Abstract: Language models (LMs) are often used as a tool to model human language processing. Recent studies suggest that severely restricting LMs' context window improves their fit to human psycholinguistic data by simulating human working memory constraints. However, it is possible that this strict memory-decay approach overlooks humans' reliance on long-range structural representations, such as discourse structre. In this work, we systematically vary the context window size of GPT-2 across four large-scale naturalistic English reading-time datasets and observe a U-shaped relationship: Although restricted contexts (< 20 tokens) successfully capture local memory limitations, expanded contexts (500--1,000 tokens) ultimately yield the highest overall psycholinguistic fit. To investigate the mechanism driving this benefit, we conduct a counterfactual inference-time experiment that disrupts cross-sentential entity chains by pronominalizing repeated discourse entities. Obscuring these structural linkages significantly degrades the predictive power of larger context windows by 20% to 40%. Our experiments demonstrate that tracking long-range coreference relations is one important factor for the alignment between LM surprisal and human reading behavior, and approximate the extent to which human comprehenders use global discourse relations during language processing.

</details>


### [24] [Typed Decision Models: An Early Evidence Audit and Evaluation Checklist](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32160)
*Lijuan Tang,Yuemeng Zheng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Early review of Jev typed decision models finds latency/cost gains but limited accuracy benefits and proposes a 14-item evaluation checklist for future work.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Typed decision models like Jev promise safer, cheaper, and faster alternatives to text-generating models by outputting probabilities over predefined options, but their true advantages in accuracy and reliability over existing label-probability methods are unclear just after release.

Method: The authors survey and synthesize results from 28 evaluation and replication papers on Jev and related typed decision models posted within nine days of Jev’s release, comparing them with prior work in label-probability classification, constrained decoding, reranking, calibration, and cascaded model systems.

Result: Across the 28 early papers, typed decision readouts do not consistently outperform standard label-probability readouts on accuracy; Jev shows its most robust advantages in lower latency and cost, while lagging on more difficult tasks. Observed methodological weaknesses across the studies motivate a set of best-practice criteria.

Conclusion: Given the limited time window and focus on a single commercial model, the review should be treated as an initial evidence map rather than a definitive judgment on typed decision models. The main takeaways are that TDMs currently offer operational benefits (speed, cost) more than accuracy improvements, and that a structured 14-item evaluation checklist is needed to strengthen future empirical work in this area.

Abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs) return probability distributions over caller-defined options without generating text. TypeSafe released Jev, a commercial typed decision model, on 15 September 2026, and a small body of evaluation and replication work appeared within days. We review 28 papers posted between 19 and 24 September and relate their findings to earlier work on label-probability classification, constrained decoding, reranking, calibration, and model cascades. In this early literature, the typed readout itself has not shown an independent accuracy advantage over comparable label-probability readouts. Jev's clearest gains are in latency and cost, while accuracy gaps remain on harder tasks. In practical deployments, confidence is often used to decide when to defer to a stronger model or a human. We use recurring weaknesses in these studies to derive a 14-item evaluation checklist for future TDM work. Because the evidence covers only the first nine days after the release of one hosted model, the review should be read as an early evidence map rather than a settled assessment of the model class.

</details>


### [25] [ScopeIF: Improving Scope-Aware Precise Instruction-Following in Large Language Models via Graded Reward Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32189)
*Bosi Wen,Yilin Niu,Xiaoying Ning,Ying Zhang,Hongning Wang,Minlie Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ScopeIF is a training framework that makes LLMs follow complex, segment-specific (scope-aware) instructions more precisely by modeling constraint scopes and providing dense, graded supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM instruction-following methods treat constraints as applying to the whole output and use coarse, binary rewards, which fail to handle constraints that apply only to specific parts of the response and give sparse learning signals for complex constraints.

Method: The authors propose ScopeIF, which starts from a unified schema that decomposes each objective constraint into Scope (where in the output it applies), Target (what aspect is constrained), and Range (the acceptable values). Based on this, they build ScopeInstruct, a large-scale dataset of instructions with scope-aware constraints, and use tools plus graded reward models to measure how severely each constraint is violated. These graded violations are then used for dense supervision in policy optimization of LLMs.

Result: Models trained with ScopeIF consistently outperform prior optimization approaches on benchmarks involving complex scope-aware constraints, while maintaining general capabilities, and specifically tuned Qwen3-4B/8B models reach or exceed the performance of strong frontier models like Gemini-2.5-Pro and DeepSeek-V3.2 on these tasks.

Conclusion: Modeling constraint scope explicitly and using graded, tool-verified supervision yields more precise instruction-following, especially for complex, segment-specific constraints, and offers a practical paradigm for training competitive scope-aware LLMs, as demonstrated by ScopeIF and the ScopeInstruct dataset.

Abstract: Precise instruction-following is a fundamental ability of large language models (LLMs), requiring their outputs to strictly satisfy objective constraints in input instructions. In complex application scenarios, these constraints often possess diverse scopes that govern specific response segments rather than the entire output. However, existing optimization methods often neglect constraint scope during data construction and rely on binary per-constraint rewards, yielding limited data diversity and sparse supervision for complex constraints. To this end, we propose ScopeIF, a novel training framework for scope-aware precise instruction-following. We first introduce a unified schema that factorizes objective constraints into three decoupled dimensions: Scope, Target, and Range. Grounded in this schema, we construct ScopeInstruct, a large-scale instruction dataset with diverse scope-aware constraints, and combine tool-grounded verification with graded reward modeling to quantify the violation degree of each constraint, providing dense supervision for policy optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScopeIF consistently outperforms existing methods, particularly on complex scope-aware constraints, while preserving general capabilities. Notably, it enables optimized Qwen3-4B and 8B models to rival or surpass strong frontier models such as Gemini-2.5-Pro and DeepSeek-V3.2, establishing an effective paradigm for advancing scope-aware instruction-following. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/thu-coai/ScopeIF.

</details>


### [26] [The Judge Is Not Its Twin: Post-training makes a model's writing more predictable but barely moves its taste, as a judge, toward predictable writing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32196)
*Arman Nik Khah,Arvin Bahreini*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies whether language models used as judges become biased toward predictable writing when the same models are made better writers via post-training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Because language models are increasingly evaluated by other language models, if training that improves writing also makes outputs more predictable, model-judges might systematically favor such predictable text. This could hide real progress on creativity and other qualities from automated evaluation, threatening the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge benchmarks.

Method: The authors track two 7B-parameter open model families, OLMo-2 and Zephyr, across their main training stages: base, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and preference training (DPO). For each stage, they evaluate models in two roles: (1) as writers of short stories for ten prompts, measuring predictability/surprisal per token, including cross-family evaluation of how surprising the texts are; and (2) as judges of paired stories, asking which is better and which is more creative, and quantifying any tilt toward the more predictable story. They also analyze side effects such as preference for length and answer position, and run a follow-up experiment to construct pairs differing in predictability but matched on quality.

Result: As writers, both model families become more predictable over training: later-stage models find earlier-stage stories increasingly familiar, and cross-family evaluation shows that more trained stories are 7.0–9.2% (OLMo-2) and 24–25% (Zephyr) less surprising per token. As judges, however, models show very little increased bias toward predictable writing. The change in probability of preferring the more predictable story as “better” is under 1 percentage point across training stages, with a one-sided 95% upper bound of 2.7 points—comparable to the base OLMo-2 judge’s initial tilt. For “more creative” judgments, trained models do not favor predictable stories more than base models. Instead, training strengthens preferences for longer stories and for a particular answer slot, and it disrupts the semantics of the “more creative” question so that trained judges no longer reliably favor intact stories over scrambled-word versions. A follow-up attempt to create pairs that vary in predictability but not quality largely failed because interventions that reduced predictability often degraded story quality below a pre-set floor.

Conclusion: Post-training clearly makes models’ writing more predictable, but this does not translate into a strong additional bias toward predictable writing when those same models act as judges—at least within the studied families and tasks. Automated LLM-as-a-judge evaluations may therefore be less compromised by predictability bias than feared, although training introduces other artifacts (e.g., preferences for length and positional biases, and degradation of “creativity” as a meaningful query). Moreover, attempts to decouple unpredictability from quality ran into practical limits, suggesting that making text less predictable without harming perceived quality is challenging in current systems.

Abstract: Language models are now routinely graded by other language models. If post-training makes a model's own writing more predictable, it may also teach the same model, acting as a judge, to reward predictable writing, so that progress on creativity would be invisible to automated evaluation. We follow two open model families, OLMo-2 and Zephyr (7B parameters each), through their public training stages and measure every stage twice, as a writer of short stories and as a judge of pairs of stories. As writers, the models drift as feared: each family's fully trained model finds the stories of its base, supervised fine-tuned (SFT) and preference-trained (DPO) stages progressively more familiar, in all ten prompts, and a model from the other family finds the trained stories 7.0 to 9.2 percent (OLMo-2) and 24 to 25 percent (Zephyr) less surprising per token. As judges, they barely move toward predictable writing. Asked which story is better, a question every judge can use to tell a story from its own words in scrambled order, no trained judge's estimated tilt toward the more predictable story grows by as much as one point in the probability of picking it. A post hoc one-sided 95% upper bound on that growth is 2.7 points on an average pair, about the size of the untrained OLMo-2 judge's own tilt. Asked which is more creative, no trained judge's estimate favors the predictable story more than its base's does. Training instead strengthens a preference for longer stories when the question is creativity, and for one answer slot, and it breaks "more creative" as a question: trained judges asked it no longer reliably prefer a story to its scrambled words. A follow-up could not build pairs that differ in predictability but not in quality, because the routes that made this writer's stories less predictable also broke some of them, often enough to fail a quality floor set in advance.

</details>


### [27] [Generalization and Memorization along the Learning Trajectory of Neural Language Models: A Geometric Account of Categorization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32199)
*Wang Bojun,Holly Jenkins,Elizabeth Wonnacott*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how neural language models shift from early-stage generalization to later-stage memorization along their training trajectory, using controlled synthetic grammars and representation-space analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand when and how neural language models generalize beyond their training data versus when they memorize observed examples, and how this balance changes over the course of training. Clarifying this dynamic can inform better model training, interpretability, and robustness.

Method: Train neural language models on controlled synthetic grammars and track both (1) the geometry of the internal representation space and (2) model behavior at multiple points in training. Analyze how unoccupied (unobserved) regions of the representation space become organized, and how models treat grammatical combinations that were and were not seen during training, across different model sizes and training durations.

Result: From very early in training, the representation space develops structured, continuous regions even where no observed tokens lie, yielding category-level geometric organization. This structure allows the model to generalize to grammatical combinations it has never seen. With extended training, especially in larger models, the models increasingly separate observed from unobserved grammatical combinations, and the initial continuous geometric structure that supported broad category-level generalization is progressively degraded.

Conclusion: Neural language models begin by learning via categorization-based generalization, enabled by smooth geometric structure in representation space that supports unseen but grammatical combinations. As training continues, they gradually transition toward exemplar-specific memorization, sharpening distinctions between seen and unseen combinations while weakening the earlier global category structure. This reveals a temporal shift from generalization to memorization in the learning dynamics of neural language models.

Abstract: We investigate how generalization and memorization develop along the learning trajectory of neural language models. Using controlled synthetic grammars, we examine both the geometry of representation space and model behaviour over training. We find that continuous regions of representation space not occupied by observed tokens become systematically structured from the earliest stages of learning, forming category-level geometric organization that supports generalization to unattested combinations. Generalization therefore emerges from the beginning of learning rather than only after extensive memorization. With prolonged training, larger models increasingly distinguish observed from unobserved grammatical combinations. At the same time, the continuous geometric structure supporting category-level generalization is gradually destructed. Together, these results suggest that neural language models initially learn through categorization-based generalization, followed by a gradual transition toward more exemplar-specific memorization.

</details>


### [28] [A model of rational interlocutors: Unification of comprehension and production](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32216)
*Hanlin Wu,Zhenguang G. Cai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a single computational “rational interlocutor” model that explains both how we interpret others’ utterances and how we tailor our own speech to different listeners.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Research on how we interpret language (speaker modeling) and how we adapt our speech to others (audience design) has evolved separately, even though both concern how interlocutors adjust to each other. There is a need for a unified theoretical and computational account that explains both comprehension and production as manifestations of the same underlying process, and that can capture systematic differences in behavior toward native speakers, L2 speakers, children, and artificial agents.

Method: The authors introduce the Rational Interlocutor (RI) model, a computational framework in which an interlocutor keeps an explicit model of their conversational partner. This partner model has three key parameters: (1) identity Π, encoding which messages and forms are typical for the partner; (2) fidelity Φ, encoding how reliably this partner maps intended messages to utterances; and (3) knowledge Λ, encoding how knowledgeable the partner is assumed to be. Comprehension and production are formalized as mirror-image Bayesian or rational-choice computations over this partner model: comprehension infers the most likely intended meaning given an utterance and the partner model, while production selects the utterance that maximizes communicative success (given the partner’s expected inference) relative to production effort.

Result: The model predicts that listeners will down-weight the evidential value of utterances from partners perceived as linguistically less competent, while speakers will increase their production effort (e.g., elaboration, clarification) for such partners. It further predicts that perceived linguistic competence can be decomposed into the fidelity and knowledge parameters and that different partner types (L2 adults, children, artificial agents) exhibit distinct profiles along these dimensions, leading to specific, testable behavioral patterns in both comprehension and production.

Conclusion: Comprehension and production adjustments to conversational partners can be understood as two sides of the same rational computation over a partner model. The RI model offers a unified account that explains asymmetries in how we interpret and design utterances for less competent speakers, and it suggests that linguistic competence is not unitary but reflects separate beliefs about a partner’s fidelity and knowledge. These components vary systematically across interlocutor types, yielding clear empirical predictions for future work.

Abstract: Who we communicate with influences both our interpretation of their utterances and the design of our own. Such adjustment to the conversational partner is studied as speaker modeling in comprehension and as audience design in production, with the two literatures having developed largely separately. We argue that both adjustments express one rational computation and propose the rational interlocutor (RI) model, a computational account unifying comprehension and production. An interlocutor maintains a model of their partner, defined by three parameters: an identity parameter Π sets the messages and forms expected from the partner; a fidelity parameter Φ sets how reliably messages and utterances map onto each other for them; a knowledge parameter Λ sets how knowledgeable the partner is believed to be. Comprehension and production are thus mirror-image modes of one computation over the partner model. Comprehension chooses the message the partner most likely intends to convey, weighing how well each candidate fits the utterance against how likely this partner is to mean it. Production chooses the utterance from which the partner will best recover the message, weighed against the effort of saying it. This explains why comprehenders appear to rely less on the forms produced by a linguistically less competent speaker, while producers tend to invest more effort in designing forms for them. We conjecture that perceived linguistic competence decomposes into two of these quantities: fidelity and knowledge. Their contrasting profiles across second-language (L2) adults, children, and artificial partners produce distinct and testable predictions.

</details>


### [29] [OptiArena: Can LLMs Improve Executable Algorithms under Fixed Resource Budgets?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32227)
*Wenjun Peng,Xinyu Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: OptiArena is a controlled testbed to evaluate how well LLMs can iteratively improve game-playing algorithms under strict resource and feedback budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing static QA and code-generation benchmarks do not adequately capture LLMs’ emerging role as interactive coding agents that iteratively optimize algorithms under constraints. There is a need for a realistic, controlled environment to study whether and how LLMs can improve executable algorithms, especially for game-playing, when limited by budgets, scaffolds, and feedback.

Method: The authors design OptiArena, a budget-controlled testbed where LLMs attempt to improve a given game-playing algorithm through up to five rounds of code edits. The environment imposes a fixed minimal code scaffold, bounded evaluator feedback, and fixed compute and cost budgets. It includes two optimization regimes, surface obfuscation controls to test robustness to representation changes, calibrated reference algorithms to define performance gaps, held-out and stress test splits, and diagnostics for degradation and exceptional failures. They evaluate twelve frontier LLMs on five different games, measuring both code improvement and robustness, while tracking LLM API costs separately from local evaluator runtime.

Result: Empirically, LLMs more reliably improve a deliberately weak starter algorithm than they do refine already competent, editable baselines. There is substantial performance variation across both games and model types. Improvements to competent baselines are less consistent and more fragile, and performance can degrade in some cases. The study also assesses whether improvements persist under surface obfuscation controls and records various failure and degradation patterns.

Conclusion: Within the five-edit, fixed-scaffold setting, LLMs show clear but asymmetric capabilities: they are good at lifting weak algorithms closer to competent references but less reliable at safely refining already competent ones. OptiArena offers a practical, controlled benchmark for measuring bounded-resource algorithm optimization and can serve as a foundation for future research on LLM-based coding agents and automated algorithm improvement.

Abstract: Static QA and code-generation benchmarks only partially capture the role that large language models (LLMs) now play as coding agents and research tools. We introduce OptiArena, a budget-controlled testbed for studying whether LLMs can improve executable game-playing algorithms through five rounds of code edits within a fixed minimal scaffold and under bounded evaluator feedback and fixed resource budgets. The testbed uses two optimization regimes, surface obfuscation controls, calibrated references, held-out/stress splits, and diagnostics for degradation and exceptional failures, with LLM API cost reported separately from local evaluator wall-clock. The empirical study asks three questions: whether models can close the calibrated gap between a designated weak starter and an editable competent baseline, whether they can refine editable competent baselines without damaging them, and whether gains survive surface obfuscation controls. Across twelve frontier LLMs and five games, models improve designated weak starters more consistently than they refine editable competent baselines, with substantial variation across games and models. OptiArena provides a practical testbed for measuring bounded-resource algorithm optimization within the five-edit, fixed-scaffold setting studied here. Code is available at https://github.com/WJ-Peng/OptiArena.

</details>


### [30] [KinyaMed: Seeds, Not Rows -- What a Corpus Requirement Written in the Wrong Unit Fails to Constrain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32234)
*Marius Bayizere*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper attempts to build an urgency classifier for patient-written Kinyarwanda triage messages but instead reports why its own data and evaluation specification cannot yield a meaningful or valid classifier, focusing on negative results and the diagnostic apparatus used.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To create an automated triage urgency classifier for patient-voice data in Kinyarwanda (and three other languages used at a Rwandan health centre) that meets a detailed data specification, and to understand whether large synthetic datasets built under that specification can genuinely ensure data and model quality.

Method: They design a multilingual data-generation and evaluation pipeline with per-language instruments: (1) author a limited set of seed sentences by clinicians in four languages; (2) automatically generate large numbers of synthetic ‘rows’ (examples) per seed; (3) enforce multiple ‘quality gates’ defined in the specification, including minimum numbers of distinct seed phrases, limits on rows per seed, and evaluation-set coverage; (4) train urgency classifiers and probe robustness by perturbing inputs (capitalisation, typos); (5) test the deployment stack, including loading models with missing tokenizers, and observe behaviours. They systematically check which gates the generated corpus passes or fails and how those gates relate to any real notion of quality.

Result: The generation process produces one million example rows in 130 seconds but fails four of nine predefined quality gates, or six when rows are attributed back to their seeds. Critically, the binding gate counts distinct authored seed phrases, and with only 165 seeds no corpus can ever pass regardless of how many rows are generated. To meet that gate would require 2,835 more distinct sentences, while another gate’s cap of 50 rows per seed implies 19,835 seeds to reach a million rows. Since rows (cheap machine-generated) and seeds (expensive clinician-authored) are constrained in a way that ignores quality, the row-count requirement is effectively meaningless. The evaluation set, comprising 17,942 rows from only nine distinct sentences, is rejected by the same gate and cannot support any formal verdict. Trained models show instability: with a uniform-surface-form corpus, urgency predictions change for 31.5% of inputs under simple capitalisation changes and 21.0% under a single typo. Furthermore, a model shipped without its tokenizer still loads, returns only class priors, and outputs well-formed probabilities for unreadable input, masking the error. None of these numbers is offered as proof of model quality; they are negative findings about the pipeline and specification.

Conclusion: The triage urgency classifier project, as specified, cannot deliver what it claims: the data-specification gates overconstrain superficial quantities (row counts) while underconstraining the crucial, expensive component (diverse clinician-authored seeds), so satisfying them says nothing about real data or model quality. The evaluation scheme itself can block any meaningful verdict when based on too few distinct sentences, and the deployment tooling can silently fail in ways that make broken models appear valid. The paper’s main contribution is therefore methodological: a set of instruments and diagnostics that reveal these structural flaws and negative results, highlighting how specification design, data generation, and tooling can invalidate the intended guarantees of a machine-learning system, and making these findings reproducible for others.

Abstract: Triage decides who is seen first. Building an urgency classifier for patient-voice Kinyarwanda, we found our specification could be met without producing anything it was meant to secure. We report that, and the instruments that detect it, instead of a classifier. Designed for the four languages a Rwandan health centre receives, with every instrument per-language: sentences are authored in all four arms and rows generate in one, because the frame slots those three need do not exist. Our requirement asked for one million examples; generation produced them in 130 seconds. It fails four of the nine quality gates in that specification, six when rows are attributed to their source sentence. The binding gate counts distinct authored seed phrases, not rows: at our 165, no corpus passes at any row count. Two shortfalls follow and differ: 2,835 further sentences to pass the seed-count gate, 19,835 to reach the stated million rows, because a separate gate caps a seed at 50 rows. Rows come from a machine at 7,700 per second; seeds from clinicians. A row count constrains the cheap quantity, leaves the expensive one free, and so does not constrain quality at all. Two further negatives follow. An evaluation set of 17,942 rows built from nine distinct sentences supports no verdict: our gate, which counts distinct sentences, refuses 38 of its cells and reports nothing. A model trained on a corpus of uniform surface form changes its predicted urgency for 31.5% of inputs under capitalisation and 21.0% under a single typo, reported as measurement and not attribution. A model directory shipped without its tokenizer loads without error and answers its class prior on input it cannot read, with well-formed probabilities. No figure here is evidence of model quality; the contribution is the apparatus and the negative results it produced, reproducible from a clean clone except where marked NOT REPRODUCIBLE.

</details>


### [31] [Solving Every Step Is Not Enough: Milestone Oracles Reveal a Composition Gap in LLM Math Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32235)
*Zhuohan Wang,Haoran Ma,Tianyu Wu,Yuanlin Duan,Zichun Liao,Jieming Yu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: OracleLadder diagnoses where large language models fail in multi-step math reasoning by progressively giving them oracle help and categorizing failures into distinct reasoning gaps, finding that composition is the dominant weakness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although LLMs can often solve individual intermediate steps of complex math problems, they still frequently fail the overall task. Existing benchmarks give only a single final-accuracy score and do not pinpoint *why* models fail or which part of the reasoning pipeline is broken. This lack of diagnostic granularity makes it hard to compare models, understand their weaknesses in compositional reasoning, or evaluate the impact of training interventions like RL or larger scales. The paper aims to build a systematic, fine-grained diagnostic tool that reveals *where* multi-step reasoning breaks down.

Method: The authors propose OracleLadder, a diagnostic evaluation framework for math reasoning. For each problem, a strong teacher LLM generates a fixed roadmap of intermediate sub-goals (called milestones). A deterministic symbolic verifier checks the correctness of milestone and final answers. The target model is then evaluated under a ladder of oracle-help conditions: (1) no help; (2) given only the roadmap; (3) given the roadmap plus correct answers to prior milestones; and (4) each milestone in isolation. By comparing performance across these settings, each failed problem is assigned to one of five specific reasoning gaps (e.g., composition gap, local-step gap). The authors apply OracleLadder to 354 NuminaMath problems and six LLMs (Qwen3, gpt-oss, Llama 3.3, DeepSeek-V3.1) ranging from 8B to 671B parameters, and they replicate key patterns on other math datasets and even code-generation tasks. They also cross-check robustness using an independent second teacher and LLM-based grading-error detection.

Result: Across all six evaluated models and multiple scales, the dominant source of failure is the **composition gap**, a stricter version of the compositionality gap: models often solve each milestone correctly in isolation but still fail to combine them into a correct overall solution. This gap accounts for 33–48% of problems, or 24–37% after filtering suspected grading errors identified by an LLM review. The diagnostic also reveals that overall accuracy and recovery under milestone help can disagree in ranking models: two models with similar accuracy can have different patterns of dependence on roadmap help, and two RLVR training runs with comparable accuracy gains shift problems across reasoning-gap categories in different ways. The roadmap effect (improvement from seeing the decomposition) replicates qualitatively on MATH500 and AIME 2024/25, and per-problem recovery patterns are consistent (83–87% agreement) when using an independent second teacher to generate roadmaps. The same help-ladder structure transfers to code-generation tasks, indicating that the diagnostic is not math-specific. All artifacts (data, roadmaps, prompts, and code) are released publicly.

Conclusion: OracleLadder provides a structured way to decompose LLM failures on multi-step math problems into interpretable reasoning gaps by progressively supplying oracle help. The analysis shows that the main obstacle for current models is not just solving local steps but **composing** correct intermediate results into a coherent global solution. This challenges the sufficiency of standard accuracy metrics and suggests that progress in multi-step reasoning should be evaluated through diagnostics that distinguish local competence from compositional integration. The framework appears robust across datasets, model families, and even domains like code, and it can be used to more precisely measure and compare the effects of model scaling and training interventions on different aspects of reasoning.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can solve every intermediate step of a multi-step math problem on its own and still fail the full problem, even when given a roadmap of the steps and all of their answers. We introduce OracleLadder, a diagnostic evaluation that locates where LLM math reasoning fails by giving the model increasing levels of oracle help. For each problem, a teacher model writes a fixed roadmap of intermediate sub-goals (milestones), and a deterministic symbolic verifier grades every answer. Testing the model with no help, with the roadmap, with the roadmap plus the milestone answers, and on each milestone alone sorts each failure into one of five reasoning gaps. On 354 NuminaMath problems and six models from 8B to 671B parameters (Qwen3, gpt-oss, Llama 3.3, DeepSeek-V3.1), the largest gap for every model is the composition gap, a stricter form of the compositionality gap. It covers 33-48% of problems, and 24-37% after removing problems that an LLM review flags as grading errors. Accuracy and milestone-help recovery rank the two strongest models differently, and two RLVR runs with similar accuracy gains move problems differently. The roadmap effect replicates on MATH500 and AIME 2024/25, per-problem recovery agrees for 83-87% of problems under an independent second teacher, and the help ladder carries over to code generation. We release the data, roadmaps, prompts, and code at https://github.com/slark-prime/OracleLadder.

</details>


### [32] [LANTERN: Illuminating Hidden Mathematical Knowledge in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32264)
*Pavel Tikhonov,Elena Tutubalina,Ivan Oseledets,Dmitry I. Ignatov,Mikhail Seleznyov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build LANTERN, a pipeline that mines internal activations of pretrained language models to automatically discover and verify new mathematical relations between integer sequences, efficiently surfacing a small number of genuinely novel results from millions of candidates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While language models can already help prove theorems, humans still decide which mathematical problems and connections to explore. Manually discovering interesting relations, such as between integer sequences, is slow and limited by human attention. The authors want to know whether hidden representations inside pretrained language models already encode signals about potentially interesting mathematical connections, and whether these signals can be turned into a scalable, automated discovery tool rather than just a proof assistant.

Method: They introduce LANTERN, a multi-stage pipeline. First, they train a classifier on top of activations from a pretrained language model to predict whether two mathematical objects (here, OEIS integer sequences) are related. Using this classifier, they rank 50 million candidate pairs drawn from 10,000 frequently referenced OEIS sequences. Then they apply staged filtering: rule-based pruning, hypothesis generation about the type of relation, executable verification (e.g., checking equations/computations over sequence terms), and then further analytical checking to confirm correctness and non-triviality. This process narrows down the initial huge candidate set to a small set of verified and interesting relations.

Result: On the OEIS corpus, LANTERN processes 50 million candidate pairs and finds 62 relations between pairs that had no existing OEIS cross-reference. After a content-quality screen, 13 relations are kept as worth presenting. Of these, 9 are judged informative or insightful by the authors, and 4 appear to be fully novel discoveries, with no record in OEIS or in the literature they searched. The entire pipeline, including classifier training, ranking, filtering, and verification, runs end-to-end in under 8 hours.

Conclusion: Internal representations of pretrained language models can be productively harnessed not just for proving given statements but for suggesting which mathematical connections are worth investigating. LANTERN shows that a classifier over model activations, combined with systematic filtering and verification, can rapidly sift through tens of millions of candidate relations and surface a small number of correct, interesting, and in some cases apparently new mathematical results. This suggests a scalable path toward semi-automated mathematical discovery using language models.

Abstract: Language models can now prove theorems, but people still decide which problems to pursue. We ask whether a model's internal representations can help identify promising mathematical connections. We develop LANTERN, a fast, cost-efficient pipeline that uses a classifier over pretrained-model activations to rank candidate relations, followed by staged filtering, hypothesis generation, executable verification, and analytical checking. Applied to the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS), LANTERN ranked 50 million pairs among 10,000 frequently referenced sequences and produced 62 verified relations between pairs without an existing OEIS cross-reference. A content screen retained 13 relations worth presenting; nine of these are informative or insightful, including four which are entirely novel to the best of our knowledge: none appears in the OEIS or in our targeted literature search. The entire end-to-end process including classifier training, candidate ranking, filtering and verification took under 8 hours.

</details>


### [33] [Before Answering: Evidence Sufficiency under Size-Matched Memory Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32269)
*Joyanta Jyoti Mondal,Md. Shifatul Ahsan Apurba,Mridul Banik,Md Masud Al Mahmud,Ibne Farabi Shihab*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how to detect when retrieved memory lacks enough evidence to answer a question and shows that common benchmarks are flawed because they leak the label through memory size; it proposes a size-matched benchmark construction and a neural estimator, MemSafe, to more fairly and effectively detect insufficient evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Question answering systems that rely on retrieved or compressed memory must know when they do not have enough information to answer safely. Existing benchmarks simulate insufficient-evidence cases by removing supporting passages, but this inadvertently correlates label with memory size, making the task artificially easy and obscuring the true difficulty of detecting missing evidence. The authors want to disentangle benchmark artifacts from genuine modeling ability and develop better estimators of when memory is unsafe or incomplete.

Method: First, the authors analyze existing benchmarks like MuSiQue and show that simply counting the number of paragraphs in memory yields near-perfect detection of insufficient evidence, revealing a dataset shortcut. They then design a size-matched construction for insufficient-evidence examples that keeps memory size constant while removing necessary support, thereby eliminating the size shortcut by design. On this improved setup, they propose MemSafe, which cross-encodes the query with each memory unit, then aggregates representations using a set transformer to output an insufficiency score. They compare MemSafe against lexical and feature-based baselines, as well as frozen pretrained cross-encoders with logistic heads, across multiple QA datasets and random seeds. They additionally evaluate MemSafe in practical gating scenarios for a 7B QA reader and against alternative gates like reader confidence, ground-truth integrity labels, and an LLM judge.

Result: On the original MuSiQue, a trivial classifier based only on paragraph counts attains an AUROC of 0.979 for detecting unsafe memory, outperforming the initial lexical estimator and demonstrating severe label leakage. Under the new size-matched construction, MemSafe achieves AUROCs of 0.968 on MuSiQue and 0.983 on HotpotQA, improving over a lexical baseline by 0.26–0.39 AUROC, while performance on 2WikiMultiHopQA appears saturated. A frozen cross-encoder with a simple logistic head recovers about 41% of the performance gap between the lexical baseline and MemSafe on MuSiQue. However, MemSafe performs poorly on some out-of-domain or differently constructed tasks: it degrades more than a weak baseline on MuSiQue’s original unanswerable questions, reaches only 0.639 AUROC on SQuAD 2.0, and needs thousands of clinical-domain examples before surpassing a hand-crafted feature-based estimator. As a gating mechanism for a 7B QA model, MemSafe reduces the error rate among answered questions from 0.850 to 0.631 at 5% coverage, surpassing both reader confidence and, on average, the ground-truth integrity labels, though a 7B LLM judge remains superior at 10% coverage.

Conclusion: Benchmark construction for insufficient-evidence detection critically affects measured performance: naïve deletions of supporting passages can introduce strong shortcuts, such as memory-size leakage, that inflate scores. A size-matched design removes these shortcuts and reveals the value of more sophisticated estimators like MemSafe, which can effectively detect unsafe memory in some multi-hop QA settings and serve as a useful gating signal for downstream readers. Nevertheless, MemSafe’s weaker generalization to datasets like SQuAD 2.0 and clinical domains, and its sensitivity to how unanswerable cases are defined, indicate that both dataset design and model architecture must be carefully matched to the target deployment to achieve robust detection of when evidence is truly insufficient.

Abstract: Agents that answer questions from compressed or retrieved memory must recognize when the evidence a query needs is no longer in memory. Benchmarks for this task usually create insufficient-evidence examples by deleting supporting passages. We show that this construction leaks the label through memory size: on MuSiQue, a classifier that only counts paragraphs reaches an area under the ROC curve (AUROC) of $0.979$ for detecting unsafe memory, higher than the lexical estimator we initially evaluated. We propose a size-matched construction that provably removes this shortcut, and use it to study MemSafe, an estimator that cross-encodes the query with each memory unit and aggregates the units with a set transformer. Across three multi-hop question answering datasets and five seeds, MemSafe reaches $0.968$ and $0.983$ AUROC on MuSiQue and HotpotQA, $0.26$ to $0.39$ above a lexical baseline, while the third dataset, 2WikiMultiHopQA, is saturated. A frozen pretrained cross-encoder with a logistic head already closes $41\%$ of the MuSiQue gap between the lexical baseline and MemSafe. At the same time, MemSafe degrades more than a weak baseline on the unanswerable questions released with MuSiQue, reaches only $0.639$ AUROC on SQuAD~2.0, and needs several thousand clinical training examples before it outperforms a feature-based estimator. Used as a gate for a 7B reader, it reduces the error rate on answered questions from $0.850$ to $0.631$ at $5\%$ coverage, outperforming both reader confidence and, on average, the ground-truth integrity label, although a 7B LLM judge is the better gate at $10\%$ coverage. These results indicate that the way insufficient evidence is constructed matters as much as the estimator that detects it.

</details>


### [34] [Supporting and Performing Culture from the Inside](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32281)
*Lea Frermann,Steven Bird*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how NLP research treats culture using the emic (insider) vs etic (outsider) distinction, highlighting how the “culture of NLP” influences research choices and proposing ways to make AI more culturally aware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cultural research in anthropology distinguishes between insider and outsider perspectives, but NLP work on culture rarely makes these assumptions explicit. As NLP systems are increasingly deployed globally across diverse cultural contexts, there is a need to scrutinize how cultural perspectives influence the entire research pipeline and to avoid implicitly imposing the norms of the NLP community as universal.

Method: The authors conceptually adopt the emic/etic framework from anthropology and use it to systematically examine recent NLP research on culture. They map emic/etic assumptions across stages: task selection, data collection, model/system design, and evaluation. They also reflect on the norms, values, and implicit assumptions of the NLP research community—what they call the 'culture of NLP.'

Result: The analysis reveals that much NLP cultural research defaults to etic, outsider-style modeling of culture, often assuming Western, English-speaking, and technologically centered norms. Emic perspectives—centered on how communities themselves conceptualize and practice culture—are underrepresented, and the culture of the NLP community itself often goes unexamined despite shaping data, tasks, and evaluation standards.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that NLP needs to explicitly recognize and balance emic and etic perspectives, critically examine its own disciplinary culture, and incorporate more participatory, community-grounded and context-sensitive practices throughout the research pipeline. This shift can lead to more culturally attuned and responsible AI systems.

Abstract: Anthropology and related disciplines which study culture have often found it useful to consider their epistemological and methodological approaches in terms of emic versus etic. This is the distinction between the insider perspective, how the world is viewed by a member of the culture, versus the outsider perspective, the scientific cataloguing of cultural knowledge and practice. We adopt this framework to systematically analyse assumptions in recent research on culture in NLP along the full pipeline of task selection, data collection, system design and evaluation. We draw attention to the `culture of NLP' which shapes the research focus and approaches of our field, and suggest pathways towards a more culturally attuned AI.

</details>


### [35] [TRAP: Understanding and Mitigating Privacy Memorization in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32293)
*Muhammed Ustaomeroglu,Ziyue Xu,Hanshen Xiao,Peter Cnudde,Guannan Qu,Holger R. Roth*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies when and why fine-tuned language models memorize sensitive training data and proposes a new regularization method (TRAP) based on a token-level memorization signal (TRA) to reduce such memorization with minimal utility loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-tuning language models on sensitive data can cause them to memorize and later reproduce private information, even when that information is rare and embedded in otherwise benign text. Existing defenses like generic regularization or differential privacy either fail to sufficiently curb memorization or significantly harm model utility. There is a need for a principled, fine-grained signal of memorization that does not require prior knowledge of which text spans are sensitive, and a corresponding training method that uses this signal to reduce memorization while preserving task performance.

Method: The authors observe that many memorization metrics and attacks effectively compare a model’s token probabilities against some reference. They formalize this as Target Reference Advantage (TRA), which measures how much more probability the fine-tuned (target) model assigns to a token than a reference model trained on the complementary half of the same corpus. TRA is computed per token, is differentiable, and indicates whether behavior is driven by record-specific memorization versus generalization across records. They empirically analyze how memorization evolves during fine-tuning (effects of training duration, dataset size, learning rate, and task difficulty), and show the limits of early stopping based on validation loss. To mitigate memorization, they introduce TRAP, a one-sided regularization term that penalizes positive TRA values, i.e., only when the target model starts to outperform the reference on a token, which suggests memorization. TRAP is integrated into the fine-tuning objective to selectively suppress memorization without broadly constraining the model.

Result: Empirical studies show that memorization continues to increase well after the point of minimum validation loss, is exacerbated by smaller datasets, higher learning rates, and harder tasks. Early stopping cuts some memorization but is least effective for rare, hard-to-predict tokens embedded in otherwise easy text, a profile characteristic of sensitive information. Applying TRAP on two benchmarks—student essays with labeled personal information and clinical cases containing patient identifiers—reduces memorization to levels comparable to an untrained model, while maintaining most of the task performance gains from fine-tuning. In contrast, common regularizers have limited effect on memorization, and differentially private training significantly degrades utility relative to standard fine-tuning.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuned language models naturally tend to memorize sensitive, hard-to-predict tokens, especially under common training regimes, and that conventional techniques like early stopping, standard regularization, or differential privacy are either insufficient or too costly in terms of utility. By formalizing a general token-level memorization signal (TRA) and introducing the TRAP regularizer that selectively penalizes it, the authors provide a practical and effective way to reduce memorization of sensitive spans without identifying them in advance and with minimal loss in model performance. This suggests a promising direction for safer fine-tuning of language models on sensitive data.

Abstract: Fine-tuning a language model on sensitive records can leave it able to reproduce them. We ask when this memorization arises and how to prevent it without knowing in advance which spans are sensitive. Our starting point is that most memorization scores and attacks share one statistical core: whether the model assigns a token more probability than some reference would. Taking as the reference a model trained on the complementary half of the same corpus gives the Target Reference Advantage (TRA), a per-token signal that separates what a model fit to a particular record from what it learned across records, and is cheap and differentiable. We then study what drives memorization during fine-tuning: it keeps growing well past the validation minimum, is larger on small datasets and at higher learning rates, and higher when the underlying task is harder. Early stopping removes much of it, but because it is chosen by aggregate validation loss it helps least for rare, hard-to-predict spans embedded in otherwise learnable text, which is exactly what sensitive information tends to be. We therefore introduce TRAP, a one-sided penalty on tokenwise TRA that acts only where the target model pulls ahead of its reference. On student essays with annotated personal information and clinical cases with patient identifiers, TRAP brings memorization near the level of an untrained model at little utility cost, where generic regularizers barely move and differential privacy gives up most of what fine-tuning bought.

</details>


### [36] [Language Distances are Practical for Equitable Cross-Lingual Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32331)
*York Hay Ng,Razan Ahsan Rifandi,Aditya Khan,En-Shiun Annie Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They study how to choose source languages for cross-lingual transfer more fairly and reliably, comparing different ways of ranking source languages, and show composite distances and trained rankers improve both equity and performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Choosing which source language to use for cross-lingual transfer greatly affects performance, but it is hard to identify the best source, especially for low-resource languages. Language distances are commonly used heuristics, yet their reliability and fairness across tasks and resource levels has not been systematically evaluated. The authors aim to fill this gap and understand equity issues in cross-lingual transfer source selection.

Method: They conduct an equity-focused evaluation of different paradigms for ranking source languages: individual language distances, training-free composite distances, trained rankers, and simple baselines like always using English. They test these methods across ten cross-lingual tasks and two multilingual models, analyzing resource-level inequality (how performance differs by resource levels of target languages) and task inequality (how performance varies across tasks). They also compare rankers based on language distances to rankers leveraging internal representations of language models to assess reliability.

Result: They find that both resource-level and task inequality are highest when using single language distances or an English-always baseline. Training-free composite distances significantly reduce these inequalities, while trained rankers almost eliminate them. Rankers using language distances are shown to be reliable and competitive with rankers that use language model internals. Overall transfer performance and equity in language selection improve with composite distances and trained rankers.

Conclusion: Language distances are an effective and practical foundation for selecting source languages in cross-lingual transfer. To achieve equitable and strong performance across languages and tasks, trained rankers should be used when task-specific transfer data is available; otherwise, composite distance-based rankers are recommended as a strong training-free alternative. This approach mitigates inequality between high- and low-resource languages and across tasks.

Abstract: Cross-lingual transfer is strongly conditional on how the source language is chosen, but it is impractical to determine the best candidate source for every target language, especially for low-resource target languages. Language distances are widely used to rank candidate sources due to their correlation with transfer efficacy and applicability in resource-sparse settings. However, the reliability of distance-based rankers across tasks and resource levels remains underexplored. We therefore present the first equity-focused evaluation of paradigms for ranking source languages, studying resource-level inequality and task inequality across ten cross-lingual tasks and two multilingual models. While both inequalities are most pronounced for individual language distances and an English-always baseline, they are substantially reduced by training-free composite distances, and nearly eliminated by trained rankers. We further demonstrate the reliability of rankers using language distances compared to rankers using language model internals. Overall, we find that language distances provide a practical basis for equitable and performant transfer language selection. We recommend using trained rankers when task-specific transfer evaluations are available, and composite distances otherwise.

</details>


### [37] [Gradients for Interventions and Activations for Detection: Targeted Feature Learning in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32355)
*Jonathan Drechsel,Steffen Herbold*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper systematically compares ways to learn a single, targeted feature for a predefined concept inside language models, contrasting them with sparse autoencoders, and shows that different signal/estimator choices trade off detection vs. causal intervention power.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most interpretability tools like Sparse Autoencoders learn many features first and only later connect them to concepts, but many real interpretability questions start from a specific hypothesis or concept of interest (e.g., a particular behavior to detect or control). There is a need to understand how best to directly learn a single internal feature that corresponds to a given, predefined concept, and to know what kinds of model-internal signals and estimators yield features that are good both for recognizing the concept and for causally manipulating the model’s behavior.

Method: The authors formalize “targeted feature learning,” where they build one feature corresponding to a specified concept rather than a whole feature dictionary. They consider three types of model-internal signals—raw activation values, activation gradients, and parameter gradients—and two estimators for turning these signals into a one-dimensional feature: (1) a simple contrastive mean estimator and (2) a learned 1D encoder–decoder mapping. Crossing these choices yields six methods, including two existing ones (CAA and GRADIEND) and four newly defined methods. They benchmark all six targeted methods versus pretrained Sparse Autoencoders on 15 tasks across three language models, measuring both (a) detection performance—how well the feature identifies when the concept is present—and (b) intervention performance—how effectively manipulating the feature changes the model’s behavior.

Result: Empirically, targeted methods based on contrastive activation values achieve the best performance at detecting the presence of the target concept across tasks and models. In contrast, gradient-based targeted methods—those using activation or parameter gradients—deliver superior performance for causal interventions, i.e., modifying model behavior by steering or editing via that feature. Sparse Autoencoder features, which are not optimized for a single concept, are outperformed on these targeted metrics by appropriately chosen targeted methods.
