Conclusion: The effectiveness of a targeted concept feature depends jointly on which model signal is used (activations vs. gradients) and how it is estimated (contrastive statistic vs. learned encoder–decoder). There is a clear trade-off: features that are best at concept detection are not necessarily best for causal manipulation, and vice versa. Detection and intervention thus capture complementary aspects of feature quality, and targeted feature learning offers a principled alternative to post hoc SAE-based interpretability when the goal is to study or control a specific concept in a language model.

Abstract: Model-internal features can be studied through both their ability to identify a specified concept and their causal effect when manipulated, e.g., through steering or weight editing. A prominent approach to feature learning is Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), which learn broad feature dictionaries whose relation to particular concepts is typically identified post hoc. However, many interpretability questions are instead hypothesis-driven and concern a concept specified in advance. We study this setting as targeted feature learning, where a single feature is constructed for such a predefined concept. We present a controlled comparison across three model signals (activation values, activation gradients, and parameter gradients) and two estimators (contrastive mean and a learned one-dimensional encoder-decoder), yielding six targeted methods, with CAA and GRADIEND as existing instances and four new methods covering the remaining combinations. We compare these methods against pretrained SAEs across 15 tasks and three language models, evaluating both detection and causal intervention. Across models, the strongest detection performance is achieved by contrastive activation value methods, whereas the strongest intervention performance is achieved by gradient-based methods. Overall, our results show that targeted feature quality depends jointly on the model signal and estimator, with detection and intervention capturing complementary properties.

</details>


### [38] [PlurVA-LLM-2026 Shared Task Track-1: Pluralistic Value Alignment in LLMs via Multilingual Fine-Tuning and Threshold Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32382)
*Vihindi Kotalawala,Nevidu Jayatilleke*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build a resource-efficient value-aligned LLM system for three countries and achieve strong accuracies using tailored augmentation and calibration strategies per language/context.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pluralistic value alignment requires adapting LLM behavior to diverse cultural and national contexts. The shared task focuses on three under-resourced, non-Western settings (China, Indonesia, Sri Lanka) where off-the-shelf models may not reflect local values or have enough labeled data. The authors aim to build an effective yet resource-constrained system that can align an open LLM to these pluralistic norms using lightweight fine-tuning and data-centric techniques.

Method: They fine-tune Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with 4-bit QLoRA to stay within resource limits. For Chinese data, they use option-permutation augmentation to expand multiple-choice training instances. For Indonesian data, they expand supervision via annotator vote expansion, presumably turning soft label distributions or multiple annotator judgments into additional training signals. For Sri Lankan data, they reformulate the task as binary classification and augment using SinhalaMMLU-style data, then post-process predictions using conditional threshold calibration to better align decision boundaries.

Result: Their system attains accuracy scores of 0.785 (Chinese), 0.715 (Indonesian), and 0.916 (Sri Lankan), leading to a macro-average accuracy of 0.805 on the shared task evaluation. This suggests strong performance, particularly in the Sri Lankan setting, under the shared task’s resource constraints.

Conclusion: A single 8B open LLM, fine-tuned with QLoRA and equipped with tailored, language-specific augmentation and calibration strategies, can achieve competitive pluralistic value alignment across multiple cultural contexts even with limited resources. Careful data-centric design per locale (option permutations, annotator vote usage, binary reformulation, and MMLU-style augmentation) is crucial for high performance in under-resourced, non-Western alignment tasks.

Abstract: We present our system for the PlurVA-LLM 2026 Shared Task Track-1, which focuses on pluralistic value alignment in the contexts of China, Indonesia, and Sri Lanka. For this resource-constrained track, we fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B Instruct using 4-bit QLoRA. Our approach combines option-permutation augmentation for Chinese data, annotator vote expansion for Indonesian data, and binary reformulation with SinhalaMMLU augmentation for Sri Lankan data. We further applied conditional threshold calibration to the predictions for the Sri Lankan data. The final system achieved accuracies of 0.785 for Chinese, 0.715 for Indonesian, and 0.916 for Sri Lankan, resulting in an overall macro-average accuracy of 0.805.

</details>


### [39] [FA-Bench: A Benchmark for Word-Level and Phone-Level Forced-Alignment and ASR Timestamps Under Clean and Noisy Conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32396)
*Wei Chu,Yuanzhe Dong,Ke Tan,Dong Han,Yichao Zhou,Ruchao Fan,Bingshen Mu,Jingbei Li,Vishwas Shetty,Sarthak Bisht,Ziyue Qiu,Massa Baali,Rita Singh,Bhisha Raj*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces FA-Bench, a standardized, open benchmarking framework for forced alignment systems, enabling fair comparison across models and APIs under consistent protocols.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of forced alignment systems use inconsistent experimental setups—different text normalizations, data splits, boundary matching schemes, and scoring metrics—making it impossible to compare reported results across papers or products. There is also a need to accurately assess systems that depend on imperfect recognition outputs and to uncover systematic timing biases that affect downstream applications.

Method: The authors build FA-Bench, a benchmark that fixes and releases all experimental components: code, dataset splits, phone mappings, text normalization rules, and scoring scripts. They define two tracks: Track 1, where systems receive the reference transcript, and Track 2, where they receive recognizer-generated transcripts for the same audio. They test on clean audio and four types of degraded audio using 21 open-source models and 9 commercial ASR APIs in a unified protocol. Scoring is done at every boundary between phones/words, considering the labels on both sides, so missed or hallucinated words incur penalties. They propose a tolerance-based F1 score as the main metric instead of mean absolute error (MAE), and they additionally analyze performance by grouping boundaries according to position and recognition correctness of adjacent words.

Result: The benchmark reveals that standard MAE substantially inflates scores—by 9–14%—for recognition-dependent systems on conversational speech, whereas the proposed tolerance-based F1 provides a more realistic assessment. The detailed boundary-level analysis exposes where systems lose performance depending on boundary context and recognition correctness. The evaluation across 21 open models and 9 commercial APIs surfaces systematic timing biases across systems.

Conclusion: FA-Bench offers a reproducible, transparent framework for evaluating forced alignment systems, enabling apples-to-apples comparisons across academic and commercial solutions. The proposed tolerance-based F1 metric and boundary-grouping analyses give more accurate and diagnostic insights than conventional MAE. The study also uncovers consistent timing biases—e.g., Whisper tending to align about 150 ms early and some commercial APIs over 50 ms late—highlighting issues that practitioners must consider when choosing or designing alignment tools. The benchmark and its public code/results aim to serve as a continually updated reference point for the community.

Abstract: Forced alignment aligns speech audio with a text transcript to generate word and phone timestamps. Published comparisons normalize transcripts, split the data and match boundaries differently, so their numbers cannot be read together. We present FA-Bench, an open framework that fixes those choices once and releases the code, splits, phone mapping, text normalization and scoring script, with results published periodically. Track 1 gives every aligner the reference transcript and Track 2 gives it a recognizer's output, on the same audio, clean and degraded four ways, with 21 open models and 9 commercial APIs under a unified protocol. We score every boundary of an utterance and check the two labels beside it, so a word the recognizer missed or invented is charged. Using a tolerance-based F1 as our primary metric eliminates the 9% to 14% score inflation that standard MAE causes on recognition-dependent systems in conversational speech. We then group boundaries by their position and how many adjacent words were recognized correctly, which shows where a system lost the score. We discovered systematic bias in how current systems time words, with Whisper about 150 ms early and several commercial ASR APIs over 50 ms late. Code and results are at https://github.com/olewave/fa-bench

</details>


### [40] [SinBrief: A Hybrid Framework for Abstractive Text Summarisation of Sinhala Legal Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32397)
*Minduli Lasandi,Nevidu Jayatilleke*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SinBrief is a hybrid, largely annotation-free abstractive summarisation framework for Sinhala legal documents that integrates domain-aware word graphs with neural sentence scoring, achieving low-overlap yet factually consistent summaries in a low-resource setting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a lack of annotated data and specialised tools for summarising legal documents in low-resource languages like Sinhala, where legal texts are complex and terminology-rich. Existing summarisation methods either rely heavily on human-annotated datasets or focus on high-resource languages, limiting their applicability to low-resource legal NLP.

Method: The authors design SinBrief, a hybrid abstractive summarisation pipeline. It constructs a domain-aware word graph over Sinhala legal documents and applies neural sentence scoring models (mBert, Llama 3.1, Falcon 7B, Laser, and a continually pre-trained Llama adapted to Sinhala legal text). These scores guide the selection and abstraction of content from the legal documents. The system is evaluated with reference-free metrics such as Coverage, Density, Compression Ratio, SummaC, and Self-BertScore on a Sinhala legal corpus.

Result: SinBrief generates summaries that have lower lexical overlap with the source text than extractive baselines, indicating more abstraction, while preserving factual consistency as measured by reference-free metrics. Among the tested sentence scoring models, the domain-adapted Llama variant is expected to perform particularly well, though exact numbers are not provided in the abstract.

Conclusion: Hybrid abstractive summarisation that combines symbolic structures (word graphs) with neural sentence scoring can work effectively in low-resource legal domains without requiring human-annotated training data. SinBrief demonstrates that such approaches are viable for Sinhala legal document summarisation and more broadly for low-resource legal NLP tasks, offering factually consistent, less extractive summaries.

Abstract: Legal document summarisation in low-resource languages presents significant challenges due to the scarcity of annotated data and the complexity of domain-specific terminology. This paper presents SinBrief, a hybrid abstractive summarisation framework for Sinhala legal documents that does not require human-annotated training data. The proposed framework combines domain-aware word graph construction with neural sentence scoring to generate abstractive summaries from Sinhala legal text. Five sentence scoring models are evaluated within the framework: mBert, Llama 3.1, Falcon 7B, Laser, and a continually pre-trained Llama model domain-adapted to Sinhala legal text. The framework is evaluated on a Sinhala legal corpus using reference-free metrics, including Coverage, Density, Compression Ratio, SummaC, and Self-BertScore. Experimental results demonstrate that SinBrief produces summaries with lower lexical overlap than extractive baselines while maintaining factual consistency, demonstrating the viability of hybrid, largely annotation-free abstractive summarisation for low-resource legal NLP tasks.

</details>


### [41] [Shared Worlds, Private Minds: Structured Memory for Long-Form Writing as World Creation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32401)
*Qiuyu Tian,Xiaowen Gu,Hang Su,Jianghan Chao,Haojie Yin,Fan Guo,Xin Zhang,Jinjing Shen,Ewing Luo,Youyong Kong,Yingce Xia,Zequn Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: NarraWorld is a structured memory system that helps LLM agents maintain consistent, coherent long-form fiction by treating memory as an evolving storyworld graph.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-form fiction writing with LLMs requires maintaining consistency with previously established story facts, character states, and plot developments. Existing memory approaches struggle with heterogeneous narrative information, cross-granularity integration (events, scenes, plots), and recovering implicit dependencies from user writing prompts. The paper aims to design a memory framework that can represent and retrieve complex, evolving storyworlds so agents can write coherent, consistent narratives over long horizons and diverse tasks.

Method: The authors introduce NarraWorld, a structured memory system that models narrative memory as world creation over a shared evidence-grounded graph. From this base graph, NarraWorld derives four interconnected views: (1) world facts (objective elements of the storyworld), (2) per-character beliefs (subjective, possibly mistaken views), (3) open developments (unresolved threads and ongoing narratives), and (4) hypothetical branches (possible-world continuations and what-ifs). It uses hierarchical aggregation with atomic closure to group low-level events into scenes, plotlines, and entire plots while preserving traceability back to source text spans. For retrieval, it performs planned reconstruction: given the current narrative situation and a preview of memory, it infers which latent dependencies a user query implies, then selects and assembles the most relevant memory records under a token budget constraint.

Result: On three long-form writing benchmarks, NarraWorld produces the best overall performance compared to baselines, indicating stronger coherence and consistency in generated stories. The structured memory further proves reusable: it transfers effectively to situated role-playing tasks, and it maintains most of its recall capability on a general-purpose long-term memory benchmark. This shows that the representation is robust and not overly specialized to a single writing setup.

Conclusion: Treating memory as an explicit, structured storyworld graph with multiple semantic views enables LLM agents to better maintain narrative coherence and consistency in long-form fiction. NarraWorld’s hierarchical, traceable aggregation and planned reconstruction retrieval provide an effective way to manage complex, evolving narrative information under token constraints. Its strong benchmark performance and transfer to other narrative tasks suggest it is a promising foundation for future long-horizon, story-centric agent systems that must sustain coherent worlds over time.

Abstract: LLM agents that write long-form fiction need an explicit memory of the evolving storyworld to keep new events consistent with established facts. Such memory must keep heterogeneous narrative information distinct, integrate story developments across granularities, and recover dependencies that a writing request leaves implicit. We present NarraWorld, a structured memory system for long-form writing that treats memory construction as world creation. From a shared evidence-grounded graph, NarraWorld derives four connected views: world facts, per-character beliefs, open developments, and hypothetical branches (possible-world continuations). Hierarchical aggregation with atomic closure consolidates events into scenes, plotlines, and plots, keeping each higher-level node traceable to its constituent source spans. For retrieval, planned reconstruction infers a query's dependencies from the current narrative situation and a preview of memory, then assembles the relevant records within a token budget. Across three writing benchmarks, NarraWorld achieves the strongest aggregate results. Its memory also transfers to situated role-playing and largely preserves recall on a general-purpose long-term memory benchmark, paving the way for agents that sustain coherent storyworlds across diverse narrative tasks.

</details>


### [42] [Automatic Speech Recognition for the Basaà Language: A Low-Resource Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32408)
*Sophie Gertrude Ngo Mock,Charles Moudina Varmantchaonala,Paul Dayang,Jean Michel Nlong,Christopher Gies*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper discusses how advances in AI-based Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) have reached near-human performance for major languages but have not equally benefited most of the world’s languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite major breakthroughs in AI, NLP, and ASR, most progress is concentrated on a few high-resource languages like English and French, leaving the majority of global languages under-served.

Method: The abstract hints that the paper surveys or builds on modern ASR techniques using deep neural networks, transformer architectures, and self-supervised learning, likely comparing their performance or applicability across languages with different resource levels.

Result: For well-resourced languages, modern ASR achieves near-human performance; for the vast majority of low-resource languages, performance lags significantly due to lack of data and tailored models.

Conclusion: Current state-of-the-art ASR technologies provide impressive accuracy for a few major languages but there is a substantial inequality in technological benefits for the rest of the world’s languages, highlighting the need for more inclusive and broader language coverage in ASR research and development.

Abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) has revolutionized the way humans interact with machines. Among the most impactful developments is Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), which enables computers to convert spoken language into text. Systems such as those built on deep neural networks, transformer architectures, and self-supervised learning have achieved near-human performance for well-resourced languages such as English and French. Yet, these advances have disproportionately benefited a small fraction of the world's languages.

</details>


### [43] [DualGuard: Dual-Mode Quality Control for Logic-Preserving Data Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32431)
*Shenghao Li,Lin Zhao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DualGuard is a dual-mode quality-control framework that makes LLM-generated logical reasoning data more reliable and improves downstream task accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can generate large amounts of data for logical reasoning tasks, but the generated examples often suffer from semantic errors, mislabeled outputs, or invalid logic. Existing methods constrain generation and filter or revise candidates, but they lack a principled control mechanism for deciding when to retain, filter, or repair data once quality judgments are available. There is also a need to use historical behavior of augmentation actions to detect anomalies and correct previous decisions.

Method: The paper introduces DualGuard, a framework with two complementary quality-control modes for logic-preserving data augmentation. Mode 1 operates locally on the current instance and its candidate batch: it performs selective retention and filtering of generated data, attribution of errors, and targeted feedback to guide improvements. Mode 2 operates globally across instances: it stores cross-instance execution records of augmentation actions and, based on per-sample diagnosis and attribution, compares new executions to each action's historical behavior. This enables retrospective anomaly inspection, targeted rollback of problematic augmentations, and bounded repair of data. Both modes rely on semantic verification of candidates, and when explicit logical forms are available, they also apply symbolic verification (e.g., via a solver such as Z3). The framework is evaluated in a Two-Stage Transfer setting across multiple downstream tasks, and ablation studies isolate components like Memory, Z3-based checks, and history-aware anomaly control.

Result: In experiments on seven downstream logical reasoning tasks under a Two-Stage Transfer setup, DualGuard achieves the highest accuracy on five tasks and consistently outperforms a no-augmentation BERT baseline on all seven. Ablation studies show that removing components such as Memory, Z3-based symbolic verification, or history-aware anomaly control degrades performance, indicating that these elements contribute complementary benefits to data quality and final task accuracy.

Conclusion: DualGuard effectively addresses the control problem of deciding how to use quality judgments for LLM-generated logical reasoning data. By combining local, per-instance quality control with global, history-aware anomaly detection and repair, and by integrating both semantic and symbolic verification, the framework produces higher-quality augmented datasets. This leads to improved performance on a range of downstream tasks and demonstrates the value of dual-mode, history-aware quality control in logic-preserving data augmentation.

Abstract: Large language models provide a practical way to generate augmented data for logical reasoning at scale, but a larger generation volume does not guarantee semantic, label, or logical reliability. Existing work has improved generation quality through generation constraints, candidate validation, filtering, and feedback-based revision; however, once a quality judgment is available, deciding whether a candidate should be retained, filtered, or repaired remains an important control problem. We propose DualGuard, a dual-mode quality-control framework for logic-preserving data augmentation. The first mode uses the current instance and candidate batch for selective retention, filtering, attribution, and targeted feedback. The second mode accumulates cross-instance execution records of augmentation actions on top of per-sample diagnosis and attribution, compares new executions against each action's own historical behavior, and supports retrospective anomaly inspection, targeted rollback, and bounded repair. Both modes share semantic verification and additionally use symbolic verification when a reliable logical form is available. Across seven downstream tasks in the Two-Stage Transfer setting, DualGuard achieves the highest Accuracy on five tasks and outperforms the no-augmentation BERT baseline on all seven. Controlled ablations further show complementary roles for Memory, Z3, and history-aware anomaly control.

</details>


### [44] [Masking Frequent Tokens Sharpens Direct Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32445)
*Harshvardhan Saini,Samyak Jha,Yiming Tang,Dianbo Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies that standard Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is dominated by high-frequency, low-information tokens that appear in both preferred and dispreferred responses, which weakens the learning signal. It proposes Anisotropic / Frequency-Hard DPO, which masks these common tokens in the objective so that gradients focus on informative, preference-specific positions, leading to better alignment without extra parameters or data changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DPO is an attractive way to align LMs with human preferences, but its token-wise reward structure allows very frequent, semantically light tokens to dominate sequence scores, even though they contribute little to preference discrimination and appear in both sides of preference pairs. This creates gradient entanglement and washes out the signal from genuinely informative tokens. The paper aims to diagnose and fix this structural flaw while keeping DPO's simplicity and efficiency.

Method: 1) Empirically analyze token frequency and sharing patterns on Anthropic HH-RLHF under Qwen tokenization, showing that a tiny set of tokens accounts for most token mass and most within-pair overlap, and that these tokens are weakly preference-specific. 2) Formalize "anisotropic" DPO as a DPO objective with non-uniform, token-level weights in the implicit reward sum. 3) Instantiate Frequency-Hard DPO by building a fixed, label-agnostic vocabulary mask that zeroes reward contributions of high-frequency, shared tokens and leaves others with weight 1. 4) Train aligned models (Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3-8B-Instruct) using this modified objective while keeping data, architecture, and parameters unchanged.

Result: On alignment benchmarks AlpacaEval, MT-Bench, and Arena-Hard, models trained with Frequency-Hard DPO consistently exceed the performance of standard DPO across both Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3-8B-Instruct backbones. The improvements show up as higher win rates and better scores, indicating that suppressing gradients from high-frequency, low-informative tokens makes preference learning more effective and robust.

Conclusion: Standard DPO suffers from a structural pathology whereby a small set of ubiquitous, high-frequency tokens dominates the objective yet carries weak preference information, causing gradient interference. Introducing anisotropic token weighting—implemented as a simple frequency-based hard mask—effectively removes this interference. The resulting Frequency-Hard DPO preserves DPO's simplicity and zero overhead (no extra parameters, no pair changes, no context removal) while yielding systematically better alignment performance, suggesting that careful control of token-level contributions is crucial for robust preference optimization.

Abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) aligns language models by optimizing over sequence-level sums of token-wise implicit reward differences. However, we identify a pervasive pathology in this formulation: a disproportionately small subset of high-frequency token types dominates cumulative sequence scores while appearing symmetrically across both preferred and dispreferred responses. Specifically, under canonical Qwen tokenization on Anthropic HH-RLHF, merely 69 token types account for $55.1\%$ of all response tokens and $85.9\%$ of within-pair shared token mass, exhibiting substantially lower preference-side specificity than the remaining vocabulary. This symmetric ubiquity induces gradient entanglement and dilutes the discriminative preference signal propagated through the objective. To resolve this issue, we introduce \emph{Anisotropic DPO} (\textsf{ADPO}) and its canonical realization, \emph{Frequency-Hard DPO}. Using a fixed, label-agnostic vocabulary mask, our method zeroes the implicit reward contribution of high-frequency response tokens while assigning unit weight to informative positions, thereby suppressing gradient interference without modifying preference pairs, discarding context, or introducing learned parameters. Here, \emph{anisotropy} designates non-uniform token-level objective weighting rather than representational geometry. Extensive empirical evaluations on AlpacaEval, MT-Bench, and Arena-Hard demonstrate that Frequency-Hard DPO consistently outperforms standard DPO across Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3-8B-Instruct, establishing that selectively masking shared high-frequency tokens offers an effective, zero-overhead mechanism for robust preference alignment.

</details>


### [45] [Self-Reports Do Not Identify Self-Models: An Identifiability Test for Counterfactual Reports](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32449)
*Phongsakon Mark Konrad,Toygar Tanyel,Serkan Ayvaz*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper examines whether language-model self-reports about their own internal states are stable evidence of an internal self-model, or just artifacts of prompts, by testing if such reports stay tied to specific interventions when the surrounding prompt environment changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is growing interest in using language-model self-reports (e.g., about being happy, sad, confident, or reflecting on internal mechanisms) as evidence of internal self-models or proto-phenomenology. However, these self-reports might simply mirror the structure of the prompts or demonstrations given to the model, rather than reflecting any autonomous reporting mechanism. The authors want to test how fragile or robust these self-reports are under changes in the prompt environment, specifically when the same activation-level intervention is paired with different contextual demonstrations.

Method: The authors use three open instruction-tuned language models and apply activation interventions that are associated with particular 'affect-like' self-reports (e.g., simulated moods or feelings). They then manipulate the demonstration environment in two ways: (1) they introduce wrong-source demonstrations that suggest the intervention comes from a different source or mechanism than it actually does, and (2) they add explicit mechanism binding, where the text clearly ties a particular pattern of self-report to a specific intervention mechanism. They measure whether the model's counterfactual self-reports under intervention stay bound to the true intervention or drift toward the answer family suggested by the demonstrations when the prompt environment changes.

Result: Across all three models tested, wrong-source demonstrations systematically pull the model's self-reports away from those associated with the true intervention and toward the reports associated with the incorrect source or answer family. However, when the prompt explicitly binds self-reports to a specific mechanism, this environmental pull is reduced, and the reports stay more closely aligned to the intended intervention. This shows that the models' self-reports are highly sensitive to prompt framing and learned associations, and only partially constrained by the underlying activation-level intervention itself.

Conclusion: Language-model self-reports about affect-like or internal states cannot be straightforwardly interpreted as evidence of an autonomous self-model or stable internal reporting mechanism. Instead, they reflect a complex interaction between activation-level interventions and the surrounding prompt environment, including demonstrations and mechanism descriptions. The authors argue that any benchmark that treats self-report accuracy as evidence for internal mechanisms should first include environment-shift invariance tests under fixed interventions, ensuring that reported states remain stable across different prompt contexts. Without such tests, we risk over-interpreting context-sensitive prompt-following behavior as genuine self-knowledge in language models.

Abstract: Language-model self-reports are evidence about behavior in a prompt environment, not by themselves evidence of a self-model. We investigate counterfactual reports about affect-like states under activation interventions and ask whether the report remains bound to the named intervention when the demonstration environment changes. Across three open instruction models, wrong-source demonstrations move reports toward the source answer family, while explicit mechanism binding reduces this pull. Self-report benchmarks should include environment-shift invariance tests under fixed intervention before treating accuracy as evidence for an autonomous report mechanism.

</details>


### [46] [What Should the Reflector See? An Empirical Study of Evidence in Reflective Prompt Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32452)
*Xiaofan Zhou,Lu Cheng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper empirically studies how different ways of feeding evidence/examples into a reflective prompt optimizer affect final performance, local reflection success, and overfitting/calibration, finding that using only failure examples often yields the largest gains but that local improvement and calibration do not straightforwardly predict test performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reflective prompt optimization methods use a model’s own behavior (successes, failures, or other examples) to iteratively revise prompts, but the field lacks a systematic understanding of what evidence should be shown to the reflecting model and how these choices affect true generalization versus overfitting. This paper aims to disentangle these factors and provide guidance on designing reflection strategies.

Method: The authors define and compare nine reflection strategies that differ along several axes: how they compose evidence (e.g., only failures vs. balanced mixes), whether examples are visible or hidden, how candidate prompts are selected, and how domain knowledge is incorporated. Within a single-parent Pareto-guided search framework, they use Qwen3.5-9B as both the task model and the reflector, and run experiments across five benchmark datasets to measure final test performance, parent-prompt improvement, and calibration properties.

Result: Experiments reveal three key patterns: (1) For final performance, the Failures-only evidence strategy achieves the highest average test gain (~+8.0 percentage points), with Balanced-mix and No-examples+Val tying for best average rank; (2) For local reflection effectiveness (improving sampled parent prompts), No-examples ranks best but yields only modest mean test gains (~+1.4 points), indicating that local success does not guarantee stronger final prompts; (3) For overfitting and calibration, Failures-only and Balanced-mix show the best (lowest) mean calibration-gap ranks, while substantially larger gaps on certain datasets (GPQA, IFBench) indicate that improvements in calibration may overstate actual held-out performance gains.

Conclusion: Reflection strategies should be evaluated along multiple axes—final test performance, effectiveness at improving parent prompts, and how well calibration improvements transfer to held-out data—because these criteria can diverge. In particular, using only failure examples can yield strong test gains and good calibration behavior, but strategies that look effective locally or in calibration metrics do not necessarily produce the best generalizing prompts, and calibration-gap should be treated as a descriptive signal rather than a direct measure of overfitting.

Abstract: Reflective prompt optimization revises instructions using examples of a model's behavior, but which evidence the reflector should receive remains unclear. We study evidence composition, visibility of examples, candidate selection and domain-knowledge policy within a single-parent Pareto-guided search. Using Qwen3.5-9B as both task model and reflector, we evaluate nine reflection strategies on five datasets. From these experiments, we find three distinct patterns. For performance improvement, Failures-only produces the largest mean test gain (+8.0 percentage points), while Balanced-mix and No-examples+Val share the best mean performance rank. For reflection effectiveness, No-examples achieves the best rank for improving sampled parents, yet yields only a 1.4-point mean test gain: local reflection success does not necessarily produce a stronger final prompt. For overfitting assessment, Failures-only and Balanced-mix share the lowest mean calibration-gap rank, while larger gaps on GPQA and IFBench show that calibration gains can overstate held-out improvement. This gap is a descriptive indicator, not a direct measure of overfitting. Together, these results show why reflection strategies should be assessed separately on final performance, parent improvement and calibration-to-test transfer.

</details>


### [47] [Streamlined Reflective Evolution for Task-Adaptive Self-Refinement Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32458)
*Xiaofan Zhou,Lu Cheng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes Workflow-Designing Agents (WDA), a framework that automatically designs and refines multi-stage prompt workflows for LLMs, yielding task-adaptive self-refinement pipelines that improve performance without changing model weights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing reflective prompt optimization methods improve LLM performance but typically use fixed, hand-designed architectures (e.g., single self-reflection step, fixed chains-of-thought). This constrains how self-refinement is organized and can lead to bloated prompts where iterative edits accumulate redundant instructions. The authors aim to automate the design of multi-stage, task-specific workflows, deciding not only what each stage should do but also how many stages are needed and how they are sequenced, while keeping model weights frozen.

Method: The authors introduce Workflow-Designing Agents (WDA), which start from a minimal initial prompt and iteratively evolve a multi-stage prompt pipeline. WDA jointly optimizes both the content of stage instructions and the structure/order of stages. During the evolution process, they observe that simple iterative refinement tends to pack many overlapping instructions into a single prompt. To counter this, they propose SPLIT, a mechanism that decomposes such overloaded prompts into multiple specialized stages, redistributing instructions across them. The search is guided by three-example reflection plus local screening to focus on promising workflow modifications. Calibration scores are used to manage a Pareto-based admission of candidate workflows and to roll back trailing updates that hurt performance. The final result is, for each task, a fixed multi-stage workflow learned from training data and then applied uniformly at test time.

Result: On five benchmarks covering knowledge-intensive tasks, mathematical reasoning, multi-hop QA, and instruction following, WDA significantly improves LLM performance without altering weights. Using Qwen3.5-9B, WDA boosts average performance to 51.24%, an 8.63 percentage point gain over the base solver and a 2.60 point gain over a WDA variant without SPLIT. On GPT-4.1-mini, WDA reaches 49.00%, improving by 5.62 points over the base solver and 3.69 points over the variant without SPLIT. These empirical results demonstrate that automatically learned, task-adaptive self-refinement workflows outperform both the initial single-stage solver and workflows evolved without explicit prompt-splitting.

Conclusion: Task-adaptive self-refinement pipelines, automatically discovered via Workflow-Designing Agents, can substantially enhance LLM performance across diverse benchmarks without modifying model weights. The SPLIT mechanism is crucial, preventing accumulation of redundant instructions in single prompts and enabling deeper, more specialized multi-stage workflows. The study suggests that learning task-specific, fixed-depth workflows is a promising, complementary alternative to generic agentic workflow search, opening a path toward more systematic and efficient design of LLM reasoning pipelines.

Abstract: Reflective prompt optimization improves large language model (LLM) systems without updating model weights, but fixed architectures constrain how self-refinement is organized. We introduce Workflow-Designing Agents (WDA), a framework for streamlined reflective evolution of task-adaptive self-refinement pipelines. Starting from a minimal prompt, WDA jointly evolves stage instructions and their sequential structure. During evolution, we find that repeated revisions can accumulate redundant instructions in a single prompt. In WDA, we propose to address this problem with SPLIT, which redistributes these instructions across specialized stages. Three-example reflection and local screening guide selective search, while calibration scores guide Pareto admission and rollback of unhelpful trailing updates. The resulting pipelines are task-adaptive: their instructions and depth are learned from task data, then fixed for all test inputs within that task. We evaluate WDA on five benchmarks spanning knowledge, mathematical reasoning, multi-hop question answering, and instruction following. On Qwen3.5-9B, WDA achieves an average score of 51.24%, improving over the initial solver by 8.63 percentage points and the variant without SPLIT by 2.60 points. On GPT-4.1-mini, it achieves 49.00%, with corresponding gains of 5.62 and 3.69 points. These results support task-adaptive self-refinement as a complementary direction to broader agentic workflow search.

</details>


### [48] [AdaTutoRank: Learning to Rerank Document Sets via Adaptive Tutoring Optimization for RAG and Deep Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32472)
*Kailin Jiang,Lei Liu,Jian Xi,Yangqi Chen,Hui Xu,Hongwei Zhao,Bin Li,Yu Lu,Haibo Shi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AdaTutoRank is a setwise document reranker for RAG/deep research that optimizes entire evidence sets, using adaptive tutoring signals to provide dense, token-level supervision and improving performance while reducing retrieval calls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard rerankers focus on individual document relevance, which fails to construct complete, complementary, non-redundant evidence sets for complex queries. Prior setwise methods use a single scalar rubric score for the whole set, leading to sparse supervision and poor credit assignment among documents (good and bad items are rewarded or punished together). On-policy distillation could help but current approaches give uniform hints to all rollouts, which are too restrictive for strong predictions and too vague for weak ones. The paper aims to provide richer, adaptive supervision for learning to compose document sets rather than just rank items.

Method: They introduce AdaTutoRank, a setwise reranker trained with Adaptive Tutoring Optimization (ATO). ATO is built around a three-level hierarchy of nine rubric dimensions that are used as silver labels, RL rewards, and distillation hints. The training uses a frozen snapshot of the policy as a teacher to generate three forms of hints, with specificity adapted to rollout quality: (1) rubric-only guidance, (2) a sibling set chosen by a self-selector under the rubrics, and (3) a self-reflector’s comparison between the rollout and that sibling set. Each rollout gets the hint type best matched to its quality. The rollout is then rescored by the hint-conditioned frozen teacher and the hint-free snapshot, and the difference is converted into a token-level advantage used in RL, complementing the usual outcome-level advantage.

Result: On ten benchmarks covering RAG, deep research, and setwise evaluation tasks, AdaTutoRank achieves the best overall performance when compared to existing rerankers and set-composition methods. It also reduces the number of retrieval calls needed, indicating more efficient evidence selection while maintaining or improving quality across tasks.

Conclusion: Optimizing evidence selection at the set level with dense, adaptive tutoring signals yields better reranking than traditional relevance-based or scalar-rubric setwise methods. AdaTutoRank’s ATO framework improves credit assignment within document sets by tailoring rubric- and teacher-based hints to rollout quality and distilling their effect into token-level advantages. This leads to state-of-the-art performance and more efficient retrieval, suggesting adaptive tutoring is a promising direction for training complex setwise rerankers in RAG and deep research systems.

Abstract: Document rerankers determine what evidence reaches the downstream model in RAG and deep research, yet mainstream rerankers select by relevance matching, and individually relevant documents rarely constitute the complete, complementary, non-redundant set a complex information need demands. Prior work rewards a set by its aggregate rubric score, shifting the objective from ranking documents to composing sets. Yet that score is one scalar shared by every document in the set, so the supervision is sparse: a redundant document is rewarded with the rest whenever the set scores well, and a decisive one penalized with the rest whenever it does not; credit assignment leaves contributors indistinguishable from free riders. On-policy distillation could densify this supervision, but existing methods give every rollout the same fixed guidance, too prescriptive for strong rollouts and too abstract for weak ones. We therefore propose AdaTutoRank, a setwise reranker trained with Adaptive Tutoring Optimization (ATO) under a three-level hierarchy of nine rubric dimensions, which supplies silver labels for the cold start, rewards for reinforcement learning, and hints for distillation. ATO draws three hint forms of increasing specificity from the policy's own frozen snapshot: the rubrics alone, a self-selector's sibling-set chosen under rubrics, and a self-reflector's reflection contrasting the rollout with that sibling-set; each rollout receives the form matched to its quality. Re-scoring that rollout under the hint-conditioned frozen teacher and the hint-free snapshot distills the hint's effect into a token-level advantage that complements the group-relative outcome advantage. Across ten benchmarks spanning RAG, deep research, and setwise evaluation, AdaTutoRank attains the best overall performance while issuing fewer retrieval calls.

</details>


### [49] [PC-SubMax: Efficient Prompt Compression via Regularized Submodular Maximization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32474)
*Ziyi Zhang,Shuang Cui,Haotian Zhang,Xiaoyu Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PC-SubMax is a submodular-optimization-based framework that compresses long prompts by selecting the most useful, diverse, and relevant sentences under a token budget, reducing cost/latency while preserving task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long prompts for LLMs cause high inference cost, latency, and the lost-in-the-middle issue. Existing selective compression either uses fixed importance scores that ignore redundancy and context-dependent contributions, or relies on expensive autoregressive LLM scoring. A more principled, efficient, and redundancy-aware selection framework is needed.

Method: Formulate selective prompt compression as regularized monotone submodular maximization under a knapsack (token budget) constraint. Define an objective U(S) - ℓ(S), where U is a monotone submodular utility over selected sentences combining information coverage, query relevance, and log-determinant-based diversity, and ℓ is a non-negative modular penalty reflecting token cost. Optimize this with the Regularized Greedy+Max (RGM) algorithm, a deterministic greedy-style method that uses encoder representations (not autoregressive scoring) and requires O(nκ) value-oracle calls, where n is the number of sentences and κ the max subset size.

Result: RGM is proven to output a feasible subset Q whose objective value satisfies U(Q) - ℓ(Q) ≥ 1/2 [U(O) - ℓ(O)], where O is an optimal solution to the regularized problem. Empirically, PC-SubMax achieves competitive or near state-of-the-art performance across seven diverse benchmarks while maintaining low computational overhead during compression, demonstrating that the method preserves task-relevant information under substantial prompt length reduction.

Conclusion: Submodular optimization with an explicit token-cost regularizer provides a theoretically justified and practical framework for selective prompt compression. By modeling coverage, relevance, and diversity with diminishing marginal returns and leveraging encoder-based scoring, PC-SubMax mitigates long-context issues like cost, latency, and information dilution, achieving strong downstream performance without expensive autoregressive scoring.

Abstract: While large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in long-context scenarios, lengthy prompts can increase inference costs and latency and exacerbate the ``lost-in-the-middle'' phenomenon. Selective prompt compression offers a model-agnostic approach to alleviating these issues. However, methods based on fixed token- or sentence-level importance scores may overlook how content contributions change with the selected subset, limiting their ability to account for inter-sentence redundancy. Compression procedures that rely on autoregressive LLM scoring can also introduce substantial overhead. We propose PC-SubMax, a theoretically grounded framework that formulates selective prompt compression as regularized monotone submodular maximization under a knapsack constraint. The objective is $U(S)-\ell(S)$, where the monotone submodular utility $U$ combines information coverage, query relevance, and log-determinant diversity, and the non-negative modular penalty $\ell$ captures token cost. Through diminishing marginal returns, the objective evaluates each sentence's contribution relative to the selected content. To optimize this objective, we develop the Regularized Greedy+Max (RGM) algorithm, which deterministically returns a feasible set $Q$ satisfying $U(Q)-\ell(Q)\geq \frac{1}{2}U(O)-\ell(O)$, where $O$ is an optimal feasible solution to the regularized problem. RGM uses $O(nκ)$ value-oracle queries, where $n$ is the number of candidate sentences and $κ$ is the maximum feasible subset size. PC-SubMax uses encoder representations and avoids autoregressive LLM scoring during compression. Experiments across seven diverse benchmarks demonstrate competitive downstream performance with low compression overhead.

</details>


### [50] [Explaining Textual Entailment with Lexical Entailments: Using LLMs to Supply Lexical Relations for Formal Proofs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32491)
*Jorryt de Jong,Stefan Moraca,Ettore Cesari,Lasha Abzianidze*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how well large language models can generate the lexical entailment knowledge needed for logic-based NLI, and how useful that knowledge is for a theorem prover.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs seem to know a lot of lexical facts and can perform natural language reasoning, but it is unclear how much of this latent lexical knowledge they explicitly and correctly use for reasoning. Logic-based NLI systems can reason transparently but require rich, structured lexical knowledge as input. The authors want to bridge these worlds: can LLMs provide the structured lexical entailments that symbolic NLI systems need, and does that actually help proof search?

Method: (1) Restrict attention to structured lexical entailments (e.g., hyponymy like chinchilla⊑small animal) as building blocks for explanations of sentential entailment. (2) Curate a dataset where each NLI entailment instance is paired with a set of lexical entailments that explain it. (3) Intrinsically evaluate various LLMs on generating such structured lexical explanations. (4) Extrinsically evaluate them in a neuro-symbolic pipeline: use LLM-generated lexical relations as input to LangPro, a natural-logic theorem prover, to see how much they improve NLI performance and proof success.

Result: The new dataset enables systematic evaluation of lexical explanation generation. Even strong proprietary LLMs struggle: their produced lexical relations are frequently incomplete and only partially correct. In the neuro-symbolic setting, feeding these LLM-generated relations to LangPro yields only moderate gains in proving entailments. Many generated relations appear overfitted to the specific NLI instance and do not represent robust, generally valid lexical knowledge.

Conclusion: LLMs, despite their apparent lexical competence, are not yet reliable providers of structured, sound lexical entailments for logic-based NLI. The proposed explanation task remains difficult, and the benefit of current LLMs for theorem provers is limited because their lexical relations are noisy, partially unsound, and problem-specific rather than general. More research is needed on extracting stable, structured lexical knowledge from LLMs or integrating them with better symbolic knowledge resources.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are highly capable of natural language reasoning and appear to store a great deal of lexical knowledge, but it is still unclear how much of this knowledge they actually use when reasoning, and whether they use it in the right way. On the other hand, logic-based Natural Language Inference (NLI) systems provide transparent and formally grounded reasoning, but they need to be supplied with rich lexical knowledge to prove inferences beyond purely logical ones. In this paper, we evaluate whether LLMs can identify all lexical knowledge needed to solve NLI problems and how much this knowledge contributes to proof search in a logic-based NLI system. Our research focuses exclusively on structured lexical entailments (e.g., chinchilla$\sqsubseteq$small animal) as a proxy for structured explanations for NLI problems with an entailment label. First, we curate a dataset for a new task of explaining sentential entailments with a set of lexical entailments. The dataset is used to intrinsically evaluate LLMs on generating structured lexical explanations. Then, we use NLI as an extrinsic evaluation in a simple neuro-symbolic setting, assessing whether LLMs can supply sufficient lexical relations to LangPro, a natural-logic theorem prover for natural language. The results show that the proposed task remains challenging even for hosted proprietary LLMs, and that their contribution to theorem proving is moderate: generated relations are often only partially sound and may be tailored to the specific NLI problem rather than representing generally valid lexical knowledge.

</details>


### [51] [Locally Sound, Globally Insufficient: The Local-Global Gap in Multi-Hop Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32496)
*Bohao Chu,Hendrik Damm,Qianli Wang,Hui Wang,Shuning Zhang,Christoph M. Friedrich,Norbert Fuhr*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies a “local-global gap” in multi-hop reasoning where every step is locally supported by evidence yet the overall reasoning fails to correctly answer the question, and proposes E-Closure, a training method that supervises three key dependencies to improve both answer accuracy and globally reliable reasoning traces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-hop QA models often produce reasoning traces that look correct step-by-step (each step is supported by evidence) but still fail to arrive at a correct or properly justified answer. Existing faithfulness verifiers mainly check local factual support against evidence and thus largely miss these globally insufficient but locally sound traces. This undermines the reliability of explanations and makes it hard to trust models’ reasoning, especially when used in high-stakes settings. The authors are motivated to formally characterize this failure regime, measure how prevalent it is, and design training-time methods to reduce it without sacrificing accuracy.

Method: 1) Define the local-global gap (LGG) as cases where each reasoning step is locally sound (supported by evidence and previous steps) but the overall trace is globally insufficient to answer the question.
2) Conduct a human-adjudicated diagnostic on 2,598 model responses from three multi-hop QA benchmarks and three models, annotating local soundness and global sufficiency to quantify the LGG and compare it with locally unsound errors.
3) Evaluate conventional faithfulness verifiers that check factual support against evidence, measuring how often they detect LGG vs locally unsound traces at high-precision thresholds.
4) Formalize three dependencies required for reliable reasoning: (a) evidence-to-step support (each step grounded in evidence), (b) question-to-trace alignment (the trace is relevant to and driven by the question), and (c) trace-to-answer closure (the trace explicitly supports the final answer).
5) Propose E-Closure, a training framework that supervises these dependencies. It uses generation supervision on both original and counterfactual responses, together with bidirectional switching constraints that encourage the model to maintain or change answers appropriately when parts of the reasoning or evidence are altered, thereby enforcing the three dependencies during training.
6) Compare E-Closure against standard fine-tuning baselines across three backbones and three benchmarks, measuring answer accuracy, local soundness, global sufficiency, and LGG rate.

Result: Empirically, the local-global gap is observed across all combinations of three multi-hop QA benchmarks and three models, accounting for nearly half of all globally insufficient responses. Faithfulness verifiers that check claims against evidence perform much worse on detecting LGG cases than locally unsound traces when tuned to keep at least 95% of reliable traces, indicating they systematically miss globally insufficient yet locally sound reasoning. Standard fine-tuning baselines increase answer accuracy and local soundness compared to base models but inadvertently worsen global sufficiency, increasing the LGG. In contrast, E-Closure improves both answer accuracy and reasoning reliability: averaged over three benchmarks and three backbone models, it achieves the best accuracy (92.8%), the highest trace reliability (89.0%), and the lowest LGG rate (6.2%) among all fine-tuned methods.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that reliable multi-hop reasoning cannot be guaranteed by enforcing only local factual correctness; models also need global alignment between question, reasoning trace, and final answer. The authors’ analysis shows that the local-global gap is widespread and largely undetected by standard faithfulness verifiers focused on local support. By explicitly supervising three key dependencies—evidence-to-step support, question-to-trace alignment, and trace-to-answer closure—during training, E-Closure significantly enhances both accuracy and global reasoning reliability while reducing LGG. This suggests future work on explainable and trustworthy reasoning models should move from purely local verification toward training and evaluation schemes that explicitly target global sufficiency of reasoning traces.

Abstract: Reliable multi-hop reasoning requires more than locally supported steps: a trace can be sound at every reasoning step yet still fail to answer the question as a whole. We call this failure regime the local-global gap (LGG), in which the trace is locally sound yet globally insufficient. Local soundness requires each step to be supported by the available evidence and preceding steps, whereas global sufficiency requires the reasoning trace to align with the question and establish the submitted answer. In a human-adjudicated diagnostic of 2,598 responses across three multi-hop QA benchmarks and three models, we find that the LGG occurs in every benchmark-model combination and accounts for nearly half of globally insufficient responses overall. However, conventional faithfulness verifiers that check claims against the evidence largely miss these failures: at thresholds retaining at least 95% of reliable traces, recall for LGG cases is substantially lower than that for locally unsound traces. To address these failures, we formalize three dependencies for reliable reasoning: evidence-to-step support, question-to-trace alignment, and trace-to-answer closure. Instead of post-hoc diagnosis, we introduce E-Closure to supervise these dependencies during training, combining generation supervision on supported original and counterfactual responses with bidirectional switching constraints. Averaged over three benchmarks and three backbones, existing fine-tuning baselines improve accuracy and local soundness over the base models, but at the cost of global sufficiency. E-Closure improves both: among all fine-tuned methods, it achieves the highest average accuracy (92.8%) and trace reliability (89.0%) while yielding the lowest LGG rate (6.2%).

</details>


### [52] [Learning an Anchored Prompt Space for Continual Adaptation of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32499)
*Rongguang Ye,Zhan Zhuang,Yichen Wu,Ming Tang,Kede Ma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces LAPS, a method to continually adapt large language models with soft prompts while preserving old capabilities and enabling knowledge transfer across tasks, outperforming prior baselines on the TRACE benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continual adaptation of large language models must balance learning new knowledge with retaining prior skills. Existing approaches that jointly adapt model parameters and task-specific soft prompts struggle because old prompts degrade as the base model changes, and cross-task prompt relationships are not explicitly modeled for transfer.

Method: LAPS first realigns historical task-specific soft prompts to the updated model via self-distillation so they remain effective after model changes. It then builds an "anchored prompt space" where vertices are these task-specific prompts and the interior is parameterized using learnable Bézier control prompts that shape the geometry. After learning this space, the method searches within it to select for each task a best-performing prompt on its validation set, effectively composing knowledge from multiple tasks.

Result: On the TRACE continual learning benchmark and across three Qwen3 model sizes, LAPS achieves higher average performance and lower forgetting compared to strong baselines, including pure distillation methods, pure prompt-based methods, and those that jointly adapt both prompts and model parameters.

Conclusion: By maintaining the usefulness of historical prompts and explicitly modeling their relationships in an anchored prompt space, LAPS enables more effective continual adaptation of LLMs, yielding better overall performance and reduced forgetting than existing adaptation techniques.

Abstract: Continually adapting large language models requires acquiring new knowledge while preserving previously learned capabilities. Jointly adapting model parameters and task-specific soft prompts offers a promising solution, but faces two key limitations: historical prompts may become less effective as the model evolves, while their transferable cross-task relationships are not explicitly learned. We propose Learning an Anchored Prompt Space (LAPS), which preserves historical prompt effectiveness and learns relationships among task-specific soft prompts to facilitate positive transfer. LAPS first aligns historical prompts with the updated model through self-distillation. LAPS then constructs an anchored prompt space whose vertices correspond to learned task-specific soft prompts and whose intermediate geometry is shaped by learnable Bézier control prompts. Once this anchored prompt space is learned, LAPS identifies the best-performing prompt for each task on its validation set, allowing the optimized prompt to draw on knowledge acquired from observed tasks. Experiments on the TRACE benchmark across three Qwen3 model scales show that LAPS consistently outperforms distillation-based, prompt-based, and joint prompt--parameter adaptation baselines, improving average performance while reducing forgetting.

</details>


### [53] [When Users Change Their Minds: Measuring and Repairing Intent Drift in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32520)
*Yanjie Zhang,Bowen Cao,Zixin Chen,Yushi Sun*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies and measures a multi-turn LLM failure mode called intent drift, where outdated user instructions still affect final outputs, and proposes explicit state tracking as a partial solution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In real-world use, LLMs act as agents over multi-turn dialogues where users revise, override, or withdraw earlier instructions. Existing benchmarks mostly use single-turn prompts, so they miss failures that arise when the model must track which parts of the evolving intent are still active. This creates safety, correctness, and reliability issues: outdated or superseded instructions can corrupt tool use, code execution, or final answers. The authors are motivated to formalize this problem (intent drift), quantify its impact, and test whether explicit mechanisms for tracking the current intent can mitigate it.

Method: 1) Define intent drift as the influence of superseded or withdrawn instructions on final model behavior. 2) Build IntentFlux, an executable benchmark that transforms verifiable tasks into multi-turn dialogues with controlled intent changes while preserving original automatic graders; this allows comparing performance between single-turn and evolving-dialogue settings. 3) Run a 627-case calibration and broader experiments across eight LLMs, varying the amount of superseded/withdrawn information and measuring task scores and correctness rates. 4) Propose StateForge, a method that explicitly maintains a representation of the active requirements (the current user intent) before generation, and test it on the General-Test benchmark. 5) Evaluate how much of the performance gap is due to state estimation by also testing with ground-truth final states.

Result: 1) As dialogues include more superseded or withdrawn information, mean task scores drop from 0.476 to 0.384 in the 627-case calibration, showing that intent drift measurably harms performance. 2) Across eight models, the fraction of fully correct solutions is significantly lower when the same final task is given via an evolving multi-turn dialogue than as a direct single-turn prompt. 3) The StateForge approach, which explicitly tracks active requirements, improves mean task score on General-Test from 0.367 to 0.467, confirming that explicit state maintenance mitigates some of the degradation. 4) Even when the ground-truth final state is provided, performance still falls short of the single-turn baseline, indicating that errors in estimating the final state are only part of the problem; multi-turn reasoning itself introduces additional difficulties.

Conclusion: Intent drift is an important, quantifiable failure mode for LLM agents in multi-turn settings, where outdated or withdrawn instructions continue to affect outcomes. The IntentFlux benchmark provides a systematic way to measure this phenomenon by generating executable, graded dialogues with controlled intent changes. Explicit maintenance of the current task state, as in StateForge, can significantly reduce but not eliminate the performance gap between multi-turn and single-turn settings. Therefore, robust multi-turn agent design will need both better state-tracking mechanisms and additional methods to handle the inherent complexity of evolving user intent.

Abstract: LLM agents often operate over multi-turn interactions in which user intent changes before execution. We study intent drift: the failure mode in which superseded parts of the user's intent continue to influence the final answer or tool action. We introduce IntentFlux, an executable benchmark that converts verifiable tasks into dialogues with controlled intent changes while preserving their original graders. In a 627-case calibration, mean task score falls from 0.476 to 0.384 as dialogues contain more superseded and withdrawn information. Across eight models, the rate of fully correct solutions is significantly lower when the same final task must be recovered from an evolving dialogue rather than given directly in a single turn. We further introduce StateForge, which explicitly maintains the active requirements before generation. On General-Test, it improves mean task score from 0.367 to 0.467. Providing the ground-truth final state improves performance further but still does not recover single-turn performance, indicating that state-estimation errors explain only part of the gap. These results establish intent drift as a measurable multi-turn failure mode and explicit state maintenance as a partial mitigation.

</details>


### [54] [Language as an Independent Information Layer: A Conceptual Model of Communication, Cognition and Decision-Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32556)
*Anastasiia Alifanova,Elena Benderskaya*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes a new way to design corporate knowledge bases by combining probabilistic word-vector spaces with ontological models to better capture business-specific knowledge and logic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional corporate knowledge bases either rely mainly on statistical methods (like vector spaces of words) or on semantic/ontological models, each with limitations: statistics lack explicit business logic, while ontologies are hard to build and maintain and often ignore language dynamics. The authors seek to unify these approaches so that corporate vocabularies, industry specifics, and business processes are accurately reflected, improving knowledge extraction and process analysis.

Method: Conceptual framework: represent the corporate vocabulary as a probabilistic vector space that encodes industry terms, subject focus, and corporate culture; integrate this with traditional ontological modeling of entities and causal relations. Treat language as a dynamic layer in the information architecture, where changes in word distributions correspond to dynamic transformations of a multidimensional solution space controlled by problem-specific input parameters. Analyze projections of the probabilistic space and mapped causal relations to locate bottlenecks in business logic.

Result: A proposed integrated concept (architectural model) for corporate knowledge bases that combines statistical language models and ontologies, and an argument that the resulting system can support efficient knowledge extraction from documents while respecting business processes and enabling identification of logic bottlenecks. The text is conceptual; no concrete experimental results are described in the abstract.

Conclusion: By integrating probabilistic vector representations of corporate language with ontological and causal models, corporate knowledge bases can more effectively capture both statistical regularities and semantic business logic. Viewing language as a dynamic, independent layer and modeling word distributions as a controllable solution space enables better problem-oriented knowledge retrieval and process analysis, including detecting bottlenecks in business logic.

Abstract: Based on an analysis of the role of language in thought and communication, this article proposes a new concept for designing corporate knowledge bases. The concept integrates the probabilistic vector space of a corporate vocabulary, reflect-ing industry specifics, subject focus, terminology, and culture, with traditional ontological modeling. This combination enables the efficient extraction of knowledge from accumulated corporate documents while strictly accounting for specific business processes. Consequently, this concept bridges statistical and semantic (cause-and-effect) methodologies. Furthermore, analyzing the projec-tions of probabilistic spaces and causal relationships can help identify bottlenecks in business logic. As a dynamic system, language functions as a separate, inde-pendent layer within the overall information architecture. Introducing a dynamic component into the probabilistic space of word distribution allows it to be mod-eled as a multidimensional solution space for various problem formulations. In this context, input data defining the problem conditions serve as control parame-ters for dynamic transformations.

</details>


### [55] [How to Reduce Whisper Hallucination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32560)
*Husein Zolkepli*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build a benchmark and fine-tuning strategy to reduce Whisper’s hallucinated transcriptions on non-speech audio while preserving (and even improving) real-speech recognition quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Whisper, a widely used multilingual ASR model, often hallucinates text on non-speech segments (e.g., silence or room tone). Existing fixes either distill from Whisper itself (thus inheriting its failure modes) or add non-speech audio to teach the model to stay quiet, which suppresses outputs indiscriminately and harms recovery of genuinely spoken phrases and repeated speech. There is a need for a method and benchmark that explicitly address hallucinations while jointly evaluating silence-handling and true-speech recognition across many languages.

Method: They construct a benchmark and training corpus explicitly targeting hallucinations. The benchmark covers 11,852 clips in eight categories (“arms”), including 6,267 synthetic positive examples, 8,296 real audio clips that cause production Whisper to fail, plus FLEURS data in 58 languages. They mine 40,891 hallucinated phrases across 100 languages, then select a text-to-speech system via empirical evaluation and synthesize these phrases as positive speech examples. During fine-tuning, the same phrases appear both as non-speech hallucinations to be suppressed and as genuine spoken phrases to be correctly transcribed. They run 33 matched pairs of fine-tunes, where the only difference is whether these positive synthetic examples are included, and compare performance on hallucination suppression and phrase recovery, including English accuracy checks.

Result: Adding the synthetic positive hallucination-phrases to training reduces hallucinations on silence and non-speech audio while improving recognition of real speech. Across 33 matched fine-tuning pairs, including the positives lowers word emission on real voice-free audio in 31/33 pairs and increases phrase recovery in 32/33; for the 30 pairs that maintain English accuracy, the improvement is 30/30. The best checkpoint cuts hallucination on pure room tone from 61.9% to 2.4%, lowers word emission on real voice-free audio from 99.9% to 47.8%, and increases phrase recovery from 69.8% to 82.7%.

Conclusion: Targeted training that exposes the model to hallucinated phrases both as content to suppress (on non-speech audio) and as content to transcribe (via TTS-generated positives) can substantially reduce Whisper’s hallucinations without sacrificing, and often improving, real-speech recognition. The released benchmark, lexicon, and synthetic corpus provide a reproducible framework for measuring and mitigating hallucinations in Whisper and similar ASR systems across many languages.

Abstract: Whisper is still what runs in production: one permissively licensed checkpoint, 99 languages, no per-language tuning. But it writes sentences nobody said. On 42 clips of pure room tone, whisper-large-v3 emits words on 61.9% of them and emits something on 100%. The usual response is to distil a student from Whisper pseudo-labels, filtering the hallucinations out of the corpus first, which deletes the evidence while leaving the behaviour in place: the student is fitted to the subset where the teacher was right, and inherits a failure mode absent from its own training data. The second response, adding non-speech audio so the model learns to stay quiet, already ships and works, but teaches suppression without discrimination. The checkpoint best on every non-speech arm here is also the one that recovers the fewest genuinely spoken phrases and deletes 58% of repeated speech. The teacher has to be fixed, with both halves of the signal. Our benchmark scores both at once: 11,852 clips over eight arms, 6,267 synthetic positives, 8,296 clips of real audio that made a production model fail, and FLEURS in 58 languages. We collect 40,891 hallucination phrases in 100 languages, choose a text-to-speech system by measurement, and synthesise those phrases as positives, so the model meets the same text both as something to suppress and as something to transcribe. Across 33 matched pairs of fine-tunes differing only by those positives, adding them lowers word emission on real voice-free audio in 31 pairs and raises phrase recovery in 32; among the 30 pairs that hold English accuracy it is 30 out of 30. The best checkpoint takes hallucination on silence from 61.9% to 2.4% and words over real voice-free audio from 99.9% to 47.8%, while raising phrase recovery from 69.8% to 82.7%. The benchmark, lexicon and synthetic corpus are released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Scicom-intl/Whisper-Hallucination

</details>


### [56] [Groupwise Agentic Grading and Advantage Redistribution for Code Agent RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32577)
*Jinhao Dong,Liang Zhao,Zihao Yue,Wenhan Ma,Linghao Zhang,Lei Li,Shicheng Li,Yifan Song,Bowen Ye,Fuli Luo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes GAGAR, a framework that redistributes RL credit among code-generation trajectories using agentic grading so that higher-quality, test-passing code is rewarded more than lower-quality but still passing solutions, improving code agent performance and training stability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL methods for code agents, like GRPO with test-based binary rewards, treat all test-passing trajectories within a group as equally good. This ignores implementation quality and task adherence, so the policy cannot learn to prefer clean, minimal, in-scope solutions over messy or over-changing ones. This leads to suboptimal behavior, trajectory bloat, and weak learning signals beyond just passing tests. A method is needed to inject quality awareness into the RL credit assignment while still using executable tests as the main objective signal.

Method: GAGAR augments group-based RL for code agents by adding a quality-aware credit redistribution step. First, it uses dynamic sampling to keep rollout groups that contain both passing and failing trajectories. Then it places all trajectories from a group into a shared workspace and uses an SFT-trained agentic grader model to jointly inspect and rank the test-passing trajectories by implementation quality and task adherence. Based on this ranking, lower-ranked passing trajectories are downweighted. To preserve the overall signal strength, the advantages of all passing trajectories are then rescaled so that their total sum matches the original GRPO advantages. This sum-preserving redistribution keeps the global reward mass from tests but shifts more credit toward higher-quality solutions while retaining relative differences induced by quality-based downweighting.

Result: On large MiMo-V2.6 models (Flash 310B and Pro 1.02T) and industrial-scale setups, GAGAR improves code agent RL outcomes. In controlled code-only experiments with Flash, it increases task performance, limits unnecessary growth in trajectory length, and makes training more stable compared to baseline GRPO-style training.
