In broader mixed-task RL settings with both Flash and Pro, incorporating GAGAR continues to provide benefits, showing that combining test-based verification with graded, groupwise quality assessment is effective at scale.

Conclusion: GAGAR demonstrates that incorporating agentic grading into group-based RL for code agents can correct a key deficiency of purely test-based binary rewards: the inability to distinguish among different quality levels of test-passing code. By redistributing the fixed total advantage within each group toward cleaner, more targeted implementations, the framework improves both solution quality and training stability. The study suggests that future RL for code agents should leverage both executable tests and learned graders operating over groups of trajectories to provide richer, quality-sensitive learning signals.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for code agents often uses executable tests to provide binary rewards. With these rewards, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) assigns identical advantages to test-passing trajectories within each rollout group, overlooking differences in implementation quality and adherence to task requirements. This leaves the policy without a learning signal that favors clean, targeted implementations over those containing unnecessary or out-of-scope changes. We introduce GAGAR, a framework for quality-aware credit redistribution in code agent RL. Built on dynamic sampling that retains groups containing both passing and failing trajectories, GAGAR places all trajectories from each group in a shared workspace, where an SFT-trained agentic grader jointly inspects them and ranks the test-passing candidates. Based on this ranking, we downweight lower-ranked trajectories and proportionally rescale the advantages of all test-passing trajectories to restore their original sum. This sum-preserving redistribution retains the relative weights established by quality-based downweighting while shifting credit toward higher-quality implementations. We evaluate GAGAR at industrial scale using pre-RL SFT checkpoints of MiMo-V2.6-Flash (310B total parameters) and MiMo-V2.6-Pro (1.02T total parameters). Controlled code-only Flash experiments show improved code agent performance, reduced trajectory-length growth, and more stable training. We further apply GAGAR in large-scale mixed-task RL with both Flash and Pro. Our results support combining test-based verification with groupwise agentic grading to improve the quality and stability of code agent RL.

</details>


### [57] [HERO-MoE: Historical Expert Routing with Scale-Preserving Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32581)
*Junxiang Qiu,Zhengsu Chen,Xinting Hu,Shuo Wang,Hengheng Zhang,Shaofeng Zhang,Changcheng Li,Boyu Shi,Qi Tian*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HERO-MoE is a new Mixture-of-Experts routing framework that reuses historical routing distributions from previous layers, fuses them in a scale-preserving way with current routing scores, and thereby improves loss with negligible compute and memory overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Mixture-of-Experts models use routers that decide expert assignment per layer based only on current activations, ignoring the rich routing distributions produced by previous MoE layers. Empirical observations suggest that routing patterns encode semantic and depth-wise information, but current designs do not explicitly leverage this history, potentially limiting training efficiency and model quality. The authors are motivated to exploit these historical routing signals without adding complex losses or significant compute overhead.

Method: They propose HERO-MoE (Historical Expert ROuting with Scale-Preserving Fusion), which augments each router with a residual contribution derived from detached, dense routing distributions from earlier MoE layers. For each token, the router still computes a standard token-conditioned routing branch, but adds a historical routing term before the softmax and top-k selection. A scale-preserving fusion mechanism normalizes the historical signal so its magnitude matches the current hidden representation and automatically adjusts for the number of contributing historical layers. This is done without extra routing losses or fusion-specific hyperparameters, and remains compatible with standard sparse dispatch schemes (top-k, group-limited).

Result: In experiments on an ~8B-parameter MoE model (0.5B active parameters) trained from scratch on 100B tokens, HERO-MoE reduces final training loss from 1.6393 to 1.6184 compared to a baseline router. The changes incur only minor overhead: peak memory increases by 0.44% and FLOPs by 0.64%. The method integrates into existing MoE backbones with minimal architectural modification while preserving standard routing operations.

Conclusion: Incorporating historical routing information via a scale-preserving residual fusion improves the efficiency and quality of MoE training with almost no additional compute or memory cost. HERO-MoE demonstrates that routing distributions from preceding layers are useful priors that can be reused to guide later routing, and this can be achieved in a modular, hyperparameter-free way that is compatible with existing sparse MoE infrastructures.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have become a standard way to scale model capacity while keeping computation sparse, yet routing remains a key determinant of MoE quality and training behavior. Prior empirical studies suggest that MoE routing reflects input semantics and upstream computation across depth, but standard routers do not explicitly use the routing distributions produced by preceding layers. We propose HERO-MoE, Historical Expert ROuting with Scale-Preserving Fusion, a routing framework that injects historical routing priors into MoE routers by reusing detached, dense routing distributions collected from preceding MoE layers. The key idea is simple: HERO-MoE preserves the original token-conditioned routing branch and adds a residual historical routing contribution before the standard softmax and top-$k$ dispatch. To stabilize this historical signal, HERO-MoE introduces a scale-preserving fusion mechanism that matches the magnitude of historical routing memory to the current hidden representation and accounts for the number of visible historical layers, without introducing an auxiliary routing loss or a fusion-specific tuning parameter. By reusing routing distributions already computed by preceding MoE layers, HERO-MoE improves training-loss reduction with modest end-to-end overhead. The resulting router remains compatible with standard sparse dispatch, including top-$k$ and group-limited routing, and can be inserted into existing MoE backbones with minimal architectural changes. Experiments on an approximately 8B-parameter MoE model with 0.5B active parameters, trained from scratch on 100B tokens, show that HERO-MoE reduces the final loss from 1.6393 to 1.6184, while peak memory and FLOPs increase by only 0.44\% and 0.64\%, respectively.

</details>


### [58] [KV-Lingo: Learning KV-Cache Translators with Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32610)
*Valérie Castin,Keitaro Sakamoto,Anastasiia Filippova,João Monteiro,Marco Cuturi,Pierre Ablin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: KV-Lingo learns to translate the key-value (KV) cache of one language model so another model can reuse it without reprocessing the context, greatly speeding up model switching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KV caches are specific to each model architecture and weight configuration. When dynamically routing or switching between models over a shared context, the new model must fully re-run the prefix to build its own cache, which is expensive for long contexts and undermines the practicality of model switching. The paper aims to avoid costly re-prefill while preserving model performance.

Method: They introduce KV-Lingo, a set of linear transformation layers (typically one per layer of the target model) that map the source model’s key and value representations into a form usable by the target model. These linear maps are applied independently to all tokens’ K and V vectors in the cache. The maps are trained via distillation: minimizing the divergence between the target model’s predictions when using its native cache versus when using the translated cache. They train separate translators for several model pairs of different sizes and architectures on a generic text corpus.

Result: KV-Lingo translators maintain strong downstream performance when transferring caches between models, both from smaller to larger models and vice versa. In practical benchmarks, performing a model switch via cache translation plus a single decoding step is significantly faster than re-prefilling: up to 9.6× speedup on a 64-token prompt for Qwen models on an Apple M3 Ultra and up to 29× speedup at 32k context length on an H100 GPU. The method also supports repeated, multi-turn switching while staying close to the performance of full re-prefill.

Conclusion: A simple, learned linear translation layer between KV caches enables efficient reuse of contextual computation across different language models, making dynamic model routing and seamless model switching far more practical. Replacing re-prefill with KV-Lingo substantially reduces time-to-first-token after a switch while preserving model quality, especially on long contexts and repeated interactions.

Abstract: Large language models represent context with a key-value (KV) cache. Caches are model-specific: for the same text, models with different architectures or weights produce incompatible representations. This makes it costly to switch models over a shared context: although the context has already been processed by one model, the incoming model must process it again to build its own cache. We introduce KV-Lingo, a method for translating the KV cache of a source model into one that can be read by a target model. KV-Lingo consists of a collection of linear maps, typically one per layer of the target model, that are applied independently on all tokens' key and value representations. We train these maps using distillation, minimising the divergence between the target model's predictions from its native cache and those from the translated cache. We consider several model pairs spanning multiple sizes and architectures, training one translator per pair on a generic text corpus. The resulting translators preserve strong downstream performance in both small-to-large and large-to-small transfers. Since a switch then costs a linear map and a single decoding step instead of a prefill, replacing re-prefill with cache translation reduces the time to first token after a model switch by 9.6x already on a 64-token prompt for Qwen models on an Apple M3 Ultra, and by up to 29x at 32k context length on an H100. These gains make KV-Lingo particularly useful for dynamic model routing: a context can be processed by one model and handed off to another only when needed, without re-prefilling the shared prefix. We finally show that KV-Lingo can be used for seamless model switching, staying close to re-prefill across repeated switches in our multi-turn evaluations.

</details>


### [59] [The Alignment Paradox: How Post-Training Amplifies Confident Hallucinations in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32617)
*Qingjia Huang,Yakai Li,Jianguo Wu,Qihang Zhou,Aimin Yu,Xiaoqi Jia,Luping Ma,Weijuan Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies that alignment training (like instruction-tuning) is a main cause of overconfident hallucinations in LLMs and proposes a margin-bounded DPO objective that significantly reduces high-confidence errors without hurting general performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs often give incorrect answers with unjustified high confidence, making it hard to detect errors using uncertainty. Prior explanations focus on missing knowledge, reasoning mistakes, or decoding stochasticity, but the authors suspect that the post-training alignment process itself may be driving these confident hallucinations and want to systematically test and address this.

Method: They compare base vs instruction-tuned variants across five model families on long-tail factual benchmarks, measuring the frequency of high-confidence errors. They use layer-wise logit lens probing to examine where in the network overconfidence emerges. Based on these diagnostics, they design a modified direct preference optimization (DPO) objective that imposes an entropy-dependent bound on logit margins during post-training, and run multi-epoch training experiments with Mistral-7B to evaluate its impact on confidence calibration and task performance.

Result: They find that unaligned base models rarely make high-confidence factual errors, while instruction-tuned models increase such errors by 10x–35x. Logit lens analysis shows that overconfidence arises in the late layers, where the margin of the wrong answer logit over others grows beyond 4.0 despite being near zero in earlier layers. Their bounded-margin DPO variant reduces high-confidence hallucinations by up to 35.3% compared with standard DPO, while preserving performance on general reasoning benchmarks.

Conclusion: Post-training alignment is a primary driver of overconfident hallucinations in LLMs (the "Alignment Paradox"), and controlling margin growth during preference-based post-training can substantially mitigate high-confidence errors without sacrificing broad reasoning performance. This suggests that future alignment methods should explicitly regulate confidence calibration, not just optimize for preference satisfaction.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can produce factually incorrect answers with high confidence, undermining their reliability and limiting the effectiveness of uncertainty-based error detection. While prior research attributes confident hallucinations to factors such as missing knowledge in training data, reasoning errors, or stochastic decoding, we uncover that post-training alignment itself is a primary driver of these errors, a phenomenon we call the \textbf{Alignment Paradox}. Across five model families evaluated on factual benchmarks, unaligned base models produce few high-confidence errors on long-tail factual queries, whereas instruction-tuned models multiply high-confidence errors ($p \ge 0.95$) by more than an order of magnitude (10$\times$ to 35$\times$). Layer-wise probing with the Logit Lens reveals that this overconfidence emerges in late layers, where wrong-answer margins expand past 4.0 points after remaining near zero across early and intermediate layers. These findings motivate limiting margin growth during post-training. We implement this principle through an entropy-dependent margin bound in direct preference optimization (DPO). In multi-epoch experiments with Mistral-7B, the bounded objective reduces high-confidence errors by up to 35.3\% relative to standard DPO while maintaining performance on evaluated general reasoning benchmarks. These results show that bounded margins mitigate confident hallucinations during post-training.

</details>


### [60] [Does CoT-Pass@k Really Check the CoT? A Multilingual Mathematical Audit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32622)
*Tarık Tuna Taşaltı,Burcu Hüdaverdi,David Semedo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper audits CoT-Pass@k, a reasoning-aware variant of Pass@k, and finds that its LLM judges largely fail to detect corrupted reasoning chains, instead keying mostly on chain-answer agreement, which undermines the metric's claims about measuring reasoning quality, especially in multilingual settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pass@k is widely used to evaluate code and math models but only checks if any of k samples is correct, not whether the model used valid reasoning. CoT-Pass@k adds an LLM-as-judge that verifies reasoning chains, implicitly assuming the judge can reliably detect flawed reasoning. This assumption had not been systematically tested, particularly in non-English languages, despite claims about reasoning ability and multilingual model use. The authors want to test whether CoT-Pass@k’s verification step actually measures reasoning quality or just agreement between chain and final answer, and how robust it is across languages and benchmarks.

Method: The authors run the first systematic audit of CoT-Pass@k’s verification step using its own evaluation protocol. They construct a multilingual benchmark suite of five mathematical datasets in English, Turkish, and Portuguese, including two datasets originally written in those languages. They take correct model solutions and apply controlled, deterministic corruptions: some that break the reasoning chain while keeping the final answer correct, and others that corrupt both reasoning and answer. These perturbed and clean solutions are then evaluated by three different LLM judges, including the CoT-Pass@k default judge, V4-Flash, and Qwen3.6, to see how often corrupted vs. clean chains are accepted or rejected. They analyze how judges’ decisions relate to reasoning quality, chain-answer agreement, and token/generation budgets.

Result: All three LLM judges accept corrupted reasoning chains at nearly the same rate as clean ones, indicating that they do not reliably detect the injected reasoning errors. V4-Flash and Qwen3.6 mostly penalize solutions only when the final numeric answer is wrong and are significantly more willing to accept incorrect answers when the explanation is internally consistent with that wrong answer. The CoT-Pass@k default judge also accepts most wrong answers. Overall, chain-answer agreement strongly dominates the two larger judges’ decisions rather than any real evaluation of reasoning correctness. As a consequence, the empirical difference between Pass@k and CoT-Pass@k has shrunk: it averages 19.7 points on an earlier solver generation but just 4.1 on a newer one, and can drop to effectively zero when token budgets and generation settings are increased—even though Pass@64 can increase by more than fifty points.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that CoT-Pass@k, in its current form and implementation, does not provide reliable evidence about a model’s reasoning quality because its LLM judges largely fail to catch systematic reasoning errors and mostly track chain-answer agreement. The small and unstable differences between Pass@k and CoT-Pass@k, especially under higher token budgets and newer solvers, show that the metric’s added complexity does not translate into dependable reasoning assessment. The authors argue that any metric using LLMs to judge reasoning should at minimum demonstrate that (1) its judges can robustly distinguish correct from corrupted reasoning chains, and (2) its scores are stable and interpretable under variations in language, benchmarks, and generation budgets before being used to make claims about reasoning ability.

Abstract: Pass@k measures whether a model reaches a correct answer under repeated sampling, but never how: a lucky guess counts the same as sound reasoning. CoT-Pass@k was proposed to close that gap, adding an LLM-as-judge that must assess a solution's reasoning chain before it counts. Its value rests entirely on one assumption: that the judge catches flawed reasoning. That assumption has never been tested inside the metric that depends on it, and never outside English, though the metric's claims concern models used in many languages. We report the first audit of that verification step, run under the metric's own protocol on a multilingual suite of five mathematical benchmarks in English, Turkish and Portuguese, two of them natively written. We corrupt correct solutions with deterministic edits that damage the chain and the final answer separately. We observe that all three judges accept corrupted chains almost as often as clean ones. V4-Flash and Qwen3.6 reject a solution sharply only when its final answer is wrong and accept a wrong answer more readily when the chain agrees with it; the metric's own judge accepts most wrong answers as well. Our study shows that chain-answer agreement dominates the two larger judges' verdicts and that all three fail to reliably detect the tested reasoning errors. Consequently the difference Pass@k - CoT-Pass@k averages 19.7 points on an earlier solver generation but only 4.1 on the current one. What little remains depends on the token budgets on both sides and on the generation mode; raising the generation budget moves Pass@64 by more than fifty points while the difference stays at zero. We close with two checks any judged reasoning metric should pass before its numbers are read as evidence about reasoning.

</details>


### [61] [MixDetect: Word-Level Localization and Quantification of AI Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32625)
*Hongrui Bao,Yubing Ren,Zhendong Pan,Fang Fang,Shi Wang,Yanan Cao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes MixDetect, a word-level method to localize and measure AI edits in text, going beyond simple AI-vs-human or scalar edit scores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI-text detectors mostly perform coarse, text-level classification (human vs AI or an overall editing score) and cannot precisely locate which parts of a text were edited by AI or how strong each edit is. As AI is increasingly used for editing rather than full generation, a more fine-grained analysis of AI involvement in text production is needed for transparency, forensics, and understanding human–AI collaboration.

Method: Introduce MixDetect, a framework that operates at the word level. For each word, it first predicts whether that word has been edited by AI and then, conditional on an edit, predicts how substantial the edit is. Training uses aligned pairs of original and edited texts to create word-level supervision signals; at inference time, only the final text is needed. Word-level predictions can be aggregated to get text-level labels or scores.

Result: MixDetect can accurately identify which words are AI-edited and can distinguish levels of editing intensity. It uncovers distinct patterns of editing scope (how many words) and intensity (how strong) across different editing degrees and operations. Quantitatively, aggregate predictions perform strongly on binary and ternary AI-text classification and are robust to domain and generator shifts. Qualitatively, it shows that AI editing magnitude grows when texts receive more AI edits, shrinks when humans edit AI-generated text, and stays nearly constant for typical human-to-human editing.

Conclusion: AI involvement in text production can be characterized more richly than a single authorship label or an overall edit score. By localizing edits at the word level and quantifying their intensity, MixDetect provides a detailed view of AI editing behavior, useful for detecting AI-assisted writing and understanding mixed human–AI authorship in diverse settings.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to edit human-written text rather than generate entire texts from scratch. Conventional AI-text detectors mainly distinguish human-written from fully AI-generated text, while recent methods for AI-edited text typically provide only a text-level label or editing-degree score. We introduce MixDetect, a word-level framework for localizing and quantifying AI editing. MixDetect separately predicts whether each word has been edited and, conditional on editing, how substantial the edit is, allowing editing scope and editing intensity to be estimated separately. During training, source--edited pairs are aligned to construct word-level supervision, while inference requires only the input text. Experiments show that MixDetect accurately localizes AI-edited words, reflects differences in editing intensity, and reveals different scope--intensity patterns across editing degrees and operations. The overall AI editing magnitude increases under additional AI editing, decreases when AI-generated text is edited by humans, and remains nearly unchanged under ordinary human-to-human editing. The aggregated text-level predictions also perform well on binary and ternary AI-text classification and remain effective under domain and generator shifts. These results show that AI editing can be analyzed beyond a single authorship label or editing-degree score by identifying both where AI editing occurs and how substantial the edits are.

</details>


### [62] [ExpVoyager: Direct Experience Navigation for Dynamic Agent Skill Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32630)
*Kwangwook Seo,Dongha Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces ExpVoyager, a framework that treats LLM agent skill synthesis as dynamic navigation over past experience, enabling on-demand, fine-grained reuse of procedural knowledge and leading to better downstream performance and continual improvement as experience grows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agent skill synthesis methods convert past experience into fixed procedural skills before knowing future task needs, which can lose potentially important knowledge and preserve unnecessary, instance-specific details. There is a need for a more flexible approach that can adaptively reuse experience based on the requirements of the current task.

Method: The authors propose ExpVoyager, where a "skill curator" dynamically navigates the raw experience space—across multiple perspectives and granularities—to identify reusable procedural knowledge relevant to the current task. The curator continually decides where to look next based on remaining knowledge gaps, progressively constructing skills that are tailored to the task on demand instead of pre-fixing them offline.

Result: Experiments show that ExpVoyager improves downstream task performance compared with baselines, gains more as the amount of available experience increases, and can work alongside existing skill systems while maintaining efficient access to experience.

Conclusion: Recasting skill synthesis as an on-demand navigation over past experience allows LLM agents to build more relevant and reusable procedural knowledge. ExpVoyager offers an effective and scalable way to continuously exploit growing experience, enhancing agent performance while remaining compatible with existing skill infrastructures.

Abstract: Learning from experience in LLM agents has become a key paradigm for developing self-evolving agents that continuously learn and expand their capabilities. Within this paradigm, synthesizing the agent skill has emerged as a promising solution for transforming accumulated experience into reusable procedural knowledge, serving as an important layer for the harness system that supplies agents at runtime. Despite its potential, existing approaches largely abstract past experience into fixed procedural knowledge before downstream demands are known, which risks discarding knowledge that later becomes critical while retaining instance-specific details irrelevant to future tasks. In this paper, we reframe agent skill synthesis as a dynamic navigation problem over past experience, where agents actively explore accumulated trajectories on demand for the current task with targeted and fine-grained access to experience knowledge. To this end, we propose ExpVoyager, a novel framework in which a skill curator navigates raw experience across different views and resolutions, continually identifying reusable procedural knowledge from what it observes while tracking remaining knowledge needs that guide where to navigate next. Extensive experiments demonstrate both the effectiveness and versatility of ExpVoyager, showing consistent improvements in downstream task performance, continual gains as the experience space scales, and practical compatibility with existing skills under efficient experience access.

</details>


### [63] [From Knowing to Abstaining: Bridging the Representation-Action Gap in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32653)
*Jialuo He,Huangxun Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces VAD-R, a benchmark and Rep2Act, a method to convert latent answerability signals in vision-language models into explicit abstention, greatly improving safe and accurate non-answering on unanswerable visual questions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for abstention in vision-language models are flawed: they leak answerability via shortcuts in images/questions and explicit "unanswerable" options, and they provide only coarse binary labels without explanatory supervision. Meanwhile, current VLMs show poor spontaneous abstention despite having internal representations that encode answerability, creating a gap between what the model implicitly knows and how it responds. The authors want a rigorous way to diagnose visual answerability and a mechanism to align internal answerability awareness with explicit abstention behavior.

Method: 1) Benchmark: They build VAD-R via a two-stage pipeline: (a) shortcut filtering and quality verification to remove samples where answerability can be inferred from superficial cues, and (b) detailed annotation of each example with step-by-step rationales and causal evidence-gap labels to explain why a question is (un)answerable. 2) Analysis: They evaluate multiple open- and closed-source VLMs on VAD-R, measure spontaneous abstention, and perform probing on hidden states to see if internal representations separate answerable vs. unanswerable cases. 3) Rep2Act: Based on the probing results, they design a representation-to-action alignment method that maps latent answerability signals in specific layers to explicit abstain-or-answer decisions, improving the model’s action policy without retraining from scratch.

Result: On VAD-R, state-of-the-art VLMs show low spontaneous abstention (recall 11.4% open-source, 16.3% closed-source), even though intermediate representations encode answerability well. Applying Rep2Act dramatically boosts action accuracy: from 56.67% to 86.33% for Qwen2.5-VL-3B and from 59.33% to 88.67% for Qwen2.5-VL-7B. On the out-of-distribution TUBench benchmark, a 3B model with Rep2Act obtains an average F1 of 53.3%, outperforming closed-source GPT-4 Turbo and GPT-4o by 16.2% and 1.1%, respectively.

Conclusion: The paper shows that modern VLMs internally distinguish answerable from unanswerable visual questions but fail to translate this into explicit abstention behavior. VAD-R enables fine-grained diagnosis of answerability without shortcut leakage, and Rep2Act effectively aligns latent answerability representations with output decisions, substantially improving safe abstention and generalizing well to out-of-distribution benchmarks.

Abstract: The ability of vision-language models (VLMs) to abstain from unanswerable questions is as important as their ability to answer answerable ones accurately. Recently, several benchmarks have emerged to evaluate and improve VLM abstention, but they have substantial limitations. First, samples often contain shortcut cues in images or questions that reveal answerability, while an explicit "unanswerable" option further prevents accurate assessment of spontaneous abstention. Second, as training data, they generally provide only binary labels without fine-grained explanations for deeper supervision. To address these limitations, we introduce Visual Answerability Diagnosis with Rationales (VAD-R), a benchmark constructed through a two-stage pipeline of shortcut filtering and quality verification to prevent answerability leakage. Each example is annotated with step-by-step rationales and causal evidence-gap labels. Evaluation of state-of-the-art open- and closed-source VLMs on VAD-R reveals limited spontaneous abstention, with average recall rates of only 11.4% and 16.3%, respectively. Probing analyses show that hidden-state representations in certain layers can effectively distinguish answerability, yet this distinction fails to manifest in final responses. Motivated by this observation, we introduce Rep2Act, a representation-to-action alignment method that translates latent answerability awareness into explicit abstention decisions. Rep2Act improves action accuracy on VAD-R from 56.67% to 86.33% for Qwen2.5-VL-3B and from 59.33% to 88.67% for Qwen2.5-VL-7B. On the out-of-distribution TUBench, Rep2Act achieves an average F1 score of 53.3% with only a 3B model, surpassing the closed-source GPT-4 Turbo and GPT-4o by 16.2% and 1.1%, respectively.

</details>


### [64] [Focusing Condition: Inference-Time Self-Contrastive Steering Elicits Better Conditional Text Embeddings in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32684)
*Zifeng Cheng,Lingyun Qian,Zhiwei Jiang,Cong Wang,Yafeng Yin,Fei Shen,Ao Zhou,Qing Gu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose a plug-and-play, training-free method to obtain higher-quality conditional text embeddings from LLMs by contrasting them with unconditional embeddings at inference time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prompt-based methods for extracting conditional text embeddings from LLMs are appealing because they need no extra data or fine-tuning, but they often fail: the obtained embeddings are entangled with general semantic information instead of being sharply focused on the target condition, which degrades performance on tasks that rely on conditional semantics.

Method: They introduce Self-Contrastive Steering (SCS), an inference-time technique that constructs unconditional text embeddings by masking out the condition via modified attention masks and positional encodings, then uses these unconditional embeddings inside the multi-head self-attention computation to refine the conditional embeddings so they focus more on the specified condition. The method is plug-and-play, training-free, and requires only one extra multi-head self-attention pass at inference.

Result: Across multiple tasks—clustering, Semantic Textual Similarity, and triplet alignment—SCS consistently improves the performance of existing prompt-based conditional embedding methods on various LLM backbones, demonstrating better conditional focus without additional training cost.

Conclusion: Inference-time self-contrastive steering using unconditional embeddings is an effective and efficient way to sharpen conditional text embeddings from LLMs, boosting downstream task performance while remaining training-free, model-agnostic, and easy to apply to existing prompt-based pipelines.

Abstract: Extracting conditional text embeddings from large language models (LLMs) is a promising paradigm, as it requires neither additional data nor fine-tuning. Existing methods incorporate conditions into prompts to guide LLMs to focus on specific aspects and elicit conditional text embeddings. However, relying solely on prompts often fails to produce high-quality conditional text embeddings, as they remain entangled with general text embeddings, ultimately degrading their quality. To this end, we propose an inference-time, plug-and-play Self-Contrastive Steering (SCS) method that constructs unconditional general text embeddings and uses them to refine conditional text embeddings, making them more focused on the target condition. Specifically, we modify the attention mask and positional encodings to mask the condition, thereby obtaining unconditional text embeddings and intervening in the multi-head self-attention computation process. Notably, our method is highly efficient, requiring only a single additional multi-head self-attention computation at inference time. Extensive experiments on clustering, Semantic Textual Similarity, and triplet alignment datasets demonstrate that our method can seamlessly improve the performance of existing prompt-based methods across different LLMs in a training-free and plug-and-play manner. Our code will be released at https://github.com/zifengcheng/SCS

</details>


### [65] [LLM Alignment--Utility Asymmetry under Semantic-Preserving Transformations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32717)
*Mohan Li,Chengyu Yu,Francesco Sovrano,Marc Langheinrich,Martin Gjoreski*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates how well LLM safety alignment holds up under synthetic, meaning-preserving changes to inputs, finding that models often keep their task performance while violating alignment more frequently.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs are aligned to be helpful and safe, it is unclear whether this alignment truly tracks semantic content or is brittle to distributional shifts in inputs. Prior jailbreak and cross-lingual work treats failures as attacks and mostly uses natural language variations likely seen in pretraining, so we still don’t know whether alignment generalizes with meaning or is anchored to superficial patterns. This gap matters for real-world robustness and for understanding if current alignment methods actually constrain model behavior at the level of semantics.

Method: The authors construct synthetic, rule-based, invertible transformations of inputs that preserve task-relevant meaning but move text beyond typical natural language variation. They apply these semantic-preserving transformations to prompts and evaluate eight LLMs (four open-weight and four commercial) under both fine-tuning and in-context learning conditions. They compare two aspects under these transformations: (1) utility (task performance on the intended task) and (2) alignment (tendency to produce harmful or misaligned outputs). The transformations are used as a controlled probe of how alignment and utility each generalize under semantic-preserving distribution shifts.

Result: Across models and adaptation regimes, once a model has learned to operate effectively on the transformed inputs (i.e., utility is largely retained), its alignment degrades disproportionately. In other words, task performance under transformation remains high while safety alignment fails more often. For example, an adapted GPT-4.1 mini shows only mild degradation in utility yet its harmful response rate jumps from 13.3% to 74.3%; Gemini 3 Flash similarly maintains near-original utility but its harmful rate increases from 2.3% to 43.0. This pattern is consistently observed and is termed “Alignment–utility asymmetry.”

Conclusion: The study concludes that current LLM alignment does not reliably generalize with semantic content under distribution shifts, even when the shifts preserve meaning. Instead, there is a recurring gap: models can generalize their task competence to transformed inputs while their safety alignment breaks down. This Alignment–utility asymmetry suggests that present alignment techniques are overly coupled to surface patterns and are insufficiently robust at the semantic level, highlighting the need for more semantically grounded and distributionally robust alignment methods.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) alignment is intended to ensure that models remain helpful and safe, but its stability under input distributional shift is not yet fully understood. Prior work shows that aligned models can fail under jailbreak prompts, alternative encodings, and cross-lingual transfer, yet these failures are usually studied as attacks rather than controlled probes of alignment generalization. Moreover, existing evidence is largely grounded in natural language variation already represented during pretraining, leaving unresolved whether alignment generalizes with semantic content or remains tied to superficial surface patterns. In this paper, we study this question using synthetic semantic-preserving transformations that are rule-based and invertible, preserving task-relevant meaning while shifting inputs beyond standard linguistic variation. Across four open-weight and four commercial models, under both fine-tuning and in-context learning, we use these transformations as a probe of alignment generalization and identify an empirical pattern we term Alignment--utility asymmetry: once models can operate effectively on transformed inputs, task utility is often substantially retained while alignment failure increases more sharply. For example, adapted GPT-4.1 mini shows only limited utility degradation under transformation while its harmful rate rises from 13.3 to 74.3; Gemini 3 Flash similarly retains near-original utility while its harmful rate increases from 2.3 to 43.0. Taken together, these results suggest that semantic-preserving distribution shifts can expose a recurring gap in how utility and alignment generalize in current LLMs.

</details>


### [66] [How Far Do Persona Effects Generalize in Language Models?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32758)
*Yufan Zhou,Yuxuan Liu,Enze Ma,Lyumanshan Ye,Zhongqi Yue,Robin De Croon,Yucheng Jin,Katrien Verbert,Zhao Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates how well persona-induced behavioral patterns in language models generalize across new questions, different models, and varied prompts, finding that such persona effects are predictable within a model but often do not reliably transfer across models or prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether persona prompting effects—changes in model behavior when instructed to act as a specific kind of person—can be systematically captured and reused to predict behavior in new settings (new questions, other models, or modified prompts), which is important for building robust, controllable, and fair language model systems.

Method: The authors analyze persona effects across 57 attributes, three behavioral domains, and seven pairs of open 7–9B language models (including OLMo-3 and Qwen2.5). They model persona effects as "gains" over a shared scaling baseline and compare several strategies: refitting gains to each target setting, borrowing gains across model pairs, allowing different numbers of target parameters (one or two amplitudes), and applying regularized updates. They also test prompt transfers via rewording, changing examples, or altering country context, and run a separate human survey comparison to evaluate how well model outputs align with human responses, including the impact of model responsiveness and temperature calibration.

Result: Persona effects are somewhat predictable but not reliably portable. In OLMo-3 and Qwen2.5, separating attribute and task gains improves prediction over simple shared scaling, with strongest evidence in OLMo-3. For OLMo-3, refitting gains on the target setting significantly outperforms borrowing gains from any other model pair. Cross-model transfer with one borrowed amplitude usually underperforms shared scaling, while a two-parameter target fit eliminates this underperformance but does not significantly beat shared scaling. Under prompt changes, refitting (with reworded prompts) beats reuse with one amplitude across all tested pairs; reuse is more robust when only examples or country context change. Regularized updates outperform reuse strategies at moderate data sizes (64 questions per attribute). The human survey shows that picking a more responsive checkpoint can degrade fit to human data due to confounding with training status; temperature calibration largely fixes this but not misordering of groups.

Conclusion: Persona-induced behavior in LLMs can be captured and predicted within a given model and setting, but these learned relationships rarely transfer cleanly across models or substantially different prompts. Effective use of persona gains in new settings generally requires some degree of target-specific calibration or refitting, and what may look like transfer can often be explained by basic calibration effects rather than genuine reuse of source relationships. Therefore, robust persona control and human-aligned behavior need careful, target-specific modeling and calibration rather than naive portability of persona effects across models or contexts.

Abstract: Persona prompts ask language models to answer as particular kinds of people. We test whether relationships learned from these effects predict responses to new questions and remain useful across models and prompts. Across 57 attributes, three behavioral domains, and seven pairs of open 7 to 9B checkpoints, persona effects can be predictable without being portable. Separate attribute and task gains improve prediction beyond shared scaling significantly in OLMo-3 and Qwen2.5, with the most robust evidence in OLMo-3. In that model, target refitting significantly outperforms gains borrowed from each of the other six pairs. Across model transfers, borrowed gains with one amplitude underperform shared scaling in most directions; allowing two target parameters removes the significant losses but yields no significant benefit over target shared scaling. After rewording, refitting significantly outperforms reuse with one amplitude in all six tested pairs, while changes of examples or country context often preserve reuse value. In the tested prompt transfers, regularized updates outperform both reuse strategies in median at 64 target questions per attribute. A separate survey comparison finds that selecting the more responsive checkpoint can worsen human fit; responsiveness is confounded with training status, and temperature calibration largely removes this cost but not errors in group ordering. Within the tested gain representation, apparent transfer can come from target calibration; source relationships must add predictive value beyond calibration and regularization. Code and data are available at https://github.com/thzva/persona-gain

</details>


### [67] [C-HAT-Bench: Benchmarking Chinese AI-Text Detection Beyond Fully Generated Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32770)
*Qing Yang,Zixiang Luo,Zhenyu Mao,Zezheng Wu,Xinghe Cheng,Haibo Chen,Qinggang Zhang,Jiapu Wang,Jingwei Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a Chinese benchmark to evaluate how well machine-generated text detectors work in realistic human–AI collaborative writing settings rather than only on purely human vs purely AI-generated texts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing machine-generated text detectors are mostly tested on a simple binary scenario—fully human versus fully AI-generated texts. However, real-world writing often involves humans and LLMs collaborating, editing, or extending each other’s drafts, which can weaken or change typical machine cues. This problem is particularly underexplored for Chinese, where language-specific factors (like tokenization and distributional properties) matter and controlled datasets across domains and generation modes are lacking.

Method: The authors build C-HAT-Bench, a unified Chinese benchmark based on 5,000 human-written source texts from five domains. They generate over 240,000 derived texts via six generative models under a baseline Prefix-Conditioned Continuation setting and three additional collaborative production modes that represent different forms of human–AI interaction. They then systematically evaluate 21 detection systems under four protocols: (1) document-level detection in zero-shot and supervised settings, (2) detection boundary localization within documents, and (3) cross-condition generalization between different production modes.

Result: Across detectors, document-level AUROC scores on collaborative production modes are on average 12.0% lower than in the simpler Prefix-Conditioned Continuation setting, with some detectors suffering up to a 44.4% relative performance drop. The study also reveals asymmetric transfer: a detector that works well in one collaborative mode does not necessarily perform well in others, indicating limited generalization between settings.

Conclusion: Performance reported on standard fully human vs fully AI benchmarks substantially overestimates the reliability of MGT detectors when applied to human–AI collaborative writing, especially in Chinese. The proposed C-HAT-Bench exposes significant weaknesses and asymmetries in current detectors across realistic collaborative scenarios, underscoring the need for more robust, collaboration-aware detection methods and evaluation practices.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly participate in writing by modifying or extending human drafts, causing machine involvement to vary in both form and extent. Yet most Machine-Generated Text (MGT) detectors are evaluated only on fully human-written versus fully AI-generated text. Because human--AI collaboration can weaken or redistribute cues associated with machine generation, strong performance under this binary setting may overstate detector reliability. This mismatch remains underexplored in Chinese: detection cues are shaped by tokenization and language-specific text distributions, yet controlled resources spanning production settings, domains, and generators remain limited. To fill this gap, we present a Chinese Human-AI Collaborative Text Detection Benchmark (C-HAT-Bench), a unified benchmark that links $5,000$ human-written source texts from five domains to more than $240,000$ variants produced using six generative models under Prefix-Conditioned Continuation as a reference setting and three collaborative production modes. We evaluate $21$ detectors through four protocols spanning zero-shot and pretrained supervised document-level detection, boundary localization, and cross-condition generalization. Relative to Prefix-Conditioned Continuation, mean AUROC across document-level detectors is $12.0\%$ lower on the collaborative production modes, with the largest detector-specific relative decrease reaching $44.4\%$. Transfer across collaborative production modes is also asymmetric, indicating that performance in a given production setting is not a reliable predictor of performance in other production settings.

</details>


### [68] [On the Behavioral Traits of LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32776)
*Haokai Zhao,Jie Gao,Yunze Xiao,Xintao Wang,Weihao Xuan,Aditya Joshi,Mark Dredze,Jen-tse Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes A-B-D, a bottom-up framework to infer AI personality traits directly from large-scale behavioral traces instead of self-reports or costly informant ratings, revealing six stable behavioral factors that only weakly align with self-reported Big Five traits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches to AI personality rely on models’ self-reports (S-data), which often diverge from actual behavior, or on informant ratings from LLM judges (I-data), which are expensive, limited in coverage, and may not reflect everyday usage. There is a need for a scalable, behavior-grounded way to characterize how different AI models systematically act and communicate in the wild, so that users, developers, and researchers can better understand, compare, and design AI agents.

Method: The authors collect 345,667 real-world trajectories from 80 AI models across 12 tasks and 50 harnesses. From these trajectories they engineer 318 candidate behavioral features capturing both functional aspects (what actions the agent takes at each step) and linguistic aspects (how it communicates). They then systematically filter features based on instance-level temporal stability within a trajectory, cross-task consistency for the same model, and ability to discriminate between models. On the remaining 79 features, they run factor analysis to uncover latent dimensions that are stable and attributable to models. They also compare the resulting factors to models’ self-reported Big Five scores to assess alignment between behavior-derived traits and self-descriptions.

Result: Factor analysis yields six robust behavioral factors—two functional and four linguistic—that consistently differentiate models. For example, Kimi-K3 ranks highest on a factor interpreted as planfulness, whereas GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 rank lowest on a factor interpreted as energetic. Across models, these behavior-based factors show only weak correlations with self-reported Big Five personality traits; even conceptually similar dimensions, such as extroversion and the energetic factor, correlate minimally (r = 0.07, p = 0.58).

Conclusion: Behavioral traces provide a scalable and informative basis for inferring stable, model-specific “personality-like” factors that differ meaningfully across AI systems. These behavior-based traits are largely distinct from what models claim about themselves via self-reported Big Five scores, highlighting a substantial “knowledge–action gap.” The A-B-D framework thus offers a principled way to characterize AI personality from what agents actually do and say in real use, with implications for how users interpret AI behavior, how developers evaluate and tune models, and how social scientists conceptualize machine personalities.

Abstract: Users increasingly describe different AI agents as distinct colleagues to work with. AI personality research aims to quantify such impressions by attributing human-like "traits" to agents. However, existing measures fall short: models' self-reports (S-data) diverge from their actual behavior, while informant ratings from LLM judges (I-data) are costly to scale and cover few everyday scenarios. In this paper, we propose A-B-D to infer traits bottom-up from behavioral data (B-data), namely how agents act on their environment and communicate with users, as recorded in existing trajectories. From 345,667 real-world trajectories spanning 80 models, 12 tasks, and 50 harnesses, we extract 318 candidate features that capture both the actions an agent takes at each step (functional) and the language accompanying them (linguistic). We retain only features that show instance-level stability, cross-task consistency, and model discriminability. Factor analysis of the remaining 79 features uncovers six stable, model-attributable factors, two functional and four linguistic. For example, Kimi-K3 exhibits the most planfulness, whereas GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 are the least energetic. Moreover, we quantify the "knowledge-action gap" in the wild: these factors correlate only weakly with self-reported Big Five scores, even for conceptually matched pairs such as extroversion and energetic (r = 0.07, p = 0.58). Our work offers a new lens for understanding AI personality, with implications for users, developers, and researchers from both computer science and social science.

</details>


### [69] [OpenTumorBoard: A Real-World Benchmark of Multidisciplinary Tumor Board Discussion Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32810)
*Anqi Li,Zhixuan Ge,Yixuan Duan,Jiarong Qian,Chi-Yu Chen,MingYu Lu,Huan-Yu Hsu,Yu Gu,Yue Guo,Sheng Wang,Wei Qiu,Hanwen Xu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: OpenTumorBoard is a large benchmark of real multidisciplinary tumor board discussions used to evaluate and train LLMs on realistic, longitudinal, multimodal oncology decision-making.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing clinical NLP and LLM benchmarks in oncology usually rely on simplified, static, and decontextualized cases, failing to capture the complex, longitudinal, and collaborative nature of real tumor board decision-making. There is a need for a realistic, large-scale benchmark reflecting true multidisciplinary discussions and patient trajectories to assess and improve LLMs intended to support cancer care decisions.

Method: The authors collected 12,534 minutes of publicly available tumor board videos from YouTube, automatically curated and transcribed them, and structured them into 611 patient cases with 19,157 discussion turns across ten specialist roles. They defined two evaluation settings: (1) SPECIALIST TURN, where an LLM must answer actual clinically important questions posed during discussions; and (2) BOARD SIMULATION, where an LLM must simulate a full multi-speaker board discussion and arrive at consensus recommendations. They then evaluated 14 general-purpose and medical LLMs on these tasks, and additionally applied supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning on a training subset. Three physicians manually checked a subset of the dataset for coverage, factuality, and fidelity of the extracted consensus conclusions.

Result: The dataset captures a broad range of real tumor board trajectories with high information coverage and factual accuracy according to expert review, and the automatically extracted consensus conclusions faithfully reflect the original discussions. When evaluated on the benchmark, state-of-the-art general and medical LLMs show clear limitations: the best model achieves an average score of 3.43/5 for clinical equivalence to human specialist answers and 2.78/5 for agreement with real board conclusions. Finetuning and reinforcement learning on the dataset yield measurable performance improvements on a held-out test set, indicating that models can benefit from exposure to real discussion trajectories.

Conclusion: OpenTumorBoard provides a realistic, large-scale benchmark and curation pipeline for evaluating and training LLMs on multidisciplinary cancer decision-making. Current frontier and medical LLMs fall short of expert performance in replicating tumor board answers and consensus decisions, but performance can be improved via targeted training on this type of data. By releasing both the benchmark and the automated pipeline, the work aims to catalyze further research on LLMs that can better understand longitudinal oncology cases and support real-world, team-based clinical decision-making.

Abstract: Multidisciplinary tumor boards integrate multimodal clinical observations and longitudinal patient histories through specialist discussions, yet benchmarks rarely capture these real-world trajectories. We introduce OpenTumorBoard, a benchmark with 611 patient cases and 19,157 discussion turns across ten specialist roles, transcribed from 12,534 minutes of publicly available tumor board recordings on YouTube. The benchmark evaluates two settings: SPECIALIST TURN, in which an LLM responds to a clinically significant question posed during a real discussion, and BOARD SIMULATION, in which it generates an entire back-and-forth discussion and reaches a consensus on therapy recommendations, surgical plans, next actions and clinical trial matching. Evaluation of 14 general-purpose frontier and medical LLMs reveals substantial limitations: the best models score 3.43 out of 5 in clinical equivalence to specialist answers and 2.78 out of 5 in alignment with recorded board conclusions. Supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning improve performance on a held-out test set, suggesting that real-world discussion trajectories can support model adaptation. Three M.D. experts review a subset of the benchmark, finding high information coverage and factuality of patient cases and strong fidelity of extracted consensus conclusions. We will release OpenTumorBoard and its automated curation pipeline to support the development and evaluation of LLMs for multidisciplinary, personalized cancer decision-making.

</details>


### [70] [ARSM: Auto-Regressive State Machine for Agentic Reasoning Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32852)
*Xiafeng Man,Siyuan Ye,Xiaosong Ma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose ARSM, a training-free framework that compresses an agent’s reasoning trace into a structured state machine to relieve LLM memory bottlenecks while preserving performance and cutting tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents in long-horizon tasks must store growing interaction histories, quickly hitting context-length and cost limits. Existing compression either needs extra training/auxiliary models or destroys the structured relations in the trajectory, causing information loss and inconsistent decisions. A method is needed that is lightweight, training-free, and preserves structured reasoning while reducing tokens.

Method: They design Auto-Regressive State Machine (ARSM) with two main ideas: (1) trajectory abstraction that restructures the agent’s interaction history into compact Hypothesis-Action-Result (HAR) micro-chains; (2) a dynamic hierarchical state machine with simple atomic operations and a compression-control parameter to manage what is stored, merged, or discarded. The system operates in an auto-regressive generation space where each LLM step both interacts with the environment and updates the internal compressed state, achieving in-situ reasoning compression without extra training.

Result: On Webshop, Multi-Objective Multi-Hop QA, and SWE-Bench Lite, ARSM keeps task success comparable to uncompressed baselines while significantly cutting token usage, showing better cost-effectiveness than prior memory compression approaches.

Conclusion: ARSM provides a simple, training-free, and structured way to compress reasoning traces for LLM agents. By representing history as HAR micro-chains and managing them with a dynamic state machine, it mitigates memory bottlenecks and token costs without sacrificing performance, suggesting a scalable path for long-horizon autonomous agents.

Abstract: While Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents demonstrate strong capabilities in long-horizon tasks by interleaving reasoning with external environment interactions, the continuous accumulation of context rapidly creates a critical memory bottleneck. Existing memory compression methods rely on task-specific optimization or external auxiliary models, introducing significant computational overhead. Furthermore, the resulting compressed representations tend to lose structured relationships, leading to information dilution, attention collapse, and degraded decision consistency.
  To address these limitations, we propose Auto-Regressive State Machine (ARSM), a lightweight training-free framework that enables in-situ reasoning compression through structured state evolution. ARSM introduces two key components: (i) a trajectory abstraction mechanism that reorganizes interaction histories into compact Hypothesis-Action-Result (HAR) micro-chains; (ii) a dynamic state machine that regulates hierarchical memory through atomic operations and a compression-control parameter. These components are unified within an auto-regressive, self-compressive generation space, where each model output jointly performs external action execution and internal state updates.
  We evaluate ARSM on Webshop, Multi-Objective Multi-Hop QA, and SWE-Bench Lite datasets. Experimental results show that ARSM maintains the task performance while simultaneously reducing token consumption, offering a practical, cost-effective route toward scalable autonomous agents for long-horizon tasks.

</details>


### [71] [Are You Sure You're Sure? Two Confounds in a Sycophancy Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32867)
*Atharv Gupta,Akshat Jindal,Lavanya Nigam,Aryan Sood*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper audits SycEval, a benchmark for measuring sycophancy in language models, and finds that its prompt templates confound timing with other factors, which reverses some of its main conclusions when corrected.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current sycophancy benchmarks, like SycEval, attribute differences in model behavior to when user objections are raised (before vs. after an answer) but may unintentionally vary multiple factors in their prompt templates. This risks misattributing effects to timing when they may actually be caused by other template features, undermining claims about model behavior and safety.

Method: The authors carefully dissect SycEval’s prompt templates and identify two confounds: whether the objection explicitly names a target answer and where the output-format instruction is placed. They then construct new, controlled templates that disentangle these factors from timing and test them on both multiple-choice questions and SycEval’s own free-form evaluation pipeline, across several model conditions. They compare follow rates (how often models adopt the user’s assertion) under different template configurations.

Result: They find that explicitly naming a target answer in the user’s objection substantially increases follow rates by 14.1–49.5 percentage points. When both preemptive and in-context objections name a target answer, the original timing result from SycEval reverses in three of five model conditions: models cave less under preemptive objections than under in-context ones. They also show that moving the output-formatting instruction from the objection into the question changes caving rates in opposite directions for different models on the same items and produces measurable effects in the free-form pipeline (e.g., −5.1pp caving on Llama-3.1-8B, no effect on Qwen3-4B).

Conclusion: The main effects reported by SycEval are partly artifacts of its prompt templates rather than genuine properties of model sycophancy. Confounds such as explicit answer naming and the placement of formatting instructions can substantially alter measured caving rates and even reverse conclusions about timing. These issues are fixable at the benchmark design stage, and the authors propose a small set of checks that benchmark creators should apply to ensure that their templates isolate the intended construct without hidden confounds.

Abstract: Sycophancy is a language model's tendency to cave when a user pushes back, abandoning a correct answer for the user's. Several benchmarks now measure it by scripting an objection and recording how often the model caves. Because that objection is a prompt template, whatever else the template varies is measured along with the property it claims to isolate. We audit SycEval, which reports that objections raised before a model answers (preemptive) cause more caving than those raised after (in-context), and attributes the gap to timing. Two features of its templates vary alongside the property each is meant to test. First, SycEval's objections escalate through four strength levels, and at the two weakest only the preemptive template names a target answer, so timing and naming vary together. We build the missing comparison and test it on multiple-choice questions and SycEval's own free-form pipeline. Naming a target answer raises the follow rate, the share of samples matching the user's assertion, by 14.1--49.5 percentage points (pp), and once both templates name one, the timing comparison reverses on three of the five model conditions we test: models cave \emph{less} under preemptive objections than in-context ones, opposite to SycEval. Second, the output-format instruction benchmarks append for automatic grading also varies with objection placement. Moving it from the pushback into the question flips its effect in opposite directions across models on the same items ($p=0.0059$). The same effect appears in SycEval's free-form pipeline: relocating its instruction lowers caving by 5.1pp on Llama-3.1-8B, while an equivalence test confirms no effect on Qwen3-4B. Both confounds live in the template rather than the models under test, so both are correctable: we close with three checks benchmark authors can apply before publishing.

</details>


### [72] [Linger and Lose: Knowledge Collapse in Low-Bit Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32902)
*Prashanna Mani Paudel,Shivanand Venkanna Sheshappanavar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that ternary-weight language models can appear good by loss and accuracy but actually store far less factual information per parameter than higher-precision models, due to a training instability that causes a late-stage collapse of knowledge capacity centered in the output head; they propose schedule and learning-rate fixes and argue that low-precision training should be evaluated by capacity during training, not just final loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard metrics like loss and downstream accuracy suggest that low-precision (e.g., ternary) language models incur only modest performance costs compared to full-precision ones. However, these metrics may not reflect how much factual information the models actually store. The authors are motivated to understand whether low-precision training fundamentally limits a model’s knowledge capacity, to diagnose any failure modes specific to low precision, and to develop training regimes that preserve information content rather than just optimizing for perplexity or loss.

Method: The authors construct synthetic biographies with precisely known information content and use them to measure knowledge capacity, defined as factual bits stored per parameter. They train GPT-2-style language models from scratch over a size range (2.5M–50M parameters) and across five numerical precisions, including ternary and fp16. Training uses different learning-rate schedules, notably the standard cosine schedule and alternative schemes (e.g., warmup-stable-decay with cooldown). They track capacity and perplexity throughout training, analyze when and how capacity collapses, and localize the failure to the output head by inspecting its weights and prediction behavior. They also experiment with modifications such as making an otherwise unpredictable output-head value predictable, adjusting the output head’s learning rate, and applying various post-training quantization methods down to sub-4-bit precision.

Result: Under conventional cosine learning-rate schedules, ternary-weight models exhibit a dramatic reduction in knowledge capacity: in some settings they retain only about 6% of the capacity of identically trained fp16 baselines despite showing only a 1.4–1.6× increase in perplexity. The capacity deficit grows with model size. Capacity over training follows a rise-and-collapse pattern: models first learn substantial information and then lose most of it. This collapse is identified as a learning-rate dwell instability occurring when the rate lingers around 1–2×10^{-4}; once collapse happens, lowering the rate later does not restore capacity. The failure is localized to the output head, where certain weights blow up on a value the model can never predict, yet the rest of its predictions remain essentially unchanged. Making that problematic value predictable, regardless of which attribute carries it, eliminates the collapse. A warmup-stable-decay schedule with a short cooldown phase markedly boosts capacity (e.g., 2.7× at 25M and 4.3× at 50M) with even larger relative gains at lower precisions. Reducing the learning rate specifically for the output head prevents collapse when training from scratch. Post-training quantization methods evaluated fail to recover any measurable capacity when going below 4 bits.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that ternary and other very low-precision language models can suffer from a severe, late-stage loss of stored factual information that is not apparent from standard metrics like loss or perplexity. This knowledge collapse is driven by a learning-rate dwell instability and is concentrated in the output head, where uncontrolled weight growth on an unlearnable value erases capacity without strongly affecting typical loss metrics. Properly designed learning-rate schedules—especially warmup-stable-decay with cooldown—and reduced learning rates in the output head can substantially mitigate or prevent this collapse, improving capacity, particularly at lower precisions. Post-training quantization below 4 bits does not recover this lost information. The authors advocate evaluating low-precision training regimes by tracking retained knowledge capacity during training, rather than relying solely on final loss or accuracy.

Abstract: Training language models with ternary weights is commonly judged by loss and downstream accuracy, which record only a modest cost relative to full precision. We show that these metrics can conceal a much larger failure. We instead measure knowledge capacity, the factual bits stored per parameter, on synthetic biographies with known information content. We train GPT-2-style models from scratch with 2.5M to 50M parameters at five precisions. Under the standard cosine schedule, ternary models retain as little as 6% of an identically trained fp16 model's capacity. The deficit widens with model size while perplexity rises by only 1.4 to 1.6 times. Measured throughout training, these models first acquire capacity and then lose most of it. We identify this knowledge collapse as a learning-rate dwell instability. Held near $1$--$2\times10^{-4}$ with no decay, a pre-collapse model collapses within a few hundred exposures, and returning to a safe rate does not restore capacity. We then locate the collapse in the output head. It happens at a value the model can never predict. The weights there grow unchecked, while every other prediction the model makes is unchanged. We find that making the value predictable removes the collapse, regardless of which attribute carries it. A warmup-stable-decay schedule with a 10% cooldown increases ternary capacity by 2.7 times at 25M and 4.3 times at 50M. Gains are larger at lower precision. Cutting the output head's learning rate prevents failure when training from scratch. The post-training quantization methods we tested recover no measurable capacity below 4 bits. Our findings suggest judging low-precision training by retained capacity during training rather than final loss.

</details>


### [73] [The Key Handoff: Retrieval in Hybrid Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32942)
*Kaan Kale,Oguzhan Baser,Sriram Vishwanath*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how two-hop reasoning happens inside both transformer and hybrid (recurrent–attention) language models, pinpointing where a bridge entity is computed, carried, and used to retrieve an answer, and showing that recurrent state can function as a queryable memory, not just a transport channel.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Two-hop questions (e.g., linking “ball” → “Alice” → “garden”) require a model to compute an intermediate “bridge” entity and then use it to retrieve the final answer. In transformers we know this seems to happen via attention in early layers, but in hybrid models with recurrent components it is unclear when and where the bridge is formed, how it is propagated, and whether retrieval depends on the key itself or on where facts sit in the prompt. The authors want to mechanistically understand these internal processes across dense transformers and hybrid architectures.

Method: The authors construct controlled two-hop reasoning setups in which a question must be answered via an intermediate entity that appears only in the context, not in the question. They compare dense transformers and sequential hybrid models (with recurrent state plus attention). They perform a hidden-state “transplantation” intervention: moving a hidden state representing the bridge entity from one story into another where different paths (via the bridge key vs. via positional prompt information) lead to different answers. By doing this around each layer, they determine where the key is computed and where it is consumed. They also modify the recurrent memory after the last attention layer by writing in alternative facts to test whether later recurrent layers can still influence retrieval. Across twelve models, they systematically observe the effect of these interventions on model answers.

Result: They find that in all tested models there exists an attention layer that converts the bridge-entity representation into a “key” used for retrieval; if they cross that layer when transplanting states, the usable effect of the key is lost, and this effect is localized to layers with no subsequent attention. In sequential hybrid models, this yields a clear division of labor: recurrent layers carry the key forward in time, and attention layers “spend” it to retrieve the answer. However, retrieval does not always end at the last attention layer. When the authors overwrite the recurrent state after the final attention layer with new, conflicting facts, the model’s answers shift toward those new facts, increasing their probability by a factor of about 1.3–2.7. Which hybrid models exhibit this behavior is not fully explained by architectural or training differences. The shift depends on the semantic key (bridge entity), not on raw position, indicating that access to recurrent memory is key-based.

Conclusion: Two-hop reasoning in both dense transformers and hybrid recurrent–attention models relies on an internal bridge-entity key that is formed by attention and then used to retrieve the answer. In hybrids, recurrent layers do more than just pass this key forward: they act as a queryable memory that later layers can read from via that key. Attention layers thus implement the conversion and spending of keys, while recurrent state can continue to store and serve facts even after the final attention layer. This challenges a purely “carrier-only” view of recurrent components in hybrid LMs and shows that detailed mechanistic behavior is not determined solely by architecture or training regime.

Abstract: A two-hop question makes a language model retrieve twice: once to produce a bridge entity, and once to retrieve with it. Transformers resolve that entity in their early layers. Hybrid models replace most of the attention with a recurrent state, so where the key becomes usable, and where it is spent on an answer, is not known. Answering "Where is the ball?" from "the ball belongs to Alice" and "Alice is in the garden" turns on Alice, a name the question does not mention. A model could reach garden through Alice, the key it computed, or through where the fact sits in the prompt. Across twelve models, dense and hybrid, we move a hidden state from one story into another where the two routes lead to different places, and read off which place the model gives. An attention layer converts the key in every model we tested, and crossing that layer removes its usable effect, all of it where no attention follows. In sequential hybrids this makes the answer a handoff: recurrent layers carry the key forward, and attention spends it. Retrieval does not always stop there. Writing a different fact into the memory of the recurrent layers that follow the last attention layer can move the answer toward that fact, multiplying its odds by 1.3 to 2.7, and which hybrids do this is not settled by their architecture or training. That read is addressed by the key, not by position: recurrent state in a hybrid is not only a carrier, but a memory that later layers can query.

</details>


### [74] [TCMQA: A 38K-Question Traditional Chinese Medicine Benchmark with a Licensed-Practitioner Reference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33014)
*Tzu-Heng Huang,Jet Lin,Eric Lin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build and release a large benchmark (TCMQA) based on Chinese TCM licensing exams, plus practitioner answers, to measure how well language models handle Traditional Chinese Medicine, and show that Chinese-pretrained models vastly outperform similarly sized Western-pretrained ones but still differ markedly from human experts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing medical benchmarks for language models almost exclusively test Western biomedicine and largely ignore Traditional Chinese Medicine, which is a distinct medical system with its own diagnostic concepts and literature. The few available TCM evaluations are tiny, narrow in scope, and usually lack human expert baselines, making it impossible to robustly assess and compare model performance on TCM reasoning or knowledge.
