There is thus a need for a comprehensive, open, and human-anchored benchmark to evaluate language models on TCM tasks.

Method: The authors construct TCMQA, a large-scale benchmark derived from Chinese TCM licensing exam questions, containing 38,279 questions. They also collect 15,151 answers from 101 licensed TCM practitioners to serve as human references. They then evaluate 29 instruction-tuned language models spanning 9 model families and parameter sizes from 0.27B to 14.8B. They compare model accuracy on the benchmark, analyze the role of pretraining data versus model size, and contrast model performance with practitioner responses, including difficulty ratings and item-level agreement between humans and models.

Result: Model accuracies span a wide 59-point range, with no model reaching ceiling performance. Pretraining data source strongly predicts TCM ability: a 12B-parameter Western-pretrained model achieves 39.6% accuracy, whereas a much smaller Chinese-pretrained model (one-eighth the size) reaches 60.8%. Nine models surpass the practitioner majority-vote accuracy of 64.9%, with the best model scoring 21.8 percentage points higher than this human baseline, and all nine top-performing models belong to the same Chinese-pretrained family. However, difficulty and correctness patterns do not align between humans and models: model accuracy is roughly constant across practitioner-rated difficulty levels, item-level agreement between any model and practitioners is near zero, and in 8.4% of items practitioners are correct while the leading model is wrong.

Conclusion: TCMQA provides a large, open, and human-anchored benchmark for evaluating language models on Traditional Chinese Medicine, revealing that Chinese-pretrained models can perform very strongly—even surpassing aggregated practitioner performance—despite being smaller than Western-pretrained counterparts. Nonetheless, the mismatch in item-level agreement and difficulty perception between models and human practitioners shows that high aggregate accuracy does not imply human-like reasoning or error profiles, underscoring the need for nuanced evaluation and caution in deploying such models for real-world TCM applications.

Abstract: Medical benchmarks for language models are built almost entirely on Western biomedicine. Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) is a separate system, with its own diagnostic framework and its own literature, and it remains largely unmeasured. The few TCM evaluations that exist are small, narrow, and rarely paired with a human reference. We present TCMQA, an open benchmark of 38,279 questions from Chinese TCM licensing examinations, paired with 15,151 responses from 101 licensed practitioners. We evaluate 29 instruction-tuned models from 9 families, spanning 0.27B to 14.8B parameters. Accuracy ranges over 59 points, and no model approaches saturation. Pretraining data predicts TCM ability far better than scale: a 12B Western-pretrained model reaches 39.6%, while a Chinese-pretrained model an eighth its size reaches 60.8%. Nine models exceed the practitioner majority vote of 64.9%, the best by 21.8 points, and all nine come from that same Chinese-pretrained family. Yet difficulty does not transfer between models and practitioners: accuracy is flat across practitioner-rated difficulty, item-level agreement is near zero for all 29 models, and on $8.4\%$ of items the practitioners are correct where the leading model is wrong. We release the corpus, the practitioner responses, the harness, and per-item model outputs at https://huggingface.co/datasets/TechTCM/TCMQA.

</details>


### [75] [Improving the Diversity of LLM Outputs without a Trade-off](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33038)
*Ryoma Sato*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DAST rearranges token IDs and uses arithmetic sampling to diversify LLM outputs while preserving the original probability distribution and adding almost no runtime cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard sampling from LLMs can repeatedly generate very similar outputs across runs, which is undesirable when brainstorming or when diversity across generations is important. Existing diversity-enhancing techniques often distort the model’s underlying probability distribution or incur noticeable computational overhead. The paper aims to obtain more diverse generations across runs without changing the marginal token distribution or slowing inference meaningfully.

Method: First, observe that token IDs in existing vocabularies are essentially arbitrary and not semantically ordered. The authors learn or compute a new permutation of token IDs such that tokens with similar meanings become adjacent in the ID space. This reindexing is a one-time, offline process taking a few hundred seconds per model and is then reused. At generation time, they apply arithmetic sampling or quasi-Monte Carlo sampling over this reordered token index space. Because these low-discrepancy sampling techniques spread samples out more uniformly, the method implicitly discourages selecting nearby (semantically similar) tokens in different runs while keeping each token’s marginal probability unchanged.

Result: The method, called DAST (Diversifying Arithmetic Sampling with TokenTour), yields more diverse generations qualitatively—e.g., more varied ideas across multiple runs from the same prompt—while incurring only microseconds of additional latency per generation. Quantitatively, the authors report significant performance gains on the ProtoQA benchmark, which evaluates models on open-ended, commonsense question answering where diversity and coverage of plausible answers matter.

Conclusion: DAST demonstrates that rearranging token IDs into a semantically meaningful order and then applying arithmetic or quasi-Monte Carlo sampling can substantially increase cross-run diversity of LLM outputs without distorting probabilities or noticeably slowing inference. This approach improves both qualitative creativity and performance on diversity-sensitive benchmarks like ProtoQA, suggesting a practical, low-cost way to obtain richer, more varied generations from existing language models.

Abstract: We propose DAST (Diversifying Arithmetic Sampling with TokenTour), a method that increases the diversity of LLM outputs without any change to the marginal distribution and with negligible generation-time overhead (a few microseconds). We observe that token IDs are often arranged in a meaningless order and reassign them so that tokens with similar meanings appear consecutively. This can be done in advance in a few hundred seconds per model, and the resulting order can be reused for all subsequent generations. By combining this order with arithmetic sampling (or quasi-Monte Carlo methods), we make similar tokens less likely to be generated across runs while preserving the distribution. Our method not only produces qualitatively good ideas but also significantly improves performance on the downstream task of ProtoQA.

</details>


### [76] [Pinned and Still Unstable: Within-Judge Verdict Variance and the Noise Floor of LLM-as-Judge Leaderboards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33044)
*Krishna Chytanya Ayyagari*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that using large language models (LLMs) as automatic judges is less reproducible than commonly assumed, even with fixed model snapshots and temperature-zero decoding on cloud platforms, and proposes metrics and reporting standards to account for this instability in leaderboards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM leaderboards and benchmarks increasingly rely on LLMs-as-judges under the assumption that fixing the model version and decoding with temperature zero yields deterministic, reproducible evaluations. However, practitioners observe unexplained variation in scores and rankings across runs, which undermines the credibility of fine-grained leaderboard claims, especially for close model comparisons. There is a need to understand the empirical magnitude, sources, and consequences of this instability and to develop ways to quantify and transparently report it.

Method: The authors empirically probe evaluation instability by repeatedly re-running the same fixed, temperature-zero judge models on the same prompts and responses across four frontier LLM judges, all hosted on a single large enterprise cloud provider. They use three standard benchmarks (Arena-Hard, AlpacaEval 2, MT-Bench) and measure how often verdicts change (flip rates) across re-runs. They introduce new metrics: (1) per-item flip rate; (2) a two-part stability profile composed of waver fraction (what fraction of items ever flip) and conditional intensity (how often they flip, given that they can); and (3) adjacency separability, which quantifies whether neighboring leaderboard positions are statistically distinguishable. They assess the impact of instability on rankings using paired hierarchical bootstrapping and cross-judge comparisons, including re-judging 13 published head-to-head claims under different judges and re-runs.

Result: They find that identical inputs to the same pinned, temperature-zero judge on the same cloud platform yield non-trivial variation: average per-item flip rates around 5% and about 40% for close-call items that typically determine leaderboard margins, with substantial variation across judges (from 0.13% to nearly 10%). For a single judge, aggregate leaderboard rankings are largely stable (0% top-K instability and 0% pooled winner flips), but the precision of fine-grained ordering is degraded: paired hierarchical bootstrap analysis shows that around 20% to 75% of adjacent positions on leaderboards are statistically indistinguishable, indicating a high noise floor. Across different judge models, leaderboards agree only on coarse ordering; middle rankings diverge, with Kendall’s tau correlations as low as 0.42–0.64 on Arena-Hard. When re-evaluating 13 public head-to-head claims, 5 of them do not hold up under a reasonable change of judge or re-run, suggesting that many reported fine-grained comparisons are not robust.

Conclusion: The apparent determinism of LLM-as-judge evaluations under fixed snapshots and temperature-zero decoding does not hold in practice on real cloud serving infrastructure; the instrument itself has a non-trivial noise floor. While single-judge leaderboards maintain stable broad rankings and overall winners, they cannot reliably support precise adjacent ordering or strong claims about small differences between models. The primary source of this uncertainty seems to be finite prompt sampling more than the judge model itself. The authors argue that current practice of reporting single point estimates without uncertainty or robustness checks misrepresents the reliability of results. They advocate a simple, low-cost reporting protocol: running multiple judge re-runs, publishing stability profiles and adjacency intervals, and providing results under at least two judge models from different families to better reflect the true uncertainty and robustness of leaderboard conclusions.

Abstract: Modern LLM evaluation assumes that pinning a judge to a fixed model snapshot and decoding at temperature zero yields reproducible verdicts. We show this assumption fails as a property of how LLM-as-Judge is operationalized on cloud serving infrastructure, not of any particular model family. Across four frontier judges all served via a single major enterprise cloud platform and three standard benchmarks (Arena-Hard, AlpacaEval 2, MT-Bench), identical inputs to the same pinned, temperature-zero judge produce different verdicts across re-runs: per-item flip rates of roughly 5% on average and about 40% on the close-call items that decide leaderboard margins, with a per-judge magnitude spanning a 40x range (from 0.13% to nearly 10%). We introduce metrics tailored to this instability: per-item flip rate, a two-part stability profile (waver fraction and conditional intensity), and adjacency separability - and report what the variance does and does not do to rankings. For a single judge the aggregate ranking is stable (0% top-K instability, 0% pooled winner flip); what degrades is precision: under a paired hierarchical bootstrap, roughly one-fifth to three-quarters of adjacent leaderboard positions are statistically indistinguishable, a noise floor we attribute primarily to finite prompt sampling rather than to the judge. Across judges, leaderboards agree on the coarse ordering but diverge in the middle (Kendall's tau as low as 0.42-0.64 between families on Arena-Hard), and of 13 published head-to-head ranking claims we re-judge, 5 fail under a defensible judge swap or re-run. We argue that leaderboards report unhedged point estimates that misrepresent the noise floor of the instrument, and we propose a minimal, low-cost reporting protocol: several judge re-runs, published stability profiles and adjacency intervals, and results under at least two judges from different families.

</details>


### [77] [Reading Too Much into Context: Passive Exposure Can Steer LLM Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33065)
*Yuxiang Zheng,Lin Tian,Marian-Andrei Rizoiu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that large language models’ decisions can be significantly shifted just by passively exposing them to extra contextual content, even when that content offers no valid reason to change the decision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM assistants increasingly browse the web and consult external tools, they are routinely exposed to large amounts of additional text. While this can provide evidence, it may also inadvertently bias or steer the model’s choices in ways unrelated to user goals or task-relevant reasons. Understanding whether mere exposure to such content can change decisions is important for reliability, safety, and alignment of LLM-based systems.

Method: The authors compare LLM decisions on the same tasks under two conditions: (1) baseline prompts without extra content and (2) prompts augmented with external content (e.g., retrieved text, online opinions) that should not rationally affect the correct or user-desired answer. They run this across multiple open-weight and closed-weight models, measuring how much the added, ostensibly irrelevant content shifts the models’ responses, including on tasks with explicit user requirements and on factual claims known to be false.

Result: All tested models, both open- and closed-weight, show systematic shifts in their decisions when exposed to the additional content. In closed-weight models, the effect size can be very large—up to roughly 50 percentage point changes in decision distributions. Similar susceptibility appears when using real-world online opinions as the added context. The effect is not confined to subjective preference questions; it also appears in tasks where user instructions or factual correctness should dominate.

Conclusion: LLM outputs are highly sensitive to what is placed in their context, even when that information provides no legitimate reason to change the answer. Passive exposure can nudge models to violate explicit user requirements and to more readily accept false statements. Therefore, the design of retrieval, browsing, and context construction pipelines is critical: simply adding more external text can inadvertently steer decisions and undermine robustness and alignment.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) assistants can now search the web and consult external sources while completing user requests. These sources can provide useful evidence, but they can also introduce additional content into the model's context. Can such passive exposure steer a decision even when the added content provides no reason to change it? We examine the stability of model decisions on the same tasks with and without such external content. Across all open-weight and closed-weight models we test, exposure systematically shifts decisions, with effects reaching nearly 50 percentage points in closed-weight models. The same pattern appears with real-world online opinions. The influence also extends beyond subjective preferences. Such exposure can steer models toward choices that violate explicit user requirements and increase their acceptance of false claims. In short, what enters an LLM's context can influence its decision even when it should not determine it.

</details>


### [78] [OneSign: Unifying Sign Language Understanding Tasks with One Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33090)
*Shiwei Gan,Yafeng Yin,Xiao Liu,Desibieer Tuerdaken,Lei Xie,Sanglu Lu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: OneSign proposes a single unified model for multiple sign language understanding tasks using a modality-adaptive mixture-of-experts to handle differences between sign and text tokens, achieving competitive or SOTA results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current sign language understanding tasks like isolated sign recognition, continuous sign recognition, and sign language translation are treated separately, each with its own architecture and pretraining/finetuning pipeline. This leads to fragmented training, multiple task-specific checkpoints, and poor knowledge sharing. Additionally, recent LLM-based methods often ignore the modality gap between continuous sign signals and discrete text tokens, simply concatenating them and processing them identically, which can hurt performance.

Method: The authors introduce OneSign, a unified framework that reformulates ISLR, CSLR, and SLT under a single training paradigm and within a single model/checkpoint. The core technical component is a Modality-Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts (MA-MoE) architecture. MA-MoE has a shared expert plus separate modality-specific experts for sign tokens and text tokens. A modality router decides, per token, which experts to activate; their outputs are combined to produce the final token representation. This lets the model specialize parameters to each modality while keeping a shared expert path for cross-modal knowledge sharing.

Result: Through experiments on multiple standard benchmarks for SLU tasks, OneSign attains competitive or state-of-the-art performance across ISLR, CSLR, and SLT, showing that a single unified model with MA-MoE can match or surpass specialized task-specific models.

Conclusion: OneSign demonstrates that diverse sign language understanding tasks can be effectively unified in one model and one checkpoint. By explicitly modeling modality differences between sign and text with a modality-adaptive mixture-of-experts, the framework enables effective parameter sharing and specialization, reducing the need for fragmented training pipelines while maintaining or improving performance on several benchmarks.

Abstract: SLU encompasses a diverse set of tasks, including ISLR, CSLR, and SLT. Although these tasks share basic semantic and linguistic foundations, they are typically addressed with task-specific architectures and training pipelines, which hinders knowledge sharing and requires costly pretraining and finetuning for each task. In this paper, we focus on two aspects of SLU tasks: (1) training and inference pipelines are highly fragmented: most methods rely on pretraining on large-scale SL datasets followed by task- or dataset-specific finetuning, which leads to multiple specialized models rather than a single checkpoint. (2) current LLM-based methods may overlook the inherent modality discrepancy between sign and text tokens, simply concatenating them and processing both modalities with the same decoder layers. In this paper, we present OneSign, a unified framework that addresses multiple SLU tasks within a single model and a single checkpoint. OneSign reformulates ISLR, CSLR, and SLT under a single training paradigm. To accommodate the heterogeneous characteristics of sign and text representations, we introduce a Modality-Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts (MA-MoE) architecture, consisting of a shared expert and modality-specific experts for sign and text tokens. A modality router dynamically activates the corresponding experts, and their outputs are aggregated to form the final token representations. By enabling modality-dependent expert specialization while preserving a shared expert path, MA-MoE can effectively model the modality differences between continuous sign representations and discrete text tokens. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that OneSign achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance on several benchmarks, highlighting its effectiveness as a unified SLU model. Datasets are available at : https://github.com/gswycf/OneSign.

</details>


### [79] [MedRouter: Demystifying Knowledge Differences Across Medical LLMs for Routing-Based Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33119)
*Lang Cao,Binghang Lu,Yuhao Shen,Yue Guo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes MedRouter, an agent system that routes medical questions to multiple specialist LLMs and combines their answers, achieving better medical QA performance than prior routing approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Different medical LLMs have complementary strengths across specialties, modalities, and tasks, so relying on a single model limits coverage and reasoning quality. Existing routing focuses on cost–quality trade-offs but does not explicitly leverage specialist competence differences to enhance medical reasoning. The authors aim to systematically exploit these differences to provide more accurate and comprehensive medical question answering.

Method: They design MedRouter, which uses an embedding-based multi-label router to select one or more specialist LLMs for each query. The selected specialists are queried, and their responses are then fed into a generator LLM that produces the final answer. They introduce SCALE (Specialist Competence-Aware Learning), a two-stage training framework: (1) supervised training of the router using labels about when each specialist is correct, and (2) reinforcement learning that optimizes routing choices via a Performance Gain Reward (PGR), which quantifies how much using specialist outputs improves the generator’s answer compared to answering without them.

Result: On eight text-only and multimodal medical QA benchmarks, MedRouter achieves an 8% average accuracy improvement over the strongest existing routing baseline. Analysis of specialist model outputs shows each specialist excels on different question types and domains, and routing can exploit this complementarity.

Conclusion: Combining multiple specialist medical LLMs via a competence-aware routing and aggregation framework yields more accurate and comprehensive medical QA than single-model or naive routing approaches. Learned routing that explicitly models specialist competence and its impact on final answer quality is an effective way to enhance medical reasoning across diverse tasks and modalities.

Abstract: Medical question answering spans diverse specialties and modalities, and individual medical large language models (LLMs) exhibit distinct strengths across tasks and domains. This heterogeneity suggests that combining specialists may enable broader coverage of medical questions than relying on any single model. However, existing LLM routing methods primarily seek to balance answer quality and inference cost, leaving open how to exploit differences in specialist competence to improve medical reasoning. In this paper, we introduce MedRouter, an agentic system that uses an embedding-based multi-label router to select and query specialist LLMs, then passes their responses to a generator to produce the final answer. We further propose SCALE (Specialist Competence-Aware Learning), a two-stage training framework that first trains the Router with specialist correctness supervision and then optimizes its selections through reinforcement learning. The second stage uses a Performance Gain Reward (PGR) that measures how specialist information affects the generator's answer correctness relative to answering without that information. Experiments on eight text-based and multimodal medical QA benchmarks show that MedRouter outperforms the strongest routing baseline by 8% in average accuracy. Our analysis of specialist outputs further reveals distinct strengths and complementary question-level coverage, motivating learned routing to combine these capabilities for more comprehensive medical reasoning.

</details>


### [80] [Classifying Dominant Temporal Orientation without Pretrained Text Embeddings: A Novel Morphosyntactic Inventory Vector Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33121)
*Jonathan Cleveland,Peter S. Bearman*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose a simple, embedding-free morphosyntactic vector representation (“Morphosyntacton”) to classify a sentence’s overall temporal orientation (past/present/future) and achieve 92% accuracy on complex English sentences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing computational methods struggle to reliably identify a sentence’s dominant temporal orientation, especially when multiple clauses with different tense/aspect cues compete. Many approaches rely on pretrained embeddings or complex sequence models, which may be unnecessary for this specific task and can be opaque or resource-intensive. The authors want a method that is simpler, interpretable, and robust for syntactically complex sentences.

Method: They introduce a fixed-length inventory vector representation for each sentence, called a “Morphosyntacton.” This vector consists of counts of part-of-speech tags, dependency relations, and explicit futurate patterns, without using pretrained embeddings, padding, sequence models, or large language models. They then train a multiclass classifier (details not in abstract, but presumably a standard ML model) to predict the sentence’s global reference interval: past, present, or future.

Result: On a dataset of 1,799 syntactically complex English sentences annotated with past/present/future global reference intervals, their method attains balanced and high multiclass classification performance, with an overall accuracy of 92%.

Conclusion: A lightweight, interpretable morphosyntactic feature representation—without embeddings or sequence models—can successfully capture a sentence’s dominant temporal orientation, even in syntactically complex cases, achieving strong performance on a challenging three-way classification task.

Abstract: Computational methods have consistently struggled to determine the dominant temporal orientation of a sentence. This difficulty is especially pronounced when a sentence contains multiple embedded clauses with competing tense and aspectual information. To address this difficulty, we propose an alternative approach for identifying a sentence's past, present, or future global reference interval. Our method does not use any form of pretrained embeddings. We rather encode sentences using fixed-length inventory vectors that are comprised of part-of-speech counts, dependency relation counts, and explicit futurate pattern counts. We term this inventory vector of a sentence a "Morphosyntacton". The method does not use any padding, sequence models, or large language models. Evaluation on 1,799 syntactically complex English sentences, annotated as past, present or future, shows balanced and high accuracy multiclass classification, achieving an overall multi-class accuracy of 92%.

</details>


### [81] [Knowing Is Not Choosing: What Explicit Verification Adds Beyond Generative Preference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33142)
*Yilong Li,Chengpo Yan,Aayan Arish,Suman Banerjee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that language models often fail factual recall not because they can’t generate the right answer, but because they don’t reliably select it among candidates; adding an explicit truthfulness-verification step improves ranking and overall accuracy across several model families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many evaluations assume that if a language model can assign high probability to a correct answer, it will also output it as the final response. However, models can generate correct and incorrect candidates together and then pick a wrong one, especially under sampling or with strong prior-answer biases. The authors want to disentangle generation from selection in factual recall, understand where failures occur, and test whether explicit truth-verification can improve which answer is ultimately chosen.

Method: They decompose factual QA into: (1) generating candidate answers, (2) ranking these candidates, and (3) selecting the final answer. Using multiple model families (Gemma, Qwen3, Llama), they first use pre-generation readouts (like token log-likelihoods) to predict recall and coverage under sampling. Then they introduce an explicit verification signal, P(True), which estimates the probability that each candidate is factually correct. They compare P(True)-based ranking against standard mean log-likelihood–based ranking, measuring AUROC improvements. In a prospectively defined cohort for Gemma, they evaluate how using verification to choose the final answer affects plurality accuracy, including comparisons to a stronger chat-template likelihood baseline. They also analyze how performance depends on answer priors and entity access (masking the entity) and compare different correctness definitions: reference-based automatic matching versus human semantic judgments.

Result: Across Gemma, Qwen3, and Llama, pre-generation metrics are good at predicting whether a model knows the fact at all and which questions sampling will cover, but they poorly predict whether the model will actually select the correct answer. Adding explicit verification via P(True) substantially improves within-question ranking over mean log-likelihood, with AUROC gains of 0.08–0.12. In Gemma’s prospective cohort, verification increases plurality accuracy by about 5 percentage points relative to a simple generative baseline and still yields about 2 points improvement over a stronger chat-template likelihood baseline. The benefit is largest for factual relations that have strong common-answer priors (e.g., popular or default answers) and critically requires access to the entity; when the entity is masked, larger Qwen models lose the ranking advantage from verification. The measured gain is also sensitive to the evaluation metric: reference-based, recall-oriented matching credits long or enumerated option lists that likelihood tends to favor, making the verification gains look smaller than they appear under human semantic correctness judgments, where verification’s advantage is more evident.

Conclusion: Factual recall in language models should be viewed as a multi-stage process where failure often arises at the ranking/selection stage, not just at generation. Simple likelihood scores are not sufficient for choosing the best answer among candidates. An explicit verification mechanism that estimates the truth probability of each candidate can meaningfully improve ranking quality and overall accuracy across different model families, especially for queries with strong prior-answer biases and when entity information is available. Standard automatic reference-matching metrics may underestimate these improvements compared to human semantic judgments, implying that better evaluation practices are needed to capture the value of verification-based methods.

Abstract: Generating a correct answer does not mean that a language model will select it. We separate factual recall into three steps: generating a correct candidate, ranking the available candidates, and selecting the final answer. Pre-generation readouts predict factual recall and which questions sampling will cover across three model families, but say little about whether an available correct answer will ultimately be selected. Explicit verification with $P(\mathrm{True})$ improves within-question ranking over mean log-likelihood in Gemma, Qwen3, and Llama, with AUROC gains of $0.08$--$0.12$. In a prospectively defined Gemma cohort, verification raises plurality accuracy by about $5$ points, and still gains about $2$ points over chat-template likelihood, a stronger generative baseline. The advantage is strongest for relations with common-answer priors and depends on access to the entity; masking the entity removes the ranking advantage in larger Qwen models. Finally, the measured benefit depends on how correctness is defined: recall-oriented reference matching can credit option lists favored by likelihood and substantially understate the improvement seen under human semantic judgments.

</details>


### [82] [CAME: Company-Aware Evidence-Memory Experts for Interpretable Quarter-Ahead Revenue Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33143)
*Ya-Wen Wu,Meng-Fen Chiang,Kuang-Da Wang,Wen-Chih Peng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A new framework, CAME, improves quarter-ahead company revenue forecasts by combining stable statistical anchors with LLM-based textual evidence and past error patterns, yielding lower errors and better interpretability than baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quarter-ahead revenue predictions must be numerically accurate at the firm level, temporally valid (no look-ahead leakage), and able to interpret company-specific narrative disclosures. Existing LLM approaches can leverage text but often misalign in scale, while pure historical/statistical methods are stable yet blind to contemporaneous qualitative signals like product changes, supply issues, and guidance. There is a need for a method that integrates the strengths of both while remaining auditable and leak-free.

Method: The authors propose CAME (Company-Aware Evidence-Memory Experts), a residual-forecasting framework. It starts from a no-leakage statistical anchor forecast and then conditionally adjusts it using two key inputs: (1) current semantic evidence extracted from narrative disclosures via LLM-style processing and (2) patterns in prior forecast errors. CAME uses these to decide when and how much to adjust the anchor forecast, while organizing the supporting textual evidence into source-linked 'evidence cards' and maintaining guarded memory traces to prevent leakage and support interpretability.

Result: On a rolling backtest covering 336 company-quarters for 12 large public technology and platform firms (with development data included in the rolling evaluation), CAME attains the lowest aggregate point-estimate error among all compared methods. It delivers statistically significant improvements in macro-sMAPE over the matched Statistical Anchor and beats a History + Guidance baseline across all six reported aggregate metrics.

Conclusion: CAME successfully combines statistical anchors with LLM-derived semantic signals and historical error patterns to improve quarter-ahead revenue forecasting. It not only enhances predictive accuracy over established baselines but also maintains interpretability and auditability by tying forecast adjustments to explicit evidence cards and controlled memory traces, aiding forecast inspection, provenance tracking, and diagnosing failures.

Abstract: Quarter-ahead revenue forecasting requires company-scale numerical accuracy, strict temporal validity, and company-specific interpretation of narrative disclosures. LLMs can distill textual evidence but can produce scale-misaligned forecasts, whereas history-based anchors are stable but miss forecast-time signals such as product transitions, supply constraints, and management guidance. We introduce CAME (Company-Aware Evidence-Memory Experts), a residual-forecasting framework that refines a no-leakage statistical anchor when current semantic evidence and prior error patterns justify an adjustment. On a development-inclusive rolling backtest of 336 company-quarters from 12 large public technology and platform firms, CAME achieves the lowest aggregate point-estimate error among the reported methods, with statistically supported macro-sMAPE gains over the matched Statistical Anchor, and outperforms History + Guidance on all six aggregate metrics. CAME also links adjustments to source-linked evidence cards and guarded memory traces, supporting forecast inspection, provenance, and failure localization.

</details>


### [83] [Generalization Dynamics of LM Pre-training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33150)
*Jiaxin Wen,Zhengxuan Wu,Dawn Song,Lijie Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that during pre-training, language models do not steadily become more intelligent but instead abruptly switch back and forth between shallow pattern-matching and deeper, generalizable reasoning, a phenomenon the authors call mode-hopping.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The common mental model is that as language models are pre-trained longer, they gradually evolve from simple pattern-matching systems into more broadly intelligent, generalizing systems. This assumption underlies how researchers interpret scaling laws, choose final checkpoints, and design training curricula. The authors suspect this picture is inaccurate and want to rigorously test how generalization and reasoning actually evolve during pre-training. They are particularly interested in understanding why models sometimes appear intelligent and aligned and at other times behave like brittle parrots, and in finding practical ways to exploit or control these dynamics.

Method: The authors construct a toy but carefully designed evaluation suite to probe different facets of generalization versus shallow behavior across pre-training. The suite includes tests that distinguish memorization or in-context pattern-matching from genuine in-context learning, System 1 (fast, heuristic) from System 2 (deliberative) reasoning, truthfulness from plausibility, multi-hop persona question answering, out-of-context reasoning, and emergent misalignment behaviors. They evaluate many intermediate pre-training checkpoints on these tasks and track performance trajectories. They analyze the dynamics of sudden performance jumps and regressions, test whether checkpoint averaging removes instabilities, and explore how capacity constraints and data ordering might induce competition between shallow and deeper circuits. They then use these insights to select specific pre-training checkpoints and data slices that improve and stabilize generalization and alignment properties.

Result: Across their eval suite, the authors find that language models do not monotonically progress from parrot-like to intelligent behavior. Instead, performance on reasoning, generalization, and alignment-related tasks exhibits abrupt phase changes: models suddenly start relying on memorized or surface patterns, switch from more reflective to purely heuristic reasoning, prefer statements that sound true over actually true ones, and fail at multi-hop persona QA and out-of-context reasoning; later, they can just as sharply revert to more generalizable behavior. These oscillations—mode-hopping—are locally stable and persist under checkpoint averaging, indicating they are not merely noise from optimization stochasticity. The behavior aligns with a capacity allocation view where shallow circuits learned early in training compete with later-emerging generalizable circuits, with the training data in each window influencing which circuits dominate. Using their suite, the authors identify intermediate pre-training checkpoints that outperform both mid- and final checkpoints on reasoning and alignment metrics, and they show that targeted pre-training data selection can shape and stabilize generalization dynamics.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that the standard view of smooth, monotonic maturation from pattern-matching to intelligence in language models is incorrect. Instead, models undergo discrete, sometimes repeated transitions between shallow and deep computation modes—mode-hopping—driven by how limited capacity is allocated among competing circuits over the course of training. This has both conceptual and practical implications: (i) evaluations of model capability and alignment should examine trajectories over many checkpoints rather than only the final model, and (ii) careful checkpoint selection and pre-training data curation can yield models with stronger and more stable generalization and alignment than those obtained by naively using the last checkpoint. Their evaluation suite offers a lightweight tool to study and control these dynamics, potentially informing better training regimes for future language models.

Abstract: People typically assume that LMs stably mature from pattern-matching parrots to generalizable intelligence during pre-training. We build a toy eval suite and show this mental model is wrong: throughout pre-training, LMs frequently and suddenly hop between parrot-like and intelligence-like computations. We call this mode-hopping. Across our suite, LMs suddenly latch onto memorized or in-context patterns instead of in-context learning, use System 1 instead of System 2 thinking, pick up what sounds true instead of what is true, fail at multi-hop persona QA, out-of-context reasoning, and emergent misalignment -- then just as suddenly revert and generalize. Mode-hopping is not explained by standard optimization dynamics: it is locally stable and cannot be fixed by checkpoint averaging. We instead think of it as a capacity allocation problem: in a capacity-bounded model, generalizable circuits must compete with the shallow ones learned early in training, and the data in each pre-training window may decide which circuits win. Our suite provides a new efficient lens on generalization. We demonstrate two concrete applications: (i) select intermediate pre-training checkpoints that strongly generalize reasoning and alignment, better than the final pre- or mid-training checkpoints, and (ii) select pre-training data that controls and stabilizes generalization dynamics.

</details>


### [84] [Where Do Test-Time Scaling and Training Fall Short in Individual Stance Prediction?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33155)
*Yuyang Zhao,Xuan Liu,HaoYang Shangm Haojian Jin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes why standard test-time scaling and post-training methods underperform on predicting an individual’s stance from their past comments, identifies four systematic failure modes, introduces a benchmark (STANCE-BENCH), and proposes a simple scoring-plus-evidence method that yields modest but meaningful gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While test-time scaling (e.g., sampling multiple outputs) and post-training methods (supervised fine-tuning and RL) have boosted LLMs on coding and math, it is unclear whether they work for personalized stance prediction—inferring how a specific person will respond in a new discussion given their history. This capability is important for applications like personalized recommendation, moderation, and modeling online communities, but standard LLM improvement techniques might behave differently in this setting. The authors aim to rigorously test these methods, uncover their failure modes, and understand how to better leverage a user’s prior discussion history when predicting stances.

Method: The authors construct STANCE-BENCH, a benchmark of 2,499 stance-prediction tasks derived from 500 Hacker News users’ histories. For each task, the model must predict the user’s stance in a new discussion using their previous comments. They systematically evaluate widely used techniques: (a) test-time scaling strategies (multiple sampling and selection schemes), and (b) post-training methods, including supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). They analyze failures across three stages—generation (what candidate stances are produced), selection (which one is chosen), and learning (how training changes behavior)—and formalize four failure modes. Based on their insights, they design a simple method: score each candidate stance directly and augment this with explicit assessments of how strongly the user’s history supports each stance, then combine these signals for final prediction. Performance is measured using discussion-specific Macro F1 on a held-out test set of 781 tasks, primarily with Qwen3-8B as the base model.

Result: Empirical evaluation on STANCE-BENCH reveals four consistent failure modes: (1) Incorrect consensus—test-time scaling yields many agreeing samples, but they converge on the wrong stance; (2) Selection failure—generation includes the correct stance among candidates, yet the selection procedure fails to pick it; (3) Response overfitting—SFT makes models better at imitating observed responses but worse at actually predicting new ones; and (4) Early plateau—RL yields small early gains that quickly saturate, providing limited additional improvement with more training. Using Qwen3-8B on the 781-task test set, the proposed combined scoring-plus-evidence method improves discussion-specific Macro F1 from 19.27 (direct scoring only) to 21.83, demonstrating a measurable but still modest gain over standard approaches.

Conclusion: Standard tools that work well for improving LLMs on coding and math—test-time scaling, supervised fine-tuning, and RL—do not straightforwardly transfer to the task of predicting an individual’s stance from their history. The identified failure modes show that problems arise in candidate generation, selection, and learned behavior, and that blindly scaling samples or training can even hurt prediction quality. A simple approach that jointly considers direct stance scores and explicit evidence from a person’s past comments achieves better performance, though there remains substantial headroom. The authors argue that future work on personalized stance prediction should: (1) evaluate generation, selection, and evidence use as separate components; (2) design methods explicitly tailored to leveraging person-specific histories; and (3) use STANCE-BENCH as a standardized benchmark for diagnosing and improving stance-prediction systems.

Abstract: Test-time scaling and post-training have improved LLM performance in coding and mathematical reasoning, but their effectiveness for individual stance prediction remains unclear. We study this question by predicting a person's stance in a new discussion from their history. We evaluate widely used test-time scaling strategies and post-training methods, such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and identify four failure modes across generation, selection, and learning: (1) incorrect consensus, where repeated samples agree on the wrong stance; (2) selection failure, where generation covers the observed stance but selection misses it; (3) response overfitting, where supervised fine-tuning improves imitation but harms prediction; and (4) early plateau, where reinforcement learning shows modest initial gains followed by limited further improvement. We expose these failures using STANCE-BENCH, which contains 2499 prediction tasks from 500 Hacker News users. Guided by this analysis, we explore a simple approach that combines direct scores for all candidate stances with explicit assessments of support from the individual's history. On the 781-task test set, this approach achieves 21.83 discussion-specific Macro F1 with Qwen3-8B, compared with 19.27 for direct scoring. Our results motivate evaluating candidate generation, final selection, and person-specific evidence use separately.

</details>


### [85] [Scoring the Wrong Question: Readout Failures in Constrained-Option Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33179)
*Jiaxuan Guo,Kejia Zhang,Shuo Xin,Jingxin Yang,Youran Sun,Haizhao Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that standard constrained-option probability scoring can completely mis-evaluate how well a model’s forecast scores track actual correctness, because the model is often about to output something else (e.g., an answer letter) with most of its probability mass. By pre-filling an answer stem and analyzing option-token mass, the authors both diagnose and substantially improve forecast quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Probabilistic evaluations of language models often rely on reading off probabilities assigned to a fixed set of options (e.g., answer choices or True/False) under the assumption that these scores reflect the model’s true beliefs about those options. However, models frequently allocate most probability to different continuations (like starting to answer a quoted question), so the constrained-option scores can be misleading and near-random as predictors of correctness. The authors aim to understand and fix these failure modes, especially in forecasting tasks such as predicting whether another model will answer correctly.

Method: The authors design a prompt that embeds a multiple-choice question and its answer instruction, then asks a forecaster model to predict whether a separate reader model, given a short note, will answer correctly. Using constrained-option scoring, they analyze output-token distributions for various checkpoints (notably Qwen3) and observe that an answer-letter token is typically the most probable first token, not the intended forecast token. They introduce: (1) a label-free diagnostic based on the total first-token probability mass allocated to the declared options in context; (2) deletion tests to trace how the answer-letter bias arises from the quoted instruction; and (3) rendering/tokenisation checks for dropped separators and overlapping first tokens. They then modify the prompt by pre-filling an answer stem before scoring the options, and systematically compare AUC/AUROC across checkpoints and tasks (MMLU, TriviaQA), including for lm-polygraph’s P(True) estimator and several alternative renormalisation strategies over the same logits.

Result: Without prompt repair, constrained-option scores yield almost chance-level discrimination of reader correctness: for Qwen3 checkpoints, the forecaster’s option ranking AUC is about 0.4929, and lm-polygraph’s default P(True) is at or below chance on MMLU and TriviaQA. Diagnostics show that, in the problematic prompts, the model assigns most first-token probability mass to unintended tokens (answer letters or schema labels) rather than the declared forecast options, indicating low support for the scored options. When the authors prefill an answer stem and then score/renormalise over the same options, the median option mass increases from below 0.5 to above 0.5 on all nine checkpoints and the Qwen3-averaged AUC improves to 0.6152. For lm-polygraph, renormalising only over the intended (A)/(B) or True/False labels—especially after an answer stem—raises AUROC up to 0.632–0.868, outperforming all fourteen default single-answer estimators on TriviaQA. Yet the original forecast, even when renormalised, remains near chance because the underlying option mass is low.

Conclusion: Constrained-option probabilities are unreliable when the model’s probability mass is not actually centered on the declared options; in such cases, renormalisation alone cannot fix the forecast quality. Simple diagnostics like checking the raw probability mass on the first tokens of the options can flag when options are poorly supported, and deletions plus tokenisation analysis can pinpoint prompt features (e.g., quoted answer instructions) that cause the model to favour unintended continuations. Pre-filling an answer stem to redirect probability mass onto the desired options can significantly improve forecast discrimination, but only if those options genuinely capture where the model wants to place its probability. Evaluators should therefore (1) measure option support directly and (2) carefully design prompts or prefill strategies, rather than trusting raw constrained-option scores or default P(True)-style estimators.

Abstract: Constrained-option scoring reads a model's probabilities for a fixed set of permitted answers, so it returns a score even when the model is about to write something else. We study a prompt that quotes a multiple-choice item, ending in the item's own answer instruction, and asks for a forecast of whether a reader model given only a short note will answer it correctly. The model can begin answering the quoted item: on three Qwen3 checkpoints an answer letter is the most probable token on nearly every passage, and the forecast ranks the reader's correctness indistinguishably from chance. Beyond prior work's argmax check and prefill repair, we contribute a label-free diagnostic of the declared options' support, their first-token mass in context; a deletion test tracing the Qwen3 answer-letter start to the quoted instruction; and rendering and tokenisation checks for dropped separators and coinciding first tokens. Prefilling an answer stem lifts the median option mass from below to above one half on all nine checkpoints scored with this prompt and, with options and renormalisation unchanged, raises the Qwen3-averaged AUC from 0.4929 to 0.6152. lm-polygraph's default P(True) estimator shows a related failure: it reads True where Qwen3 without thinking favours an answer letter (MMLU) or the prompt's (A)/(B) label (TriviaQA), and its Qwen3-averaged AUROC is indistinguishable from chance on MMLU and below chance on TriviaQA. Scoring and renormalising the (A)/(B) labels after an answer stem raises it to 0.632 and 0.868, renormalising True against False in place reaches 0.660 and 0.860, and on TriviaQA both exceed all fourteen default single-answer library estimators. The original forecast is renormalised too, yet stays indistinguishable from chance: option mass flags low support in both settings without labels, and only checking the intended target shows which score still ranks.

</details>


### [86] [Identifying Temporal Features within Transcoders for Time Sensitive Factual Recall](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33183)
*Sanjay Govindan,Yang Song,Maurice Pagnucco*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper maps how specific MLP features in LLMs implement time-sensitive factual recall, revealing parallel chrono-semantic mechanisms and introducing transcoders as a stronger interpretability tool than existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs often output outdated or temporally inconsistent facts because their training data mixes information from different times. Existing fixes like fine-tuning or RAG are costly and do not explain *how* time is internally represented. Prior interpretability work focuses on coarse components (layers, heads), lacking a fine-grained, feature-level view of temporal recall, so the authors aim to uncover the internal feature circuits responsible for time-aware factual recall and misalignment.

Method: Use transcoder circuit tracing to isolate individual MLP features involved in temporal recall across several models (Gemma 2 2B, LLaMA 3.2 1B, Qwen3-4B). Analyze how these features activate during time-sensitive factual queries and categorize them into three node types (common temporal, common-to-year, chrono-semantic). Compare their structure and layerwise behavior to prior attributions obtained with EAP-IG and study their interactions to infer the computation of a temporal filter for factual recall.

Result: They produce a feature-level map of temporal recall, identifying three interacting node categories that together form a temporal filter for factual recall. They show that temporal processing is not a simple linear, layer-by-layer pipeline but a parallel, mixed syntactic-semantic process distributed across layers. They also find higher-layer temporal components that existing EAP-IG attribution methods fail to capture, demonstrating that transcoder-based analysis recovers additional, important temporal circuitry.

Conclusion: Temporal knowledge in LLMs is implemented via distributed, parallel MLP feature circuits that mix syntactic and semantic information instead of a single linear pipeline. Transcoder circuit tracing reveals previously hidden temporal components, making it a more complete interpretability tool than standard EAP-IG methods. The identified MLP features and node types offer concrete targets for future interventions to improve time-sensitive factual recall without costly fine-tuning or heavy RAG setups.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) suffer from temporal misalignment, often due to the contradictory nature of their training corpora. While current mitigation strategies rely on computationally expensive fine-tuning or context-heavy retrieval augmented generation (RAG), the internal mechanisms governing time-sensitive recall remain under-explored. Unlike prior studies that identify temporal components such as attention heads and MLP layers, we provide the first feature-level map of temporal recall by isolating individual MLP features via transcoder circuit tracing. We identify three node categories (common temporal, common to the year, and chrono-semantic) which interact to generate a temporal filter during factual recall. By analysing Gemma 2 2B, LLaMA 3.2 1B, and Qwen3-4B, we show that these features do not follow a simple linear pipeline but represent time through a parallel and mixed syntactic-semantic interplay across layers. We additionally discover a class of higher-layer temporal components invisible to existing EAP-IG methods, establishing transcoders as a more complete lens for temporal interpretability in time-sensitive factual recall. These findings present MLP components for potential targeted interventions in time-sensitive factual recall

</details>


### [87] [Turning Speech Language Models into Multilingual Listeners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33204)
*Tolúlopé Ògúnrèmí,Dan Jurafsky,Chris Manning,Ahmet Üstün,Martijn Bartelds*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build a large multilingual spoken QA dataset and benchmark to improve and evaluate Speech Language Models across 23 languages, showing synthetic data can significantly boost multilingual SLM performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Speech Language Models mainly support a few high-resource languages because there is a lack of large-scale, instruction-style spoken QA data covering many languages. This limits access for speakers of low- and mid-resource languages and hinders fair evaluation of multilingual SLMs. The authors want to close this resource gap and provide both training data and a standardized benchmark for multilingual spoken question answering.

Method: They synthetically generate a massive multilingual spoken QA dataset (MULTISPEECHQA) and then apply human verification for quality control. The dataset consists of 9200 hours and 10.8 million spoken question–answer pairs in 23 typologically diverse languages. From it, they construct MULTISPEECH-BENCH, a multi-task evaluation benchmark for SLMs in those languages. They then compare a cascade pipeline (ASR + text LLM) with various open-weight and proprietary SLMs on the benchmark, and finally finetune Qwen 2.5-Omni on MULTISPEECHQA to measure performance gains.

Result: MULTISPEECHQA provides large-scale, high-quality multilingual spoken QA data across 23 languages, and MULTISPEECH-BENCH offers a standardized evaluation suite. Experimental results show the cascade system outperforms existing open-weight SLMs but still lags behind the best closed-source SLMs on the benchmark. Finetuning Qwen 2.5-Omni on MULTISPEECHQA leads to improved performance on MULTISPEECH-BENCH, validating the dataset’s effectiveness.

Conclusion: High-quality, synthetically generated and human-verified speech QA data can substantially improve the multilingual capabilities of Speech Language Models in a cost-effective way. MULTISPEECHQA and MULTISPEECH-BENCH fill an important resource and evaluation gap for 23 diverse languages and enable both better training and more systematic comparison of multilingual SLM systems.

Abstract: Speech Language Models (SLMs) that understand spoken language questions support only a few high-resource languages, limiting access to millions of people worldwide. This gap stems from the scarcity of multilingual speech instruction-tuning datasets. We present MULTISPEECHQA, a large-scale, synthetically generated and human-verified dataset comprising 9200 hours of 10.8 million spoken question-answer pairs in 23 typologically diverse languages. Using MULTISPEECHQA, we also introduce MULTISPEECH-BENCH, a multi-task benchmark for evaluating SLM performance on 23 languages. We compare the performance of a cascading system to open-weight and closed SLMs on MULTISPEECH-BENCH and find that the cascading system outperforms open-weight SLMs but not all closed SLMs. We use MULTISPEECHQA to finetune Qwen 2.5-Omni, which improves its performance on our benchmark. Our findings show that high-quality synthetic datasets offer a cheap solution to improving the multilingual capabilities of SLMs.

</details>


### [88] [Beyond Calibration: Do a Typed-Decision Model's Probabilities Obey the Probability Axioms?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33209)
*Keyi Li,Yihao He,Quanyi Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates the probabilistic coherence of typed-decision models (which output probabilities over answers rather than text) by checking whether their probabilities over logically related queries are mutually consistent, revealing substantial incoherence even in a model specifically designed for probabilistic outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional evaluation of typed-decision models focuses on accuracy and calibration for individual questions, but ignores whether probabilities assigned to logically related questions (e.g., a proposition and its negation) are mutually consistent. Systems that use these probabilities for downstream decision-making require logically coherent probability assignments; inconsistencies can induce irrational or exploitable behavior. The authors aim to fill this gap by proposing a label-free, logic-based coherence test and applying it to both a purpose-built probabilistic model (Jev) and a standard language model (Qwen3.8-27B).

Method: The authors construct a battery of logically linked yes/no and multiple-choice queries that do not require ground-truth labels. Using 160 three-label items from ChaosNLI and PubMedQA, they ask four related questions per item: (1) whether the label is X, (2) whether it is not X, (3) whether it is one of the other two labels, and (4) which of the three labels applies. This yields 480 negation pairs of the form “label is X” vs “label is not X.” They then examine the extent to which model-assigned probabilities respect the logical constraints—for example, that P(label is X) + P(label is not X) ≈ 1, and that the three single-label probabilities sum to 1. They compare Jev (a typed-decision model) with Qwen3.8-27B, using both first-token readouts and verbalized probabilities, and analyze where and how the coherence violations arise, also comparing them against Jev’s repeat-call noise.

Result: On the 480 negation pairs, Jev’s probabilities for “label is X” and “label is not X” fail to sum to 1 by an average of 0.064 (95% CI [0.055, 0.072]). Qwen3.8-27B is substantially worse: the mismatch is 0.293 using first-token probabilities and 0.122 using verbalized probabilities. Jev’s incoherence is still statistically significant, with violations about five times larger than its own repeat-sampling noise and with a tendency to over-endorse individual labels so that the three single-label probabilities sum to about 1.14 on average. Qwen3.8-27B’s first-token readout systematically under-assigns probability to complements of labels regardless of the presence of “not,” frequently rejecting both a statement and its negation (196 out of 480 pairs), and it does not become more coherent on higher-confidence items. In contrast, Jev’s largest violations cluster on questions where its own answers are uncertain. The study documents that both models fail coherence but with qualitatively distinct patterns.

Conclusion: Typed-decision models and standard LMs can exhibit substantial probabilistic incoherence across logically related questions, even when they perform adequately in terms of accuracy and calibration on isolated items. The proposed label-free coherence checks reveal inconsistencies and biases that are invisible to standard evaluations and that may severely limit the reliability of probabilistic outputs for downstream decision-making. Jev, despite being designed for probabilistic output, still shows meaningful incoherence—though less severe and differently structured than Qwen3.8-27B’s first-token probabilities. The authors argue that future development and evaluation of probabilistic NLP models should explicitly target coherence across logically related questions, not just item-wise accuracy or calibration, and that their methodology provides a practical diagnostic tool for uncovering such issues.

Abstract: Typed-decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev answer a declared yes/no or multiple-choice question about a state with a probability instead of text, and their evaluations report accuracy and calibration. Neither requires that the probabilities a model gives to logically related questions fit together item by item, which is what a system that acts on those probabilities needs. We test this property, coherence, with a battery of logically linked questions that needs no labels. For 160 items from ChaosNLI and PubMedQA, each with three mutually exclusive labels, we ask whether the label is X, whether it is not X, whether it is one of the other two labels, and which label applies. On 480 negation pairs, Jev's probabilities for "the label is X" and "the label is not X" miss summing to one by 0.064 on average (95% CI 0.055 to 0.072). Qwen3.8-27B, run from its official BF16 weights, misses by 0.293 with first-token probabilities and by 0.122 with verbalized probabilities. The gap to the first-token readout persists on pairs where both systems give similar probabilities, without double-negation labels, and after averaging Jev's repeated calls. Jev is not coherent either: its violations are about five times its repeat noise, and it over-endorses statements about single labels, so that its three single-label probabilities sum to 1.14 on average. The two systems also fail differently. Qwen3.8-27B's first-token readout under-endorses the complement of a label whether or not the question contains "not", rejecting both a statement and its negation in 196 of 480 pairs, and it does not become more coherent where it is more confident, whereas Jev's violations concentrate where its answer is uncertain. Because the checks need no labels, they expose biases that appear only when question forms are compared, and inconsistencies within items.

</details>


### [89] [CoLMbo-SV: A Grounded Language Model for Explainable Speaker Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33212)
*Massa Baali,Sarthak Bisht,Ziyue Qiu,Joseph Konan,Rita Singh,Bhiksha Raj*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces CoLMbo-SV, a speaker verification model that joins a pretrained speaker encoder with a language model to provide both high-accuracy verification and interpretable, acoustically grounded comparison reports, along with a new dataset (VoxReason) and evaluation framework for aligning explanations with model decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional speaker verification systems are highly accurate but opaque: they do not expose which acoustic cues drive their decisions, and existing explanation approaches either reduce accuracy or restrict reasoning to what can be verbalized. The authors aim to build a system that keeps state-of-the-art verification performance while producing structured, checkable, and acoustically grounded natural-language explanations of its judgments, and to rigorously evaluate how explanations relate to encoded information and decision-making.

Method: The authors connect a strong pretrained speaker encoder to a language model and feed it explicit acoustic measurements so the model can generate natural-language comparison reports grounded in measurable acoustic properties, while still relying on the full latent representation for verification decisions. They construct VoxReason, a dataset of paired recordings annotated with measured acoustic properties and curated comparison reports that pass numerical and qualitative checks, to supervise both verification and explanation. They also design an evaluation framework that disentangles: (1) what acoustic information is present in the speaker representation, (2) what information influences the verification score, and (3) what information is verbalized in the explanation, with metrics including EER and numerical grounding scores.

Result: On the VoxCeleb1-O benchmark, CoLMbo-SV achieves a 0.99% equal error rate (EER), an ~80% relative error reduction compared to the strongest audio-language baseline fine-tuned on VoxReason. It also attains a numerical-grounding score of 0.82, indicating that its textual reports are largely consistent with explicit acoustic measurements. Analyses show that while the system can be acoustically correct in its explanations, this correctness does not fully capture whether the explained factors actually drive the verification decision, highlighting a gap in current explanation metrics.

Conclusion: CoLMbo-SV significantly narrows the performance gap between audio-language speaker verification models and dedicated speaker encoders while adding structured, acoustically grounded, and checkable natural-language explanations. The new VoxReason dataset and the proposed evaluation framework enable systematic study of how explanations relate to internal representations and decisions, revealing that acoustic correctness and decision relevance are distinct and both need to be considered. These contributions advance inspectable speaker verification and provide tools for empirically tying natural-language explanations to the decisions they purport to justify.

Abstract: Speaker verification systems achieve high accuracy but provide little account of the acoustic evidence behind their judgments. Making these systems inspectable requires exposing interpretable evidence while retaining the richer information on which their decisions depend. We present \textbf{CoLMbo-SV}, a speaker language model that combines strong speaker discrimination with structured, acoustically grounded comparison reports. By connecting a pretrained speaker encoder to a language model and supplying explicit acoustic measurements, CoLMbo-SV makes voice comparisons inspectable without restricting verification to the evidence verbalized in its reports. We additionally introduce \textbf{VoxReason}, paired recordings with measured acoustic properties and comparison reports filtered through numerical and qualitative checks, providing supervision for this combined capability. We also develop an evaluation framework that separates what acoustic information a speaker representation encodes, what influences the verification score, and what the generated report discusses. On VoxCeleb1-O, CoLMbo-SV achieves 0.99\% EER, reducing verification error by approximately 80\% relative to the strongest audio-language baseline fine-tuned on VoxReason, while attaining a numerical-grounding score of 0.82. Our analysis further demonstrates that acoustic correctness and decision relevance are distinct properties of an explanation, exposing a gap that numerical-grounding metrics miss. Together, these contributions substantially advance audio-language speaker verification, bring its accuracy toward that of dedicated speaker encoders while adding checkable acoustic reporting, and establish an empirical framework for connecting natural-language explanations to the decisions they explain.

</details>


### [90] [Beyond Memory Construction: Rethinking Memory Access for LLM-based Conversational Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33226)
*Donghua Cai,Yongheng Deng,Yifei Wang,Zijun Shen,Ju Ren*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes Threader, a memory system that drops LLM-based rewriting and instead keeps raw conversations, segments them by topic, and retrieves them with multi-view, multi-signal methods to get better accuracy and lower cost in long, complex dialogues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-centric memory construction pipelines for conversational agents work in small or simple contexts but fail in long, high-entropy dialogues: they lose information, become unstable, and are too expensive due to repeated LLM calls.

Method: Introduce Threader, which treats raw conversational interactions as primary memory, performs lightweight incremental topic segmentation to form coherent segments, builds multi-view representations of these segments, and at query time uses multi-signal retrieval combining segment-level selection with fine-grained evidence matching.

Result: Experiments show Threader yields higher answer accuracy and better evidence recall than prior LLM-based memory construction approaches, while also greatly cutting the computational and monetary overhead associated with memory construction.

Conclusion: Shifting from heavy LLM-based memory construction to efficient, structure-aware access over raw interactions—via segmentation, multi-view representation, and multi-signal retrieval—provides a more accurate and cost-effective memory system for long, complex conversational agents.

Abstract: Memory is a core component of conversational agents, enabling coherent and context-aware behavior over long interactions. Recent approaches commonly rely on LLM-based memory construction, where raw interactions are rewritten into structured memory units and later retrieved via a RAG pipeline. While effective in controlled settings, we show that this paradigm breaks down in long-horizon, high-entropy conversations: memory construction becomes increasingly lossy and unstable as context length and information complexity grow, and incurs prohibitive cost due to repeated LLM invocation. To address these limitations, we propose Threader, a memory system that shifts the focus from memory construction to efficient, structure-aware access over raw interactions. Instead of rewriting interactions, Threader preserves them as first-class memory, organizes them into topic-coherent segments via lightweight incremental segmentation, and enables accurate retrieval through multi-view representation. At query time, it performs multi-signal retrieval that combines segment-level access with localized evidence matching, ensuring both completeness and coherence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Threader consistently improves answer accuracy and evidence recall, while significantly reducing the memory construction overhead.

</details>


### [91] [The Text Beside the Image: Detection, Utility and Leakage for Trustworthy Multimodal Medical Data and Beyond](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33280)
*Andreas Maier,Monica Hinrichs-Mayer,Franziska Weber,Niklas Lackner,Matthias May,Bernhard Kainz,Siming Bayer*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates how well different pseudonymisation policies protect identities in text associated with medical images while preserving utility, using multi-language, multi-domain corpora and multiple detectors and linkage attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Releasing medical images with accompanying text reports can leak patient identity even if images are protected. There is a lack of systematic, quantitative evaluation of text pseudonymisation policies that considers both detection performance and residual identity leakage across languages and domains.

Method: The authors compare 15 identifier detectors and three release conditions (likely different pseudonymisation policies) across four text corpora: medical reports, legal judgments, news/other genres, and e-mails in German, English, Chinese, and Arabic. They measure detector sensitivity and specificity, then perform two re-identification attacks: frequency matching against public name lists and cross-document linkage, both with and without training, to quantify residual identity leakage. A fixed ensemble of 13 detectors (union) is the main configuration under test.

Result: The 13-detector ensemble achieves very high person sensitivity with moderate to high specificity across domains: 0.9998/0.8686 on medical reports, 0.9958/0.8504 on legal judgments, 0.9352/0.9318 on news/other, and 0.9906/0.6235 on e-mails. Frequency-matching attacks recover zero identities via alignment when the ensemble is used; any correctly guessed names are those missed and left in clear text. Cross-document linkage still recovers some identities but at sharply reduced rates compared with unmodified text: on e-mail, 0.93% (no training) and 3.94% (with training) vs 71.98% on unmodified text; on medical reports, 0% (no training) and 0.71% (with training) vs a 2.73% ceiling on unmodified text.

Conclusion: A strong ensemble pseudonymisation strategy using multiple detectors can provide very high coverage of person identifiers across languages and domains, substantially reducing identity leakage from both simple frequency-based and more advanced cross-document linkage attacks, while still leaving some small but nonzero residual risk. The work offers an empirical framework and baseline metrics for evaluating text pseudonymisation in medical and related document releases.

Abstract: Medical images are released with the reports that describe them, and protecting the image does not protect the report. This paper measures the text component of such releases. We measure identifier detection, downstream utility and residual identity leakage on the same documents, with the pseudonymisation policy as the variable under test: 15 detectors, three release conditions and four corpora of medical reports, legal judgments, news and other genres, and e-mail, in German, English, Chinese and Arabic. A fixed 13-detector union reaches a person sensitivity of 0.9998 at specificity 0.8686 on the medical reports, 0.9958 at 0.8504 on the legal judgments, 0.9352 at 0.9318 on news and other genres, and 0.9906 at 0.6235 on e-mail. With this ensemble, frequency matching with a public name list recovers zero identities by alignment across the four corpora; the names it got right were ones the detector missed, left in clear text. Cross-document linkage ranks the correct person first for 0.93% of e-mail queries without training and 3.94% with it, against 1/3697 chance and 71.98% on unmodified text. On the medical reports it recovers nothing without training and 0.71% of 138 queries with it, against 1/207 chance and a 2.73% ceiling on unmodified text.

</details>


### [92] [Calibration, Not Answer Selection: Distilling Internal Confidence in Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33290)
*Yadong Xi,Rongsheng Zhang,Tangjie Lv,Ziyang Luo,Ruochen Zhao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They find that current RL-trained reasoning models produce overconfident, poorly calibrated verbal confidence scores, and propose using a linear probe on internal states plus a self-distillation method (Probe-SD) to train models whose confidence is much better calibrated without changing test-time architecture.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reasoning models trained with reinforcement learning on binary correctness rewards tend to learn how to get answers right but not how to assign accurate probabilities to those answers.
