Their verbalized confidence correlates with willingness to commit, not true likelihood of correctness, and simple post-hoc rescaling of these scores fails to transfer across settings. There is a need for confidence signals that are both well-calibrated and usable without complex extra machinery at test time.

Method: The authors analyze internal activations between chain-of-thought and final answer and train a linear probe to predict correctness, evaluating its calibration versus verbalized confidence on factual QA tasks. They then introduce Probe-guided Self-Distillation (Probe-SD): sample multiple reasoning traces from the model, score each with the learned probe, overwrite the trace’s stated confidence with the probe’s score, and finetune the base model on these probe-labeled examples so that the model internalizes the calibrated confidence without needing the probe at inference.

Result: Across four benchmarks and two model families, the linear probe’s expected calibration error (ECE) is 5–38× lower than verbalized confidence, although it does not identify the best answer among multiple samples as well as an oracle. Using Probe-SD on Qwen3-14B yields a large calibration improvement: ECE drops from 0.178 to 0.024 in-domain and from 0.542 to 0.113 out-of-domain, outperforming post-hoc recalibration and self-consistency distillation, and enabling effective weighted voting using the model’s own calibrated confidence.

Conclusion: Internal representations in reasoning models contain a well-calibrated signal of certainty that is distinct from their ability to choose the correct answer among candidates. This signal is best used as a probability estimate, not as a selector. By distilling the probe’s calibrated confidence back into the base model via Probe-SD, one can obtain models whose verbalized confidences are substantially better calibrated and practically useful, achieving behaviors similar to RL-based methods using only supervised finetuning and without added inference-time complexity.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with binary correctness rewards trains correctness, not calibrated confidence. The confidence that reasoning models verbalize is systematically overconfident, and the problem is not merely one of scale: verbalized confidence tracks how willing a model is to commit to an answer, not how likely the answer is to be right. Post-hoc rescaling therefore fits one distribution but rarely transfers. We look inside the model instead. On factual question answering, a linear probe on the hidden state between the chain of thought and the answer is substantially better calibrated: its expected calibration error is 5 to 38 times lower than that of the verbalized score across four benchmarks and two model families. However, when used to pick among N sampled answers, that same probe nearly ties majority voting yet falls far short of the oracle. Internal states answer "how certain am I" well and "which answer is right" poorly, so the signal should be reported as a confidence rather than used to select answers. As a result, we introduce probe-guided self-distillation (Probe-SD): score a model's own sampled traces with the probe, overwrite the confidence each trace states, and finetune the base checkpoint of the same family, so nothing but the model itself remains at test time. On Qwen3-14B, Probe-SD cuts ECE from 0.178 to 0.024 in-domain and from 0.542 to 0.113 out-of-domain, where it also beats post-hoc recalibration and self-consistency distillation. The resulting confidence is well-calibrated and useful for weighted voting, behaviors previously attributed to online RL, here obtained with supervised finetuning alone.

</details>


### [93] [BaatCheet: A Multilingual Corpus for Dialogue Translation in Indian Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33296)
*Priyanka Dasari,Yuvrajsinh D. Bodana,Vandan Mujadia,Arafat Ahsan,Dipti Misra Sharma,Parameswari Krishnamurthy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces BaatCheet, a large multilingual Indic dialogue translation corpus and shows that fine-tuning open-source LLMs on it significantly improves dialogue translation quality over zero/few-shot baselines, evaluated via automatic, LLM, and human methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most translation models and resources for Indic languages focus on sentence-level, formal text and therefore fail to handle conversational dialogue phenomena like informality, speaker interaction, and discourse coherence. There is also a lack of appropriate benchmarks to evaluate dialogue translation quality for such phenomena, especially for Indic languages.

Method: The authors construct BaatCheet, a multilingual dialogue corpus with around 49,000 dialogues covering five translation directions. They then fine-tune five open-source LLMs under seven different training data configurations for dialogue translation. They assess model performance using automatic metrics, LLM-as-a-judge evaluations, and human evaluations via an SQM-guided Direct Assessment protocol.

Result: Fine-tuning the open-source LLMs on the BaatCheet dialogue corpus produces substantial performance improvements compared to zero-shot and few-shot baselines across the evaluated translation directions and setups, as shown by both automatic metrics and human/LLM judgments.

Conclusion: A specialized multilingual dialogue corpus like BaatCheet significantly enhances the ability of translation models to handle conversational Indic language, and the proposed multi-pronged evaluation (automatic, LLM-as-judge, and SQM-based human DA) provides a more complete picture of dialogue translation quality for these under-resourced settings.

Abstract: Existing translation models are typically trained on sentence-level and formal text, limiting their ability to capture everyday conversational dialogue phenomena such as informality, speaker interaction, and discourse coherence. Most existing Indic translation resources and evaluation benchmarks focus on sentence-level or formal text, making it difficult to assess translation quality of the dialogue phenomena. In this work, we introduce BaatCheet, a multilingual dialogue corpus named after the Hindi term for conversation or chitchat, containing approximately 49,000 dialogues for dialogue translation across five translation directions. We fine-tune five open-source LLMs across seven training data configurations and find that fine-tuning yields substantial gains over zero- and few-shot baselines. To comprehensively evaluate dialogue translation quality, we employ multiple evaluation strategies, including automatic metrics, LLM-as-judge, and human assessments using an SQM-guided Direct Assessment (DA) Protocol.

</details>


### [94] [Hesitation-Aware On-Policy Distillation for Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33301)
*Jianguo Huang,Lipeng Wan,Yanchen Deng,Bo An*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Hesitation-Aware On-Policy Distillation (HOPD) for diffusion LLMs, leveraging not only committed tokens but also intermediate, uncommitted token proposals (“hesitations”) during iterative unmasking to improve distillation efficiency, accuracy, and decoding speed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing trace-based on-policy distillation (TOPD) for diffusion LLMs only supervises the student model on tokens that the decoder finally commits to at each denoising step. However, diffusion LLMs produce full token distributions at all masked positions, and a large portion of the teacher–student divergence lies in the uncommitted token proposals (“hesitations”). Ignoring these hesitations wastes a strong training signal that could improve model quality and decoding efficiency.

Method: The authors analyze teacher–student divergence across state-position pairs and find that hesitations, though fewer in number, account for most of the divergence. They propose HOPD, which extends teacher distribution matching from only committed positions (as in TOPD) to all masked positions at each denoising step. HOPD uses hindsight from the completed trajectory to reweight supervision: it assigns higher loss weight to positions where early proposals differ from the final committed token and to blocks where first-step proposals rarely survive to the final output. This is implemented without extra forward passes—only additional loss evaluations at more positions—since both teacher and student already output distributions at all positions during decoding.

Result: In experiments distilling SDAR-1.7B and SDAR-4B students from a TraDo-8B-Instruct teacher, HOPD outperforms baseline distillation methods, including TOPD, on five math and coding benchmarks under both static and dynamic decoding settings and at both model scales. Quantitatively, for SDAR-4B, the HOPD student exhibits fewer hesitations and commits about 11% more tokens per denoising step than TOPD while achieving higher accuracy.

Conclusion: HOPD demonstrates that supervising on all masked positions, with hindsight-based weighting of hesitations, significantly improves the effectiveness of on-policy distillation for diffusion LLMs. This approach better exploits the rich intermediate signal produced during iterative unmasking, leading to higher accuracy and faster decoding without extra forward passes, suggesting a more efficient way to train and deploy diffusion-based language models.

Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text by iterative unmasking. At each denoising step, a dLLM proposes a token at every masked position, but the decoder commits only a confident subset of these proposals. Trace-based on-policy distillation (TOPD) builds on this process by matching the student to a stronger teacher, yet only at the committed positions. We argue that this discards much of the useful signal, which resides in the uncommitted proposals, where the student has made a prediction but is not yet confident enough to commit it. We call these proposals hesitations. In our pilot study on an SDAR-4B student, hesitations make up only 24% of supervisable state-position pairs but carry 66% of the teacher-student divergence. To exploit this signal, we propose Hesitation-Aware On-Policy Distillation (HOPD), which extends teacher distribution matching to every masked position of each denoising step. Because hesitations are not equally informative, we further allocate supervision using hindsight from the completed trajectory, placing more weight on positions whose proposal was later disagreed with the final token and on blocks where first-step proposals rarely survive. Since both models already produce distributions at all masked positions, HOPD requires no additional forward passes over TOPD. The only extra cost is evaluating the loss at more positions. With SDAR-1.7B and SDAR-4B students distilled from TraDo-8B-Instruct, HOPD achieves the best average score among the evaluated methods on five math and coding benchmarks, under both static and dynamic decoding and at both scales. It also speeds up decoding. On SDAR-4B, the HOPD student hesitates less and commits 11% more tokens per denoising step than TOPD, while reaching higher accuracy.

</details>


### [95] [CertMark: Distortion-Free Multi-Bit Watermarking with Certified Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33332)
*Paweł Batorski,Przemysław Spurek,Paul Swoboda*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CertMark is a watermarking scheme for language models that embeds multi-bit messages without changing the model’s sampling distribution and provides certified, abstaining decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-bit watermarks bias next-token probabilities, degrading text quality and lacking guarantees on when decoders should abstain versus output a possibly wrong message. There is a need for a watermarking method that both preserves the model’s native text distribution and offers mathematically certified guarantees on decoding correctness or abstention.

Method: CertMark seeds an exact Gumbel-max sampler with the watermark message instead of altering token probabilities, ensuring the original sampling distribution is preserved. It introduces two decoders: (1) a model-agnostic text-only decoder that operates only on the generated text, and (2) a model-aware decoder that additionally uses the model’s next-token probability distributions. Both decoders are designed with certified abstention rules that upper-bound the probability of outputting an incorrect message.

Result: On tasks like text completion, summarization, and story generation, CertMark’s generated text matches the perplexity of unwatermarked outputs, indicating no loss in text quality. The method reliably recovers embedded multi-bit messages, and the model-aware decoder achieves higher bit accuracy than state-of-the-art probability-biasing watermark baselines.

Conclusion: CertMark provides a practical, distribution-preserving multi-bit watermarking scheme for language models with certified decoding guarantees. By using message-seeded Gumbel-max sampling and abstaining decoders, it avoids the usual quality–robustness trade-off of probability-biased watermarks and offers stronger, quantifiable reliability in watermark recovery across diverse language generation tasks.

Abstract: Leading multi-bit watermarking methods for language models encode messages by biasing the model's next-token probabilities, creating a trade-off between message recovery and text quality. Their decoders typically return the highest-scoring candidate from accumulated token-level evidence, without a certified abstention rule that bounds the probability of outputting an incorrect message. We introduce CertMark, a distribution-preserving multi-bit watermark with certified decoding. Rather than modifying probabilities, CertMark uses the embedded message to seed an exact Gumbel-max sampler, thereby preserving the model's original sampling distribution. We propose two scalable decoders: a model-agnostic, text-only decoder and a model-aware variant that leverages the original next-token distributions for stronger recovery. Both support certified abstention with mathematical bounds on the probability of returning an incorrect message. Across text completion, summarization, and story generation, CertMark matches the perplexity of unwatermarked text while reliably recovering multi-bit messages. The model-aware decoder further achieves higher bit accuracy than probability-biasing baselines. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Batorskq/CertMark.

</details>


### [96] [Does Learning to Predict the World Help Agents Act? Auditing World-Model Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33335)
*Xinyu Che,Hang Yan,Yanchen Liu,Haochen Liu,Ruifeng Li,Anran Shi,Heng Wang,Jun Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates why world-model style next-observation prediction training improves agent performance, finding that much of the benefit does not actually come from accurate future prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World-model methods train agents to predict future observations and use those predictions as rewards or supervision. These approaches reliably improve performance, but it is unclear whether the gains truly come from learning accurate environment dynamics or from side effects of the training setup (e.g., exploration pressure, regularization, or better use of the action space). The authors aim to disentangle these effects and identify the real sources of improvement.

Method: The authors systematically break the link between prediction quality and performance by corrupting the supervision and rewards used in world-model training. First, they replace ground-truth next observations with in-distribution but mismatched observations, which substantially reduces next-observation prediction accuracy. They then measure how much task performance remains. Second, they create a setting where prediction-based rewards are replaced with independent random signals that contain no information about the environment. They evaluate agents in two interactive text environments and in the multimodal VisualWebArena benchmark, using metrics such as pass@64, number of candidate actions considered, and looping behavior.

Result: Even when next-observation targets are mismatched, reducing prediction accuracy by 15.3–61.6%, agents still achieve substantial gains over the base model in the text environments. These trained models explore more candidate actions and get stuck in loops less often than the base model. In the random-reward setting, agents still expand task coverage (pass@64) despite the rewards containing no environment information. On VisualWebArena, training with random rewards alone increases pass@64 by 14.3% over the base model, without any observation-matching rewards or external multimodal teacher for shaping rewards.

Conclusion: The performance improvements of world-model-style training cannot be fully attributed to learning accurate next-observation predictions or using informative, environment-aligned rewards. Instead, a large fraction of the gains appears to come from auxiliary effects of the training process—such as encouraging broader action exploration, breaking looping behaviors, and generally reshaping the agent’s search and decision patterns. This calls for reinterpreting the role of world models in agent training and motivates designing training objectives that directly target these beneficial side effects rather than focusing solely on prediction accuracy.

Abstract: Predicting how an environment will change before acting is a natural route to better decision making for agents. Recent post-training methods therefore require agents to predict the next observation and turn that prediction into a reward or a direct supervision signal, which is called world model. Existing next-observation training methods help the agent to learn the environmental content. However, they additionally involve an optimization process, which may introduce several effects other than learning to predict the world. Consequently, where the performance gain comes from during the training process remains an open question. We answer this research question through replacing true next-observation targets with in-distribution mismatched observations during the training process. Across two interactive text environments, mismatched targets lower prediction accuracy by 15.3-61.6% relative to ground-truth targets, yet retain substantial task gains over the base model. Compared with the base model, trained models consider more candidate actions and exhibit less looping. We also introduce a setting that replaces prediction-based rewards with independent random signals. This training expands task coverage (pass@64) even when the reward carries no environment information. We also generalize this finding to VisualWebArena, where random-reward training raises pass@64 by 14.3% relative to the base model, without observation-matching rewards or an external multimodal teacher for reward construction.

</details>


### [97] [CHI: A Composite Hallucination Index Unifying Entity, Relation, and Quantity Dimensions for Summarization Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33343)
*Praveenkumar Katwe,Rakesh Chandra Balabantaray,Kali Prasad Vittala*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes CHI, a unified metric for measuring hallucinations in abstractive summaries, combining entity, relation, and quantity hallucination into a single interpretable score that correlates well with human judgments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing faithfulness metrics for abstractive summarization focus on isolated hallucination types (e.g., wrong entities, incorrect relations, or numerical errors) and fail to model their co-occurrence and interaction, limiting their diagnostic power and reliability as comprehensive faithfulness measures.

Method: The authors design CHI (Composite Hallucination Index), which decomposes hallucinations into three orthogonal dimensions: entity hallucination (EHI), relation hallucination (RHI*), and quantity hallucination (QHI). Each dimension uses a shared architecture that applies a softmax over Venn-diagram-based factors capturing extractiveness, positive and negative hallucination, over-focus, and lost focus. QHI introduces a tolerance-aware numerical matching scheme with exact, epsilon, derived, and temporal comparison modes. The three dimension scores are then combined via a harmonic mean to form a single composite hallucination score. The metric is evaluated on 800 documents from four domains with summaries from five systems, and further assessed via correlation with human judgments and ablation studies.

Result: The three hallucination dimensions are shown to be largely independent (mean Spearman rho = 0.148), indicating that they capture distinct error types. CHI achieves the strongest system-level correlation with human faithfulness judgments on SummEval (rho = 0.66, p = 0.006), outperforming ROUGE (rho = 0.53), the entity-only metric EHI (rho = 0.58), and all individual CHI components. Ablation experiments reveal that removing any dimension degrades performance, demonstrating that all three contribute unique explanatory variance and enabling more fine-grained diagnostic insights than single-score baselines.

Conclusion: CHI is an effective, unified hallucination metric for abstractive summarization that is decomposable into entity, relation, and quantity components, each capturing distinct aspects of unfaithfulness. Its composite score correlates better with human judgments than existing baselines while providing interpretable, fine-grained diagnostics, making it suitable for both offline evaluation and real-time monitoring of summarization systems.

Abstract: Faithfulness evaluation of abstractive summaries remains an open challenge, with existing metrics addressing only isolated hallucination types: factual entity errors, relational inconsistencies, or numerical fabrications, without capturing their co-occurrence or interaction. We introduce CHI (Composite Hallucination Index), the first unified hallucination metric that decomposes faithfulness errors into three orthogonal dimensions: entity hallucination (EHI), relation hallucination (RHI*), and quantity hallucination (QHI). Each dimension employs a shared softmax-normalized architecture over Venn diagram-derived factors representing extractiveness, positive hallucination, over-focus, negative hallucination, and lost focus. The novel QHI component introduces tolerance-aware numerical matching with exact, epsilon, derived, and temporal comparison modes. We fuse the three dimensions via harmonic mean to produce a single composite score that penalizes weakness in any dimension. We validate CHI on 800 source articles spanning four domains (news, medical, legal, financial) with summaries from five generation systems. Empirical results demonstrate that: (i) the three dimensions are statistically orthogonal (mean rho = 0.148), confirming they capture distinct error types; (ii) CHI achieves the highest system-level correlation with human judgments (rho = 0.66, p = 0.006) on SummEval, outperforming ROUGE (rho = 0.53), EHI (rho = 0.58), and all individual components; and (iii) ablation studies confirm that all three dimensions contribute unique variance, with the full composite outperforming any individual component while providing decomposable error diagnostics unavailable from single-score baselines. CHI provides practitioners with a decomposable, interpretable, and efficient faithfulness metric suitable for both offline evaluation and online monitoring of summarization systems.

</details>


### [98] [Language Discrimination Improves Linguistic Learning in Multilingual Speech Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33345)
*Maureen de Seyssel,Jie Chi,Zakaria Aldeneh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how making multilingual self-supervised speech models better at distinguishing languages during pretraining can close the performance gap with monolingual models, without losing cross-language sharing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multilingual self-supervised speech models promise data efficiency and cross-lingual transfer, but under a fixed total data budget they still underperform monolingual models trained on a single language. Understanding why this multilingual gap occurs and how to reduce it is important for building effective multilingual speech systems, especially for low-resource languages.

Method: Using a controlled bilingual English/French HuBERT setup with a matched total pretraining data budget, the authors introduce and compare two ways to strengthen language discrimination during pretraining: (1) adding an auxiliary language classification objective to HuBERT, and (2) using separate per-language k-means clusterings to generate HuBERT targets. They measure the effects of these interventions on multiple linguistic evaluation benchmarks (phone-ABX for phonetic discrimination, sWUGGY for lexical performance, and ProsAudit for prosodic/lexical prosody) and analyze how the timing of the interventions across HuBERT training stages affects performance and language-wise segregation in the learned representations.

Result: Both interventions that improve language discrimination reduce the performance gap between bilingual and monolingual HuBERT models. Phone discrimination error (phone-ABX) improves from 11.6% in the bilingual baseline to 10.4%, outperforming the monolingual score of 10.8%. Lexical performance on sWUGGY increases from 52.1% to 56.7%, approaching the monolingual 58.5%. Prosodic lexical performance on ProsAudit rises from 68.9% to 72.9%, slightly surpassing the monolingual 72.6%. The largest gains occur when language discrimination mechanisms are introduced in the first HuBERT iteration; later or repeated interventions yield smaller benefits and lead to more pronounced language-wise segregation in the representations.

Conclusion: Explicitly strengthening language discrimination during multilingual self-supervised pretraining can substantially reduce, and in some measures close, the gap to monolingual models under a fixed data budget, while preserving cross-language sharing. Early introduction of language discrimination objectives is most effective, and excessive or late-stage interventions can increase language-wise segregation with diminishing returns. These findings suggest that the ability to distinguish languages plays a causal role in mitigating the additional cost of multilingual learning in self-supervised speech models.

Abstract: Multilingual self-supervised speech models can benefit from sharing information across languages, but under a matched total pretraining data budget they still fall short of monolingual models. We show that strengthening the model's ability to discriminate languages during pretraining reduces and, on some measures, closes this multilingual gap on continuous phonetic and higher-level linguistic measures, while preserving substantial cross-language sharing. Using a controlled English/French HuBERT setting, we test two interventions which strengthen language discrimination: an auxiliary language classifier and per-language k-means targets. Across interventions, continuous-feature phone discrimination error (phone-ABX, lower is better) decreases from 11.6% in the bilingual baseline to 10.4% (monolingual: 10.8%), while lexical performance (sWUGGY, higher is better) increases from 52.1% to 56.7% (monolingual: 58.5%) and prosodic performance (ProsAudit, lexical subtask, higher is better) from 68.9% to 72.9% (monolingual: 72.6%). Across HuBERT training stages, the strongest gains on most linguistic measures occur when language discrimination is introduced in the first iteration, whereas later or repeated interventions yield smaller improvements and are accompanied by increased language-wise segregation. These results support a causal role for language discrimination in reducing the additional cost of multilingual learning.

</details>


### [99] [NLPG: Natural-Language Policy Gradients for Self-Evolving Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33379)
*Xu Liu,WenZhang Wei,Jun Cao,Dehua Peng,Huan Chen,Zhipeng Gui,Huayi Wu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Natural-Language Policy Gradients (NLPG), a method that improves fixed LLM agents by storing and reusing local, natural-language corrections derived from execution traces, leading to significant performance gains across multiple benchmarks without changing model weights or program structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents increasingly use complex, multi-step programs for tasks like retrieval, tool use, and reasoning. Their failures are often due to local procedural mistakes (e.g., a specific tool call or routing decision) rather than a global prompt flaw or model limitation. Existing approaches such as RL fine-tuning or prompt optimization typically treat behavior with scalar rewards or modify entire prompts, making it hard to (1) attribute errors to specific steps, (2) store and reuse local procedural improvements, and (3) keep the underlying agent frozen (no weight updates) while still benefiting from experience. The paper aims to create a mechanism that can learn from past procedural failures in a localized, interpretable way that augments a fixed agent.

Method: The authors propose Natural-Language Policy Gradients (NLPG), an external policy-memory mechanism wrapped around an otherwise frozen LLM agent. NLPG works by: (1) recording execution traces of the agent’s compound program (modules, tool calls, routing decisions); (2) diagnosing failures using downstream feedback (e.g., final task success or evaluation signals); (3) propagating this feedback backward along the module graph to identify which local decisions likely caused errors; (4) converting these recurring local failures into natural-language corrections that specify better behavior for particular routes or contexts; and (5) aggregating these corrections into bounded, localized policy updates that are consulted in future executions, effectively biasing the agent’s decisions without altering its weights or global prompt. This creates a form of gradient-like improvement in natural-language space over a structured program graph.

Result: Across six benchmarks targeting memory, reasoning, instruction following, and evidence verification, NLPG consistently improves performance of fixed LLM agents. It outperforms the strongest listed baseline on each benchmark, with an average gain of 8.71 percentage points. This demonstrates that the external policy-memory and local correction mechanism is effective across diverse tasks that require different kinds of procedural competence.

Conclusion: Evaluated procedural experience from LLM agents can be turned into localized, interpretable policy updates expressed in natural language and attached to specific parts of a compound program. NLPG shows that such an external policy-memory can continually improve a frozen agent—without changing its parameters or overall program—while yielding sizable performance gains across varied tasks. This suggests a practical path for making LLM agents more reliable over time by learning from their procedural mistakes in a targeted, reusable way.

Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly rely on compound programs for retrieval, tool use, reasoning, and verification, yet their failures often arise from local procedural decisions. Existing reinforcement-learning and prompt-optimization approaches typically rely on scalar rewards or repeatedly modify entire prompts, making it difficult to capture and reuse procedural improvements while preserving a frozen agent. To address this problem, We propose Natural-Language Policy Gradients (NLPG), an external policy-memory method for improving a fixed agent without changing its model parameters or program structure. NLPG diagnoses execution traces, propagates downstream feedback backward through the module graph, and converts recurring failures into route-local natural-language corrections that are aggregated into bounded policy updates for subsequent executions. Across six benchmarks covering memory, reasoning, instruction following, and evidence verification, NLPG also outperforms the strongest listed baseline for each benchmark by 8.71 percentage points on average. These results provide evidence that evaluated procedural experience can be transformed into local and interpretable policy updates, enabling continual improvement of frozen agents.

</details>


### [100] [From Position Risks to Block Survival: Faster Generation for Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33390)
*Siwei Chen,Yuxiang Wan,Yifan Yu,Fan Lai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes BRISK-DLM, a framework to make diffusion language models faster and more effective by aligning how they propose token blocks with how those tokens are actually accepted during decoding, improving throughput without hurting quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion language models can generate multiple tokens in parallel, but their proposal mechanism is misaligned with the final verification-based decoding: (1) tokens inside a block are predicted without conditioning on earlier choices in that same block, even though their correctness depends on the realized prefix; (2) in proposal-verification decoding, an early error can cause rejection of the entire block, making later correct proposals useless. This leads to asymmetric, inefficient progress and suboptimal speed-quality tradeoffs, motivating a method that better optimizes proposals for verified decoding progress.

Method: BRISK-DLM introduces a training and inference framework tailored to proposal-verification decoding. During training, the model generates its own sequences and uses risk-reward weighting to focus learning on token positions that most affect verified progress and decoding cost. At inference, a lightweight prefix-conditioned corrector re-ranks already proposed tokens within a block, conditioning on the tokens that have been actually accepted so far. This corrector distills preferences from the model’s verifier, reuses the backbone model’s parallel representations, and is executed in a fused way so that it does not require extra backbone evaluations and has minimal overhead.

Result: Experiments show that BRISK-DLM increases end-to-end decoding throughput by as much as 37.4% compared to baseline diffusion language model decoding methods, while maintaining the same task quality. This establishes a better speed–quality tradeoff compared to prior approaches for diffusion language model generation.

Conclusion: By jointly optimizing how diffusion language models learn proposals and how they are selected during decoding, BRISK-DLM reduces the mismatch between parallel token prediction and verification-based acceptance. Its risk-reward training and lightweight, prefix-conditioned corrector enable substantial throughput gains without quality degradation, defining a new frontier in efficient DLM generation.

Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can accelerate generation by predicting multiple tokens in parallel, but there is a mismatch between how these tokens are predicted and how they ultimately contribute to generation. Parallel predictions can hardly condition on the tokens selected earlier within the same block, even though their validity depends on this realized prefix. Under the popular proposal-verification decoding, this mismatch makes errors highly asymmetric: an early rejection prevents all subsequent proposals from contributing decoding progress. We introduce BRISK-DLM, a framework that addresses both mismatches by optimizing proposal learning and selection for verified progress. BRISK-DLM trains on self-generated sequences, using risk-reward weighting to dynamically prioritize positions by their impact on verified progress and decoding cost. During inference, a lightweight prefix-conditioned corrector reranks existing candidates using previously selected tokens and preferences distilled from the model's own verifier. The corrector reuses the backbone's parallel representations and requires no additional backbone evaluation, while fused execution keeps its overhead small. BRISK-DLM improves end-to-end throughput by up to 37.4% while preserving task quality, establishing a new quality-throughput frontier for DLM generation.

</details>


### [101] [Preserving Morphemes: Morphology-Guided Pre-Tokenization for Nepali](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33395)
*Kalash Shrestha,Nikhil Pradhan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates a linguistically informed pre-tokenizer (Papaya) for Nepali that splits stems and affixes before byte-level BPE, finding modest perplexity gains but limited downstream impact compared to plain BPE and other tokenizers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Byte-level BPE treats each inflected Nepali word form as a distinct sequence, causing stems to fragment across many case-marked forms. The authors want to know if adding explicit morphological segmentation before BPE can yield better subword units, improved language modeling, and downstream NLP performance for a morphologically rich, low-resource language like Nepali.

Method: They build Papaya, a pre-tokenizer that segments Nepali words into stems and affixes using a finite-state transducer derived from an existing grammar, with regex-based fallbacks, and then applies standard byte-level BPE unchanged. They evaluate segmentation quality on 607 manually annotated words (7 annotators), compare tokenization properties vs. plain BPE, and train a 17M-parameter language model with fixed corpus, vocabulary size, model architecture, and number of training steps. They compare bits-per-byte under various training regimes (equal steps vs equal epochs) and against an unsupervised Morfessor segmentation. They also test downstream performance on NER, POS tagging, and news classification, and benchmark against existing Nepali tokenizers. They release annotated boundaries, an affix list, and code.

Result: Papaya’s segmenter attains 0.96 boundary F1 on the annotated set and preserves stems as intact tokens far more often than plain BPE. In language modeling, it reduces bits per byte by about 1% at equal training steps; at equal epochs, the apparent larger gain largely comes from the additional training steps enabled by longer token sequences. An unsupervised Morfessor-based segmentation yields similar language modeling improvements. For downstream tasks, gains are small: NER improves only on entities containing OOV words, POS tagging and news classification show no change, and existing Nepali tokenizers achieve comparable performance.

Conclusion: Morphology-aware pre-tokenization for Nepali can slightly improve intrinsic language modeling metrics and stem preservation but has limited impact on standard downstream tasks under the tested conditions. Carefully engineered rule-based or unsupervised segmenters both offer similar modest benefits, suggesting that while explicit morphology helps BPE in principle, its practical value for downstream applications in this setup is small. The released datasets and tools provide useful resources for further research on Nepali tokenization and morphology.

Abstract: A byte-level BPE vocabulary learns each inflected form of a Nepali word as a separate string, so a noun stem is spelled differently in each of its case-marked forms. We test whether splitting words into stem and affixes before BPE helps, with the corpus, vocabulary size, model and number of training steps held fixed. Our pre-tokenizer, Papaya, uses a finite-state transducer built from a published grammar of Nepali, falls back to regular expressions, and leaves the BPE trainer unchanged. On 607 words annotated by seven native speakers its segmenter reaches 0.96 boundary F1, and the resulting tokens keep stems intact far more often than plain BPE does. In a 17M-parameter language model it lowers bits per byte by about 1% at equal training steps; most of the larger gain seen at equal epochs comes from the extra steps that longer token sequences buy, and an unsupervised Morfessor segmentation gives the same improvement. Downstream the effect is small: NER improves only on entities that contain words unseen in training, POS tagging and news classification do not change, and published Nepali tokenizers perform about as well. We release the annotated boundary set, a 556-affix dataset and the code.

</details>


### [102] [Dense Is Not Enough: Hierarchical Supervision Allocation for Long-Horizon On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33409)
*Yuhao Sun,Binrui Wu,Zhuoer Xu,Ming Wen,Haoxiang Xu,Bin Chen,Yan Lin,Qianzijing Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes LENS-OPD, a hierarchical on-policy distillation framework that selectively allocates teacher supervision in long-horizon language-agent tasks to improve student performance more efficiently than standard OPD and curriculum/selection baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard on-policy distillation uniformly matches teacher and student token-by-token on the student’s rollouts, which is inefficient for long-horizon agentic tasks. Large local discrepancies may not matter for future success, and important strategic guidance may be either too hard for the current student to learn or may not persist without special inputs. There is a need for a distillation approach that focuses teacher supervision on the most impactful and learnable parts of trajectories, and that adapts as the student improves.

Method: The authors reframe long-horizon OPD as a hierarchical supervision allocation problem and propose LENS-OPD, a coarse-to-fine three-stage framework: (1) Locate: adaptively choose which parts of the trajectory to expose and select a candidate decision point for teacher intervention based on the student’s evolving competence; (2) Validate: test counterfactually whether providing teacher guidance at that decision actually improves the same student’s subsequent behavior; (3) Refine: distill the improved guided behavior into the deployable policy by focusing token-level supervision on the most decisive teacher–student conflicts within the validated decision turn. Each finer level of supervision is conditioned on decisions from the coarser level, instead of independently scoring tokens or steps.

Result: Across several long-horizon agent benchmarks and multiple student–teacher model pairings, LENS-OPD consistently yields higher task performance than vanilla OPD as well as strong curriculum-learning and data-selection baselines. This demonstrates that their hierarchical, adaptive supervision allocation leads to more effective distillation in complex, multi-step tasks.

Conclusion: Effective long-horizon distillation requires not just more supervision, but supervision that is targeted in depth (coarse-to-fine), timing (which decision to intervene on), and granularity (which tokens within that decision). By organizing OPD into nested Locate–Validate–Refine stages, LENS-OPD better aligns supervision with both future utility and current student learnability, leading to more efficient and successful transfer of capabilities from large teachers to smaller students in agentic settings.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers the capabilities of a large language model to a smaller student by providing teacher supervision on the student's own rollouts. In long-horizon agentic tasks, however, uniform token-level matching can allocate supervision poorly: a large local discrepancy need not improve future behavior, while consequential guidance may be beyond the current student's reach or fail to persist without privileged input. We formulate long-horizon OPD as hierarchical supervision allocation and argue that productive guidance lies at the intersection of future utility and current learnability. Crucially, this intersection evolves as the student learns. Based on this principle, we propose LENS-OPD, a coarse-to-fine framework that organizes supervision through Locate, Validate, and Refine. Locate adapts trajectory exposure to the student's evolving competence and proposes a candidate decision for intervention. Validate tests whether teacher guidance at that decision improves the same student's subsequent behavior. Refine internalizes the beneficial guided behavior into the deployable policy and concentrates token-level supervision on decisive teacher-student conflicts within the validated turn. These stages are nested: each finer allocation is conditioned on the coarser decision, rather than being optimized as an independent importance score. Experiments across multiple long-horizon agent benchmarks and student-teacher configurations show that LENS-OPD consistently improves task performance over vanilla OPD and strong curriculum- and selection-based baselines. Our results suggest that effective long-horizon distillation requires teaching at the right depth, the right decision, and the right token.

</details>


### [103] [Grounding Memory Summarization in Utility Intent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33417)
*Zhenyu Lei,Mingjia Shi,Xingbo Fu,Haoyu He,Qi R. Wang,Jundong Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes MemSuit, a utility-aware memory summarization and retrieval framework that conditions on query-answer pairs to preserve evidence most useful for future queries, achieving better performance than existing summarizers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional memory summarizers are optimized for human-facing qualities like faithfulness and readability, which do not directly optimize for the system’s real objective: retaining information that will be useful to answer future queries. This misalignment can cause important evidence to be lost in summarization, reducing answer quality in conversational systems that rely on long-term memory.

Method: The authors introduce MemSuit, a self-distillation framework. First, a teacher summarizer takes conversation blocks plus observed query–answer pairs and generates utility-aware memory entries that focus on evidence needed to support those queries. To avoid losing information relevant to other possible future queries, the teacher decomposes each block into multiple small, self-contained entries, each capturing a distinct query-relevant facet. Then a student model is trained to reproduce these teacher-style entries using only the raw conversation (without access to query–answer pairs), effectively distilling utility-aware behavior. Additionally, the embedding-based retriever is fine-tuned with a contrastive objective using these teacher entries so that it better retrieves compact, fact-dense memories.

Result: When evaluated on a diverse set of conversational query types, the MemSuit framework produces higher-quality answers than state-of-the-art baseline summarization and memory systems. The experiments show that conditioning on query–answer pairs yields more useful memory representations, that this utility-aware style can be transferred to a student that no longer sees queries, and that retriever fine-tuning further improves performance.

Conclusion: Grounding memory summarization and retrieval in downstream utility—specifically, the ability to support future queries—leads to more effective conversational memory systems than optimizing for generic summarization criteria. MemSuit demonstrates that self-distillation from a utility-conditioned teacher, combined with facet-level memory decomposition and retriever alignment, consistently improves answer quality across diverse conversational tasks.

Abstract: Existing summarizers for memory systems are typically optimized for human-facing criteria such as faithfulness, which misaligns with their true objective: preserving the evidence needed to support future queries. We show that conditioning summarization on query-answer pairs substantially improves answer quality, and that this utility-aware behavior is transferable across queries. Motivated by these findings, we propose MemSuit, a self-distillation framework in which a teacher summarizer, conditioned on observed query-answer pairs, produces utility-aware memory entries that a student learns to reproduce from the raw conversation alone. To prevent collateral erasure where conditioning on a single query-answer pair discards evidence relevant to other plausible queries, the teacher decomposes each block into multiple self-contained entries that preserve distinct query-relevant facets as independently retrievable units. To align the retriever with the compact, fact-dense style of teacher entries, we further fine-tune the embedding model with a contrastive objective supervised by teacher entries. Across a diverse suite of conversational query types, MemSuit consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, confirming the value of grounding memory in downstream utility.

</details>


### [104] [TeacherGRPO: Closing the Capacity Gap in Reasoning Distillation via Teacher Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33426)
*Zhenyu Lei,Zihan Chen,Yaochen Zhu,Shangbin Feng,Zaiyi Zheng,Ruocheng Guo,Yushun Dong,Jundong Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper tackles the “Gap Curse” in reasoning distillation from powerful teacher models to smaller students by aligning the teacher to the student’s capabilities via a new RL-based method, TeacherGRPO, which improves distillation performance without reducing data coverage or reasoning quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As teacher models become more capable, their reasoning distributions diverge from what smaller student models can represent, leading to worse distillation performance (the Gap Curse). Existing fixes either drop hard examples or use weaker intermediate teachers, both of which reduce the coverage or quality of supervision. The authors want a way to keep the strong teacher and full data while making its behavior compatible with the student.

Method: They introduce Teacher Alignment, where the teacher itself is adapted toward the student’s distribution. Instead of naive KD, they formulate this as a reinforcement learning problem and propose TeacherGRPO, based on Group Relative Policy Optimization. TeacherGRPO adds (1) Curriculum Selective Alignment: token-level and distribution-level curricula that emphasize important reasoning discrepancies and downweight trivial or noisy parts; and (2) Importance-Adaptive Length Regularization: a mechanism that discourages redundant verbosity while protecting essential reasoning steps. After alignment, the modified teacher is used in standard distillation pipelines to train students.

Result: Experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks and with different distillation schemes show that TeacherGRPO-trained teachers yield students that significantly outperform baselines, including data-selection and assistant-teacher approaches, as well as naive KD-based alignment. The improvements are consistent and robust across settings.

Conclusion: Aligning a powerful teacher to a student’s representational limits via RL-based TeacherGRPO mitigates the Gap Curse without sacrificing data coverage or reasoning quality. Careful curriculum design and length regularization are key to avoiding catastrophic collapse of the teacher while making its reasoning more distillable, resulting in better-performing student models on reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Reasoning distillation from powerful teacher models to smaller students faces the Gap Curse: as teachers grow more sophisticated, their complex distributions increasingly diverge from what students can approximate, causing performance degradation. Existing mitigation strategies either filter out challenging examples through data selection or introduce weaker intermediate assistant models, inherently compromising supervision coverage or quality. We propose Teacher Alignment, which directly adapts the teacher toward the student's distribution without discarding data or degrading reasoning quality. However, naive alignment through standard knowledge distillation triggers catastrophic collapse of the teacher's reasoning capabilities. To address this, we reformulate teacher alignment as reinforcement learning and introduce TeacherGRPO, built on Group Relative Policy Optimization with two key innovations: (i) Curriculum Selective Alignment applies dual token- and distribution-level curricula to focus rewards on high-signal reasoning gaps while filtering noise from trivial tokens and uncertain tail distributions, and (ii) Importance-Adaptive Length Regularization selectively penalizes verbose redundancy while preserving pedagogically critical reasoning steps. The aligned teacher then distills knowledge to students via standard pipelines. Extensive experiments show TeacherGRPO significantly outperforms baselines across diverse reasoning benchmarks and distillation methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/LzyFischer/TeacherGRPO.

</details>


### [105] [MIC: Explaining Image-Claim Inconsistencies in AI-Generated Multimodal Misinformation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33441)
*Ruihong Zeng,Jonathan Tonglet,Preslav Nakov,Iryna Gurevych*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes MIC, a multimodal inconsistency checking framework that detects and explains AI-generated image–text misinformation by focusing on semantic inconsistencies rather than just detecting synthetic images.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-generated images paired with textual claims are increasingly used for misinformation. Existing automated fact-checking mainly detects if an image is AI-generated via low-level artifacts, but does not check if the image content is semantically consistent with the associated claim, which is what human fact-checkers typically do. There is a need for systems that can identify and explain such multimodal inconsistencies to better assist human fact-checkers.

Method: The authors propose MIC (Multimodal Inconsistency Checking), an automated fact-checking framework. MIC first uses supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to adapt a base model to the multimodal fact-checking task. Then it applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a reinforcement learning method, to directly optimize verifiable component-level rewards for several subtasks: predicting the overall verdict, classifying the type of inconsistency, generating visual evidence descriptions, and producing world-knowledge-based explanations. They also construct MIC-Bench, a benchmark of 8,812 image-claim pairs built from 4,406 claims, each paired with both an authentic image and a controlled AI-generated counterpart introducing specific contextual inconsistencies.

Result: Using GRPO on top of SFT leads to improved performance over SFT alone. Macro-F1 scores increase by 4.67 points on in-distribution data and 4.11 points on out-of-distribution data. Additionally, the quality of generated visual evidence descriptions and world-knowledge explanations improves, as measured by higher semantic similarity to human reference annotations on the MIC-Bench dataset.

Conclusion: MIC demonstrates that directly optimizing for verifiable, component-level rewards via GRPO can substantially improve multimodal inconsistency detection and explanation over standard SFT. The newly introduced MIC-Bench provides a controlled benchmark for evaluating AI-generated image–text misinformation detection. The framework better aligns automated fact-checking with human fact-checkers’ practice of checking semantic consistency between claims and visual evidence, and offers more informative explanations to support human verification.

Abstract: Claims paired with AI-generated images are a rapidly growing form of misinformation. Existing automated fact-checking (AFC) methods mainly treat this as a provenance problem, detecting low-level synthesis artifacts to decide whether an image is AI-generated. However, such methods do not verify what human fact-checkers often check: whether an image's content is consistent with the context implied by its accompanying claim. To address this gap, we introduce MIC (Multimodal Inconsistency Checking), an AFC framework that assists human fact-checkers by detecting AI-generated multimodal misinformation and explaining inconsistencies using world knowledge. MIC first uses supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for task adaptation and then applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to directly optimize component-level verifiable rewards for verdict prediction, inconsistency type classification, visual evidence description, and world-knowledge explanation. We further introduce MIC-Bench, a benchmark comprising 8,812 image-claim instances derived from 4,406 claims, where each claim is paired with an authentic image and an AI-generated counterpart that introduces a controlled contextual inconsistency. Compared with SFT alone, GRPO further improves Macro-F1 by 4.67 and 4.11 points in the in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, respectively, while also improving the semantic similarity of visual evidence descriptions and world-knowledge explanations to reference annotations. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/UKPLab/arxiv2026-mic.

</details>


### [106] [Context Spanning: A Communication Framework for Full-Duplex Speech Models and External LLM Backends](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33443)
*Seonghyeon Go,Yongwoo Kim,Hyeonjin Cha,Jaeho Shin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They introduce a way to inject external LLM text directly into a full-duplex speech model in real time, boosting conversational and QA performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing full-duplex speech dialogue systems can talk and listen simultaneously but are generally limited to their parametric (pretrained) knowledge. Even when they query external tools or LLMs, the returned information is often compressed into latent representations before being fed to the speech model, which can cause information loss and limit real-time reasoning over fresh, external knowledge.

Method: They propose Context Spanning, a framework that connects a full-duplex speech model with an external LLM backend. Retrieved information is streamed in via real-time chunked prefill and injected as frames that are encoded in a single forward pass within the system’s tight real-time frame budget. Crucially, the external information is delivered to the speech model in raw text form rather than as compressed latent vectors, allowing the model to reason over it directly while maintaining full-duplex behavior.

Result: Using Context Spanning, the authors’ duplex speech system achieves strong performance on Full-Duplex dialogue benchmarks and competitive scores on Question Answering tasks, indicating that the model can effectively use injected external knowledge during real-time conversation.

Conclusion: Directly injecting external information as raw text into a duplex speech model via context spanning is both simple and effective. It avoids information loss from latent compression, supports real-time interaction within latency constraints, and significantly enhances the conversational and QA capabilities of full-duplex speech systems.

Abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models can listen and speak simultaneously like the real-time dynamics of human conversation. For natural dialogue, the ability to search for external information in real-time is also an important capability. Many models remain trapped in parametric knowledge, leaving them unable to access real-time information and tool execution. Furthermore, even when Large Language Models (LLM) retrieve information, many duplex speech models process it within a compressed latent space rather than in its raw text form, which can lead to information loss from compression. To address this issue, we propose Context Spanning, a framework for information injection between a full-duplex speech model and an external LLM backend via real-time chunked prefill. The injected frame is encoded in a single forward pass inside the real-time frame budget. It feeds the retrieved information to the speech model as-is, enabling it to reason over the information independently and generate responses. With this approach, our model achieves high performance on Full-Duplex benchmarks and strong results on Question Answering tasks, demonstrating its conversation potential. Context Spanning shows that external information can be injected directly into a duplex speech model, introducing a new simple and powerful mechanism for duplex systems.

</details>


### [107] [Rethinking Token Reweighting for SFT: Suppress, Reverse, and Extrapolate Learned Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33463)
*Cunchun Li,Haonan He,Yifan Gao,Minglei Li,Jingqi Ye,Qingyu Yang,Peng Ye*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies a limitation of standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT)—it can only amplify or suppress learned behaviors, not reverse or extrapolate them—and proposes SCALE, a method that freezes both the base model and the SFT update and then learns gated controls to selectively suppress, reverse, or extrapolate SFT-induced features using entropy minimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard SFT updates the model most where it is most wrong, which helps it learn new behaviors but also amplifies noise and can overwrite useful pretrained knowledge. Existing token-reweighting or policy-loss variants only re-scale positive update directions and thus cannot undo harmful features once learned or extrapolate them in a controlled way. The authors want a principled mechanism to correct or enhance already-learned SFT residuals without destabilizing or re-running SFT, and to better manage the trade-off between task performance (e.g., math and coding) and general capability retention.

Method: The authors present a unified policy-loss perspective on SFT and existing token-reweighting approaches, showing that these methods effectively apply nonnegative coefficients to demonstrated tokens, which limits them to suppression or amplification of the SFT direction. They then introduce SCALE (Selective Control of Adaptation via Local Entropy). SCALE: (1) performs a standard SFT run to obtain an SFT delta relative to a frozen pretrained model; (2) freezes both the base model and this SFT delta; and (3) learns bounded, token- and module-specific gating scalars that modulate the SFT residuals. The learning signal is predictive entropy alone: gates are optimized so that their application leads to lower output entropy, thereby selectively suppressing, reversing (negating), or extrapolating (amplifying beyond 1×) SFT features where they are entropy-reducing. Because the reference SFT delta is fixed, changes correspond to controlled use of known directions rather than new directions in parameter space.

Result: On multiple math-focused LLMs (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Qwen3-4B-Base), SCALE increases average mathematical reasoning scores to 37.84, 43.60, and 36.57, outperforming the strongest baselines. It also yields the best average code-generation performance on HumanEval, HumanEval+, and MBPP for all three models tested. At the same time, it remains competitive on general capability retention benchmarks, suggesting that its corrections to SFT do not significantly degrade broader model abilities.

Conclusion: The study concludes that simply changing token weights during SFT is insufficient for correcting harmful or suboptimal learned behaviors because such methods cannot reverse or extrapolate learned features in a stable way. By freezing both the pretrained model and the SFT delta and learning entropy-guided gates over that delta, SCALE can selectively suppress, reverse, or amplify existing SFT-induced features. This leads to better performance on targeted tasks like math reasoning and code generation while preserving general abilities, indicating that effective SFT correction hinges on how learned residuals are deployed, not just how they are originally acquired.

Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) learns most aggressively from tokens that the model deems least likely. This helps acquire new behaviors, but also amplifies noisy or conflicting supervision and can overwrite useful pretrained knowledge. Through a unified policy-loss view, we revisit existing token-reweighting methods and show that they assign nonnegative coefficients to demonstrated tokens. Consequently, they can suppress or amplify supervised updates, but cannot reverse harmful features once learned. Moreover, larger training weights do not amount to feature extrapolation, since they change the optimization trajectory rather than scale a fixed SFT direction. We argue that reversal and extrapolation require a stable reference frame defined by a fixed SFT delta. Motivated by this, we propose SCALE (Selective Control of Adaptation via Local Entropy), an entropy-guided adaptation-strength-control method that freezes the pretrained model and the SFT delta and learns bounded token- and module-specific gates by minimizing predictive entropy alone. These gates suppress, reverse, or extrapolate frozen SFT features according to their alignment with entropy reduction. Across Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen2.5-Math-7B, and Qwen3-4B-Base, SCALE achieves mathematical-reasoning averages of 37.84, 43.60, and 36.57, exceeding the strongest corresponding baselines while remaining competitive on general-retention benchmarks. It also attains the best average code-generation performance across HumanEval, HumanEval+, and MBPP for all three models. These results suggest that effective SFT correction can benefit from controlling how already learned residuals are used, rather than only modifying how they are learned.

</details>


### [108] [GSM: Efficient Language Modeling with Shared Global State](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33465)
*Yunao Zheng,Bin Wen,Xiaojie Wang,Kaiyu Jiang,Xuanyu Zheng,Changyi Liu,Hongyi Fu,Jianxiong Wang,Tianke Zhang,Haonan Fan,Yingxin Li,Jiankang Chen,Xu Wang,Tingting Gao,Han Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes Global State Model (GSM), an efficient language model architecture that centralizes long-range context processing in an encoder to keep decoder cost and cache size independent of history length.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard transformer language models become inefficient with long sequences because each layer repeatedly attends over and reprocesses the full history, making both per-token computation and KV cache grow with context length. The authors aim to design an architecture that can still exploit long-range information while reducing both compute and memory overhead, especially the repeated selection and processing of historical context across layers.

Method: Introduce the Global State Model (GSM), a causal encoder–decoder architecture. The encoder performs multiple stages of history retrieval, progressively pulling relevant long-range information into representations at recent positions within a fixed-size window, forming a shared global state. The decoder then has all layers attend only to this fixed-size shared state, using layer-updated queries but avoiding reconstruction of historical key–value representations and long-range indexing at each layer. This design decouples decoder attention cost and KV cache size from total history length.

Result: In experiments (not detailed in the abstract), GSM achieves better computational efficiency and lower KV cache usage than standard approaches, while maintaining language modeling quality and the ability to exploit long-range context.

Conclusion: Centralizing long-range context processing into an encoder that builds a fixed-size shared state enables an efficient language model architecture whose decoder cost and cache size do not scale with history length, while preserving model depth and performance. GSM provides a practical shared-state design for efficient long-context language modeling.

Abstract: Efficient language models must reduce not only the cost of individual accesses to past context but also the overhead of repeatedly selecting and processing historical information across layers. We introduce the Global State Model (GSM), a causal encoder--decoder architecture that concentrates the selection and aggregation of long-range information in the encoding stage. Through multiple stages of history retrieval, the encoder progressively incorporates long-range information into representations at recent positions, forming a shared state with a fixed window size. Each decoder layer accesses this same state using queries updated from the preceding layer, preserving computational depth while avoiding repeated construction of historical key--value (KV) representations and long-range indexing. As a result, neither the decoder's per-step attention cost nor its KV cache size grows with the history length. Experiments show that GSM improves computational efficiency and reduces cache overhead while maintaining model performance and the ability to use long-range information, offering a shared-state architecture for efficient language modeling.

</details>


### [109] [DISCO: Distributed Long Context Scaling with Grounding-Reasoning Disaggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33485)
*Guanzheng Chen,Viet Dac Lai,Subhojyoti Mukherjee,Branislav Kveton,Seunghyun Yoon,Franck Dernoncourt,Qizhe Xie,Trung Bui*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces DISCO, an architecture that splits long-context processing into many worker LLMs for grounding and a central driver LLM for reasoning, eliminating context rot and improving long-context QA accuracy and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs with million-token context windows suffer from 'context rot', where reasoning quality degrades sharply as input length grows because the model’s single representation has to simultaneously retrieve relevant information and perform complex reasoning. The authors want a scalable way to use very long contexts without losing reasoning performance or incurring huge computational costs.

Method: They propose DISCO (Grounding-Reasoning Disaggregation via DIStributed long COntext scaling), a distributed framework inspired by systems like Apache Spark. Long input context is partitioned and sent to multiple Worker LLMs that focus purely on localized grounding (extracting relevant evidence). A central Driver LLM, trained via reinforcement learning (GRPO), plans and orchestrates the process: it decomposes the query into atomic extraction subtasks, routes them to appropriate workers, and then aggregates the workers’ evidence to produce the final answer, thus structurally separating grounding from reasoning.

Result: On the RULER-QA benchmark with 1M-token contexts, DISCO maintains 78.4% accuracy where conventional single-LLM baselines experience severe performance collapse. On LongBench v2, it outperforms full-context models by up to 9.8 accuracy points. It also matches the performance of strong proprietary systems like Gemini-3-Pro-Preview while cutting inference costs by over 80%, demonstrating both performance and efficiency gains.

Conclusion: Disaggregating grounding and reasoning across a distributed system of LLMs can effectively eliminate context rot, enabling robust reasoning over million-token contexts. DISCO shows that long-context inference can be made both more accurate and more cost-efficient, suggesting a new architectural paradigm for scaling LLM context windows beyond monolithic designs.

Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) advertise million-token context windows, reasoning quality often collapses as inputs grow -- a phenomenon termed context rot. This failure stems from a structural entanglement in monolithic architectures, where the massive search burden of contextual grounding exhausts the representational capacity needed for complex reasoning. To resolve this, we propose Grounding-Reasoning Disaggregation via DIStributed long COntext scaling (DISCO). Inspired by distributed computing frameworks like Apache Spark, DISCO partitions long context across a fleet of Worker LLMs dedicated exclusively to parallel, localized grounding. A central Driver LLM, trained via Reinforcement Learning (GRPO) to optimize planning, orchestrates execution by dynamically mapping queries into atomic extraction tasks and reducing the gathered evidence to synthesize a final answer. By isolating reasoning from raw context noise, DISCO effectively eliminates context rot. On RULER-QA (1M tokens), it maintains 78.4% accuracy where standard baselines collapse. Furthermore, it outperforms full-context models by up to 9.8 points on LongBench v2 and matches frontier models like Gemini-3-Pro-Preview while reducing inference costs by over 80%, establishing a highly efficient paradigm for robust long-context inference.

</details>


### [110] [LLMs Trust Their Own: Identity-Dependent Conformity in Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33495)
*Liron Soffer,Ravid Shwartz-Ziv,Chen Shani*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that large language models exhibit group-based social influence: they conform more to wrong answers from in-group agents and less to wrong answers from out-group agents, even when group identity is arbitrary, revealing a novel manipulation surface for multi-agent AI systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used in multi-agent systems where they read and respond to each other’s outputs, their patterns of social influence become a safety concern. Prior work mostly studies accuracy, alignment, or simple consensus effects, but we lack understanding of whether LLMs are sensitive to social identities (e.g., in-group vs. out-group agents) in ways analogous to human in-group favoritism and out-group derogation. This is crucial, because identity-conditioned influence could be exploited to systematically bias LLM decisions in collaborative settings, independent of factual correctness.

Method: The authors design judgment tasks with objectively correct answers and embed LLMs in simulated multi-agent settings. Target models receive answers from other agents that are intentionally incorrect, and these peer agents are labeled with various social identities: AI vs. human, different model families, or minimal arbitrary groups. The key manipulations are whether peers are in-group or out-group relative to the target model and whether there is a unanimous majority or the presence of an ally offering the correct answer. They systematically test 12 open-weight models across nine tasks, comparing response conformity rates to the incorrect majority under different identity and ally configurations. They also evaluate how prompting with Chain-of-Thought and safety-aligned labels for peers modulates these effects.

Result: Across all evaluated models and tasks, the authors find a consistent bidirectional group-identity effect on conformity to incorrect answers. When incorrect answers come from in-group agents, models are more likely to conform (in-group favoritism); when they come from out-group agents, models are less likely to conform and may actively diverge (out-group divergence). Unlike humans, whose conformity sharply drops when even one ally breaks the majority consensus, LLMs show little sensitivity to allies that belong to the majority’s group. Furthermore, a correct ally from the opposing group amplifies the identity-based conformity patterns instead of mitigating them. Chain-of-Thought prompting significantly reduces the size of these social-identity effects, but does not fully remove them: in-group allies still reduce conformity to an incorrect out-group majority. Labeling peer agents as safety-aligned shifts overall conformity levels but does not eliminate the in-group vs. out-group asymmetry.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that LLMs do not simply aggregate peer information based on correctness or numerical consensus; they also use group identity cues in a way that mimics human-like in-group favoritism and out-group divergence, even for arbitrary groupings. This introduces a novel manipulation surface for multi-agent AI systems, as an adversary could strategically assign or present identities to shape model behavior. While Chain-of-Thought and safety-aligned labels can dampen overall conformity, they do not fully remove identity-conditioned influence. The authors argue that robust multi-agent AI design must explicitly account for and mitigate these social-identity dynamics when deploying LLMs that interact with each other or with humans at scale.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings, where agents observe and influence one another, making social influence a key dimension of AI behavior and safety. We investigate whether LLMs' responses depend on the social identity of other agents, beyond the effect of their consensus. We construct judgment tasks with a single correct answer, and place models in a multi-agent setting where they receive incorrect answers from other agents whose social identities (AI or human, model family, or an arbitrary minimal group) are either shared with or distinct from their own. Across 12 open-weights models and nine tasks, we find a bidirectional effect of group identity on conformity to incorrect answers: in-group consensus increases conformity (in-group favoritism), whereas out-group consensus decreases it (out-group divergence). Unlike humans, for whom one ally breaking the consensus sharply reduces conformity, models are unmoved by an ally from the majority's group. Worse, a correct ally from the opposing group intensifies this bidirectional effect. Chain-of-Thought reasoning suppresses most of these effects, yet an in-group ally still reduces conformity to an incorrect out-group majority. Labeling peers as safety-aligned shifts overall conformity but leaves in-group favoritism and out-group divergence intact. These results show that group identity shapes how LLMs aggregate information across agents, independently of its correctness, and identify a manipulation surface for multi-agent AI systems.

</details>


### [111] [E-CONAN (Entailment, CONtradition And Neutral) Diagnostics Dataset Investigating Linguistic Phenomena in Arabic Natural Language Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33530)
*Khloud AL Jallad,Nada Ghneim,Ghaida Rebdawi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose a standardized hierarchical framework for fine-grained, cross-lingual NLU error analysis and instantiate it for Arabic with a new diagnostic dataset (E-CONAN), then compare pretrained models and LLMs across linguistic phenomena.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: NLU systems struggle with various linguistic complexities (lexical ambiguity, syntax, reasoning), and existing diagnostic benchmarks are heterogeneous: they use different labels, macro/micro categories, and sets of phenomena. This lack of standardization makes cross-model and cross-language error analysis difficult and hinders systematic understanding and improvement of NLU models.

Method: The authors design an initial cross-lingual hierarchy of macro- and micro-level linguistic phenomena suitable for NLU error analysis, with a specific methodology to derive an NLI-oriented hierarchical framework.
