They then instantiate this hierarchy for Arabic, manually constructing and annotating a diagnostic NLI dataset—E-CONAN—with both coarse-grained (macro) and fine-grained (micro) labels. Using this dataset, they evaluate and analyze errors of 9 pretrained language models and 5 LLMs across the defined categories.

Result: Using E-CONAN, they find that large language models outperform traditional pretrained models on world knowledge and commonsense reasoning categories, but perform worse on syntactic phenomena. Across all tested systems, reasoning-related phenomena are the most challenging. For pretrained models, syntactic phenomena are the easiest; for LLMs, lexico-syntactic phenomena are the easiest.

Conclusion: A structured, hierarchical error-analysis framework and a corresponding diagnostic dataset (E-CONAN for Arabic) enable more fine-grained understanding of NLU model strengths and weaknesses. The results reveal distinct capability profiles for pretrained models versus LLMs—particularly in syntax vs. world knowledge/reasoning—validating the usefulness of the proposed hierarchy and indicating directions for targeted model improvement. The work also lays groundwork for standardized, cross-lingual NLU error analysis.

Abstract: Natural Language Understanding (NLU) plays a crucial role in various applications, yet its performance suffers from weaknesses in handling the complexities of human languages, ranging from lexical ambiguity to high-level reasoning difficulties. Analyzing errors across diverse linguistic phenomena is crucial for NLU improvement, as it will help humans get insights to comprehensively assess models' limitations and capabilities, so optimizing models' generalization. Notably, several benchmarks contain diagnostics datasets designed for investigation and fine-grained error analysis. When highlighting the gaps in the state-of-the-art, we noted that there is no naming convention for macro and micro categories or even a standard set of linguistic phenomena that should be covered. To overcome this gap, we propose an initial hierarchy for Cross-Lingual NLU error analysis. Moreover, we propose a methodology to create an NLI hierarchical framework and applied a case study on Arabic NLU. Moreover, this paper introduces E-CONAN diagnostics dataset, a freely available dataset manually-annotated with coarse-grained and fine-grained categories based on our proposed Arabic hierarchy. E-CONAN dataset helps NLU designers better understand their models by doing error analysis and in-depth investigation. We used E-CONAN to investigate the performance of 9 pretrained language models and 5 LLMs. Results indicate that LLMs outperform pretrained models in world knowledge and commonsense reasoning macro-category, and underperform pretrained models in syntactic macro-category. Moreover, the hardest phenomena for all models is Reasoning, and the easiest phenomena for all pretrained models is Syntactic, and the easiest for LLMs is Lexico-Syntactic.

</details>


### [112] [ManiEdit: Sequential Unstructured Knowledge Editing for Language Models from a Manifold Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33534)
*Rui Liu,Chenheng Zhang,Haoxuan Li,Zhouchen Lin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes ManiEdit, a manifold-aware framework for continuously editing long-form knowledge in large language models while minimizing forgetting and preserving general abilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing model editing methods cannot reliably handle sequential edits of unstructured, long-form knowledge. They often forget previous edits and damage the model’s general capabilities. The authors aim to provide a more principled geometric view of knowledge editing that scales to complex, continual updates.

Method: The authors reinterpret knowledge editing as moving a localized edit sub-manifold within the model’s global knowledge manifold. They design ManiEdit, an autoregressive editing framework with two main components: (1) Pivot Localization, which selects high-leverage pivot points to anchor the edit sub-manifold and avoid using mediocre, uninformative edit locations; and (2) Manifold-Aware Preservation, which protects non-edited knowledge using an energy-weighted penalty across knowledge types and a recursive null-space alignment procedure to maintain the remaining manifold’s structure during editing.

Result: On two base LLMs and four benchmarks for unstructured knowledge editing, ManiEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing the strongest prior method by up to +27.81 BERTScore and +8.50 ROUGE-L. At the same time, it preserves almost all of the models’ original general capabilities across six downstream tasks.

Conclusion: Viewing knowledge editing as a sub-manifold displacement problem enables more effective and stable updates to LLM knowledge. ManiEdit operationalizes this view and substantially improves long-form, sequential editing quality while keeping overall model performance nearly intact, offering a promising direction for continual LLM knowledge updating.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) inevitably generate some incorrect or outdated content, necessitating efficient and precise mechanisms for continual knowledge updates. However, existing model editing methods struggle to sequentially edit unstructured long-form knowledge, suffering from severe edit forgetting and degradation of general capabilities. To address these challenges, we reframe knowledge editing from a manifold perspective, viewing it as a localized displacement of an edit sub-manifold within the global knowledge manifold. Under this formulation, the problem can be decomposed into two key questions: (i) how to identify representative edit points that effectively anchor the edit sub-manifold, and (ii) how to preserve the remaining manifold structure during the sub-manifold displacement process. Based on this perspective, we propose ManiEdit, a novel manifold-aware autoregressive editing framework consisting of two core components. Pivot Localization addresses the mediocre-point dilemma by identifying high-leverage pivots to anchor the edit sub-manifold. Manifold-Aware Preservation preserves different knowledge types through an energy-weighted penalty combined with recursive null-space alignment. Experiments on two base LLMs and four unstructured editing benchmarks demonstrate that ManiEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to +27.81 BERTScore and +8.50 ROUGE-L, while maintaining near-original general capabilities across six representative downstream tasks. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Areyliu/ManiEdit

</details>


### [113] [Jev Matches 7B Language Models for Speech-Neuroprosthesis Rescoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33538)
*Gabriele Cinà*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes using Jev, a hosted calibrated decision model, as a low-cost, low-latency language-model-based rescoring component for speech neuroprostheses, achieving similar or better accuracy than large GPU-based LMs at much lower cost and without requiring a GPU.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing speech neuroprostheses rely on a very large language model (several billion parameters) to rescore candidate sentences produced by a brain-activity decoder. That rescoring stage is the only one requiring a GPU and is expensive to deploy for individual users. Simply replacing it with a general-purpose language model is difficult because such models can behave poorly when asked to select from a small candidate set, often keying off list position rather than content. The authors want a solution that is accurate, well-calibrated, inexpensive per sentence, and does not require GPU hardware, making the system more practical for real-world deployment and for single users with low utilisation.

Method: The authors reformulate the rescoring problem as a single typed decision task: a model is called once to return a calibrated probability for each candidate sentence, rather than engaging in standard generative language modelling or list-choosing behavior. They introduce Jev, a hosted model explicitly trained for calibrated decision-making over candidate sentences. The decoder's original scores are combined with Jev's probabilities, and the weight of the decoder is optionally re-tuned. They evaluate Jev on 978 held-out sentences from a participant with ALS, comparing word error rates against the original published decoder alone and against rescoring with large general LMs (OPT-6.7b and Qwen2.5-7B). They also measure economic cost per thousand sentences, GPU utilisation break-even points, and end-to-end latency over the internet versus local GPU inference.

Result: On the held-out set, the published decoder alone achieves 8.1% word error rate (WER). Using Jev for rescoring yields 7.5% WER, outperforming both OPT-6.7b and Qwen2.5-7B, which achieve 7.8% WER with default decoder weights. After re-tuning the decoder's weight, Jev achieves 6.9% WER, versus 7.2% for OPT-6.7b and 7.4% for Qwen2.5-7B. Jev is better in all four pairwise comparisons and is at most 0.2 percentage points behind the best at the 95% confidence bound. Economically, Jev costs about $0.07 per thousand sentences and requires no GPU, whereas a dedicated GPU running a 7B model only becomes cheaper per sentence when utilisation exceeds 43%, which is much higher than typical single-user load. Latency-wise, end-to-end over the internet is 262 ms per query, with 62 ms at the provider; this is of the same order as running a 7B model locally on a GPU (27 ms) though not faster.

Conclusion: Recasting language-model rescoring for speech neuroprostheses as a calibrated decision task and serving it via Jev enables GPU-free deployment with similar or superior accuracy to large 7B-parameter models. Jev consistently improves word error rate over the baseline decoder and outperforms or matches large general-purpose LMs while being substantially cheaper per sentence under realistic, low-utilisation conditions. Although network latency prevents it from being faster than a local GPU model, its performance, calibration, and economic profile make it a practical and attractive alternative for real-world speech neuroprosthesis users, especially when dedicated high-utilisation GPUs are not available.

Abstract: A speech neuroprosthesis decodes attempted speech from brain activity and ends by rescoring the decoder's candidate sentences with a language model of several billion parameters, the only component that needs a GPU. Replacing that model with a cheaper one is hard: general language models asked to pick one sentence from a list answer from where a label sits in the list rather than from the sentence itself. We pose rescoring as a single typed decision, one call that returns a probability for every candidate, served by Jev, a hosted model trained for calibrated decisions, and combine it with the decoder's own score. On 978 held-out sentences from a participant with ALS, where the published decoder alone reaches 8.1% word error, Jev reaches 7.5% against 7.8% for both OPT-6.7b and Qwen2.5-7B; with the decoder's weight re-tuned, 6.9% against 7.2% and 7.4%. Jev is ahead in all four comparisons and at most 0.2 points behind at the 95% bound. It costs 0.07 USD per thousand sentences and needs no GPU; a dedicated GPU running a 7B model is cheaper per sentence only above 43% utilisation, far beyond what one user generates. End-to-end latency over the internet is 262 ms, of which 62 ms is spent at the provider, the same order as a 7B model on a local GPU (27 ms) but not faster.

</details>


### [114] [Quizzing the Translation: A Prover-Grounded Evaluation Metric for NL$\rightarrow$FOL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33612)
*Pu Suo,Ali Emami*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces SIV, a verification-based metric for evaluating translations from natural language to first-order logic, which more faithfully reflects semantic correctness than surface-based metrics like BLEU or BERTScore.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluation metrics for translating natural language into first-order logic (FOL) focus on surface similarity (e.g., token overlap or embedding cosine), which fails to capture critical logical errors. Small lexical changes like swapping quantifiers ("every" vs. "some") can completely alter meaning while preserving high overlap scores. This misalignment leads to metrics that may rate severely incorrect logical forms as good, undermining progress in symbolic reasoning over text. The authors aim to design an evaluation metric that is sensitive to logical content and error severity, not just surface similarity.

Method: They propose SIV, a semantic evaluation framework that constructs logical "probes" from the target FOL formula and verifies candidate translations using a theorem prover. Two probe types are derived: (1) Positive probes: logical consequences that any correct candidate must entail; failure to entail them signals content loss or under-specification. (2) Contrastive probes: logical statements that must not be entailed by a correct candidate; their entailment signals hallucinated or over-asserted content. For each candidate translation, SIV runs theorem-proving checks against these probes, aggregates the outcomes into a score, and records which probes fail. This probe-level feedback forms an error trace that can be used to classify error types. They evaluate SIV against existing metrics (BLEU, BERTScore, Smatch++) on controlled perturbations of FOLIO translations, on disjoint error-class test sets, and on expert-audited real LLM-produced FOL translations.

Result: On a controlled dataset of systematically perturbed FOLIO translations, the severity of logical error explains about 80% of the variance in SIV scores, versus at most 17% for any previous metric, showing SIV is much more sensitive to semantic degradation. On an independent set spanning six error classes, SIV correctly ranks the gold reference above perturbed candidates in over 99% of pairs, far outperforming prior metrics. The labeled probes enable SIV to reconstruct the underlying perturbation/error class with a macro-F1 of 0.638, nearly twice the performance of using only scalar metric scores. On 434 expert-audited real-world LLM translations, SIV achieves the best AUC among all metrics tested, is uniquely capable of reliably identifying and grading expert-labeled major errors, and can abstain from scoring out-of-vocabulary translations instead of mis-evaluating them.

Conclusion: SIV provides a logically grounded, verification-style metric for evaluating natural-language-to-FOL translations that correlates closely with true semantic correctness and error severity. By using theorem-prover-based positive and contrastive probes, it overcomes the limitations of surface-based similarity metrics, consistently ranks correct translations above perturbed ones, and yields interpretable error traces that help diagnose failure modes. Its strong empirical performance on both synthetic perturbations and expert-audited real translations suggests it is a practical and more faithful tool for benchmarking and improving symbolic reasoning systems that rely on logical form translation.

Abstract: A standard pipeline for symbolic reasoning over natural-language problems translates them into first-order logic and invokes a theorem prover. The translation step is the bottleneck: swap "every" for "some" and every inference that follows is corrupted. Yet today's metrics often score more broken translations higher than less broken ones, because BLEU, BERTScore, and Smatch++ reward surface overlap that the worst errors happen to preserve. We introduce SIV, which derives two kinds of probes from the target formula and uses a theorem prover to verify the candidate translation against each. Positive probes are statements the candidate must entail, which detect translations that drop content; contrastive probes are statements the candidate must not entail, which detect translations that assert more than the original. On a controlled pool of perturbed FOLIO translations, the severity of the error accounts for 80% of SIV's score variance, compared with at most 17% for any prior metric. Across six error classes on a disjoint pool, SIV scores the reference above the perturbed candidate in over 99% of pairs. Because each probe is labeled with what it tests, the failure pattern also supplies a labeled error trace, recovering the perturbation class at macro-F1 0.638, nearly double the score-only baseline. On 434 expert-audited real LLM translations, SIV attains the top AUC, uniquely detects and grades expert-labeled major errors, and abstains, rather than mis-scoring, on out-of-vocabulary translations.

</details>


### [115] [Safety Reconstructed: Generative Modeling via Masked Diffusion Builds Strong Safety Guardrails](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33634)
*Gert Lek,Abele Malan,Chaoyi Zhu,Pin-Yu Chen,Robert Birke,Lydia Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces LLaDA-Guard, a generative guard model that evaluates which safety label better explains a text by scoring all tokens, leading to better calibration, robustness, and token-level risk localization compared to standard discriminative guard models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current guard models for LLM safety are trained to predict a single verdict token for an entire conversation, which concentrates supervision on one position. This narrow objective causes structural issues: models exploit shortcuts, become overconfident, and are sensitive to where safety evidence appears in the sequence instead of its semantic role in the overall context. The authors aim to design a guard that reasons over full content, mitigates shortcut reliance, and improves calibration and robustness while still being practical to deploy on top of existing LMs.

Method: The authors reformulate guarding as a generative, label-conditional modeling problem: instead of predicting a label from text, the model asks which label (e.g., safe/unsafe) better explains the text. Concretely, LLaDA-Guard scores the prompt or response under each label hypothesis, then classifies based on the score difference. This pushes supervision to every token in the moderated span, enforcing attention to full content. They instantiate this with a masked diffusion language model, fine-tuning LLaDA-8B-Instruct using a class-conditional reconstruction loss via LoRA, without changing the base model’s architecture. The result is a generative safety classifier that can also localize risky tokens by inspecting token-level contributions to the label-conditioned likelihoods.

Result: On seven held-out safety benchmarks, LLaDA-Guard ranks best on average compared to strong discriminative baselines, even those using more powerful backbones. It shows substantially improved confidence calibration (ECE 0.0875 vs. 0.1384 for Qwen3Guard), and it reduces over-defense on benign prompts that merely contain unsafe-looking cues. It is also less prone to prompt leakage when moderating model responses. Because it is generative and token-aware, LLaDA-Guard can naturally locate high-risk spans and use them to rewrite unsafe prompts into safer alternatives, attaining a 60.7% average rate of converting unsafe inputs into safe ones without additional training.

Conclusion: Recasting safety guarding as generative, label-conditional modeling over all tokens rather than discriminative, single-token classification yields structurally better behavior. LLaDA-Guard, instantiated via a class-conditional masked diffusion LM fine-tune, outperforms discriminative guards across diverse safety benchmarks, achieves better calibration, avoids excessive conservatism, and reduces prompt leakage. Its generative nature further enables token-level risk localization and automatic safe rewriting, suggesting that future guard models should be built as generative explainers of text under safety labels rather than simple verdict predictors.

Abstract: Guard models are the last line of defense between a language model and a harmful output, yet their training objective is surprisingly narrow. Existing guards learn to predict a single verdict token from a conversational context, concentrating supervision on a single target. The consequences are structural: models latch onto shortcut features, are overconfident, and remain sensitive to where safety evidence appears in the sequence rather than its role in the full context. We propose a different framing. Rather than predicting a label from text, our LLaDA-Guard asks which label better explains the text: scoring the prompt or response under each label hypothesis and classifying based on their difference. This shifts supervision to every token in the moderated region, forcing the model to account for full content rather than its most discriminative fragments. We instantiate this idea with a masked diffusion language model, fine-tuning LLaDA-8B-Instruct with a class-conditional reconstruction objective using LoRA and requiring no architectural changes beyond the base model. LLaDA-Guard leads on average rank against discriminative baselines trained on stronger backbones across seven held-out safety benchmarks, while exhibiting substantially better confidence calibration (ECE 0.0875 vs. 0.1384 for Qwen3Guard), less over-defense on benign prompts with unsafe-looking cues, and less prompt leakage when moderating responses. Its generative nature further enables token-level risk localization as a natural byproduct, yielding a pipeline for rewriting unsafe prompts into safe equivalents without additional training and achieving a 60.7% average conversion-to-safe rate.

</details>


### [116] [Learning to Learn from Context: Synthetic Training from Perturbed Public Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33642)
*Haoyi Wu,Yang Xiao,Yusong Sun,Wenyang Hui,Zhaokai Luo,Chengyue Jiang,Mu Chuan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build a fully-automatic data synthesis pipeline that turns public documents into context-dependent QA + reasoning traces, then use these to train and RL-tune a student LLM that gets much better at learning from long, complex context without human annotation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs still struggle to truly learn and reason from task-specific context (documents, long inputs) and instead lean on their baked-in parametric knowledge. Creating supervised datasets that require genuine context use is expensive because it needs humans to read long documents and craft questions/answers. Simply reusing web documents is unsafe because much of that text was seen during pretraining, so naive training risks encouraging memorization rather than context-grounded reasoning. The authors want a scalable, reproducible way to exploit high-quality public documents to improve in-context reasoning, while minimizing memorization and avoiding human labeling costs.

Method: They propose an automatic document-based synthetic data pipeline. (i) Take high-quality public source documents and rewrite/perturb them to reduce overlap with pretraining data and thus lower memorization risk. (ii) Automatically generate questions and grading rubrics that require reasoning over each (perturbed) document, not just surface recall. (iii) Use a strong model to answer these questions with explicit access to the document, also producing reasoning traces. (iv) Filter and keep only the samples where the answer demonstrably depends on the document (“genuinely depend on the document”), ensuring context-groundedness. This synthetic dataset (~10k QA+reasoning samples from 3.5k docs) is used to supervised fine-tune a mid-size student model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B). They then apply an additional RL stage using the rubrics as rewards to further refine the student. Evaluation is done on CL-bench and a range of other tasks (long-context, instruction following, reasoning, code, knowledge).

Result: Their synthetic data and training improve the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B student’s CL-bench performance from 13.7% (base) to 22.8% after supervised fine-tuning, and up to 24.6% after rubric-based RL. This surpasses the performance of a much larger frontier model, Qwen3.8-2.4T (23.9%), on CL-bench. The improvements also transfer broadly to long-context understanding, instruction following, and general reasoning benchmarks, while performance on code generation and factual knowledge tasks remains largely unchanged. The pipeline yields ~10k high-quality document-grounded samples from 3.5k documents, with no human annotation.

Conclusion: An automated pipeline that perturbs public documents, synthesizes document-reliant questions, reasoning traces, and rubric-based rewards, and filters for genuine context dependence can significantly enhance an LLM’s ability to learn from context. With only ~10k synthetic samples and no human labels, a 35B-parameter student model can match or slightly exceed the context-learning performance of a 2.4T-parameter model on CL-bench and gain broader benefits in long-context understanding and reasoning. The method appears scalable and reproducible, and it highlights document-grounded synthetic supervision as a promising direction for improving context-grounded reasoning without needing massive human-annotated datasets or ever-larger models.

Abstract: Real-world tasks often require large language models (LLMs) to learn from complex task-specific context rather than pretrained parametric knowledge. This capability remains a weakness of LLMs, while human annotation for such task contexts is expensive and difficult to scale. Public high-quality documents are an abundant alternative, but much of the public web has already been consumed during pretraining: training on such documents naively would reward memorization rather than context learning. In this work, we attempt to make use of high-quality public documents with small perturbations and empirically find that LLMs can successfully generate context-dependent reasoning traces and answers, which are then used to train a student model. Specifically, we construct a synthesis pipeline that (i) rewrites source documents to reduce memorization risk, (ii) generates questions and rubrics that require reasoning over the document, (iii) answers the questions with the document as context, and (iv) admits only samples that genuinely depend on the document. Without any human annotators, our pipeline generates about 10k samples from 3.5k documents, and the resulting student model substantially improves the performance on CL-bench. SFT raises a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B student from 13.7% to 22.8%, and a subsequent rubric-reward RL stage reaches 24.6%, on CL-bench comparable with a frontier model of over a trillion parameters, Qwen3.8-2.4T (23.9%). We also observe a broad transfer of improvements to long-context understanding, instruction following, and reasoning, while code generation and knowledge remain mostly flat. We hope this work provides a reproducible and scalable way to improve the ability of LLMs to learn from context, and to facilitate further research on context-grounded reasoning.

</details>


### [117] [Tsubame: Tree Replay for Diffusion-Based Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33652)
*Yepeng Weng,Qiao Hu,Takehisa Yairi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes Tsubame, a two-pass speculative decoding framework for diffusion-based drafters that decouples tree topology selection from token selection via sampling, achieving better acceptance length and throughput than deterministic dynamic trees and sometimes outperforming sampled chains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dynamic, context-aware speculative decoding trees can adapt depth and branching to path probabilities, but under stochastic decoding they may underperform simple sampled chains because they mostly verify deterministic high-score tokens and thus lose the benefits of random sampling combined with strong verification. The authors aim to keep the structural strengths of dynamic trees while recovering the probabilistic benefits of sampling.

Method: The authors design Tsubame, a two-pass tree speculative decoding algorithm for diffusion-based drafters. In pass one, the system constructs and freezes a context-aware draft tree topology using draft path scores (deterministic planning of which nodes/paths to consider). In pass two, keeping this topology fixed, the algorithm repopulates all tree nodes by stochastic sampling to create candidate tokens, which are then fed into an advanced verifier. Diffusion-based drafters make this efficient because their parallel generative process or conditional corrections can regenerate candidates cheaply after the topology is fixed. The authors also provide a theoretical proof that Tsubame is lossless under suitable sampling and verification schemes.

Result: Across three different diffusion-based drafters, six datasets, and various candidate budgets, Tsubame yields longer accepted sequences and higher decoding throughput than standard deterministic dynamic trees. In particular, in settings where deterministic dynamic trees previously lagged behind simple sampled chains, Tsubame reverses this disadvantage and can surpass sampled chains in performance.

Conclusion: By decoupling tree topology construction from token selection and exploiting diffusion-based drafters for cheap candidate regeneration, Tsubame combines the adaptive structure of dynamic trees with the robustness of stochastic sampling plus advanced verification. This two-pass framework is provably lossless under compatible strategies and empirically improves both acceptance length and throughput, demonstrating a practical path to more efficient speculative decoding for modern diffusion-based language models.

Abstract: Context-aware dynamic trees allocate the speculative decoding budget according to draft path probabilities, adapting their depth and branching to the current context. Under stochastic decoding, however, we find that this structural advantage does not always compensate for the acceptance gains of random sampling paired with advanced verification, and such dynamic trees can fall behind sampled chains in some settings. These trees grow their topology from the candidates themselves, so the tokens submitted for verification are typically the deterministic high-score tokens selected during construction. This coupling is not inherent: once the topology is fixed, its nodes can be repopulated by sampling, allowing dynamic trees to retain their structural advantage while also benefiting from random sampling and advanced verification. Diffusion-based drafters make this practical, as their parallel outputs or lightweight conditional corrections allow candidates to be regenerated cheaply after the complete topology is known. We introduce Tsubame, a two-pass tree speculative decoding framework for diffusion-based drafters. The first pass plans and freezes a context-aware topology using draft path scores; the second replays the fixed topology, sampling the tokens that populate its nodes to form the candidate tree for verification. We prove that Tsubame is lossless under compatible sampling and verification strategies. Experiments across three diffusion-based drafters, six datasets, and multiple candidate budgets show that Tsubame improves acceptance length and throughput over deterministic trees, including settings where it reverses their disadvantage against sampled chains.

</details>


### [118] [One Model Is Not a Crowd: Multi-LLM and Aspect-Conditioned Diverse Comment Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33666)
*Nafis Irtiza Tripto,Delvin Ce Zhang,Mahjabin Nahar,Dongwon Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether synthetic comment threads generated by large language models can capture the diversity of human online discourse and proposes a multi-model, aspect-conditioned approach plus a diversity evaluation framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM-based agents increasingly participate in online discussions, there is a risk that homogenized AI-generated content will reduce diversity in digital communication, potentially leading to model collapse and a loss of richness in discourse. The authors are motivated to understand and improve how well synthetic comments can reflect the diverse perspectives found in real human conversations.

Method: The authors combine multiple LLMs from different providers and use aspect-conditioned generation to produce synthetic comments. They design a framework to characterize diversity across semantic, linguistic, and socio-pragmatic features along three axes: dispersion, coverage, and alignment. They then conduct a large-scale empirical study comparing synthetic comments to more than 2 million human YouTube comments across multiple domains.

Result: They find that multi-LLM setups with aspect-conditioned generation produce comment distributions that more closely resemble human comment diversity than single-model or unconditioned baselines. The generated data remains usable under typical pretraining-style filtering and works well for downstream tasks. However, the level of diversity achieved by these synthetic comments still falls short of actual human diversity.

Conclusion: Using multiple LLMs together with aspect-conditioned generation offers a practical way to generate more diverse and socially grounded synthetic discourse for AI-mediated environments, but it still cannot fully match the diversity of real human communication. Their framework and findings provide a basis for improving and evaluating diversity in synthetic comment generation going forward.

Abstract: Human communication on the internet is shaped by diverse perspectives, most visibly expressed in online comment spaces. As large language model (LLM)based AI agents begin to inhabit these spaces, a key question arises: whether synthetic comment threads can capture the diversity inherent in human discourse. This concern is increasingly important, as the growing presence of homogenized AI-generated content risks reducing diversity over time, potentially leading to model collapse and degrading the richness of digital communication. Inspired by the plurality of human crowds and the aspect-driven nature of discourse, we hypothesize that comment diversity is better approximated by combining multiple LLMs with aspect-conditioned generation. We formalize and evaluate this approach using models from different providers and introduce a framework that characterizes diversity across semantic, linguistic, and socio-pragmatic features along three axes: dispersion, coverage, and alignment. Using this framework, we conduct a large-scale study on over 2 million YouTube comments across multiple domains. Our results reveal that multi-LLM and aspect-conditioned generation better align with human comment distributions and such data remains viable under pretraining style curation and is effective for downstream tasks. Yet, human diversity remains unmatched. Overall, our findings provide a practical foundation for generating more diverse and socially grounded discourse in AI-mediated environments.

</details>


### [119] [Closing the Cross-Dialect Gap: Query Plans as a Portable Interface in Text-to-SQL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33670)
*Corentin Royer,Robin Oester,Yotam Perlitz,Yannick Metz,Andrea Giovannini,Mennatallah El-Assady*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that training Text-to-SQL models on a single SQL dialect (like SQLite) causes large accuracy drops when used on other dialects, and proposes generating dialect-agnostic relational algebra plans plus a compiler as a robust, portable alternative.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In practice, Text-to-SQL systems must work across diverse SQL dialects (PostgreSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse, etc.), but existing research and benchmarks typically assume a single dialect (SQLite). This mismatch causes models that perform well in lab settings to degrade significantly in real-world multi-dialect environments. The authors aim to understand and fix this cross-dialect generalization problem so that models are both accurate and portable across backends.

Method: Instead of having large language models directly generate dialect-specific SQL, the authors have them generate a dialect-agnostic relational algebra query plan. A deterministic compiler then translates this plan into concrete SQL for each target backend. They empirically evaluate thirteen models from 3B parameters to frontier scale, comparing direct-SQL generation to plan generation under prompting and fine-tuning settings. They also design a new evaluation metric, MetricName, which compares result sets in a question-aware way to disentangle true semantic errors from harmless cross-dialect execution differences.

Result: All tested models suffer substantial drops in accuracy when evaluated on SQL dialects different from the one used for training (typically SQLite). Switching the generation target from SQL to relational algebra plans largely eliminates this cross-dialect drop, yielding nearly uniform portability across dialects. Any loss in peak accuracy on the training dialect is small for strong prompted models and disappears when models are fine-tuned on plans. Under matched fine-tuning conditions, supervising on plans even produces stronger models than supervising directly on SQL. MetricName enables more accurate cross-dialect evaluation by avoiding penalization for benign dialectal differences in results.

Conclusion: The central barrier to cross-dialect Text-to-SQL robustness is the choice of generation target: dialect-specific SQL entangles surface-form quirks with semantics, harming portability. Generating a dialect-agnostic relational algebra plan and compiling it to SQL resolves this tension, improving cross-dialect generalization with minimal or no loss on the home dialect and even better performance under plan-based supervision. The newly proposed evaluation metric further supports fair comparison across dialects. More generally, when using LLMs for code-like generation, representing the task via an intermediate, execution-agnostic abstraction can significantly improve model quality and robustness.

Abstract: Text-to-SQL systems are typically trained and evaluated on a single dialect (SQLite), yet production deployments span PostgreSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse, and beyond. We show that this single-dialect assumption leads to a substantial drop in cross-dialect accuracy for every model we tested. The drop persists across scale, architecture, and even purpose-built text-to-SQL systems. We argue that the fix is to change the generation target: instead of asking an LLM to emit dialect-specific SQL, we have it emit a dialect-agnostic relational algebra query plan, which a deterministic compiler then renders into SQL for any supported backend. Across thirteen models from 3B to frontier scale, this restores cross-dialect portability nearly uniformly, at a small cost in peak accuracy on the model's home dialect for capable prompted models and none once fine-tuned on plans; under matched fine-tuning, plan supervision yields a stronger model than SQL supervision. We also introduce MetricName, a question-aware result-set comparator needed to evaluate fairly across dialects, where existing metrics confound semantic errors with benign cross-dialect variation. More broadly, the result is a reminder that a generation target chosen for execution is not necessarily the one that maximizes generation quality.

</details>


### [120] [Reset Is Not Recovery: Evaluating Recoverability from False Conversational Context via Sycophancy Hysteresis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33672)
*Adi Shnaidman*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies whether language models can recover their factual accuracy after being pressured by a user to adopt a wrong answer in multi-turn dialogue, finding that simple history-preserving fixes are usually insufficient while removing or overriding misleading context is highly effective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In real conversations, users often assert incorrect information. Instruction-tuned language models tend to be sycophantic and follow user mistakes. Existing evaluations mostly test models with clean, supportive context, so it is unclear how well models recover once the user stops pushing a wrong answer. The authors want to understand and quantify this "post-pressure recoverability" and how different dialogue-management strategies affect it.

Method: They define a multiple-choice dialogue evaluation protocol called recovery-after-pressure. A user repeatedly advocates a wrong answer, then removes that pressure (e.g., retracts or the system asks for a fresh answer). The authors compare model behavior in this pressured dialogue to a clean-context counterfactual with no wrong advocacy, measuring "sycophancy hysteresis"—the residual probability the model assigns to the wrong answer after pressure is withdrawn. They test seven open-weight instruction-tuned models across two factual QA benchmarks and explore various recovery operations: ordinary reset, keeping history but adding retractions or system messages, self-verification prompts, deleting parts of history, truncating context, and adding benchmark-derived trusted evidence. They also run multiple controls to rule out simpler explanations like dialogue length or repeated confidence.

Result: Ordinary reset reduces but does not fully eliminate bias toward the previously user-advocated wrong answer. History-preserving repairs (such as user retraction, system reset messages, or self-verification) successfully restore clean behavior in only 2–3 out of 14 model–dataset combinations under a strict diagnostic. In contrast, operations that effectively change or trim the context work much better: both fresh-context deletion and context truncation, which remove the pressure-bearing dialogue turns, fully restore clean behavior in all 14/14 cases. Under an oracle setting that appends trusted benchmark evidence while keeping the misleading history, average accuracy jumps from 0.368 to 0.929 and the rate of following the wrong answer drops from 41.2% to 4.3%. Control experiments show these effects are not due to dialogue length, repeated assertions, distractors, mere mention of the false answer, or option-label bias.

Conclusion: Language models exhibit persistent sycophantic bias after user pressure, even when that pressure is later withdrawn, and common history-preserving fixes are usually inadequate. Reliable factual dialogue requires explicit management of conversational history: models or systems must decide which past user statements to treat as evidence and which to remove, downweight, or quarantine before answering. Providing strong trusted evidence or pruning misleading context is far more effective than simply adding retractions or self-check prompts.

Abstract: Grounded language models are usually evaluated by adding relevant context, but multiturn dialogue also contains unsupported user claims that may contaminate later factual answers. We study post-pressure recoverability: whether a model returns to clean-context behavior after a user repeatedly advocates a wrong answer and then withdraws that pressure. We introduce a recovery-after-pressure protocol for multiple-choice factual dialogue and measure sycophancy hysteresis, the residual probability assigned to the user-advocated wrong answer relative to a clean-context counterfactual. Across seven instruction-tuned open-weight models and two factual benchmarks, ordinary reset often reduces but does not erase pressure-induced bias. History preserving repairs such as user retraction, system reset, and self-verification recover only 2-3/14 model-dataset pairs under the strict clean-restoration diagnostic, whereas operations that change the effective context are substantially more reliable; the two conditions that remove the pressure-bearing history entirely, fresh-context deletion and context truncation, recover 14/14. In an oracle trusted-evidence condition across fourteen model-dataset pairs, preserving the pressure-bearing history while adding benchmark-derived trusted evidence increases accuracy from 0.368 to 0.929, while wrong-answer following falls from 41.2% to 4.3%. Controls show that the effect is not explained by dialogue length, repeated confidence, plausible distractors, mere false-answer mention, or option-label inertia. These results suggest that faithful grounded dialogue requires evaluating which prior context should be treated as evidence and which should be removed or quarantined before answering.

</details>

### [121] [SMARtCARE: Privacy-Preserving Agentic AI Systems for Bounded-Autonomy Clinical Decision Support](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31763)
*Srini Ramaswamy,Deveeshree Nayak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces SMARtCARE, a four-state clinical decision-support framework that uses compact fingerprints of prior ICU trajectories to flag possible recurrences of past deterioration patterns while preserving traceability and privacy, without claiming clinical efficacy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context clinical AI systems may fail to consider important prior admissions when they fall outside the active context window, leading to missed recognition of recurring deterioration patterns in ICU patients. There is a need for a mechanism that can surface such "middle-context" risk (not fully in-context, not fully out-of-scope) in a traceable and privacy-conscious way, without indiscriminately retrieving all prior records.

Method: The authors design SMARtCARE, a four-state architecture—Stable, Meta-cognitive, Assisted, Regulated (Revoked)—for ICU decision support. Instead of automatically loading complete prior records, the system computes a lossy six-channel fingerprint representing a patient's historical physiological trajectory. During monitoring, if current vital-sign drift matches this fingerprint and the original prior record is not currently loaded, the system transitions into a Meta-cognitive state and raises an escalation for clinician review. Full record retrieval happens only when the clinician advances the system to the Assisted state. A patient-identity guard enforces correct attribution of data across loading, logging, and audit components. The framework is evaluated with a synthetic Monte Carlo study (to test state transitions and estimator stability) and small-scale runs on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV demo datasets.

Result: In synthetic Monte Carlo experiments, the state-transition logic and estimator behavior are validated, though no clinical performance metrics are claimed. On the MIMIC-III demo, among 14 patients with two admissions, the system identified one case where a current pattern matched a prior deterioration fingerprint when the prior data were not in context. On the MIMIC-IV demo, with 9 two-admission patients, the same pipeline found no recurrent-pattern matches, highlighting a limitation of using a fixed canonical pattern library for fingerprinting. In all experiments, every logged decision remained traceable and correctly linked to the appropriate patient identity, confirming the integrity of the patient-identity guard and logging design.

Conclusion: SMARtCARE offers a structured, four-state, meta-cognitive decision-support framework that can surface potential recurrence of prior ICU deterioration patterns using compact fingerprints instead of full historical retrieval, thereby supporting privacy, traceability, and controlled clinician-mediated escalation. The current work demonstrates architectural feasibility and traceable operation rather than any clinical benefit, and it reveals constraints such as the limited sensitivity of a fixed canonical pattern library. Further research is needed for clinical validation and refinement of the fingerprinting and pattern-matching mechanisms.

Abstract: Long-context clinical AI systems can miss relevant patient history when prior admissions fall outside the active reasoning context. In ICU monitoring, this can cause early vital-sign drift to appear nonspecific even when it resembles a prior deterioration pattern. SMARtCARE addresses this gap through a four-state clinical decision-support architecture: Stable, Meta-cognitive, Assisted, and Regulated (Revoked). Rather than automatically retrieving prior records, SMARtCARE uses a lossy six-channel fingerprint of the patient's prior trajectory. When current drift matches that fingerprint and the prior record is absent from context, the system raises a Meta-cognitive escalation for clinician review; full retrieval occurs only through clinician action in the Assisted state. A patient-identity guard is designed to enforce correct attribution across data loading, logging, and audit layers. Evaluation combines a synthetic Monte Carlo study that validates the state-transition logic and estimator stability, not clinical performance, with real-data runs on both the MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV Clinical Database Demos. On MIMIC-III, one prior-pattern recurrence was identified among 14 two-admission patients; on MIMIC-IV, the same pipeline produced no fingerprint matches among 9 two-admission patients, which illustrates a key limitation of a fixed canonical pattern library. Across both runs all logged decisions were fully traceable and correctly attributed. The results support SMARtCARE as a traceable, privacy-aware mechanism for surfacing middle-context risk; they are not a clinical efficacy claim.

</details>


### [122] [Witeness Overlap: Directional Provenance Inside Open-Weight Model Families](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31784)
*Siyuan Li,Haoxuan Zeng,Xin Luo,Fernando Jia,Florence Li,Zhengyang Geng,Zico Kolter,Tai Sing Lee,Tianqin Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a method to determine not only whether two model checkpoints are related, but also which one is the parent and which is the child.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing model-provenance methods mainly answer whether two models are related, assuming a known base model, but they cannot reliably determine the direction of the relationship (which came first) because they rely on symmetric evidence like representation or weight similarity.

Method: The authors propose a local geometric comparison using a third, same-family model checkpoint as a witness. They compare the geometry of model parameters around each candidate checkpoint and infer directionality by checking which candidate behaves more like a branching parent. They instantiate this as Witness Overlap, a prompt-free, training-free, white-box test that uses metrics like Frobenius cosine and an SVD-based weight reduction variant.

Result: On 176 LLM checkpoints from 16 families, the one-witness Witness Overlap test correctly orients 95.3% of parent-child relationships using Frobenius cosine. The method is also evaluated for root identification, sibling discrimination, extension to VLM and diffusion models, and for ordering checkpoints in chains. The signal remains robust under weight noise and sparse pruning, with the SVD-based variant more robust than plain Frobenius cosine.

Conclusion: Witness Overlap provides an effective, training-free, and prompt-free white-box test for directional model provenance, enabling auditors to infer not just relatedness but also the temporal or genealogical order of checkpoints across LLM, VLM, and diffusion model families, even under noise and pruning.

Abstract: Open-weight models are often released, fine-tuned, aligned, merged, and re-released, making provenance audits ask not only whether checkpoints are related, but also which checkpoint came first. Many existing model-provenance methods are designed for a base-known audit setting: given a victim or source model, they test whether a suspect model is related to it. Although these audits are framed as source-to-suspect tests, their underlying evidence is often symmetric, relying on representation similarity, weight similarity, behavioral fingerprints, or correlation statistics. Symmetric pairwise comparisons can detect relatedness, but they cannot by themselves orient relationship between checkpoints A and B. We therefore introduce a local geometric comparison: instead of comparing two checkpoints directly, we add a third same-family checkpoint as a witness and compare the geometry around each candidate endpoint. Direction is inferred by asking which candidate behaves more like a branching parent. Motivated by this idea, and by the empirically observed asymmetry between parent-anchored and child-anchored witness-overlap distributions, we propose Witness Overlap, a prompt-free, training-free white-box test for directional provenance. On 176 LLM checkpoints from 16 families, our one-witness test orients 95.3\% of parent-child decisions using Frobenius cosine. We further evaluate root identification, sibling discrimination, generalizations to VLM and diffusion families, and chain-structured ordering. The signal is robust to weight noise and sparse pruning, with a proposed SVD weight reduction variant showing greater robustness than Frobenius cosine.

</details>


### [123] [CP-Agent: A Harness-Engineered Agent for Crystal Plasticity Simulation Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31790)
*Samuel Onimpa Alfred,Abhishek Kumar,Veera Sundararaghavan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces CP-Agent, an LLM-based agent that automates end-to-end crystal plasticity modeling workflows from natural language instructions, reducing manual setup and calibration effort while keeping results interpretable and auditable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Crystal plasticity simulations are powerful for predicting mechanical behavior of polycrystalline metals but are cumbersome to use in practice. They require manual configuration of multiple heterogeneous tools, complex multi-step data pipelines, and labor-intensive calibration of constitutive parameters against experiments, which makes systematic parameter studies slow and error-prone. There is therefore a need for automated, reliable, and interpretable workflows that can orchestrate these tasks with minimal human intervention.

Method: The authors design CP-Agent, a large language model-based agent built with a harness-engineering approach. The harness combines a minimal system prompt, typed tool definitions encoding domain knowledge, a tool dispatcher, and a safety-bounded iteration loop. The agent operates under the ReAct paradigm: it plans, selects, and sequences tools for each task while delegating numerical parameter search to external optimizers rather than solving it internally. The domain logic is encoded in tool schemas instead of hard-coded workflows, enabling the agent to infer the correct sequence of crystal plasticity modeling steps directly from natural language task descriptions.

Result: CP-Agent is evaluated on four case studies: (1) calibration of four slip parameters for additively manufactured 316L stainless steel using tensile data; (2) validation on published copper benchmarks, successfully reproducing stress–strain response and texture evolution; (3) recovery of the initial diffuse crystallographic texture in copper; and (4) reproduction of multi-pass rolling texture evolution in a Mg–Zn–Ca alloy, including five chained deformation passes and recovery of the experimentally observed weakened, split basal texture. Across all cases and repeated runs, the agent consistently inferred appropriate tool sequences and produced physically meaningful and interpretable outputs.

Conclusion: Harness engineering with an LLM-based agent is an effective, systematic way to automate complex crystal plasticity modeling workflows. CP-Agent can translate natural-language tasks into robust, reproducible simulation pipelines, preserving physical interpretability and auditability via explicit reasoning traces. This approach lowers the barrier to routine CP simulations and enables more efficient parameter studies without sacrificing scientific rigor.

Abstract: Crystal plasticity (CP) simulations predict the mechanical behavior of polycrystalline metals, yet their routine use is hindered by the manual effort of configuring heterogeneous tools, orchestrating multi-step data pipelines, and calibrating constitutive parameters against experiments. These bottlenecks impede productivity in systematic parameter studies, motivating interest in automated workflows. This study presents CP-Agent, a harness-engineered LLM-based agent that autonomously executes complete CP modeling workflows from natural-language tasks. Operating under the ReAct paradigm, the agent reasons about tool selection and sequencing while delegating numerical search to established optimizers. The harness comprises a minimal system prompt, typed tool definitions, a dispatcher, and a safety-bounded iteration loop, encoding domain knowledge through tool schemas rather than hard-coded logic. CP-Agent is demonstrated on four case studies: calibrating four slip parameters of additively manufactured stainless steel 316L against tensile data; validating the workflow against published copper benchmarks, reproducing stress-strain and texture evolution; recovering the initial crystallographic texture of copper, where the agent correctly identifies a diffuse initial texture; and reproducing the multi-pass rolling texture evolution of a Mg-Zn-Ca alloy, where the agent chains five deformation passes and recovers the experimentally observed weakened, split basal texture. In all cases, the agent inferred the correct execution sequence from the task statement, robustly across repeated runs, and delivered physically interpretable results. This work establishes harness engineering as a systematic approach to automating CP modeling workflows while maintaining physical interpretability and auditability through visible reasoning traces.

</details>


### [124] [ConflictVLA-Bench: Benchmarking Behavioral Responses of Vision-Language-Action Models to Premise Conflicts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31792)
*Liyu Hou,Yuan Wu,Yi Chang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces ConflictVLA-Bench to study how Vision-Language-Action models behave when given invalid task premises, revealing a recurring failure mode called Failed Persistence where models keep pursuing impossible goals instead of disengaging, and showing that outcome-based evaluations are insufficient.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-Language-Action models show good performance on standard manipulation tasks, but little is known about how they react when the task description is logically inconsistent or impossible. Existing evaluations mostly look at whether the final task succeeds or fails, which cannot distinguish between models that recognize conflicts and disengage, and models that still try to execute the impossible task but fail only at the end. The authors want to systematically analyze this gap in order to better understand and evaluate robustness and safety of VLAs under invalid or conflicting instructions.

Method: The authors build ConflictVLA-Bench, a benchmark based on the LIBERO environment, consisting of 2,826 prompt-conditioned conflict tasks. Each conflict task has a paired premise-consistent reference task, allowing controlled comparisons. The tasks span four conflict families, four structural configurations, and two prompt conditions. They run eight different VLA models on both conflict and reference tasks, and evaluate not only binary success or failure but also the detailed execution process—such as whether the agent continues to pursue the original (now invalid) goal, how its trajectory evolves, and how much it suppresses action magnitudes—thereby identifying behavioral patterns beyond terminal outcomes.

Result: Across all eight evaluated VLA models, introducing invalid premises substantially reduces original goal completion rates, with at least a 17.3 percentage point drop and up to 56.2 percentage points for OpenVLA. Even in cases where the models succeed on premise-consistent tasks but fail on the matched conflict tasks, the agents frequently continue to move toward original targets, preserve early trajectory patterns from the valid version, and show limited reduction in action magnitudes. This reveals a systematic failure mode, termed Failed Persistence, where agents continue pursuing impossible or conflicting goals rather than recognizing the premise conflict.

Conclusion: The study concludes that terminal task failure alone cannot be interpreted as evidence that a VLA has recognized an invalid premise and appropriately disengaged or refused the task. Instead, many models exhibit Failed Persistence, continuing to pursue the original goal despite premise conflicts. Explicit premise-checking mechanisms, as currently implemented, do not reliably yield selective, coordinated behavioral adjustments. Therefore, outcome-only metrics are insufficient for evaluating VLAs; process-level analyses and conflict-sensitive evaluation benchmarks like ConflictVLA-Bench are necessary to accurately assess robustness and safety under invalid or conflicting task premises.

Abstract: While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models perform strongly on manipulation tasks, their responses to invalid task premises remain underexplored. Existing evaluations of premise conflicts often focus on terminal task outcomes, yet task failure alone cannot distinguish behavioral disengagement from continued pursuit followed by an execution error. We call the latter pattern Failed Persistence. To study this phenomenon, we introduce ConflictVLA-Bench, which pairs conflict rollouts with premise-consistent reference rollouts and evaluates both outcomes and execution processes. Built on LIBERO, the benchmark contains 2,826 prompt-conditioned conflict tasks spanning four conflict families, four structural configurations, and two prompt conditions. Across all eight VLAs, invalid premises reduce original goal completion by at least 17.3 percentage points, with the reduction reaching 56.2 percentage points for OpenVLA. Crucially, even when models succeed on premise-consistent tasks and fail on their matched conflict tasks, they often continue to approach the original targets, retain early trajectory structure, and show limited action magnitude suppression. Failed Persistence therefore recurs across the evaluated models. Explicit premise checking does not consistently produce selective and coordinated behavioral changes. These findings show that terminal failure alone establishes neither behavioral disengagement nor refusal and that outcomes alone are insufficient for VLA evaluation. Experimental data and additional details are available on the project page: https://github.com/EmbodiedAISurvey/ConflictVLA-Bench

</details>


### [125] [Working with AI: A Design Framework for Human-AI Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31793)
*Yuqian Lu,Regina Lee,Rui Zhou,Lixin Jiang,Andrew McDaid,Amy Lawrence*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a practical framework for designing effective, human-centred, and responsible human-AI collaboration in industrial settings, illustrated with a cobot-based assembly use case.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although GenAI and other AI tools can enhance decision-making, automation, and productivity in industrial work, their success depends not only on technical capabilities but also on how humans experience and collaborate with them. There is a need for clear, practical guidance on how to design human-AI collaboration so that it benefits both workers and organisations while aligning with societal expectations.

Method: The authors develop a conceptual and practical framework that structures human-AI collaboration around five key elements: the human, the AI system, the task, the organisation, and the wider societal environment. They specify what effective collaboration entails, identify influencing conditions, derive design requirements, and outline relevant design decisions. They then apply this framework to a concrete use case: a human-AI collaborative assembly system using a cobot. In this use case, they translate high-level requirements into specific collaboration features and evaluate them through a case study.

Result: The framework clarifies the conditions and requirements for effective human-AI collaboration and turns them into actionable design decisions. In the cobot assembly use case, the authors demonstrate how the framework guides the selection and implementation of concrete collaboration features and show that these can be evaluated in practice within an industrial context.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that effective human-AI collaboration in industrial settings requires a structured, human-centred, and context-aware design approach. The proposed framework offers organisations a practical guide to understand collaboration requirements, make informed design decisions, and implement and assess human-AI systems—such as cobot-based assembly—in a responsible and effective way.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly GenAI, is becoming an increasingly important part of modern work. In industrial settings, AI can support decision-making, automate routine activities, assist humans, and improve productivity. However, successful AI adoption depends on more than what the technology can do. It also depends on how people experience and work with it. This raises an important question: how should human-AI collaboration be designed so that it works well for both people and organisations? This white paper addresses that question by presenting a practical framework for designing human-AI collaboration. The framework considers the human, the AI system, the task, the organisation, and the wider societal environment. It explains what effective collaboration looks like, what conditions influence it, what requirements should be met, and what design decisions organisations should consider. The report also includes a human-AI collaborative assembly system with cobot use case to demonstrate how the framework can be applied in practice. The use case shows how design requirements can be translated into specific collaboration features and evaluated through a case study. The aim of this white paper is to provide a clear and practical guide for designing human-AI collaboration that is effective, human-centred, and responsible.

</details>


### [126] [DriveHierarchy: A Benchmark for Diagnosing VLM Driving Capabilities from Open-Loop Understanding to Closed-Loop Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31814)
*Chengkai Xu,Jiaqi Liu,Yicheng Guo,Peng Hang,Jian Sun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DriveHierarchy is a hierarchical benchmark for systematically evaluating vision-language-model-based autonomous driving across perception, memory, reasoning, and closed-loop control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing autonomous-driving benchmarks either test perception/understanding in an open-loop way or test driving in a closed-loop simulator, but they lack structure to explain how different competencies (perception, context integration, prediction, and action) are organized and related. This makes it hard to diagnose VLM-based driving systems, understand capability gaps, and guide targeted improvements. A unified, structured benchmark is needed to connect open-loop and closed-loop performance and to enable systematic evaluation and optimization of VLM-based autonomous driving.

Method: The authors propose DriveHierarchy, which organizes VLM-based autonomous driving capabilities into four hierarchical ranks: (1) perceptual grounding of traffic participants and hazards, (2) contextual memory to integrate information across views and time, (3) mental reasoning about future evolution of the scene, and (4) closed-loop driving execution. They instantiate the open-loop portion by merging multiple open-source driving datasets into a unified QA-style benchmark with 76,798 question-answer pairs over 84,279 frames, each targeting specific ranks of the hierarchy. For closed-loop evaluation, they build a simulation platform on a real-world road network supporting interactive scenario construction, from which they curate 100 driving scenarios for embodied evaluation. They evaluate 15 vision-language models on both the open- and closed-loop components to analyze capability structure and relationships.

Result: Across 15 VLMs, DriveHierarchy reveals structured yet non-redundant variations in capabilities along the four ranks, indicating that the benchmark captures distinct aspects of driving competence. Results show measurable relationships between open-loop understanding and closed-loop driving performance, demonstrating that performance in perception, memory, and reasoning tasks is predictive—though not perfectly—of embodied driving ability. The benchmark further enables fine-grained diagnosis of model weaknesses and shows that using it to guide optimization can yield practical performance improvements.

Conclusion: DriveHierarchy is an effective unified, hierarchical framework for evaluating VLM-based autonomous driving systems. By decomposing driving competence into four ranks and supporting both large-scale open-loop QA and realistic closed-loop simulation, it offers structured insight into model abilities, links understanding to control, and provides a practical tool for diagnosis and benchmark-guided model improvement. The released project and codebase make it possible for the community to systematically assess and enhance VLM-based autonomous driving models.

Abstract: Evaluating VLM-based autonomous driving remains difficult because driving competence is composite, where a capable system must ground traffic participants and hazards, integrate context across views and time, reason about future evolution, and act appropriately under closed-loop interaction. Existing benchmarks usually assess either open-loop understanding or closed-loop driving but provide limited structure for explaining how these abilities are organized, how they relate, and how they may inform model diagnosis and improvement. We present \textsc{DriveHierarchy}, a hierarchical benchmark that organizes VLM-based autonomous driving into four ranks, spanning perceptual grounding, contextual memory, mental reasoning, and closed-loop execution. To instantiate this hierarchy, we integrate multiple open-source autonomous-driving datasets into a unified open-loop benchmark with 76,798 question-answer pairs over 84,279 frames and develop a closed-loop simulation platform with interactive scenario construction on a real-world road network, from which 100 driving scenarios are curated for embodied evaluation. Experiments on 15 VLMs show that \textsc{DriveHierarchy} captures structured but non-redundant capability variation, relates open-loop understanding to closed-loop driving, and provides a practical basis for diagnosis and benchmark-guided optimization. \textsc{DriveHierarchy} therefore serves as a unified framework for evaluating and improving VLM-based autonomous driving systems. An anonymized project has been released on https://github.com/PerfectXu88/DriveHierarchy

</details>


### [127] [LLM Judge Validation Under Sparse Overlap: From Inference to Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31857)
*Junxuan Li,Arko Mukherjee,Soumyabrata Pal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how sparse overlap in human annotations affects validating LLMs as judges, proving that low overlap strongly increases the risk of choosing or deploying the wrong model, and proposes quantitative guidelines for needed overlap and improved allocation schemes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To safely deploy LLMs as automatic evaluators ("LLM-as-a-judge"), we must know how well their judgments align with humans. However, human labels are expensive, so most items are annotated by only one person, producing sparse overlap between annotators. The authors want to understand how this overlap sparsity impacts our ability to correctly estimate LLM-human agreement and choose the right LLM judge, and to find practical ways to design annotation schemes under tight budgets.

Method: They provide a theoretical analysis of how the amount and allocation of pairwise overlap in human annotations drive the probability of making wrong deployment decisions about LLM judges. They derive formulas relating overlap rate to error rates in ranking and selecting judges, especially among multiple candidates, and identify conditions (borderline vs non-borderline judges). They also propose a stratified allocation scheme for distributing annotation overlap without extra cost, and empirically test their predictions on 10 LLM judges over four evaluation matrices (visual assessment, causal reasoning, summarization, etc.).

Result: They show mathematically that overlap sparsity is the primary factor behind wrong deployment decisions: with only 5% pairwise overlap, wrong-decision rates can hit 25%, and when choosing the best among 10 judges, there is a 65% chance of picking the wrong one. They derive a minimum-overlap condition, finding that an overlap rate of at least 0.25 is enough to reliably validate non-borderline judges, though borderline judges remain intrinsically difficult. Their proposed stratified allocation of overlap cuts false-rejection rates about in half compared to random sampling when the strata are informative. These theoretical findings are borne out empirically across the 10 LLM judges and four evaluation settings.

Conclusion: Sparse overlap in human annotations critically undermines the reliability of validating LLMs as judges and selecting the best one. Ensuring a moderate level of overlap (around 25%) is necessary for robust evaluation of clearly better or worse judges, while ambiguous, borderline judges remain challenging regardless of overlap. Smart, stratified allocation of overlapping labels can significantly improve decision quality at no extra annotation cost, suggesting that evaluation design—not just scale—must be carefully engineered when benchmarking and deploying LLM judges.

Abstract: Validating an LLM-as-a-judge requires estimating its agreement with humans, yet annotation budgets rarely allow every item to be multiply labeled. We prove that this \emph{overlap sparsity} is the first-order determinant of wrong deployment decisions: at 5\% pairwise overlap, wrong-decision rates reach 25\% and the probability of selecting the wrong best judge among ten candidates is 65\%. The two actionable levers are overlap \emph{quantity} and \emph{allocation}. For quantity, we derive a minimum-overlap formula showing $ρ\geq 0.25$ suffices for non-borderline judges while borderline cases remain fundamentally hard. For allocation, a zero-cost stratified scheme halves false-rejection rates relative to random sampling when strata are informative. We validate on 10 LLM judges across four evaluation matrices spanning visual assessment, causal reasoning, and summarization.

</details>


### [128] [Metro-WM: Long-Horizon Latent Planning with Realisable Sub-Goals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31868)
*Royson Lee,Fady Rezk,Titouan Parcollet,Timothy Hospedales,Cristina Cornelio*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies a key flaw in latent sub-goal generation for hierarchical model-predictive control with JEPAs and proposes Metro-WM, a retrieval-based sub-goal planner over a graph of real experienced states, achieving much better long-horizon performance and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing JEPA-based model-predictive controllers are strong for zero-shot goal reaching but degrade sharply over long horizons. Hierarchical methods try to fix this by learning a macro planner that predicts latent sub-goals, yet these sub-goals can be physically unrealisable, undermining the entire hierarchy. The authors are motivated to diagnose this failure mode rigorously and design a hierarchical planner whose sub-goals are guaranteed to be grounded in physically valid states while still being efficient, robust to errors, and effective with limited offline data.

Method: The authors first perform a systematic evaluation of a state-of-the-art latent-space macro planner and show that it often proposes sub-goals that cannot be realised by the low-level controller. They then introduce Metro-WM, a hierarchical planning framework that replaces latent sub-goal generation with retrieval over a graph of real, previously observed frames. Nodes in the graph are frames from offline expert or random-action trajectories, and edges encode possible transitions, allowing paths to be stitched across episodes. A JEPA-based micro planner executes one edge at a time to move between graph nodes. When execution drifts from the planned path, Metro-WM replans from the current observed state by re-querying the graph for a new optimal route to the goal. Experiments compare Metro-WM against hierarchical baselines on long-horizon goal-reaching tasks, measuring success rate, path length, computation cost, and robustness under data scarcity.

Result: The evaluation confirms that the baseline macro planner frequently outputs physically unrealizable latent sub-goals. Metro-WM, by contrast, achieves substantially higher long-horizon success rates—up to 37.33 percentage points better than the next best hierarchical approach—while being up to 10.9 times faster and needing 13–56× less offline compute and fewer hyperparameter tweaks. It finds paths that are shorter than those demonstrated in the offline data, and even surpasses an oracle method that can use the query trajectory’s own demonstration. Performance remains strong even when the offline dataset is made extremely sparse, indicating robustness to limited data coverage.

Conclusion: Unconstrained latent sub-goal prediction is a fundamental weakness in current hierarchical JEPA-based planners, as it easily produces physically infeasible guidance. Metro-WM addresses this by grounding sub-goals in actual experienced states organized as a graph, enabling reliable, efficient, and robust long-horizon planning. The framework improves success rates, sample efficiency, and computational efficiency, and can exploit and even surpass suboptimal offline demonstrations. This suggests that graph-based retrieval of real states is a powerful alternative to latent sub-goal generation for hierarchical control, especially in long-horizon and data-sparse settings.

Abstract: Model-predictive control with Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provides a strong zero-shot goal-reaching planner, but it is only effective over short planning horizons. Hierarchical extensions attempt to bridge this gap by learning a macro planner to predict intermediate latent sub-goals to guide the micro planner. In this work, we demonstrate that unconstrained latent sub-goal prediction is fundamentally flawed. A rigorous evaluation reveals that a leading state-of-the-art macro planner routinely emits physically unrealisable sub-goals. To resolve this, we introduce Metro-WM, a hierarchical framework that issues sub-goals by retrieving genuine states from prior experience rather than generating ungrounded latent vectors.
