Specifically, Metro-WM constructs a graph whose vertices are observed frames from offline expert demonstrations or random-action trajectories, allowing frames from different episodes to be connected and stitched into routes to the goal. Planning over the full graph also makes the system highly robust to execution errors: if the micro planner drifts off course, Metro-WM instantly finds a new optimal path from the current state. Our experiments show that Metro-WM achieves superior long-horizon success rates of up to 37.33 percentage points over the next best hierarchical approach while being up to 10.9 times faster, requiring both 13-56 times less offline compute and fewer tuned hyperparameters. Additional analysis reveals that Metro-WM finds shorter paths than the offline demonstrations, outperforms an oracle relying on the query's own demonstration, and maintains robust performance under extremely sparse dataset conditions.

</details>


### [129] [IndustryLLM: Failure-Driven LLM Training for Industrial Procurement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31871)
*Liang Ding,Zhiang Xu,Yuyang Sheng,Bin Chen,Songlin Bai,Run Zhu,Dingjun Wu,Hui Xu,Yandi Wang,Fulin Shi,Leilei Gan,Linlin Yu,Qihuang Zhong,Keqin Peng,Yalong Li,Chengfu Huo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: IndustryLLM is an open-weight industrial language model tailored for procurement that uses failure-driven continued pre-training and fine-tuning on standards, transaction records, and rewritten domain text to robustly map informal buyer queries to formal engineering specs under strict safety constraints, yielding higher accuracy and better business metrics in production.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial procurement workflows rely on translating messy, colloquial buyer language into precise, standard-compliant product specifications, but generic LLMs handle this poorly because they lack exposure to authoritative standards, real transaction data, and the specialized ways people describe parts in practice. The authors want a domain-specialized model that can safely interpret informal jargon, resolve ambiguous or erroneous part descriptions, and respect engineering constraints, while being efficient enough for real-world deployment and available as open weights.

Method: They start from Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base (with a frozen vision encoder and about 3B active parameters per token) and apply a failure-driven adaptation pipeline combining continued pre-training (CPT) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). For CPT, they curate a ~100B-token corpus mixing: (1) 5B tokens of national standards and technical archives, (2) 10B tokens of de-identified industrial transactions and inquiries, and (3) 60B tokens of general replay, with the rest reconstructed via multi-register rewriting of domain text across 10 genres and 8 styles. They add confidence-routed minimal factual editing and error-targeted QA synthesis to fix typical domain errors (colloquial typos, ambiguous numeric codes, conflicting specs). For deployment, they introduce an evidence-gated constraint-evaluation interface based on three-valued logic, so any requirement without explicit product evidence is treated as unknown instead of satisfied, enforcing stricter safety and compliance. They then perform offline evaluation on procurement-query structuring tasks and randomized online A/B tests in production.

Result: Offline, IndustryLLM shows consistent performance gains on procurement-query structuring, improving exact match by +2.97 percentage points with a 95% confidence interval of [2.11, 3.86] in a No-Think setting. In live A/B tests within a production procurement system, the model drives a +4.25% increase in gross merchandise value (GMV), an +8.3% rise in satisfied inquiries, and a sharp latency improvement from 6–7 seconds to about 1.5 seconds per query.

Conclusion: Failure-driven continued pre-training plus supervised fine-tuning on carefully curated and reconstructed industrial text, combined with a conservative evidence-gated constraint-checking interface, yields an industrial language model that better understands informal procurement language, aligns it with engineering standards, and safely evaluates constraints. This approach not only improves offline structuring metrics but also delivers tangible business and user-experience gains in real production settings, and the released open weights make it available for broader industrial use and further research.

Abstract: Industrial procurement requires language models to bridge informal buyer jargon, sparse marketplace attributes, and authoritative engineering standards under strict safety tolerances. We present IndustryLLM, an open-weight industrial language model trained from Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base (35B total parameters with ~3B activated per token, with the vision encoder frozen). Rather than relying on generic text scaling, we introduce a failure-driven adaptation recipe spanning continued pre-training (CPT) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). CPT leverages a curated ~100B-token corpus integrating 5B tokens of national standards (e.g., GB/T) and technical archives, 10B tokens of de-identified real-world industrial transaction and inquiry records, and 60B tokens of general replay. To overcome register mismatch and factual brittleness, we systematically reconstruct an estimated 20B-token domain subset via multi-register rewriting across 10 genres and 8 writing styles, confidence-routed minimal factual editing, and error-targeted QA synthesis (resolving colloquial typos like '42-luo-mu' -> 42CrMo, expanding ambiguous codes like '16674' -> GB/T 16674, and clarifying conflicting dimensional specs). For downstream deployment, we formalize an evidence-gated constraint-evaluation interface enforcing three-valued logic where unverified product evidence remains unknown rather than satisfied. Offline evaluations demonstrate consistent gains on procurement-query structuring (+2.97 percentage points in exact match, 95% CI [2.11, 3.86] in No-Think mode), while randomized online A/B experiments in production yield substantial improvements (+4.25% GMV, +8.3% satisfied inquiries) alongside a latency reduction from 6-7 s to 1.5 s. Model weights and configs are released at https://huggingface.co/alibaba-multimodal-industrial-ai/IndustryLLM.

</details>


### [130] [COUNTERMEM: World-Model Verified Counter-Factual Memory for Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31874)
*Hongji Pu,Ruixiang Tang,Yongfeng Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: COUNTERMEM is a framework that builds and uses verified counterfactual memories for RL-style LLM agents, improving success and efficiency over ReAct and Reflexion by exploring and storing 'what-if' alternatives after failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most agent memory frameworks only store experiences from actual interactions with the world (e.g., executed actions and received feedback). They rarely explore counterfactuals—what would have happened under alternative actions—because doing so online can be expensive and may irreversibly change the environment. The authors aim to create a principled way to construct and reuse such counterfactual memories across tasks, to improve agent performance and reduce interaction costs without changing the base LLM.

Method: COUNTERMEM is a reinforcement-learning framework that, after an agent takes a failed action, copies or resets the original state and explores local alternative actions using executable world models such as tests, proof checkers, or solvers. It verifies which alternatives lead to better outcomes and stores these as counterfactual memory records, including: the original and corrected actions, the verified outcomes, and conditions under which they apply. A learned policy then decides at inference time whether to use retrieved memory entries or to ignore them, trading off between success rate and interaction cost. The underlying LLM agent is kept fixed; only the memory and the memory-use policy are trained, then frozen for evaluation.

Result: COUNTERMEM is evaluated on 12 benchmarks across six domains and consistently improves the performance of ReAct and Reflexion agents when using the gpt-oss-120b backbone, achieving an average improvement of 12.6 percentage points over the unaugmented baselines. In a subset of four domains and two model backbones, it also reduces runtime token usage per task by 7.7–42.0% (not counting the offline cost of training the selector policy). Ablation studies show that omitting verification or persistent storage decreases performance gains, and that applying counterfactual corrections in contexts where they do not fit can negate the benefits.

Conclusion: Verified, task-general counterfactual memories—constructed via offline exploration of alternative actions in copied or reset states and managed by a learned selector policy—can significantly improve the effectiveness and efficiency of LLM-based agents over standard memory frameworks. The work highlights the importance of verification, persistent storage, and careful selection of when to apply counterfactual corrections, and demonstrates that substantial gains can be achieved without modifying the underlying LLM.

Abstract: Existing agent memory frameworks mainly create memory through an agent's interaction with the factual world, e.g., remembering feedback from actions taken to improve performance on future tasks. However, these frameworks seldom ask the "what if" question during memory construction: what if a different action had been taken, would the feedback have changed, and how could this feedback become useful memory? Obtaining such feedback directly in an active environment can be expensive and can alter the state needed for comparison. In this work, we introduce COUNTERMEM, a reinforcement-learning framework for constructing and using verified counterfactual memory across tasks. After a failed action, COUNTERMEM evaluates local alternatives from a copy or reset of the original state using executable world models, such as tests, proof checkers, and solvers. It stores improvements with the original and corrected actions, checked outcomes, and conditions for reuse. A learned memory-use policy selects a retrieved record or skips memory to balance task success and interaction cost, while the base LLM remains fixed. Both memory and policy are frozen during held-out evaluation. We evaluate COUNTERMEM on 12 benchmark settings across six domains. With gpt-oss-120b, COUNTERMEM improves both ReAct and Reflexion on all 12 benchmarks across six domains, averaging a gain of 12.6 percentage points over their unaugmented versions. In the four-domain comparison across two backbones, task-run tokens decrease by 7.7-42.0%, excluding offline selector-training costs. Further analyses show that removing verification or persistent storage weakens the gains, while applying verified corrections to unsuitable decisions can reverse them. Code will be released upon acceptance.

</details>


### [131] [Context-dependent agent evaluation with orthogonal equilibrium learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31897)
*Haorui Ma,Zehua Zang,Jiangmeng Li,Yi Li,Fanjing Xu,Stefan Feuerriegel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose NashEval, a framework to evaluate agents under varying contexts using offline human feedback, by framing evaluation as a contextual game and learning Nash equilibria robustly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing offline evaluation methods like Bradley-Terry assume a single transitive preference ordering over agents. This assumption breaks when human preferences are heterogeneous across contexts, so these methods cannot faithfully capture collective preferences conditioned on prompts, tasks, or user groups. Moreover, in contextual settings each context only reveals feedback for a subset of agents, so naive estimators of context-specific performance can be biased and unstable.

Method: The authors recast agent evaluation as a two-player contextual game. For a given context, each player chooses a mixed strategy (a distribution over agents), and receives payoffs governed by collective preferences from offline human feedback. The set of winners for that context is defined as the support of a Nash equilibrium of this game. They introduce NashEval, which (1) builds debiased estimates of the contextual payoff matrix from partial offline comparisons using nuisance function estimation, and (2) learns a mapping from context to equilibrium strategies using a specially designed orthogonal loss so that a separate game need not be solved for every context. The orthogonal loss is constructed so that first-stage estimation errors (of the nuisance functions/payoffs) only enter higher-order terms of the equilibrium learning risk.

Result: Theoretical analysis shows that estimation errors in the nuisance functions underlying the payoff matrix influence the exploitability (risk) of the learned equilibrium only through higher-order terms, indicating robustness of the procedure. Empirically, across multiple experimental setups, NashEval leads to more robust learning of equilibria from offline data and more reliably recovers the set of top-performing agents across different contexts compared to existing score-based and plug-in approaches.

Conclusion: By formulating contextual agent evaluation as a game and learning Nash equilibria with orthogonalized objectives, NashEval overcomes limitations of score-based, transitivity-assuming models and naive plug-in estimators under heterogeneous preferences. It provides a more robust, theory-grounded way to identify context-specific top agents from offline human feedback, with both theoretical guarantees and empirical evidence supporting its effectiveness.

Abstract: Many applications require to evaluate agents under contextual information (e.g., a prompt, task, or user group). We study how to perform such context-dependent agent evaluation from offline feedback. Existing score-based models for this purpose (e.g., Bradley-Terry) impose a transitive preference ordering, which fails to reflect collective preferences when human judgements are heterogeneous. Inspired by social choice theory, we frame evaluation as a contextual game between two players, each selecting a distribution over agents as the strategy to receive greater collective preference than the other. Then, the support of the Nash equilibrium defines a context-specific set of winners. However, learning context-specific equilibria from offline logs is difficult because each context reveals human feedback on only a subset of agents, and, hence, a naive plug-in estimator can therefore be biased. To address these challenges, we propose NashEval, a general framework for robust contextual equilibrium learning. NashEval first constructs debiased estimates of the contextual payoff matrix that characterizes the game. NashEval then learns the context-to-equilibrium mapping with a tailored orthogonal loss, which avoids the need to solve a separate game for each context. We show theoretically that errors in estimating the nuisance functions underlying the payoff matrix affect the risk of the learned equilibrium (i.e., exploitability) only through higher-order terms. Across various experiments, NashEval improves robustness of equilibrium learning and consistently identifies the set of top-performing agents across contexts.

</details>


### [132] [Choir: An Open Protocol for Distributed Multi-Agent Autoformalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31903)
*Yidi Qi,Melanie Weber*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents Choir, an open, distributed protocol that lets many independent contributors run their own AI agents to collaboratively formalize mathematics in proof assistants, coordinated via GitHub.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current state-of-the-art AI formalization of mathematics in systems like Lean is powerful but centralized: a single team typically runs all the agents, pays the full compute and API costs, and manages the infrastructure. This centralization limits scalability, openness, and community participation. The authors want a way to turn formalization into a massively parallel, open, crowdsourced process where anyone with an LLM account can contribute safely and efficiently.

Method: The authors design Choir, a protocol and software framework that decomposes a formalization project into modular tasks (e.g., formalizing specific theorems or files). Each task can be picked up by any independent contributor running their own AI agent with their own LLM subscription. Coordination, task assignment, and result integration occur via a GitHub repository. A deterministic verification gate checks each proposed contribution (proof scripts, definitions) before merging, ensuring that only correct and compatible changes are integrated. Choir is implemented to support multiple proof assistants (Lean 4, Isabelle, Rocq) and is architected in a modular, open-source way so individual components (tasking, agents, verification) can be swapped or extended.

Result: They obtain a working open-source implementation of Choir that successfully supports distributed AI-agent-based formalization over GitHub for multiple proof assistants. Independent contributors can run agents locally, contribute formalizations, and have them automatically checked and merged via the deterministic gate, demonstrating that large formalization projects can be safely parallelized and crowdsourced. The protocol’s modular design shows that it can be adapted to different tools and workflows beyond the initial implementations.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that distributed, community-driven AI formalization is both feasible and practical. By shifting from centralized infrastructures to an open protocol with deterministic verification and GitHub-based coordination, Choir enables scalable collaboration across many independent AI agents and users. This architecture lowers barriers to participation, spreads computational cost, and provides a flexible foundation for future extensions and broader adoption in formal mathematics and software verification communities.

Abstract: AI agents can now formalize entire textbooks and major theorems in proof assistants such as Lean, but current efforts are typically centralized: a single team runs all agents and bears the full computational cost. We introduce Choir, an open protocol for distributed formalization. Choir decomposes a project into tasks that can be completed by independent contributors, each running their own agent with their own LLM subscription, while coordinating entirely through the project's GitHub repository. To support open participation, every contribution is checked by a deterministic gate before merge. Choir supports Lean 4, Isabelle, and Rocq, and is open source and modular, allowing projects to replace individual components or extend the protocol.

</details>


### [133] [EmailBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agents on Enterprise Email and Productivity Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31906)
*Mukul Singh,Mansi Uniyal,Devin Devlin,Wen Xie,Big Thadawasin,Ritam Dutt,Vivian Lai,Hyeonsu B. Kang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EmailBench is a benchmark to evaluate end-to-end email agents on realistic, tool-based enterprise email workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent benchmarks include some productivity tasks but do not focus deeply on typed email workflows in a self-contained, tool-API-driven environment. There is a need to rigorously test whether language-model-based agents can actually complete multi-step email and productivity tasks, not just make valid tool calls.

Method: The authors build EmailBench, a suite of 206 scenarios across 16 task categories based on email and related productivity tasks. They define a typed email API with provider-neutral naming, generate a deterministic synthetic corpus inspired by Enron emails, and construct scenarios guided by real aggregate task-intent telemetry. For evaluation, they use a hybrid protocol combining 258 executable static assertions (automatic checks) with 211 LLM-based rubric evaluations. They then test eight different language-model configurations on a fixed single-user corpus.

Result: Across the benchmark, the best-performing model configuration successfully completes only 33.5% of scenarios, even though 99.7% of its tool calls do not trigger observable API failures. Performance varies a lot across different task categories, exposing weaknesses in current systems’ ability to handle complex email workflows end-to-end.

Conclusion: Correct and reliable use of tools is far from sufficient for successful completion of email-agent tasks; substantial reasoning and coordination gaps remain. EmailBench offers a controlled environment for measuring these abilities and highlights avenues for future work, including broader tool sets, testing multiple user personas, and repeated-run robustness assessments.

Abstract: Enterprise email agents must combine information retrieval, structured state changes, temporal reasoning, and multi-step coordination. Recent agent benchmarks include productivity tasks, but few center on typed email workflows in a self-contained environment. We introduce EmailBench, a benchmark of 206 email and productivity scenarios across 16 task categories. The benchmark couples a typed email API specification with provider-neutral naming, a deterministic synthetic Enron-inspired corpus, and a scenario suite whose topic selection was informed by aggregate task-intent telemetry from an interactive prototype. Its hybrid evaluation protocol combines 258 executable static assertions with 211 LLM rubrics. We evaluate eight LM configurations on a fixed single-user corpus. The best-performing configuration passes only 33.5% of scenarios despite 99.7% of its tool calls completing without an observed API failure, with pass rates varying substantially across task categories. This gap shows that valid tool execution is not equivalent to task completion. EmailBench provides a self-contained environment for end-to-end email-agent evaluation, with broader tool coverage, multi-persona testing, and repeated-run evaluation as future work areas.

</details>


### [134] [Improving Medical Calculation of LLMs with Embedded Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31908)
*Tianshi Ming,Yingying Zhang,Xian Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces MedCode, a framework that makes large language models reliable at medical calculation tasks by having them generate executable code instead of doing arithmetic in natural language.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although LLMs score well on medical exams and QA benchmarks, they are unreliable at precise numerical medical calculations—such as drug dosing, organ function assessment, and clinical risk scores—where even small errors can be dangerous. There is a need for methods that ensure both correctness and transparency of calculations in high-stakes clinical settings.

Method: The authors propose MedCode, where an LLM, given a clinical context, (1) identifies the appropriate medical calculator, (2) extracts the necessary input variables, and (3) generates an embedded, executable script that offloads arithmetic to a deterministic interpreter. The system then executes this script to obtain the final numeric result, an explanation, and the correct units. They build supervised fine-tuning and preference-learning datasets based on the MedCalc benchmark and an additional ICU-focused calculation dataset. They also introduce weighted Direct Preference Optimization (wDPO), which gives more weight to preference pairs that the model finds harder to tell apart, to better align model outputs with desired behavior.

Result: On several base models (LLaMA3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B), MedCode yields absolute accuracy improvements of about 20–30 percentage points on medical calculation benchmarks, indicating substantially more reliable numeric performance compared with standard LLM behavior.

Conclusion: Embedding code generation into LLMs, combined with specialized training data and the wDPO alignment method, significantly improves accuracy on medical calculation tasks. This approach addresses a key reliability gap in current medical LLMs and suggests that delegating arithmetic to deterministic interpreters is an effective way to make LLM-based systems safer for high-stakes clinical calculations.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well on medical examinations and question-answering benchmarks, but remain unreliable on medical calculation tasks that require exact numerical outputs. These calculations support high-stakes decisions such as medication dosing, organ-function assessment, and prognostic scoring, for which even small errors can have serious clinical consequences. We introduce MedCode, a framework that improves medical calculation by training LLMs to generate embedded executable code. Given a clinical context, the model identifies the relevant calculator, extracts its input variables, and produces a script that delegates arithmetic operations to a deterministic interpreter. Executing the script returns the calculated value together with an explanation and the appropriate unit. We construct supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference datasets from the MedCalc benchmark and additionally curate a dataset for calculation tasks in Intensive Care Unit (ICU) scenarios. We further propose weighted Direct Preference Optimization (wDPO), which adaptively emphasizes preference pairs that are difficult for the model to distinguish. Experiments with LLaMA3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B show absolute accuracy gains of 20--30 percentage points, demonstrating the effectiveness of embedded code generation for medical calculation.

</details>


### [135] [BioDyad: Synchronize Biomedical Discovery and Machine Learning Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31939)
*Xingbo Du,Fadli Aulawi Al Ghiffari,Leonard Song,Loka Li,Duzhen Zhang,Zixiao Wang,Xiuying Chen,Le Song*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BioDyad is an agentic biomedical ML framework that jointly manages scientific discovery and ML engineering using a dual-hierarchy Monte Carlo graph search, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the BioXArena benchmark under tight time budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic ML systems in biomedicine must not only generate models but also actively acquire and integrate external biomedical evidence while staying within limited computational and time budgets. Existing approaches partially connect evidence acquisition and program search but struggle to coordinate them end-to-end: new evidence often doesn’t effectively guide later candidate designs, execution feedback is not systematically reused, and validation and retraining steps may be misaligned with search constraints. A unified framework is needed to tightly couple biomedical reasoning (what knowledge to use and discover) with ML engineering (how to build, evaluate, and refine executable models) across diverse biomedical tasks.

Method: The authors propose BioDyad, an agent framework that structures program search with two intertwined hierarchies within Monte Carlo graph search. The scientific hierarchy plans and performs biomedical evidence acquisition, combining prior domain guidance with iterative discovery and storing links between biomedical plans, retrieved knowledge, and execution outcomes for reuse across candidate solutions. The engineering hierarchy manages the lifecycle of candidate ML programs, progressing them through stages: lightweight “smoke” execution, more thorough train/validation evaluation, and eventual full-data retraining. Both hierarchies jointly guide exploration of the program search space while staying within a fixed time budget and using large language models as backends for program synthesis and reasoning.

Result: On the 76-task BioXArena benchmark, evaluated with a two-hour per-task budget and three different but matched LLM backends, BioDyad attains the highest penalized all-task score and the highest task success rate compared with four other agent-based methods and a one-shot baseline under each backend configuration. This indicates consistent improvements in both performance quality and robustness across heterogeneous biomedical ML tasks when using the dual-hierarchy coordination strategy.

Conclusion: Coordinating biomedical knowledge discovery with ML engineering decisions through a dual-hierarchy Monte Carlo graph search enables more effective agentic ML in biomedical domains. By systematically linking evidence acquisition, candidate construction, staged evaluation, and retraining, BioDyad can better integrate external biomedical knowledge into executable ML programs under realistic computational budgets, yielding improved performance across a wide variety of biomedical tasks. This suggests that tightly coupled scientific and engineering planning is a promising direction for future biomedical agent systems.

Abstract: Agentic biomedical machine learning (ML) draws on complementary advances in biomedical evidence acquisition and executable program search. Existing systems connect aspects of these capabilities, but coordinating them throughout program search remains challenging. New evidence must guide candidate construction, execution outcomes must inform subsequent discovery and reuse, and validation demands must fit the search budget. We introduce BioDyad, which couples biomedical discovery and ML engineering through two hierarchies within Monte Carlo graph search. Its scientific hierarchy combines prior biomedical guidance with iterative discovery, then links biomedical plans to execution outcomes in memory for reuse across candidates. Its engineering hierarchy moves candidate programs from smoke execution, through train/validation evaluation, to full-data retraining. We evaluate BioDyad on the 76-task BioXArena benchmark under a two-hour per-task budget with three matched LLM backends. It achieves the highest penalized all-task score and task success rate among four agent methods and a one-shot baseline under each backend. These results support coordinating biomedical discovery and ML engineering to integrate external knowledge into executable programs across heterogeneous biomedical tasks.

</details>


### [136] [Symbolic Guidance for LLM Agents in Distributed Multiagent Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31963)
*Ben Rachmut,Ning Zhang,Yevgeniy Vorobeychik,William Yeoh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how different levels of symbolic guidance (from free-form reasoning to strict algorithms) affect LLM agents’ ability to perform distributed coordination tasks, and finds that intermediate, partially guided autonomy works best.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are being used as autonomous agents in multi-agent systems, but their reliability in running classic distributed coordination protocols is unclear; full autonomy often leads to inconsistent or poor performance in complex settings. The authors want to understand and improve how LLM agents coordinate by systematically controlling how much algorithmic structure they follow.

Method: They propose the Symbolic Guidance Taxonomy (SGT), a spectrum of autonomy levels for LLM agents, from open-ended natural language reasoning to fully specified algorithmic execution, with several intermediate levels where agents are guided by partial pseudocode or symbolic hints. Using the AgentsNet benchmark for LLM-based distributed coordination, they evaluate how agents perform under these different autonomy levels on various protocols and tasks.

Result: Across the tested distributed coordination tasks, agents operating at intermediate autonomy levels, with partial pseudocode or symbolic guidance, consistently achieve higher performance and more reliable coordination than both unguided, fully free-form agents and agents forced to follow rigid, fully prescriptive specifications.

Conclusion: Regulating LLM agent autonomy via structured symbolic guidance—rather than giving them either complete freedom or entirely fixed algorithms—is crucial for robust distributed coordination. Autonomy regulation emerges as a core design principle for building effective multi-agent systems with LLM-based agents.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in multi-agent systems, yet their ability to reliably execute distributed coordination protocols remains poorly understood. While AgentsNet, a benchmark framework for distributed coordination among LLM agents, enables such coordination, granting full reasoning autonomy often leads to inconsistent or degraded performance in complex domains.
  We hypothesize that coordination can be improved by regulating agent autonomy through symbolic guidance derived from established algorithms. To investigate this, we introduce the \emph{Symbolic Guidance Taxonomy (SGT)}, which characterizes a spectrum of autonomy ranging from open-ended natural language reasoning to fully prescribed algorithmic execution, with intermediate levels providing partial pseudocode guidance. Our results show that intermediate autonomy levels consistently outperform both unguided agents and fully prescriptive specifications. These findings identify autonomy regulation as a key design principle for LLM-based distributed coordination.

</details>


### [137] [Goal-Persistent Coding Agents as Scientific Performance Engineers: A Fixed-Radius Nearest-Neighbor Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31980)
*Xiangyang Ju*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper demonstrates that off-the-shelf coding agents (Codex, Claude Code) can autonomously optimize a scientific CUDA application at repository scale, achieving substantial performance gains while maintaining exact correctness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While coding agents can write and modify code, it is unclear whether they can perform rigorous, hypothesis-driven performance engineering on complex scientific software, especially at repository scale with strict correctness requirements. The authors aim to test if general-purpose code agents can act as experimental performance engineers rather than just code autocompleters.

Method: Starting from a PyTorch-dependent CUDA implementation of fixed-radius nearest-neighbor (FRNN) search for particle tracking, the authors specify an executable goal containing exact correctness tests, profiling requirements, and non-prescriptive acceptance criteria. They then let off-the-shelf Codex and Claude Code agents independently optimize the repository. The agents remove the PyTorch dependency, propose and test performance hypotheses, and iteratively modify the code while being constrained by the executable contract. Performance is evaluated via a standalone C++/CUDA library with a synchronous NumPy interface, and results are compared to the original GPU-resident PyTorch interface across multiple GPU architectures and software stacks.

Result: In the main optimization trajectory, the agents successfully eliminated the PyTorch dependency and produced a standalone C++/CUDA FRNN library that exactly reproduces the reference results. The NumPy-based interface—despite incurring host-device transfers—achieved a 1.6x speedup over the original PyTorch GPU-resident implementation, with similar gains across different GPUs and software environments. A separate rerun, following a different chain of optimization hypotheses, reached even better performance on the same workload, demonstrating both robustness and diversity in optimization paths.

Conclusion: Goal-persistent coding agents, when guided by precise executable scientific contracts, can function as effective experimental performance engineers on non-trivial scientific codebases. Executable contracts are crucial both for constraining the search space (guidance) and for verifying that aggressive optimizations preserve exact scientific correctness. This suggests a viable pattern for using general-purpose code agents in high-stakes scientific and engineering optimization tasks.

Abstract: Coding agents can pursue persistent objectives across many tool-use turns, but evidence that general-purpose agents can conduct rigorous scientific performance engineering remains limited. We present a repository-scale case study in which off-the-shelf Codex and Claude Code agents optimize fixed-radius nearest-neighbor (FRNN) search for particle tracking. Starting from a PyTorch-dependent CUDA implementation, the agents follow an executable goal that specifies exact-correctness tests, profiling requirements, and acceptance criteria without prescribing code transformations. In the primary sequential trajectory, they autonomously remove the PyTorch dependency and conduct hypothesis-driven optimization experiments. The resulting standalone C++/CUDA library exactly reproduces the targeted reference result. Its synchronous NumPy interface achieved 1.6-fold speedup over the original GPU-resident PyTorch interface, despite including host transfers. Similar speedups were observed across different GPU architectures and software stacks. An independent optimization rerun followed a different sequence of hypotheses and reached even better performance on the target workload. These results show that goal-persistent coding agents can act as experimental performance engineers, and that executable scientific contracts are needed both to guide and to validate their optimization.

</details>


### [138] [CSI-Agent: LLM-Assisted Few-Shot Adaptation for Cross-Domain Wi-Fi CSI Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31990)
*Tianya Zhao,Chuan Liu,Xuyu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces CSI-Agent, an LLM-based decision-making framework that adapts Wi-Fi CSI sensing models to new domains at deployment time, improving cross-domain human activity recognition performance, especially in low-shot scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wi-Fi CSI enables device-free sensing like human activity recognition, but models often fail when deployed in new domains (different users, environments, devices) due to domain shift. Existing methods address this as an offline model design problem with stronger pretraining or a single, fixed adaptation strategy, which is inadequate when labeled target data are scarce and when different classes are affected differently by the same domain shift. A more flexible, deployment-time, class-specific adaptation mechanism is needed.

Method: The authors propose CSI-Agent, an evidence-seeking agent system built around a large language model (LLM). Instead of directly handling raw CSI or making sample-level predictions, CSI-Agent aggregates target-domain behavior into class-level, sensing-grounded evidence using complementary CSI views. It sets up a strong, target-adaptive default behavior for each class, then uses an LLM planner to decide per class whether to keep this default or trigger specialized adaptation actions. The framework incorporates deterministic verification and bounded execution to limit unreliable or excessive interventions during adaptation.

Result: CSI-Agent is evaluated on four public Wi-Fi CSI datasets with five types of cross-domain splits that include device, user, environment, and compositional shifts. Under a 1-shot adaptation regime, CSI-Agent consistently yields the best target-domain performance across all splits, improving average Macro-F1 by about 16% compared to the strongest existing baseline method.

Conclusion: Treating cross-domain CSI adaptation as a deployment-time decision-making problem and leveraging an LLM-based agent to operate on class-level evidence leads to significantly more robust and effective adaptation than conventional offline or single-strategy approaches. CSI-Agent particularly excels in low-shot settings, demonstrating that adaptive, class-specific interventions guided by an LLM can substantially enhance cross-domain generalization for CSI-based sensing applications.

Abstract: Wi-Fi channel state information (CSI) has enabled device-free sensing applications such as human activity recognition. However, CSI sensing models remain brittle in cross-domain deployment, where changes in users or environments can produce incorrect predictions. Existing solutions usually treat this problem as an offline model-design problem, by pretraining a stronger representation or applying one fixed adaptation method to the entire target domain. In practice, labeled target data are scarce and different classes may fail in different ways under the same domain shift. To address this, we propose CSI-Agent, an evidence-seeking LLM agent that reformulates cross-domain CSI adaptation as a deployment-time decision-making problem. Rather than processing raw CSI or making sample-level predictions, CSI-Agent summarizes target-domain behavior into sensing-grounded class-level evidence. It establishes a strong target-adaptive default from complementary CSI views and uses an LLM planner to determine whether each class should retain the default or invoke a specialized action. Deterministic verification and bounded execution further reduce unreliable interventions. We evaluate CSI-Agent on four public datasets using five cross-domain splits covering device, user, environment, and compositional shifts. Under 1-shot adaptation, CSI-Agent achieves the best target-domain performance across all splits and improves the average Macro-F1 by about 16\% compared to the strongest baseline method.

</details>


### [139] [SenseAgent: An LLM Agent for Adaptive Cross-Domain IMU Sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32000)
*Tianya Zhao,Chuan Liu,Xuyu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces SenseAgent, an LLM-guided agent that dynamically manages cross-domain IMU activity recognition by diagnosing domain shifts and selecting appropriate sensing tools at runtime.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: IMU-based activity recognition models degrade when deployed to new domains (different users, devices, or body positions). Existing approaches handle domain shift with static model designs—better pretraining, augmentation, or a single predetermined adaptation method—assuming ample target data and labels. In reality, the target domain appears gradually, labels are scarce, and different shifts require different actions. There is a need for a flexible, online, label-efficient mechanism that can detect domain shifts and choose tailored adaptation strategies safely during deployment.

Method: SenseAgent wraps an IMU backbone with an LLM-driven decision agent. Rather than letting the LLM classify raw signals, it serves as a high-level planner operating over: (1) sensing tools (e.g., gravity-aware sensing, prototype transfer, style normalization); (2) source-domain experience memory; (3) online target-domain memory; and (4) verification modules. From the incoming unlabeled target IMU stream, the agent builds a label-free diagnosis report describing inferred domain shifts. Based on this report, it chooses between standard raw inference or invoking specialized tools. Verifiers evaluate source calibration, the reliability of target memory, and ‘no-harm’ constraints to guard against unsafe or performance-degrading adaptations. The system can also incorporate scarce user feedback without retraining the backbone or replacing the default label-free path.

Result: Across several IMU datasets and deployment shifts (including challenging body placements and compound domain changes), SenseAgent’s verified tool/route selection improves cross-domain activity recognition compared with static pipelines and single adaptation methods. Performance gains are particularly strong under harder shifts and are further enhanced when limited user feedback is available.

Conclusion: By reframing cross-domain IMU sensing as a closed-loop process, SenseAgent can diagnose target-domain shifts online, select appropriate sensing tools, and avoid harmful adaptations via verification. This LLM-guided planning framework yields more robust and adaptable cross-domain IMU activity recognition than fixed inference pipelines, and it remains effective even with scarce labels and incremental target observations.

Abstract: Deep learning has improved inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensing for mobile and wearable applications. However, an IMU model trained in one domain often becomes unreliable when it is used with a new user, device, or body position. Existing methods usually treat this problem as a static model-design task: they pretrain a stronger representation, add data augmentation, or select one adaptation method before deployment. In practice, the target domain is only gradually observed, labels are scarce, and different domain shifts require different sensing actions. This paper presents SenseAgent, an LLM-guided sensing agent for cross-domain IMU activity recognition. Instead of asking an LLM to classify raw IMU signals, SenseAgent uses the LLM as a runtime planner over sensing tools, source-domain experience memory, online target memory, and verifiers. The agent builds a label-free diagnosis report from the target stream and uses it to decide whether to keep raw inference or invoke specialized tools, including gravity-aware sensing, prototype transfer, and style normalization. Verifiers check source calibration, target-memory reliability, and no-harm criteria before accepting high-risk tool decisions. SenseAgent also supports scarce feedback without retraining the backbone or replacing the label-free route. This design converts cross-domain IMU sensing from a fixed inference pipeline into a closed-loop sensing process that diagnoses target shifts, selects suitable sensing actions, and rejects unsafe adaptations. We evaluate SenseAgent across multiple IMU datasets and deployment shifts. Results show that its verified route selection improves cross-domain sensing, especially under harder placement and compound shifts, and further benefits from limited user feedback.

</details>


### [140] [What Does the Rank Buy? A Spectral and Distributional Analysis of Low-Rank Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32002)
*Babak Barazandeh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper challenges the common belief that the LoRA rank r directly controls model capacity and generalization. Under realistic norm constraints, any capacity or displacement measure is maximized by rank‑one updates, so higher rank does not increase capacity. Instead, rank mainly determines which spectral updates are reachable and how costly it is to cancel certain directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LoRA is widely used for efficient adaptation of large models, and practitioners often tune the rank r as if it were a direct capacity knob (smaller r → simpler model → better generalization). This intuition influences practical hyperparameter choices but lacks rigorous justification under the kinds of norm and weight‑decay constraints actually used. The paper aims to clarify what role rank truly plays in LoRA, whether and how it affects capacity, and under which conditions it matters for generalization and adaptation quality.

Method: The authors analyze a linear-readout model with LoRA-style low-rank updates, under hard per-factor norm constraints that idealize weight decay and norm control. They characterize the set of reachable updates as matrices of rank at most r within a nuclear-norm ball. Over this set, they examine several complexity and displacement measures (including Rademacher complexity and distributional shift metrics) and show that they are maximized by rank-one updates, rendering the rank cap non-binding. They then modify the constraint to a joint norm budget on the product matrix and derive data-dependent, rank-sensitive complexity bounds. Finally, they perform a spectral analysis of the pretrained weights and LoRA updates to relate rank and budget to the ability to cancel leading singular directions, providing matching upper and lower bounds on the minimal rank needed for a target alignment under specified spectral decay assumptions.

Result: Under per-factor norm budgets, the LoRA update space is exactly the set of rank-≤r matrices inside a nuclear-norm ball, and for all studied complexity and displacement functionals, the extremal cases are achieved by rank-one updates. Consequently, the effective model class for linear readouts is the same for every r ≥ 1, the Rademacher complexity is independent of r, and the maximal source-distribution displacement is bounded by a rank-independent limit that is tight. When the constraint is changed to a joint product budget, rank can influence complexity, but only in a data-dependent way and not in the worst case. In the spectral analysis, the authors show that canceling leading singular directions of the pretrained weights requires both adequate rank and budget; they give upper and lower bounds on the minimal rank needed to achieve a target alignment, which coincide under two-sided spectral decay conditions.

Conclusion: The work overturns the standard view of LoRA rank as a direct capacity control parameter under realistic per-factor norm constraints. In that regime, capacity and generalization measures are essentially rank-insensitive once r ≥ 1; rank does not bound how complex the model can be. Instead, rank governs which spectral directions of the pretrained model can be modified and how expensive it is, in norm budget, to cancel or reorient them. When using joint product budgets and for suitably spread features, rank can impact data-dependent complexity, but the worst-case behavior remains rank-free. Overall, rank should be understood primarily as determining reachability and spectral cancellation cost of updates, not as a simple knob on model capacity.

Abstract: The rank $r$ in LoRA is widely treated as a capacity control: a smaller rank is assumed to yield a simpler model that generalizes better. We show that, under hard per-factor norm budgets---the idealization of the weight decay and norm control used in practice---this intuition breaks down. The reason is structural: under such budgets, the updates LoRA can reach are exactly the matrices of rank at most $r$ inside a nuclear-norm ball, and every complexity and displacement functional we analyze is maximized over this set by a rank-one update---so the rank cap never binds. The consequences follow directly. The linear-readout model class we study is identical for every $r \ge 1$, its Rademacher complexity carries no dependence on $r$, and the distance the adaptation can move the source distribution obeys a rank-independent upper bound that we show is sharp. If rank does not control capacity, where does it act? We identify two places. Statistically, replacing the per-factor budgets with a joint budget on the product restores a data-dependent, rank-sensitive complexity bound---though the gain appears only for well-spread feature distributions, and the worst case remains rank-free. Spectrally, rank sets the price of adaptation: canceling the leading singular directions of the pretrained weight requires both sufficient rank and sufficient budget. We bound the smallest rank achieving a desired source--target alignment, with upper and lower bounds that match under two-sided spectral decay. Together, these results recast rank as governing which updates are reachable and what cancellation costs---not how much capacity the model has.

</details>


### [141] [Decentralized Master-Mind: Joint Action Refinement through Iterative Intent Denoising in Multi-Agent Pathfinding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32019)
*Valeriy Vyaltsev,Anton Andreychuk,Taisia Zlotnikova,Konstantin Yakovlev,Aleksandr Panov,Alexey Skrynnik*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose DMM, a decentralized multi-agent pathfinding method that refines agents’ action intents over several communication rounds, improving coordination and coverage versus existing learnable baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In decentralized MAPF with partial observability, agents must coordinate to avoid collisions. Learnable per-agent policies trained from expert data work fairly well but break down when multiple valid coordinated joint actions exist. Independent per-agent sampling can accidentally combine locally valid actions into a globally invalid joint action, even if each agent’s action distribution is correct. Thus, there is a need for a decentralized mechanism that couples agents’ final action choices so that they form compatible joint actions, without resorting to centralized control.

Method: They introduce DMM (Decentralized Master-Mind), which replaces one-shot action sampling with discrete, multi-round refinement of per-agent action intents, inspired by denoising in diffusion models. Each agent starts with a random action intent, then iteratively refines it across several communication rounds, exchanging local information so that their eventual choices become coupled before final commitment. DMM is first pretrained with imitation learning on expert MAPF solutions, and then fine-tuned using MICPO, a critic-free, group-relative reinforcement learning algorithm tailored to multi-agent, multi-round intent refinement, optimizing for success and solution quality.

Result: Compared to learnable baselines on standard MAPF benchmarks, DMM typically achieves higher success rates and lower solution costs. On 1,600 MovingAI tasks, the MICPO fine-tuned DMM solves 1,598 tasks, the highest task coverage among evaluated methods, while its solution costs are similar to those of the best competing approaches. The method further scales to scenarios with over one million simultaneously acting agents in environments with many obstacles, maintaining effective coordination.

Conclusion: Round-level intent refinement via iterative communication lets decentralized agents couple their action choices, improving joint-action coordination without sacrificing decentralized execution. DMM demonstrates that such refinement can significantly increase task coverage and maintain competitive solution quality in MAPF, and can scale to very large multi-agent systems in complex environments.

Abstract: Decentralized multi-agent path finding (MAPF) with communication requires agents to reach individual goals without collisions under partial observability. Learnable policies trained on expert data provide an effective approach to this problem. However, when several coordinated joint actions are valid in the same context, independently sampling from per-agent distributions can recombine locally valid choices into incompatible joint actions. This failure can arise from the final sampling mechanism even when the per-agent action distributions are learned correctly. DMM (Decentralized Master-Mind) addresses this by replacing one-shot action sampling with discrete, iterative refinement of action intents across communication rounds, inspired by denoising in diffusion models. Agents initialize random action intents and refine them through local communication, coupling their choices before commitment. DMM is pretrained with imitation learning on expert MAPF solutions and further optimized with MICPO, a critic-free group-relative reinforcement-learning method designed for multi-agent, multi-round action refinement. DMM generally achieves higher success rates and lower solution costs than the evaluated learnable baselines. On 1,600 MovingAI tasks, DMM fine-tuned with MICPO solves 1,598, the highest coverage among the evaluated methods, while achieving solution costs close to those of the strongest baselines. DMM also scales to over one million simultaneously acting agents in obstacle-rich environments. These results show that round-level intent refinement can improve joint-action coordination while preserving decentralized execution.

</details>


### [142] [A Benchmark for LLM's Understanding of Middle School and High School Science Topics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32020)
*Noah L. Schroeder,Yessy Eka Ambarwati,Yuji Zhang,ChengXiang Zhai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper builds an NGSS-aligned benchmark to evaluate how well various open-weight LLMs handle middle and high school science content and explores the role of human review in improving synthetic test items and future educational uses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are entering K-12 education, but current benchmarks mostly test general language skills or advanced scientific reasoning, not the actual standards-based content taught in secondary science. Educators therefore lack reliable, NGSS-aligned tools to judge whether specific models are appropriate for classroom use and how they perform on real curriculum-relevant material.

Method: The authors created a comprehensive benchmark aligned with NGSS for middle and high school science using a synthetic question-generation pipeline, multiple independent judges to validate items, and item-level psychometric analysis to assess quality and difficulty. They then evaluated nine open-weight LLMs of varying sizes on this benchmark. Finally, they added a human-in-the-loop phase where human reviewers checked LLM-generated items for true NGSS alignment and pedagogical appropriateness.

Result: Several smaller, locally deployable open-weight LLMs performed strongly on the NGSS-aligned benchmark, often matching or approaching the accuracy of larger models. Model size did not systematically correlate with performance, highlighting that bigger models are not always better for standards-based K-12 science tasks. Human review revealed that many synthetically generated items deviated from full NGSS alignment, despite scoring well by automatic and multi-judge criteria.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that NGSS-aligned benchmarks for K-12 science are feasible and that smaller open models can be viable for classroom use, but also that automated synthetic item generation alone is insufficient to guarantee standards and pedagogical alignment. Effective educational deployment requires deliberate model selection plus human-in-the-loop item development, and future benchmarks should move beyond static question answering to assess LLMs’ ability to provide interactive, evidence-based feedback to students.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into educational settings, yet educators lack robust, standards-aligned tools to evaluate their effectiveness in K-12 science contexts. Existing benchmarks predominantly assess general language or advanced scientific reasoning, leaving a critical gap in understanding LLMs' performance on content directly relevant to secondary science curricula. To address this gap, we developed a comprehensive NGSS-aligned benchmark for both middle and high school science using a rigorous synthetic data pipeline, multi-judge validation, and item-level psychometric analysis. Nine open-weight LLMs were systematically evaluated using this benchmark, indicating that several smaller, locally deployable models achieved high accuracy across diverse science domains and question types. Our findings indicate that model size did not consistently predict performance, emphasizing the importance of intentional model selection for educational deployment. We then incorporated a human reviewer into the loop, reviewing the items generated by the LLMs for alignment with NGSS standards. The human review indicated that synthetically generated items were not in perfect alignment with the NGSS standards, indicating the benefits of human-in-the-loop item development, the need to explore the intersection of content and pedagogical knowledge, and the need to extend benchmarks to evaluate LLMs' capacity for interactive, evidence-based feedback in educational scenarios.

</details>


### [143] [Reasoning Concentrates Errors, and Self-Consistency Never Notices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32035)
*Asaad Althoubi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that chain-of-thought style reasoning often makes multiple samples from the same model agree on the same wrong answer, undermining self-consistency methods like majority voting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-consistency and confidence-weighted ensembling assume that when a model is unsure, independently sampled answers will disagree, so that agreement indicates correctness. This assumption underlies many current techniques for improving large language model performance by sampling multiple chains of thought and aggregating them. The authors want to test whether this assumption actually holds when you turn on explicit reasoning modes, while keeping model weights fixed.

Method: Using eight language models across five benchmarks, the authors compare a 'reasoning' mode (e.g., chain-of-thought or similar) with a 'non-reasoning' mode while keeping model weights constant. They draw 74,944 independent samples and perform dataset-scale comparisons of how often two independently drawn wrong answers coincide, how many distinct answers are produced, and how answer probabilities are distributed. They analyze settings with unbounded answer spaces (open-form outputs) and bounded answer spaces (fixed option sets), and evaluate different aggregation methods: plain majority vote, confidence-weighted voting using several confidence signals (e.g., answer log-probability), and a learned combination of six such signals. They also examine in-domain vs out-of-domain performance and perform statistical testing (e.g., p-values) on error concentration effects.

Result: Turning on reasoning consistently concentrates the model’s errors: two independently sampled wrong answers are more likely to be identical under reasoning than under non-reasoning, with this effect observed in all ten dataset-scale comparisons and in nine of nine comparisons when conditioning on problems that both modes answer incorrectly. In open answer spaces, reasoning reduces the number of distinct answers to 43–65% of the non-reasoning baseline; in bounded spaces, reasoning instead concentrates probability mass on the shared option set, in a way not explainable by positional priors at fixed weights. While this concentration should, in theory, hurt self-consistency methods significantly, the observed aggregate performance drop is smaller because reasoning also reduces the subset of problems where diversity between samples could help, by about 2.7x in all ten cells. After normalizing for this reduced 'headroom', both reasoning and non-reasoning settings exploit only about a quarter of the potential diversity benefit. Confidence-weighted voting does not recover the lost performance: across 280 method-dataset-model combinations, none outperforms plain majority vote after correction; weighted voting matches majority vote on 98.5% of problem-method pairs and is correct only 56.3% of the time when it disagrees. Moreover, the relationship between confidence signals and correctness can flip: answer log-probability is positively correlated with correctness without reasoning but predicts errors when reasoning is enabled. A learned combination of six confidence signals fails to generalize out of domain.

Conclusion: Explicit reasoning modes, such as chain-of-thought, cause language models’ wrong answers to become more self-consistent with each other, reducing answer diversity exactly where self-consistency schemes rely on it. This undermines common practices like majority voting over chains of thought and confidence-weighted ensembling, which assume that disagreement between samples signals uncertainty and that agreement implies correctness. The paper concludes that confidence signals and self-consistency methods must be evaluated based on their impact on actual decision quality, not just on their ability to discriminate correct from incorrect answers, and that reasoning-induced changes in error structure can invalidate naive confidence-based aggregation even when model weights remain fixed.

Abstract: Self-consistency assumes that independent samples disagree when a model is unsure, so agreement is evidence of correctness. Holding weights fixed and toggling only a reasoning mode, over five benchmarks and 74,944 samples, we show that reasoning concentrates a model's errors: the probability that two independently drawn wrong answers coincide rises in all ten dataset-scale comparisons (p = 0.00098), and in nine of nine after restricting both arms to the problems each gets wrong. Where the answer space is unbounded, reasoning cuts the distinct answers produced to 0.43-0.65 of the non-reasoning count; where it is bounded, both arms hold an identical option set and reasoning concentrates mass on it instead, which no positional prior can explain at fixed weights. The aggregate cost is smaller than the mechanism predicts, because reasoning also shrinks the set of problems where answer diversity can decide anything, in ten of ten cells and by 2.7x; normalized for available headroom, both arms convert a quarter of it in domain. Confidence weighting does not recover what is left. Across 280 method-dataset-model combinations on eight models and five benchmarks, not one beats plain majority voting after correction; weighted voting agrees with it on 98.5% of problem-method pairs and is right 56.3% of the time on the rest; and a signal's direction can invert within fixed weights, with answer log-probability predicting correctness when reasoning is off and error when it is on. A learned six-signal combination gains nothing out of domain. Confidence signals should be evaluated on decisions, not on discrimination.

</details>


### [144] [Receiver-Conditioned Latent Communication gives 94% CacheBack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32046)
*Maximillian Rossi,Prajwal Raghunath,Haoqing Xuan,Yusen Zhang,Eugene Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces CacheBack, a method for efficient latent communication in multi-agent LLM systems by sending only receiver-relevant compressed KV cache states.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Latent communication via full KV cache sharing between LLM agents avoids text generation overhead and can boost accuracy and latency, but KV caches scale linearly with both context size and number of agents, quickly exhausting GPU memory and context windows. The paper is motivated by the need to retain the benefits of KV-based communication while drastically reducing its memory and context footprint in realistic multi-agent deployments.

Method: Proposes receiver-conditioned communication: the receiving agent first sends a compact description of its information needs to the sender. The sender then filters and compresses its KV cache accordingly, transmitting only the parts useful for the receiver’s local task. CacheBack is a concrete, training-free implementation that uses the sender’s attention weights to select and compress the most relevant KV states before sending them.

Result: On the FanOutQA benchmark with Qwen 3, CacheBack removes about 75% of the KV state that would otherwise be transmitted, while improving accuracy by 14.7 percentage points and reducing median end-to-end latency by 3.2x versus standard text-based communication. Similar gains are observed across different model architectures, including dense Transformers, Mamba-attention hybrids, and sliding-window attention models.

Conclusion: Receiver-conditioned latent communication, instantiated as CacheBack, can significantly reduce memory and communication overhead in multi-agent LLM systems while simultaneously improving accuracy and latency, and it works robustly across diverse model architectures without additional training.

Abstract: Multi-agent systems distribute large contexts across agents that communicate to solve a task. Text messages are compact but require decoding and may omit evidence the receiving agent needs. Recent latent communication instead transfers KV caches. This avoids text generation and can improve accuracy and latency. However, a full KV cache grows linearly with both the context an individual agent processes, and the number of agents that coordinate together. This raises memory and context costs, often far exceeding available GPU resources and context window sizes. Our key observation is that agents need only send what the receiving agent requires for its local task -- which we call receiver-conditioned communication. The receiver agent passes the sender a small description of its information needs, which serves to filter and compress the sender agent's KV cache. CacheBack is a simple, robust, training-free instance of receiver conditioning based on the sender's attention weights. On FanOutQA, CacheBack with Qwen 3 removes 75% of the state the agent would otherwise receive, improving accuracy by 14.7 percentage points and reducing median task-completion latency by 3.2x relative to text communication. We show comparable improvements across model families that span dense Transformers, Mamba-attention hybrids, and sliding-window attention.

</details>


### [145] [EngramRAG: Dynamic Usage-Weighted Topology and Synaptic Consolidation for Multi-Hop Agentic Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32049)
*Bhavyateja Potineni,Lohit Giri,Anu Jain,Vadim Kutsyy,Rajasekhar Pentakota*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EngramRAG is an adaptive memory and retrieval architecture for long-term LLM agents that mitigates common failures in multi-session use by combining graph-based, vector, and lexical retrieval with biologically inspired consolidation and topology adaptation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory architectures for autonomous LLM agents in long, multi-session settings fail in three key ways: (1) they are bad at multi-hop relational reasoning over stored memories (Associative Blindness); (2) they forget stable user or agent traits over time due to recency-based eviction (Scaffolding Amnesia); and (3) they use static knowledge graphs that do not adapt as usage patterns change (Static Topology Stagnation). The authors aim to design a memory system that maintains long-term, persona-level invariants, adapts its structure based on usage, and supports robust retrieval for temporal and relational reasoning, while still being fast enough for interactive use.

Method: The paper introduces EngramRAG, inspired by Complementary Learning Systems, with two operational modes: a low-latency Waking State for fast retrieval and an asynchronous Dreaming State for consolidation and topology updates. Key components include: (1) Usage-Modulated Personalized PageRank (U-PPR), which adjusts graph transition probabilities via a Hebbian-like rule so that frequently co-activated entities become high-centrality hubs; (2) Consolidation-Activated Topology Decay (CATD), which decays or prunes edges and nodes based on their structural importance rather than pure recency, with a grace period to protect new memories; (3) a directed SUPERSEDES DAG that explicitly encodes fact mutations and suppresses outdated or conflicting states during retrieval; and (4) a triple-source hybrid retrieval pipeline that combines dense vector search, BM25, and U-PPR graph retrieval, fused using Reciprocal Rank Fusion, to rank candidate memories. The system is evaluated on the LoCoMo benchmark of long-term conversations, temporal reasoning tasks, and controlled mutation tests and long-duration simulations.

Result: On the LoCoMo benchmark (1,982 QA pairs across 10 long-term conversations), EngramRAG improves Recall@5 from 38.29% to 53.21% (a 38.9% relative gain) and MRR from 0.2937 to 0.4203 (a 43.1% relative gain) over a dense-vector-only RAG baseline. It also outperforms Okapi BM25 (48.66% Recall@5) and static graph retrieval (8.50%). For temporal reasoning subsets, EngramRAG attains 62.33% Recall@5, 16.67 points higher than dense vector retrieval. In controlled fact-mutation experiments, the SUPERSEDES mechanism eliminates split-brain hallucinations, reducing them from 70% to 0%. In 90-day simulation studies, the system maintains 100% retention of core scaffolding information while preserving interactive latency, with an average retrieval time of about 26.21 ms.

Conclusion: EngramRAG demonstrates that a biologically inspired, adaptive memory architecture with dual operational states, usage-modulated graph dynamics, and explicit mutation handling can substantially improve long-term recall, temporal reasoning, and hallucination resistance for LLM agents in multi-session settings. By decoupling structural retention from raw recency and leveraging hybrid retrieval, the system preserves core persona and task scaffolding over extended periods without sacrificing interactive latency, suggesting a promising direction for building more robust long-lived AI agents.

Abstract: As autonomous LLM agents are deployed across multi-session environments, conventional memory architectures suffer from Associative Blindness (inability to traverse multi-hop relational dependencies), Scaffolding Amnesia (temporal decay evicting core persona invariants), and Static Topology Stagnation (immutable graphs ignoring usage dynamics). Grounded in Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) principles, we propose EngramRAG, an adaptive memory architecture coupling a low-latency Waking State reflex with an asynchronous background Dreaming State consolidation cycle. EngramRAG introduces: (1) Usage-Modulated Personalized PageRank (U-PPR), where transition probabilities adapt via Hebbian plasticity to promote persistent entities into high-centrality Epistemic Macro-Hubs; (2) Consolidation-Activated Topology Decay (CATD), which scales retention half-life by topological load-bearing weight rather than wall-clock recency, protected by a cold-start grace period (N_grace >= 4); (3) Directed SUPERSEDES DAG filtering to suppress obsolete state during fact mutations; and (4) Triple-source hybrid retrieval fusing dense vectors, BM25, and U-PPR via dynamic Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). Evaluating on all 1,982 QA pairs across 10 long-term conversations in the LoCoMo benchmark, EngramRAG achieves +38.9% relative improvement in Recall@5 (53.21% vs. 38.29%, p < 0.001) and +43.1% in MRR (0.4203 vs. 0.2937) over dense vector RAG, significantly outperforming Okapi BM25 (48.66%) and isolated static graph retrieval (8.50%). On temporal reasoning, EngramRAG reaches 62.33% Recall@5 (+16.67 points over dense vectors). In controlled mutation tests, SUPERSEDES suppresses split-brain hallucinations from 70.0% to 0.0%, while 90-day simulations show 100.0% scaffolding retention under a 26.21ms interactive retrieval reflex.

</details>


### [146] [Contract monitoring: governing AI via separation of powers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32061)
*Enric Boix-Adsera*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a contract-based AI safety framework where worker agents are constrained by explicit contracts, with monitoring and judging agents enforcing these constraints using asymmetric computational resources, enabling empirical measurement of statistical safety guarantees across scenarios like code security and box-escape tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI systems become more capable and autonomous, ensuring they behave safely and within specified limits is challenging. Existing approaches often lack clear, enforceable guarantees or are hard to measure empirically. The paper is motivated by the need for a practical framework that can formally constrain AI agents’ behavior, reliably detect violations, and provide measurable, statistical safety guarantees in realistic tasks such as secure coding or preventing agents from escaping restricted environments.

Method: The authors design a multi-agent safety architecture centered on contracts that explicitly define the allowed actions of a worker agent. They introduce monitor agents that observe worker behavior and judge agents that adjudicate potential violations, with each role given distinct responsibilities. A key design choice is to give monitors and judges asymmetric (typically stronger or differently structured) computational resources compared to workers, so they can effectively detect and evaluate rule violations. The framework is instantiated in various experimental settings (e.g., code security, escape-the-box tasks) where contracts, monitoring procedures, and judging criteria are concretely defined, allowing empirical evaluation of how often safety violations occur and are caught.

Result: The framework is shown to be implementable across multiple domains such as secure code generation and containment scenarios. Experiments yield empirical, statistical measurements of safety performance: how frequently worker agents violate contracts, how reliably monitors detect such violations, and how accurately judges evaluate them. The results demonstrate that contract-based constraints combined with specialized monitoring and judging agents can provide quantifiable safety assurances in practice.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that contract-bound worker agents supervised by dedicated monitors and judges, especially with asymmetric computational resources, offer a practical pathway to measurable AI safety. This architecture can be adapted to diverse domains and supports empirical estimation of statistical safety guarantees, representing a step toward more rigorous and testable control of advanced AI systems.

Abstract: We propose an AI safety framework that binds worker agents to contracts specifying their permitted actions. We show how these contracts can be enforced and specified by assigning distinct responsibilities to monitor agents and judges, and asymmetric computational resources to monitors and workers. Our framework allows us to empirically measure statistical safety guarantees. The framework applies to a wide range of settings, including code security and escape-the-box scenarios.

</details>


### [147] [Toward Interactive Understanding of Code APIs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32081)
*Dhananjay Ashok,Jesse Thomason,Jonathan May*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose PAU, a benchmark where models must infer the functionality of Python APIs using only black-box interaction, revealing large performance gaps and overconfidence in current LMs, and show an AAC-style post-training method that improves exploration and performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current code-focused language model agents assume direct read access to code, which breaks down for external or black-box APIs. There is a need to systematically study whether models can understand tools purely through interaction, and to quantify and improve this capability.

Method: They build PAU (Python API Understanding), a benchmark of Python methods exposed only via API-level, black-box access. Models can send exploratory inputs, observe outputs, and must produce natural language descriptions of each snippet’s true behavior. They evaluate frontier models on this benchmark, analyze their error patterns (especially overconfidence and premature stopping), and then adapt the Asymmetric Actor Critic (AAC) paradigm from robot learning to post-train models for more effective interactive code exploration and understanding.

Result: On PAU, even strong models perform poorly: the best baseline, Claude-4-Opus, fails on more than 45% of the test cases and exhibits systematic overconfidence and insufficient exploration.
