Applying AAC-style post-training leads models to explore the API space more actively, and an AAC-tuned Qwen3-8B attains performance comparable to a stronger baseline model, GPT-5-mini.

Conclusion: Understanding black-box tools via interaction alone is considerably harder for current LMs than traditional code-understanding tasks with source access. PAU exposes this gap and highlights overconfidence and under-exploration as key failure modes. AAC-inspired post-training can significantly improve interactive exploration and understanding, narrowing the performance gap between smaller and larger models.

Abstract: Empowered by advances in Language Model agents, systems have made substantial strides in code generation and understanding. However, these approaches often rely on read access to the relevant code, an assumption which does not hold when dealing with external APIs. In this work, we introduce the PAU (Python API Understanding) benchmark, where we provide models with black-box, API-level access to code snippets. Models must query the API with exploratory inputs and draw insights from the resulting outputs, with the goal of describing the snippet's true functionality. By treating the code snippets as external tools that must be understood via interaction alone, PAU studies the more general problem of unsupervised tool understanding, specifically for tools implemented as Python methods. Despite recent progress in coding agents, even frontier models struggle to achieve high performance on PAU, with the best model (Claude-4-Opus) failing to understand over 45% of the PAU test set. An investigation into the common error modes reveals that models are overconfident; they often overrate the quality of their current hypothesis, leading to insufficient exploration and premature termination. Finally, we take inspiration from the Asymmetric Actor Critic (AAC) paradigm, frequently used in robot learning, to post-train models for interactive code understanding. Models trained with AAC conduct more active exploration of the APIs, with an AAC-tuned Qwen3-8B model matching the performance of GPT-5-mini.

</details>


### [148] [Memory as Middleware for Self-Improving AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32091)
*K. R. Jayaram,Vatche Isahagian,Vinod Muthusamy,Gegi Thomas,Punleuk Oum,Gaodan Fang,Ashwath Vaithinathan Aravindan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes treating AI agent memory as independent, pluggable middleware rather than bespoke, agent-specific logic, and presents ALTK-Evolve as a reference implementation for self-improving agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI agents are stateless across sessions, causing them to forget past failures, fixes, preferences, and successful strategies. Existing solutions use custom, tightly coupled memory implementations tied to specific agents and storage backends, leading to fragmentation and limited reusability, sharing, or isolation of memory components.

Method: The authors conceptualize AI agent memory as a middleware layer and articulate six key systems challenges that such middleware must address: two-sided pluggability (decoupling agents and memory backends), host-native interposition, multi-tenant isolation, write-path consistency, federated sharing with provenance, and lifecycle governance. They then design and implement ALTK-Evolve as a concrete reference system embodying these principles for self-improving agents.

Result: The paper delivers ALTK-Evolve, a working prototype of memory middleware that demonstrates how agent memory can be modularized, plugged into different agents and storage systems, and governed in a principled way along the six identified dimensions. It shows that memory can be managed as a separate infrastructure layer rather than bespoke per agent.

Conclusion: Agent memory should be elevated to a first-class middleware concern, analogous to data access or messaging layers in traditional systems. The ALTK-Evolve implementation illustrates the feasibility and benefits of this approach and lays out a broader research agenda for developing robust, pluggable, shared, and governable memory middleware for self-improving AI agents.

Abstract: AI agents are stateless across sessions by default and therefore operationally amnesic: each session begins with little durable knowledge of prior failures, repairs, preferences, or successful strategies. As a result, agents repeat the same mistakes and discard hard-won experience. The dominant fix is \emph{bespoke memory}---retrieval, persistence, and learning logic hand-wired into one agent and bound to one storage engine. This creates a fragmented landscape where memory cannot be swapped, shared, isolated, or reasoned about independently of the agent that owns it. We argue that this is a middleware problem: agent memory deserves a first-class, pluggable layer, just as data access, messaging, and persistence each became middleware concerns.
  We develop this vision through six systems challenges: two-sided pluggability, host-native interposition, multi-tenant isolation, write-path consistency, federated sharing with provenance, and lifecycle governance. We present ALTK-Evolve, a reference implementation of memory middleware for self-improving agents, and use it to motivate a broader research agenda for future memory middleware.

</details>


### [149] [GameBoyWorlds: A Testbed for Self-Improvement in Embodied Video Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32093)
*Dhananjay Ashok,Adam Shen,Aslan Huo Feng,Chinmay Khanna,Jun Rui Huang,Raghav Sarmukaddam,Surendira Balaji Natarajan,Xiaotong Cui,Xincan Zhang,Thomson Yen,Hongseok Namkoong,Jonathan May,Jesse Thomason*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces GameBoyWorlds, a benchmark to test whether agents can autonomously self-improve in Game Boy video-game environments, showing that current frontier models and self-improvement methods fall far short.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern agents can follow human guidance in interactive environments but it is unknown whether they can reliably self-improve using only their own experience, without demonstrations, documentation, or explicit rewards. The authors want a rigorous, challenging benchmark to measure this capability and expose the gaps in current methods.

Method: They build GameBoyWorlds, a testbed consisting of (1) GameBoyWorlds-Execution: short-horizon tasks across 5 game series, where agents get separate training games and must infer how to act via self-directed exploration and experience; and (2) GameBoyWorlds-Playthrough: full playthrough objectives in two fan-made Pokémon games, where agents must progress only via learning from interaction, using tools like multimodal memory, hierarchical subgoals, world models, autonomous skill discovery, and curiosity-driven guide writing. They evaluate frontier multimodal models and several self-improvement strategies on these benchmarks.

Result: Frontier models, without extra self-improvement mechanisms, solve under half of 500 short-horizon tasks, largely due to failures in multimodal grounding. Established self-improvement techniques like world modeling and autonomous skill discovery do not substantially improve performance, and even a new curiosity-driven guide-writing approach only partially helps. In the long-horizon playthrough setting, a sophisticated agentic pipeline using memory and hierarchical subgoals still fails to reach the first major milestone in either Pokémon game, despite models having prior exposure to related official titles.

Conclusion: GameBoyWorlds is a difficult and discriminative benchmark for agentic self-improvement: it shows that current frontier models and state-of-the-art self-improvement pipelines cannot reliably learn to play and complete unfamiliar games from scratch purely through their own interaction. The benchmark thus sets an ambitious target and highlights the need for more powerful methods for multimodal grounding, exploration, knowledge extraction from experience, and long-horizon autonomous learning.

Abstract: Powered by expert guidance, agents can operate in interactive environments; however, it is unclear whether they can learn autonomously from their own experience. To evaluate such self-improvement methods, we introduce GameBoyWorlds, a testbed for agentic self-improvement in video games. GameBoyWorlds-Execution evaluates task execution on a collection of 5 distinct game series. Agents are allowed access to dedicated training games but are provided no demonstrations, documentation, or rewards. Agents must ground themselves in the environment through self-directed exploration and by inferring actionable knowledge from their own experience. At test time, agents must complete short-horizon tasks that evaluate their ability to navigate, interact, and engage with game-specific mechanics in unseen games. Out-of-the-box frontier models complete fewer than 50% of the 500 tasks due to failures in multimodal grounding, establishing that self-improvement methods have room to push performance. We demonstrate that contemporary approaches to self-improvement are lacking, with world modelling and autonomous skill discovery failing, and a novel strategy that uses curiosity-based exploration to write guides achieving only partial success. GameBoyWorlds-Playthrough tests end-to-end game completion in two fan-made Pokémon games. We show that while frontier models have been pre-exposed to official releases such as Pokémon Red, they lack essential information on the games in our testbed. Instead of relying on their parametric knowledge to succeed, agents must learn from their own experience and autonomously improve over the course of the playthrough. We show that a sophisticated agentic pipeline with multimodal memory and hierarchical subgoals fails to reach even the first major milestone in both games, establishing GameBoyWorlds as an ambitious target for self-improving agents.

</details>


### [150] [Residual Streams Read, Recurrent States Remember: The Global Workspace in Mamba Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32102)
*Wenlong Wang,Fergal Reid*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Study of how a global-workspace style interpretation of internal representations applies to state-space language models like Mamba.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Global-workspace explanations have mostly been developed for transformer residual streams; it is unclear whether similar mechanisms and interpretability tools apply to newer state-space models whose core representations are recurrent states rather than residual streams.

Method: Fit Jacobian lenses (linear probes / readouts) to both residual streams and recurrent states across several Mamba model variants, using a standard 1000-prompt probing setup. Compare recovery of known intermediate concepts using residual-only, state-only, and joint residual+state readouts across different task families. Analyze temporal maps and word-list retention to study how information persists in states vs residuals. Propose and test a new intervention method, sign-guarded steering, and compare it to coordinate exchange for causal editing of internal representations, evaluating effects on verbal report and relational question answering.

Result: Joint residual+state readouts recover intermediate concepts better than residual-only lenses on most task families and checkpoints. In Mamba-2, probes on the recurrent state alone outperform both residual and logit lenses on all task families, and a normalized joint readout usually performs best. Temporal and word-list analyses show that earlier content remains readable from the recurrent state even when it is less visible in residuals. Sign-guarded steering improves top-5 accuracy on targeted verbal-report interventions in five models, with recurrent state alone being sufficient for this access. However, these improvements are inconsistent for relational questions: guarded edits often surface the edited concept directly, and on Mamba-3 joint interventions can harm otherwise successful state-only steering.

Conclusion: State-space language models like Mamba contain a complementary "workspace" in their recurrent state, distinct from the residual stream, that better preserves and exposes intermediate concepts for both measurement and causal intervention in many cases. However, effective use of this workspace—particularly for complex relational reasoning—requires tools that separately measure recovery, persistence, and causal effects in state vs residual channels, as naive joint editing can degrade performance.

Abstract: Can the global-workspace account of transformer representations extend to state-space language models? We fit Jacobian lenses to the residual streams and recurrent states of Mamba-1, Mamba-2 and Mamba-3, using the original 1000-prompt recipe. Joint residual--state readouts improve recovery of known intermediate concepts over the residual lens on at least five of six task families in every tested Mamba checkpoint. On Mamba-2, state alone exceeds residual and logit lenses on all six families; a normalised joint readout improves on both components on five. Temporal maps and word-list experiments show earlier content remaining state-readable as residual visibility changes. We also propose sign-guarded steering, which improves target top-five success over coordinate exchange on matched verbal-report trials in five models. Recurrent state alone supports this verbal access. These gains do not extend consistently to relational answers: guarded edits often output the edited concept itself, and Mamba-3's joint edits can disrupt successful state-only redirection. Recurrent state thus provides a complementary carrier of workspace content, whose recovery, persistence and causal uses require separate measurements.

</details>


### [151] [Escaping Alignment: A Physical Trap Model of Best-of-N Jailbreaking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32116)
*Marco Biroli*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper analyzes and models how “best-of-N” jailbreaking attacks succeed against aligned language models, showing that previously assumed power-law scaling in N is misleading and proposing a simple four-parameter barrier model that predicts attack success across prompt, sampling, and temperature budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Best-of-N jailbreaking—issuing many slightly modified unsafe prompts and choosing the best response—has become a standard way to bypass LLM safety, but existing work mostly studies only the dependence on the number of prompt augmentations N and claims the attack success rate follows a power law. There is little understanding of how success scales jointly with both the number of augmentations N and the number of generations per augmentation M, nor how it changes with temperature T. This gap makes it hard to rigorously compare defenses, extrapolate to stronger attackers, or design principled safety evaluations.

Method: The authors empirically re-examine the scaling of attack success rate (ASR) with the number of augmentations N, showing that the apparent power law exhibits exponent drift and an exponential crossover due to finite-size artifacts in the adversarial dataset. They then propose a simple “barrier model” in which each unsafe prompt has a baseline safety level, and each augmentation is associated with a random, thermally activated barrier determining whether the safety filter is overcome. This model is parameterized by four interpretable quantities corresponding to distinct safety mechanisms, and it specifies the full attack surface over (N, M) and temperature T. The parameters are fit using data at moderate N and a single temperature, then used to make out-of-sample predictions.

Result: The authors show that the best-of-N scaling previously fit with a power law actually deviates systematically as N grows, with the power-law exponent drifting and an exponential crossover emerging that is attributable to finite-size effects in the adversarial dataset. Their four-parameter barrier model accurately predicts the ASR across a wide range of N and M, extrapolating from N ≤ 100 up to N = 10^4. When applied to five distinct models, the ASR curves collapse onto a common scaling function once expressed in terms of the barrier-model parameters. Furthermore, the model can predict ASR at different sampling temperatures from parameters fitted at a single temperature, indicating that temperature effects are captured by the thermally activated barrier mechanism.

Conclusion: Best-of-N jailbreaking behavior is not well-described by a simple power law in the number of augmentations; instead, a finite-size, barrier-crossing picture better captures how attacks scale with prompt and sampling budgets and with temperature. A four-parameter barrier model provides a compact, interpretable description of the entire (N, M, T) attack surface, enabling reliable extrapolation to stronger attack regimes and unifying the behavior of multiple models under a common scaling function. This offers a more principled basis for analyzing and benchmarking LLM safety against BoN-style attacks.

Abstract: Best-of-$N$ jailbreaking (BoN) bypasses safeguards of aligned models by drawing $N$ independent augmentations of an unsafe prompt and sampling $M$ completions of each. Previous works have shown that the attack success rate (ASR) seems to follow a power-law in $N$, which we challenge. The exponent drifts with $N$, with an exponential crossover which is a finite-size artifact of the adversarial dataset. Little work has been done to explore the entire two-budget ($N, M$) attack surface as well as its dependence on the generation temperature $T$. We introduce a simple barrier model where each prompt has a baseline safety level and each augmentation a random thermally activated barrier. Then four numbers, each backed by an interpretable safety mechanism, determine the entire ($N, M$) attack surface. They extrapolate predictions from $N \leq 100$ to $N = 10^4$, collapse five distinct models on the same scaling function and predict ASR at different temperatures from the one they were fitted at.

</details>


### [152] [READ-Bench: Benchmarking Historical Instance Retrieval for Time-Series Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32123)
*Gerardo Pastrana,Haojun Li,Dhruv Mehta,Anoushka Vyas,Sina Khoshfetrat Pakazad,Henrik Ohlsson,John Paparrizos*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces READ-Bench, a benchmark for retrieving relevant historical time-series diagnostic cases, and shows that simple reranking with light supervision outperforms fancier representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing time-series diagnostic systems rarely use case retrieval, and when they do, they only evaluate retrieval indirectly via prediction accuracy. Moreover, relevance is usually tied to signal similarity instead of sharing the same underlying fault, and the impact of modern representation learning and reranking strategies on retrieval itself is unclear. There is a need for a systematic benchmark and study of time-series case retrieval grounded in diagnostic relevance.

Method: The authors build READ-Bench, a benchmark across 12 multivariate time-series diagnostic datasets where relevance is defined by matching fault/event type rather than signal shape. They model retrieval as a two-stage process: a base retriever followed by a reranker. They comprehensively evaluate classical distance measures, symbolic retrieval methods, self-supervised and foundation-model embeddings, and their combinations, as well as label-aware and LLM-based rerankers. Experiments vary levels of supervision, data pollution, and corpus size, using a unified interface and statistical significance testing. A key reranker is a Gaussian-process model that propagates labels in embedding space from a small set of resolved cases.

Result: Pretrained representation-based retrievers (self-supervised and foundation models) show no statistically significant advantage over strong classical and symbolic baselines when used only for search. The main performance gains come from adding a small amount of supervision at the reranking stage via the Gaussian-process label-propagation reranker, which remains effective even under data pollution and large-scale corpora. Based on this insight, the authors propose a fused retriever combining a normal-residual-scored embedder with a dynamic time warping leg using reciprocal-rank fusion, followed by the Gaussian-process reranker, which improves NDCG@10 across all 12 datasets, by +0.11 over its own search stage and +0.16 over the strongest individual base retriever.

Conclusion: For historical-case retrieval in time-series diagnostics, better reranking with light supervised signal-label propagation matters more than sophisticated pretrained representations or language-model reasoning at the retrieval stage. READ-Bench provides a standardized way to evaluate such systems. A fusion-based base retriever plus a Gaussian-process reranker yields consistent and significant gains in ranking quality across diverse diagnostic datasets, highlighting that modest supervision at reranking is the decisive ingredient for effective fault-type-based retrieval.

Abstract: Time-series diagnostic systems rarely rely on retrieving relevant historical cases, and when they do, retrieval is evaluated only indirectly through downstream prediction. We introduce READ-Bench, a benchmark for historical-case retrieval across 12 diagnostic datasets, centered on multivariate time series, that defines relevance by shared fault or event type rather than signal shape, so visually different traces of the same fault count as relevant while similar-looking traces of different faults do not. Treating retrieval as a base retriever followed by a reranker, we evaluate classical distances, symbolic retrievers, self-supervised and foundation-model embedders, and their fusion, plus label-aware and language-model rerankers, under one protocol that varies supervision, pollution, and corpus scale with significance testing. Under a common channel-independent interface, pretrained representations offer no statistically detectable advantage over strong classical and symbolic baselines for search alone. The decisive factor is a small amount of resolved-case supervision at reranking, namely a Gaussian-process reranker that propagates a few neighbor labels in embedding space, which helps far more than more sophisticated representations or language-model reasoning and holds under pollution and at full corpus scale. Guided by these findings, we fuse a normal-residual-scored embedder with a dynamic time warping leg via reciprocal-rank fusion, then rerank with the Gaussian-process reranker, improving NDCG@10 over its own search stage on all 12 datasets, by +0.11 from reranking and +0.16 over the strongest single base retriever.

</details>


### [153] [PastForward: Faster On-Device GUI Agents via Computational Experience Reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32166)
*Taehwan Park,Changmin Lee,Hayeon Lee,Taesik Gong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PastForward speeds up on-device GUI agents by reusing past computations and interaction histories while preserving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Running GUI agents on edge devices improves privacy by keeping interaction data local, but per-step VLM inference is too slow and costly. Existing reuse approaches are too coarse and brittle in dynamic mobile environments and often require fine-tuning or offline exploration. The paper aims to enable efficient, accurate, and practical on-device GUI agents by reusing computation from normal task executions in a fine-grained and validated manner.

Method: PastForward records prior VLM output sequences and GUI transitions during normal use. At each decoding step, it retrieves previously generated output token sequences as multi-token proposals tailored to the current device context and verifies them in a single VLM forward pass. Across action steps, it predicts the next screen based on prior GUI transitions and starts the next-step inference speculatively while the device executes the current action. If the predicted screen matches the observed one, PastForward reuses the corresponding KV cache (attention states) to skip redundant computation; otherwise, it discards them and falls back to normal inference.

Result: Evaluated on AndroidWorld benchmarks that reflect realistic mobile usage, and using multiple VLM backbones on both server and edge hardware, PastForward yields 1.63–2.36× speedups in per-action latency on-device without degrading task success rates.

Conclusion: Fine-grained, validated reuse of past computations and GUI interaction histories can substantially accelerate on-device GUI agents while preserving effectiveness. PastForward demonstrates that such reuse can be implemented in a device-adaptive way, using speculative decoding and KV cache forwarding across action steps, achieving significant speedups without sacrificing task success.

Abstract: Running GUI agents on edge devices can keep sensitive screens and interaction histories local, but the computational cost of inference at every action step makes deployment challenging. Existing GUI agent systems either perform full vision-language model (VLM) inference at each action step or reuse coarse-grained knowledge matched to prior tasks. However, dynamic mobile environments and user tasks make it difficult to fully utilize prior task executions without additional fine-tuning or task-specific offline exploration. To address this challenge, we present PastForward, a system that accelerates GUI agents through validated, fine-grained reuse of computational experience accumulated during ordinary task execution. During decoding, PastForward retrieves prior output sequences as device-adaptive multi-token proposals and verifies them in a single VLM forward pass. Across action steps, it uses prior GUI transitions to begin next-step inference while the device executes the current action, retains the early computation only when the predicted screen matches the observed screen, and carries reusable KV states forward. We evaluate PastForward on AndroidWorld workloads derived from real mobile usage patterns using multiple VLM backbones across server and edge platforms. On device, PastForward achieves action-step latency speedups of 1.63-2.36$\times$ while maintaining task success rates.

</details>


### [154] [Noisy Test-Time Reinforcement Learning for Code LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32172)
*Xikai Yang,Hieu Trung Nguyen,Dunyuan Xu,Yuzhi Zhao,Jinpeng Li,Wenao Ma,Pheng-Ann Heng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose NTRL-Code, a test-time reinforcement learning framework that makes code LLMs more robust to noisy, vague user instructions using only unlabeled noisy data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Code LLMs work well on clean benchmarks but struggle with real-world user prompts that are vague, noisy, and error-prone. Robustness-oriented fine-tuning usually needs expensive paired clean-noisy data and complex noise simulation. The authors want a way to improve robustness to noise without such labeled resources, and to adapt models at test time directly on noisy inputs.

Method: They introduce NTRL-Code, a noisy test-time reinforcement learning framework for code LLMs. At test time, given only noisy prompts, the model first performs conservative self-denoising to construct a cleaner semantic anchor for the underlying task. It then generates multiple candidate programs and aggregates them using an abstract-syntax-tree (AST) based structural mechanism to estimate a proxy target. Using this proxy, they optimize the policy on the original noisy prompts with a hybrid reward containing: (1) format validity, (2) code similarity to the proxy target, and (3) anti-repetition signals. This constitutes a self-evolution loop that doesn’t require clean labels or paired data.

Result: On three benchmarks with systematically injected perturbations at character, word, and paragraph levels, NTRL-Code consistently improves robustness and stabilizes predictions over various base code LLMs. It achieves higher performance than baselines across perturbation types and strengths, showing that the approach generalizes and works in multiple noisy conditions.

Conclusion: NTRL-Code provides an effective way to enhance the robustness of code LLMs to noisy, vague instructions using only unlabeled noisy data at test time. By combining self-denoising, AST-based aggregation, and hybrid rewards in a test-time RL framework, it achieves consistent gains without requiring curated clean-noisy pairs, offering a practical path for deploying more reliable code LLMs in real-world settings.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across various code-related tasks. However, unlike carefully curated datasets that are typically high-quality and error-free, real-world user instructions are often vague and error-prone, posing significant challenges to the robustness of code LLMs. Furthermore, robustness-oriented fine-tuning relies on paired clean-noisy samples, which are costly to curate and require sophisticated noisy simulation techniques. To address these challenges, we propose the Noisy Test-time Reinforcement Learning framework (NTRL-Code), which enables robust self-evolution of code LLMs using only unlabeled noisy data during the testing stage. Specifically, NTRL-Code uses conservative self-denoising to obtain a cleaner semantic anchor for target estimation, and employs an abstract-syntax-tree (AST)-based structural aggregation mechanism to estimate a proxy target from multiple candidate programs. The policy is then optimized on the original noisy prompts with a hybrid reward that combines format validity, code similarity, and anti-repetition signals. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks, each incorporating character-level, word-level, and paragraph-level perturbations, demonstrate that NTRL-Code yields robust and consistent improvements, stabilizing the predictions of various base models. Our code is available at https://github.com/Xikai97/NTRL-Code.

</details>


### [155] [AI Harness: Certification under Proposal-Conditioned Information for Foundation-Model Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32184)
*Hailin Zhong,Shengxin Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies when collapsing model proposals and histories into a state-only interface preserves or destroys safety certification for foundation-model agents, and characterizes when proposal–history correlation at the model–tool boundary is necessary.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Foundation-model agents are commonly treated as policies over observed states, but real deployed runtimes often only see and can intervene on semantic proposals emitted by the model. This means proposals serve both as action candidates and as observations derived from the model’s internal history. Existing abstractions that collapse this structure into a simple state-based interface may be invalid for safety certification: they might preserve the set of proposed actions while losing crucial information about correlations between history and proposals that are needed to guarantee robust safety. The paper is motivated by the need to understand exactly when such collapses are safe or unsafe from a certification standpoint.

Method: The authors model a “finite robust interface” where a runtime safety controller can intervene on proposals from a history-conditioned model. They define and analyze viability kernels (sets of states from which safety can be maintained) both in a history-augmented space and in a collapsed state-only space. Using this formalism, they prove inclusion relations between the viability kernels of the collapsed and history-augmented models, and characterize when the collapse is lossless via a “common robust-safe intervention” condition on each proposal-conditioned fiber. They further derive a dual result where observing the current proposal can expand the robustly feasible set when it separates latent modes that require incompatible interventions. They extend the one-step analysis to multi-step horizons using exact finite belief states and standard fixed-point operators for safety and reachability. Finally, they validate the theory with controlled model-in-the-loop experiments where telemetry or effect verification is removed or intervention authority is constrained, demonstrating the predicted safety obstructions.

Result: The main results are: (1) In a finite robust interface, the viability kernel of the collapsed state-only model is always contained in the physical projection of the history-augmented viability kernel, meaning collapsing never increases the certifiable safe set. (2) The collapse is lossless for certification exactly when, for every proposal, all corresponding history-conditioned states admit a common robust-safe intervention; otherwise, safety guarantees are strictly weakened. (3) This gap between the true and collapsed kernels can be maximal even when proposal and history alphabets are of constant size, emphasizing the practical severity of the issue. (4) The same common-action condition produces a dual insight: observing the current proposal can restore robust feasibility by distinguishing latent modes that require mutually incompatible interventions. (5) Extending to multi-step settings via belief-based fixed-point calculations separates indefinite operational viability from finite-horizon worst-case verified progress. (6) Model-in-the-loop experiments confirm that removing telemetry, eliminating effect verification, or restricting intervention authority induces the predicted failures in safety certification.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that certification of foundation-model agents cannot, in general, rely on a collapsed state-only view of model proposals. Maintaining and exploiting proposal–history correlations at the model–tool boundary is sometimes essential for robust safety guarantees. A collapse to a proposal envelope is certifiably lossless only under a stringent common-robust-intervention condition for each proposal; otherwise, the certifiable safe set can shrink dramatically. Observing proposals can also be beneficial, enabling recovery of robust feasibility when proposals disambiguate latent modes. Overall, the work does not propose a new fixed-point framework but clarifies when and why interface design—specifically, how proposals and histories are exposed to the runtime—determines the possibility of formal certification for foundation-model agents.

Abstract: Foundation-model agents are often modeled as policies over an observed state. In deployed systems, however, a runtime may intervene only after the model has emitted a semantic proposal, making the proposal both an action candidate and a decision-time observation generated by a history-conditioned process. We show that collapsing this structure into a state-only proposal envelope can preserve proposal coverage while destroying certifiability. In a finite robust interface, the viability kernel of the collapsed model is contained in the physical projection of the history-augmented kernel, and the collapse is lossless exactly when every proposal-conditioned collapsed fiber retains a common robust-safe intervention. This gap can be maximal even with constant-size proposal and history alphabets. The same common-action condition yields a dual result: observing the current proposal can restore robust feasibility when it separates latent modes requiring incompatible interventions. We extend these one-step results over time using exact finite beliefs and standard safety and reachability fixed points, separating indefinite operational viability from finite worst-case verified progress. Controlled model-in-the-loop tests reproduce the predicted obstructions when telemetry or effect verification is removed or intervention authority is restricted. Thus, our contribution is not a new fixed-point calculus, but a characterization of when proposal--history correlation at the model--tool boundary is necessary for certification.

</details>


### [156] [CoMemBench: Benchmarking Collaborative Memory Boundaries across Multi-Agent Workflow Topologies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32192)
*Sen Zhao,Ruiqi Kong,Zuyu Zhang,Lifeng Shen,Xinyu He,Ding Zou,Xu Zhang,Qinghua Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes CoMemBench, a benchmark to evaluate how well multi-agent systems share and isolate information across workflow topologies, focusing on topology-conditioned collaborative memory boundaries rather than just retention or coordination.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-agent workflows, agents need access only to task-relevant information while being shielded from irrelevant, outdated, or incompatible data. This selective sharing is governed by the workflow topology, which defines where intermediate artifacts are valid and for whom. Existing benchmarks either test memory as retention/retrieval or multi-agent systems as coordination and completion, but they do not specifically measure how well systems handle memory boundaries shaped by workflow structure. This leaves a key aspect of collaborative intelligence—controlled sharing and isolation across complex workflows—unaddressed.

Method: The authors build CoMemBench, an execution-grounded benchmark that generates 800 composite workflows across four domains using source-grounded dependency graphs. Each node in a workflow has a local specification; intermediate artifacts passed between nodes are verifiable; and there are native evaluators to check correctness. For each workflow, matched isolation challenges are constructed so that certain information should not be accessible to specific downstream agents. The benchmark then evaluates multi-agent systems on multiple workflow topologies, tracking how they share and isolate memory under realistic execution conditions.

Result: CoMemBench yields quantitative metrics including workflow completion rates, verified progress at each node, reliability of required artifact handoffs, robustness of isolation against leakage or misuse of information, and token cost. Experimental results across different systems and topologies show a clear trade-off: giving agents broader shared context increases access to needed information and can help completion, but it also reduces isolation robustness, leading to more violations. The relative performance ranking of systems changes depending on the workflow topology and the nature of artifact isolation challenges.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that collaborative memory in multi-agent workflows must be evaluated not just on retention or coordination, but on how well systems respect topology-conditioned memory boundaries. CoMemBench exposes a fundamental sharing–isolation trade-off and demonstrates that system performance is highly topology-dependent. The benchmark provides a principled way to stress-test and compare multi-agent memory designs, encouraging future methods that can dynamically balance context breadth with strict isolation according to workflow structure.

Abstract: Multi-agent workflows require task-relevant information to be shared across agents, while irrelevant, stale, unverified, or incompatible information must remain isolated. We call this task-conditioned scope of information a collaborative memory boundary. Workflow topology determines which intermediate artifacts are applicable to which downstream workers and when they cease to be valid, thereby providing a structural stress dimension for sharing and isolation. Existing memory benchmarks primarily evaluate retention and retrieval, whereas multi-agent benchmarks emphasize coordination and end-to-end completion, leaving topology-conditioned memory boundaries largely unmeasured. We introduce CoMemBench, an execution-grounded benchmark for collaborative memory sharing and isolation across multi-agent workflow topologies. It constructs 800 composite workflows across four domains from source-grounded dependency graphs, with node-local specifications, verifiable artifact handoffs, native evaluators, and matched isolation challenges. CoMemBench measures workflow completion, verified node progress, required-handoff reliability, isolation robustness, and token cost. Experiments reveal a sharing-isolation trade-off: broader context improves information availability but can weaken isolation, while system rankings shift across topologies and artifact violations.

</details>


### [157] [Instruct, Not Answer: Using Instruction Privileges in On-Policy Context Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32201)
*Hantao Yu,Sandy Han,Udaya Ghai,Ferhat Erata,Joe Lilien,Aman Goel,Ali Torkamani*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies On-Policy Context Distillation (OPCD) and finds that simple, global instructions tailored to common model errors can be better training privileges than instance-specific gold answers/demonstrations, especially out-of-distribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior OPCD work typically uses gold answers or gold demonstrations as privileged information for the teacher model. However, many studies show that this can hurt training performance, particularly on out-of-distribution data. The authors aim to understand whether a more abstract, general form of privilege—short instructions that address recurrent student mistakes—can provide better transfer and robustness while preserving in-domain performance.

Method: The authors design short, general instructions that describe how the student should avoid common errors observed on the training data (e.g., formatting, reasoning patterns), and use these instructions as the privileged context for the teacher in OPCD instead of instance-specific gold solutions. They evaluate this OPCD setup on autoformalization tasks across multiple datasets (ProverQA, ProofWriter, ProntoQA) and model families (Qwen3-Thinking, Olmo3-Thinking), comparing matched-instruction privileges against gold-privilege baselines on both in-domain and out-of-distribution test splits.

Result: Across 7 out of 8 experiments, the OPCD setup using matched instruction privileges improves out-of-distribution accuracy by 4–17 points relative to using instance-specific gold, while maintaining comparable in-domain performance. In autoformalization, a simple formatting-oriented instruction as privilege can significantly outperform gold on OOD benchmarks. Importantly, each instruction is only a few sentences long and is applied uniformly across all training samples, yet still surpasses the richer, instance-specific gold privileges in transfer.

Conclusion: General, domain-agnostic instructions that systematically target common student mistakes can serve as highly effective privileged information in OPCD, often more transferable than detailed, instance-specific gold solutions. This suggests that well-chosen, compact instructions that are shared between source and target domains may be a better inductive bias for OPCD, yielding robust OOD gains without sacrificing in-domain accuracy.

Abstract: On-Policy Context Distillation (OPCD) has recently emerged as a powerful technique for transferring context to student models and for self-improvement. In OPCD, the teacher is conditioned on privileged information, and the goal is to minimize the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the privileged teacher and the student, evaluated on student-generated tokens. Many existing studies show that using instance-specific gold answers or gold demonstrations as the default privilege can hurt training performance, especially out-of-distribution (OOD). In this work, we instead design general instructions that target common student mistakes observed on the training samples, and show that such simple instructions can outperform gold as the OPCD privilege. In autoformalization tasks, using a matched formatting instruction as the privilege could outperform gold in OOD accuracy by a large margin. In 7 out of 8 experiments using ProverQA, ProofWriter, and ProntoQA as datasets, and Qwen3-Thinking and Olmo3-Thinking families as models, matched instruction privileges outperform gold in OOD by 4 to 17 points, while remaining on par with gold in-domain. Each instruction is only a few sentences (and thus contains much less information compared to all instance-specific gold) and is applied uniformly to every training sample. These results indicate that a general instruction, which applies equally to source and target domain examples, can be substantially more transferable than instance-specific gold in OPCD while maintaining in-domain performance.

</details>


### [158] [Witness: Discovery, Deciphering, and Epiphany in Interactive Puzzle Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32208)
*Guanghan Ning,Ping Liu,Linyi Li,Huangjie Zheng,Arjun Neervannan,Huu Nguyen,Michael Sklar,Deniz Zorlu,Nicolai Ouporov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces WITNESS, a grid-based rule-discovery benchmark to test how well language-model-based agents learn hidden rules by interaction, showing that even frontier models struggle with rule acquisition and that reinforcement learning offers modest but transferable gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated science requires agents that can infer the governing rules of unfamiliar environments through active experimentation. Existing evaluations of language models focus mostly on static benchmarks or explicit reasoning, not on interactive discovery of hidden rules. The authors aim to systematically measure where current models fail in rule discovery, how sensitive they are to interfaces and agent setups, and whether reinforcement learning can improve generalization to new rules and real-world-like tasks.

Method: The authors design WITNESS, a 2D grid-based puzzle environment with precise ASCII observations and controllable hidden rules. They build an agentic pipeline to automatically generate games, split into WitnessGym for RL training and WitnessBench for evaluation, with a public validation set and a private test set. The validation set is structured to separately probe generalization to new compositions of seen rule primitives and to entirely unseen primitives. Under a shared evaluation harness, they test 18 frontier proprietary and open-weight language models in interactive play. They then provide some models with explicit ground-truth rules to isolate rule-acquisition versus rule-execution difficulty, and train an open-weight 27B model with RL on WitnessGym to measure performance gains on both the benchmark and four external discovery tasks.

Result: Across 18 models, the best performance on the private test set is only 24% of level slots solved, and performance is highly sensitive to observation format and agent configuration. When given explicit rules, Opus-5’s validation RHAE-L5 jumps from 59.9 to 97.8, indicating that its main weakness lies in inferring the rules rather than executing them. In contrast, a 27B open-weight model improves by just 2.1 RHAE-L5 points with rules provided, revealing substantial deficits even in rule-following. RL training on WitnessGym improves the 27B model’s private test RHAE-L5 from 2.1 to 5.4 and produces an average gain of 4.1 points on four external rule-discovery benchmarks, demonstrating some transfer of learned capabilities.

Conclusion: The study concludes that rule acquisition from interaction is a central bottleneck for advanced language models such as Opus-5, while smaller open-weight models are additionally hampered by difficulties in executing rules even when they are known. The WITNESS environment and WitnessBench benchmark expose these weaknesses under controlled conditions, and RL on hidden-rule puzzles can partially mitigate them and transfer to other rule-discovery tasks. Overall, the work frames interactive rule learning as a key challenge for building automated scientific agents and provides a standardized suite for future research in this area.

Abstract: Automated science needs agents that can work out the rules of an unfamiliar environment by interacting with it. Interactive rule-discovery puzzles offer a controlled setting for studying this ability: an agent infers hidden rules through experimentation and uses what it has inferred to reach a stated goal. We ask what limits current language models on these puzzles and whether reinforcement learning (RL) improves performance on rules held out from training. To study both, we introduce WITNESS, a 2D grid-based puzzle environment with ground-truth ASCII observations and controlled access to rules. An agentic pipeline generates games for WitnessGym, the RL training suite, and WitnessBench, comprising public validation and private test games. The validation set separately tests new compositions of trained rule primitives and primitives absent from training. Under a shared harness, the best of 18 frontier proprietary and open-weight models solves only 24\% of private test level slots, with scores sensitive to the observation interface and agent configuration. Providing ground-truth rules raises Opus-5's validation RHAE-L5 (relative human action efficiency over the first five levels) from 59.9 to 97.8, whereas a 27B open-weight model gains only 2.1 points and remains limited even with the rules provided. RL on WitnessGym raises the 27B model's private test RHAE-L5 from 2.1 to 5.4 and yields a mean gain of 4.1 points on four external discovery benchmarks. Together, these results point to rule acquisition as a major difficulty for frontier models like Opus-5 while smaller models further struggle on rule-based execution, and indicate that RL on hidden-rule puzzles transfers to broader rules and real-world tasks beyond training. Benchmark is available at: https://witnessbench.ai

</details>


### [159] [Fracast-0: Fractal Weight Sharing for a Time Series Foundation Model with Only 85K Parameters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32209)
*Tianxiang Zhan,Huanyao Zhang,Yuanpeng He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Fracast-0 is a tiny (85k-parameter) probabilistic time-series foundation model that reuses the same operator across temporal scales to achieve strong multi-domain forecasting performance with far fewer parameters than prior models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Time series foundation models need to handle many domains, provide probabilistic forecasts, and capture multiple temporal scales (e.g., daily, weekly, yearly patterns). Existing models often allocate separate representations or modules to each scale, causing parameter counts to grow, which is problematic for deployment on resource-constrained devices and for efficient pretraining across diverse datasets. The authors aim to design a model that maintains forecasting quality and multi-domain generality while drastically reducing parameter count by sharing computation across temporal scales.

Method: The authors propose Fracast-0, a compact probabilistic forecasting foundation model that leverages temporal self-similarity to reuse the same neural operator across different temporal scales. A parameter-free detector identifies significant seasonal structure in the series. The encoder applies a single shared local block repeatedly along a geometrically dilated ladder of time scales, conditioned on the current scale, to capture multi-scale patterns without adding per-scale parameters. The decoder fuses context representations with an explicitly modeled seasonal future state and then reuses a second shared block along another dilation ladder, before generating probabilistic forecasts as nine output quantiles. The model is pretrained on six heterogeneous time series corpora to achieve multi-domain generalization within just 85,001 parameters.

Result: On the GIFT-Eval benchmark with 97 different evaluation configurations and no per-dataset fine-tuning, Fracast-0 is the smallest among 28 evaluated checkpoints yet remains on the Pareto frontier of the parameter-vs-accuracy trade-off. It attains a Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE) of 0.808 and a Weighted Quantile Loss (WQL) of 0.564. Compared with TinyCast, Fracast-0 uses 42.0% fewer parameters, while TinyCast’s MASE and WQL are only modestly better by 4.2% and 3.3%, respectively, demonstrating competitive accuracy despite substantial compression.

Conclusion: Cross-scale weight reuse via shared operators along dilated temporal ladders is an effective strategy for compressing time series foundation models while retaining strong multi-domain probabilistic forecasting performance. Fracast-0 shows that a model with only ~85k parameters can remain competitive on standardized benchmarks like GIFT-Eval without per-dataset fine-tuning, suggesting that future time series foundation models can be made much smaller and more deployment-friendly by exploiting temporal self-similarity and parameter-efficient multi-scale design.

Abstract: Time series foundation models must preserve multi-domain breadth, probabilistic output, and multiple temporal scales, but parameter count grows when each scale receives a separate representation. We introduce Fracast-0, a probabilistic forecasting foundation model that exploits temporal self-similarity to reuse one operator across scales. A parameter-free detector extracts significant seasonal structure. The encoder applies a shared local block along a geometric dilation ladder with scale conditioning, while the decoder combines context-gathered states with an explicit seasonal future state and reuses a second block along another ladder before emitting nine quantiles. Pretraining across six corpora preserves multi-domain breadth within 85,001 parameters. On 97 GIFT-Eval configurations without per-dataset fine-tuning, Fracast-0 is the smallest of 28 evaluated checkpoints and remains non-dominated in the aggregate parameter-accuracy plane with MASE 0.808 and WQL 0.564. It uses 42.0% fewer parameters than TinyCast, whose MASE and WQL are 4.2% and 3.3% lower. These results support cross-scale weight reuse as a practical route to further time series foundation model compression.

</details>


### [160] [A bilingual AI audiologist built through rubric-guided playbook induction outperforms human audiologists in a blinded evaluation of simulated cases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32220)
*Linkai Li,Changgeng Mo,Hanlin Yu,Congxi Lu,Shangqiguo Wang,Matthew B Fitzgerald,Shan X Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build and test a bilingual AI audiologist that uses a structured consultation playbook plus audiogram interpretation and retrieval to match and exceed human audiologists on simulated cases, without fine-tuning the base language model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world audiology consultation involves complex, structured tasks (history-taking, audiogram interpretation, patient communication), but curated real clinical dialogue data are scarce, especially across languages. There is a need for specialist medical consultation agents that work well in low-data settings and can handle technical test results and patient interaction without expensive model fine-tuning.

Method: They combine a general-purpose large language model with three main components: (1) rubric-guided playbook induction—using a 21-item consultation rubric and an AI patient simulator to derive a 19-rule consultation policy from 73 bilingual training cases; (2) multimodal audiogram interpretation—allowing the model to understand audiometric plots; and (3) retrieval-augmented grounding—supplying relevant reference information at inference. They then evaluate the resulting “AI audiologist” on 58 independent simulated consultation cases (30 Chinese, 28 English), using a pre-specified, source-blinded comparison against 17 practising audiologists, scoring performance on a 5-point composite and per-rubric items.

Result: Across 58 simulated cases, the AI audiologist scored higher than all human audiologists on every case (58/58), with a mean paired score difference of +1.35 on a 5-point composite scale, a very large effect size (Cohen’s d = 1.84), and an extremely small p-value (P = 4.5 × 10^-20). It outperformed humans on 20 of 21 rubric dimensions and in both English and Chinese consultations. Ablation experiments showed that the rubric-induced playbook contributed the most to the performance gains.

Conclusion: A structured playbook layered on top of a general-purpose large language model, plus audiogram interpretation and retrieval grounding, can produce a bilingual specialist consultation agent that substantially outperforms human audiologists on simulated cases, even in a low-data regime and without fine-tuning the underlying LLM. This suggests that playbook-style policy induction is a practical pathway for building specialist medical consultation systems in other data-scarce domains.

Abstract: Audiology consultation requires structured history-taking, audiometric interpretation and patient-centred communication, yet real-world case material is scarce. We present a bilingual AI audiologist pairing a general-purpose large language model with rubric-guided playbook induction, multimodal audiogram interpretation and retrieval-augmented grounding, without fine-tuning the language-model backbone. Using a 21-item rubric and an AI patient simulator, we induced a 19-rule consultation policy from 73 training cases (43 English, 30 Chinese) and evaluated the system on 58 independent simulated cases (30 Chinese, 28 English) in a pre-specified, source-blinded comparison with 17 practising audiologists. The AI audiologist outperformed human audiologists on every case (58/58; mean paired $Δ$ = +1.35 on a 5-point composite, Cohen's d = 1.84, $P = 4.5 \times 10^{-20}$), on 20 of 21 rubric items and in both languages. Component ablation identified the playbook as the largest contributor, offering a practical route to specialist consultation agents in low-data medical domains.

</details>


### [161] [RAO-Nav: Probing Omni-Language Models for Zero-shot Semantic Audio-Visual Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32224)
*Qilang Ye,Meng Liu,Yu Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes RAO-Nav, a zero-shot Semantic Audio-Visual Navigation pipeline that leverages Omni-Language Models (OLMs) and a Latent Navigation Reasoning (LNR) module to outperform specialized trained models on SAVN benchmarks, without using any task-specific training data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Specialized multimodal navigation models, even state-of-the-art ones, still struggle to achieve robust, generalist semantic audio-visual navigation and require extensive task-specific training. With the emergence of powerful Omni-Language Models that inherently encode rich audio-visual and world knowledge, the authors are motivated to investigate whether these OLMs can be directly used as embodied agents for zero-shot navigation, thereby reducing or eliminating the need for training while improving generalization and reasoning capabilities.

Method: The authors introduce RAO-Nav (Reasoning All-in-One OLM), a deployment pipeline that re-purposes an Omni-Language Model as an embodied navigation controller. The OLM is used to jointly process audio-visual observations and language instructions, enabling the agent to "hear," "see," "reason," and "act" in an environment via its generative outputs. To better exploit the OLM’s internal reasoning, they design a test-time Latent Navigation Reasoning (LNR) module, which operates in the model’s decoding space. LNR guides the generative process to focus on target-relevant observations and to produce more effective navigation decisions, effectively acting as a lightweight inference-time reasoning scaffold without any extra training data.

Result: Comprehensive experiments on public Semantic Audio-Visual Navigation benchmarks demonstrate that RAO-Nav, used in a zero-shot manner (i.e., without any task-specific training), surpasses existing state-of-the-art baselines that are explicitly trained for these tasks. The framework exhibits stronger generalist navigation behavior and better exploitation of multimodal cues than prior specialized approaches.

Conclusion: The study concludes that Omni-Language Models, when appropriately deployed through the RAO-Nav pipeline and enhanced with the Latent Navigation Reasoning module, can serve as effective zero-shot embodied navigation agents for audio-visual environments. This challenges the prevailing assumption that strong semantic navigation requires extensive task-specific training. Additionally, the newly proposed Global Navigation Instruction setting highlights that OLMs have promising potential as general-purpose controllers for complex, instruction-driven navigation tasks.

Abstract: We explore whether Omni-Language Models (OLMs) can be directly applied to zero-shot Semantic Audio-Visual Navigation (SAVN). Recent work demonstrates that even state-of-the-art specialized models still struggle to achieve generalist multimodal navigation, despite extensive task-specific training. In this paper, we introduce RAO-Nav, short for Reasoning All-in-One OLM, a deployment pipeline for zero-shot SAVN. By leveraging the rich implicit audio-visual knowledge encoded in OLMs, the embodied agent is enabled to ``hear'', ``see'', ``reason'', and ``act'' in the environment. To further elicit the built-in thinking ability of OLMs, we propose a test-time Latent Navigation Reasoning (LNR) module that can be seamlessly integrated into the decoding space. LNR encourages the model to retrieve more target-relevant observations and make effective navigation decisions. Through comprehensive experiments, we show that our framework surpasses existing state-of-the-art baselines on public SAVN benchmarks without using any training data. Moreover, we introduce a new \emph{Global Navigation Instruction} setting to further evaluate the ability of OLMs to serve as embodied navigation agents. Code: https://github.com/rikeilong/OmniAV\_Nav.

</details>


### [162] [Certifying Interventional Agreement Among Observationally Equivalent Causal Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32247)
*Sourena Khanzadeh,Daniel Platnick,Marjan Alirezaie,Hossein Rahnama*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Interventional Separation Selection (ISS), a procedure that uses targeted interventions to distinguish between observationally equivalent causal models and certify their agreement with the true system on all admissible interventions within a cost bound.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Observational data alone cannot distinguish between causal models that make identical predictions on naturally occurring data but differ under interventions, especially in complex systems such as neural networks. This limitation prevents us from certifying what a system will do under novel interventions or edits, even with unlimited observational data. The authors want a principled way to audit and certify the causal behavior (causal abstraction) of learned models using a limited budget of interventions.

Method: The authors propose Interventional Separation Selection (ISS), an iterative procedure over a candidate set (version space) of causal models. At each step, ISS: (1) finds an admissible intervention, within a specified cost bound, on which at least two surviving candidate models disagree; (2) queries the true system under this intervention; (3) eliminates all candidate models inconsistent with the observed outcome; and (4) repeats until there is no admissible intervention that can separate any remaining candidates. Crucially, the stopping condition depends only on the surviving models, not on the unknown true system. For continuous variables, the candidate set is infinite; the authors formulate the separation and stopping conditions as mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs) to decide exactly whether any admissible separating intervention exists, up to a numerical tolerance. They then apply ISS to a colored MNIST causal abstraction task, where ink hue spuriously tracks digit size, using candidate causal abstractions of trained convolutional networks.

Result: On a three-digit colored MNIST task where ink hue correlates with digit size, standard convolutional networks achieve zero held-out error but disagree with shape-based labels on 26% of single-digit edits, performing no better than hue-based labels, revealing strong reliance on spurious cues. Applying ISS to these networks, the authors are able to certify each network’s causal abstraction using on average 13.6 interventions per image, where each certificate is guaranteed (under the assumption that the true abstraction is among the candidates) to agree with the network’s behavior on all admissible interventions. They also show a failure mode: when a network bypasses a unit that all candidate abstractions assume is used, ISS can return certificates that are in fact void for interventions on that unit. Empirically, they find that 20 random validation interventions can falsify 69% of such silently invalid certificates.

Conclusion: ISS provides a way to move beyond purely observational evaluation of models by using carefully chosen interventions to both shrink the version space of candidate causal models and certify that all surviving models agree with the true system on a bounded set of possible interventions. This yields guarantees that are impossible with observational data alone. The method scales to continuous settings via MILP formulations and is practically useful for auditing neural network causal abstractions, though it can produce silently void certificates when modeling assumptions about which components are used by the system are violated. Additional validation interventions can help detect these invalid certificates.

Abstract: Observationally equivalent causal models can still disagree about what happens under intervention, because interventions create inputs that never occur in observational data. We introduce Interventional Separation Selection (ISS), which repeatedly queries the true system with an admissible intervention on which the surviving candidate models disagree, discards the candidates the outcome contradicts, and stops once no intervention within a cost bound separates the survivors. If the true system is among the candidates, this stopping condition certifies that every survivor agrees with it on every admissible intervention within the bound, a guarantee that no observational learner can give, however much data it sees. The stopping condition depends only on the survivors, so it can be checked without knowing the truth. For continuous variables the candidates form an infinite version space, and mixed-integer linear programs decide the stopping condition exactly over all of it, with agreement holding up to a tolerance. On a three-digit colored MNIST causal abstraction task in which ink hue tracks digit size, plain convolutional networks trained on examples reach zero held-out error, yet disagree with shape-based labels on 26% of single-digit edits, as often as hue-based labels do. Auditing the causal abstractions of networks observed only on such images, ISS certifies what each network perceives with 13.6 interventions per image on average, and each certificate, checked against every admissible intervention, holds whenever the network's true abstraction is among the candidates. When a network bypasses a unit that every candidate abstraction relies on, certificates covering interventions on that unit can be silently void, and twenty random validation interventions refute 69% of them.

</details>


### [163] [Why Directly Learning Periodic Trajectories Can Fail](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32254)
*Kaixin Zheng,Anita Layton*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies why standard ways of collecting and representing simulation data make operator learning of periodic solutions hard, and proposes a phase-aligned, period-normalized representation that is easier to learn and generalizes better.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In operator learning for dynamical systems with periodic solutions, practitioners must choose how long to simulate and how to represent trajectories as learning targets. A common approach is to simulate until transients decay and then take a time window that covers at least one full period for all trajectories. However, even when the underlying periodic orbits depend smoothly on parameters, learned operators often generalize poorly, both within and beyond the training distribution. The paper aims to understand the mechanism behind these failures and to design a representation that leads to more regular targets and better generalization.

Method: The authors analyze operator learning of periodic trajectories under standard data collection choices: (1) unaligned trajectories in a fixed time window after transients and (2) phase-aligned trajectories still represented over a fixed physical-time window. They show theoretically that small frequency differences cause phases to diverge over time, making the target mapping highly oscillatory in parameter space and inducing an irreducible error floor (population MSE), plus a per-sample lower bound in the fixed-window case. Motivated by this analysis, they introduce a decoupled representation: learn a phase-aligned, normalized waveform and its period separately. They prove that, under common ODE assumptions, these decoupled targets vary smoothly with parameters, and then test the approach empirically on ODE systems and a PDE case study.

Result: Theoretical results demonstrate that both unaligned trajectories and phase-aligned trajectories represented in a fixed physical-time window lead to highly non-smooth target maps due to accumulated phase differences, which imposes lower bounds on achievable prediction error for typical operator learners. In contrast, the proposed representation—separately learning an aligned, normalized waveform and its period—avoids these degeneracies: the associated target maps are shown to be regular under mild ODE conditions. Experiments on several ODE examples and a PDE benchmark confirm that this representation yields substantially improved in-distribution generalization and avoids large errors on trajectories with periods outside the training range.

Conclusion: Standard practices for recording and representing periodic trajectory data in operator learning create targets that are intrinsically hard to approximate, due to phase accumulation and resulting rapid variation with respect to parameters. This leads to poor generalization and irreducible error floors, even when the true periodic orbits depend smoothly on parameters. By instead decoupling the learning problem into an aligned, normalized waveform and its period, one obtains smoother target mappings that standard operator learning models can approximate more accurately. The proposed representation is both theoretically justified and empirically effective across ODE and PDE settings, suggesting it as a better default for learning periodic solutions.

Abstract: Operator learning of periodic solutions requires deciding how simulation data should be recorded and represented. A natural choice is to integrate long enough for transients to decay and record a window wide enough to contain at least one full period of all trajectories. We find that these conservative choices can make the resulting trajectories difficult to learn, even when the underlying periodic orbits vary regularly with system parameters. Unaligned trajectories generalize poorly even within the training distribution. Phase alignment substantially improves in-distribution generalization, but models trained on a fixed physical-time window still have large errors on trajectories with periods outside the training range. We explain both failures through a common mechanism: frequency differences accumulate over time, so the target phase varies rapidly with the parameters. Predictors that cannot track this variation incur a population MSE floor in both settings; for fixed window prediction, we also derive a per-sample lower bound. We then study one of the simplest representations that escape these floors: learning an aligned, normalized waveform and its period separately. We establish regularity of the decoupled targets under ODE assumptions and show experimentally that this approach avoids both failures in ODE systems and a PDE case study.

</details>


### [164] [Clarify the User or Verify the World? Uncertainty Routing for Proactive Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32255)
*Zhaofeng Li,Xuan Zhang,Xiaokui Xiao,Yang Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces PROUR, a framework for large language model (LLM) agents that proactively decide whether to act, clarify with the user, or verify information in the environment, improving task success and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing tool-using LLM agents struggle to decide not just if they need more information, but from where it should come: the user (clarification) or the environment/tools (verification). Prior proactive methods typically specialize in only one of these behaviors and lack an explicit mechanism to select the correct information source based on the type of uncertainty. This limitation leads to inefficient or suboptimal interactions, especially in domains like retail and airline booking where both user goals and world state can be uncertain. The paper is motivated by the need for a principled way to route uncertainty to the right information source to improve success rates and reduce interaction steps.

Method: The authors formulate proactive decision making as an uncertainty routing problem among three modes: ACT (proceed with an action), CLARIFY (ask the user), and VERIFY (query the environment/tools). Their framework, PROUR, decomposes the agent’s action uncertainty into two components: (1) disagreement across plausible user-goal interpretations, interpreted as user-side ambiguity that should trigger CLARIFY; and (2) remaining entropy within each fixed interpretation, interpreted as missing world-side evidence that should trigger VERIFY. They then train a query generator conditioned on the selected mode, using an information-gain-based reward. Under CLARIFY, the reward encourages queries that best identify the user’s true goal; under VERIFY, it encourages queries that best identify the optimal next action given the environment. The overall policy thus jointly decides when to act, clarify, or verify and how to formulate targeted queries in each mode.

Result: On τ-bench in retail and airline domains, PROUR attains a 28.17% average success rate, surpassing the strongest existing method by 4.57 percentage points while using 2.17 fewer interaction steps on average. The learned routing and query policy also generalizes without retraining to stronger downstream task agents and to transactional domains in τ^3-bench, indicating robustness and transferability of the uncertainty-routing approach.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that explicitly modeling and routing uncertainty between user-related ambiguity and environment-related missing evidence leads to more effective proactive LLM agents. By decomposing uncertainty and aligning query generation with the appropriate information source, PROUR improves both task success and interaction efficiency. Its ability to generalize to new agents and related benchmarks further suggests that source-aligned uncertainty resolution is a promising direction for building scalable, proactive tool-using LLM systems.

Abstract: Tool-using LLM agents must decide not only whether additional information is needed, but also which source can resolve the uncertainty. Existing proactive approaches often specialize in either user clarification or environment verification, without explicitly determining the appropriate information source for each decision. We formulate this problem as uncertainty routing among ACT, CLARIFY, and VERIFY, and propose PROUR, a proactive uncertainty routing framework. PROUR decomposes action uncertainty into disagreement across plausible user-goal interpretations, which signals user-side ambiguity, and the entropy remaining within each interpretation, which signals missing world-side evidence. To acquire information from the routed source, a query generator is trained with a mode-conditioned information-gain reward, targeting user-goal identification under CLARIFY and next-action identification under VERIFY. On $τ$-bench, PROUR achieves 28.17% average success rate across retail and airline, outperforming the strongest prior method by 4.57% while using 2.17 fewer interaction steps. The learned policy further generalizes to stronger task agents and transactional domains of $τ^3$-bench without retraining, demonstrating the benefit of source-aligned uncertainty resolution for proactive agents.

</details>


### [165] [LAM: Efficient Lossy Agent Memory Framework With A Retrieval-Score Error Bound](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32256)
*Baixi Sun,Le Chen,Anjir Ahmed Chowdhury,Xiaolong Ma,Chih-Hsuan Yang,Mingze Xia,Syed Zawad,Sheng Di,Rajkumar Kettimuthu,Huihuo Zheng,Rajeev Thakur,Venkatram Vishwanath,Feng Yan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces LAM, a lossy memory system for LLM-based agents that safely compacts growing histories to reduce tokens and latency while tightly bounding the impact on retrieval quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents accumulate long interaction histories as they read inputs, reason, and call tools. This growing memory increases inference cost, can exceed the model’s context window, and makes systems slower and more expensive. Existing LLM-based summarization techniques for trimming history are slow, add latency, and provide no explicit guarantees or bounds on how much important information is lost or how retrieval quality is affected. The authors are motivated to design a memory management method that is efficient, has predictable cost, and comes with explicit bounds on how much it perturbs retrieval scores, while also integrating well with system scheduling to minimize end-to-end latency.

Method: They propose LAM (Lossy Agent Memory), which has three key components: (1) A deterministic deduplication rule for compacting memory that comes with a substitution bound on retrieval scores. This bound quantifies the maximum perturbation in similarity/retrieval scores caused by replacing detailed observations with compacted representations, but it does not guarantee that the ranking of retrieved items is unchanged. (2) A memory manager that always preserves the cached prefix of the interaction history and overlaps the compaction process with ongoing inference, so that compaction work is done in parallel with the model’s main computation to reduce visible latency. (3) A performance model that, given a fixed deletion/compaction policy, estimates the cost and speedups of compaction prior to deployment, enabling system designers to understand tradeoffs and expected end-to-end performance benefits, specifically comparing removing records before prefill versus deleting tokens after prefill.
