To align this algorithmic design with system efficiency, we further introduce the Replica Expert Mechanism (REM), which improves load balancing through a two-tiered strategy: adjusting replica expert placement at the global-batch level and performing real-time token dispatching at the micro-batch level. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our method outperforms the evaluated routing algorithms on downstream tasks for both 4.8BA0.5B and 30BA3B MoE models, while maintaining comparable training efficiency.

</details>


### [184] [Opening LLM Judges: Recovering Preference Signals Beyond the Final Verdict](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32407)
*Sourabrata Mukherjee,Sunayana Sitaram*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether large language model (LLM) evaluators ("judges") internally encode correct evaluation information even when their final verdicts are biased or wrong, showing a large gap between what is present in internal activations and what is expressed in outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM judges are increasingly used to automatically evaluate model outputs, but their decisions are often systematically biased by surface features like answer length or position, sometimes preferring worse answers. It is unclear whether such errors stem from a lack of underlying knowledge or from failures to express that knowledge in their outputs. Understanding this distinction matters for building more reliable evaluation systems and for knowing when and how to trust LLM-based judgments.

Method: The authors study 64 open-weight evaluator models on 14 datasets, focusing on LLMBar, where superficial answer quality cues are inverted. They compare raw judge verdicts to signals extracted from internal activations using small linear probes without updating model weights. They also perform causal interventions on 41 judges by editing activations mid-run to see if verdicts change, and they measure how well surface features alone (e.g., length, position) predict human labels. They analyze the relation between surface-feature predictiveness and the performance gain from probing internals, and they test both pairwise evaluation and rubric-based single-answer scoring tasks.

Result: On LLMBar, raw judge verdicts match human labels only 0.456 of the time, whereas a probe on the same activations achieves 0.846 accuracy, or 0.686 after residualizing out surface features (vs. 0.507 with shuffled labels). Similar gaps appear across eight benchmarks and multiple model families. A pre-computable score of how well surface features predict the label strongly correlates with the eventual gain from probing (Spearman ρ = 0.90). On single-answer rubric tasks without exploitable surface cues, probing internals provides no benefit. Activation-editing interventions show that modifying mid-network activations can flip verdicts and reveal specific pathways carrying length and position biases. Using the recovered internal signal allows judges to better detect when they are likely wrong and to produce higher-quality labels for preference learning under the same label budget.

Conclusion: LLM judges often internally represent information sufficient for correct evaluation even when their final outputs are biased or incorrect, especially on tasks where surface features are misleading. Bias arises not from an absence of evaluative knowledge but from how that knowledge is read out. A simple diagnostic based on surface-feature predictiveness can identify when probing internals is likely to help, enabling more reliable automatic evaluation and improved training signals for preference learning. Wrong verdicts, therefore, do not necessarily indicate missing knowledge, and internal signals can sometimes be systematically recovered and exploited.

Abstract: LLM judges are widely used to evaluate model outputs, but their verdicts can be unreliable: a judge may favor the worse answer for its position, length, or other surface features. When a judge is wrong, is the information needed to judge correctly absent from the model, or present in its internal representations but not reflected in the output? We study this across 64 open-weight evaluators and 14 datasets, including causal interventions on 41 judges (editing activations mid-run to see whether the verdict changes). On LLMBar, built so the superficially better answer is the worse one, the verdicts of 50 judges agree with human labels only 0.456 of the time, even after averaging both answer orders. Yet a small probe on the same judges' activations, with no weight updates, reaches 0.846, and 0.686 once surface features such as length and position are residualized out (0.507 with shuffled labels). The gap holds across eight benchmarks and model families, but is not universal: a score of how well surface features alone predict the human label, computed before any probe is trained, predicts the size of the gain (Spearman rho = 0.90). On rubric tasks that score one answer at a time, leaving no surface cue to exploit, reading the internals gives no advantage. The interventions also show that editing activations mid-network already changes the verdict, before it can be read off directly, and locate the pathways carrying position and length bias. At the same label budget, the recovered signal lets a judge flag cases where it is likely wrong and yields better labels for preference learning. A wrong verdict, then, does not mean the judge lacks the information, and a simple diagnostic shows when it is worth recovering.

</details>


### [185] [Carnator: Fast Text-to-Video Generation with Generation-Native Compatibility-Guided Cross-Request Reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32420)
*Xingkun Yin,Xuebin Tang,Mingkun Xu,Hongyang Du*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Carnator, a framework to speed up video diffusion transformers by safely reusing computation across different user requests using internal model signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos but require many iterative denoising steps, leading to high inference latency that limits interactivity and scalability. Existing acceleration methods mainly optimize single-request computation, missing opportunities to reuse work across different but related requests. Recent cross-request reuse methods try to share computation based on semantic similarity between prompts, but semantic similarity does not reliably indicate whether internal generation states are compatible, causing either quality loss (over-aggressive reuse) or lost speedups (over-conservative reuse).

Method: Carnator is a cross-request acceleration framework that bases reuse decisions on the model’s internal diffusion states rather than external semantic similarity. It performs a lightweight early probe during the generation process to build an Early Signature capturing generation-native evidence of compatibility. Using this signature, Carnator makes risk-aware decisions about whether cached computation from previous requests can be safely reused. It also uses the same evidence to determine how much and which parts of the computation to share, by localizing target-specific regions and enabling joint reuse of historical latent trajectories and sparse attention connectivity patterns.

Result: Evaluated on three different text-to-video diffusion backbones, Carnator achieves higher effective cache-hit rates and better end-to-end acceleration than other cross-request reuse baselines, even though it accepts cache reuse more selectively. It reaches up to a 2.17× speedup in generation time while preserving competitive video quality compared to the original full-compute baselines.

Conclusion: Generation-native compatibility signals derived from internal diffusion states enable more accurate and risk-aware cross-request reuse decisions than coarse semantic similarity. By probing early internal states to form an Early Signature, Carnator can selectively and jointly reuse latent trajectories and attention structures, yielding substantial speedups (up to 2.17×) without degrading video quality. This demonstrates that internal-state-driven cross-request acceleration is an effective strategy for scalable, interactive video diffusion serving.

Abstract: Video diffusion transformers produce high-quality videos, yet iterative denoising incurs substantial inference latency, limiting interactive and large-scale serving. Most existing acceleration methods focus on individual requests, thereby restricting efficiency gains to redundancy within a single generation trajectory. Recent cross-request reuse offers an additional source of savings, but existing approaches often infer reusability from coarse semantic similarity. This conflates semantic relatedness with generation-level computational compatibility, so aggressive reuse may accept incompatible historical computation while conservative reuse leaves substantial acceleration unrealized. We present \emph{Carnator}, a cross-request acceleration framework that addresses this challenge by extracting and using generation-native compatibility evidence directly from the model's evolving internal states. Specifically, \emph{Carnator} performs a lightweight early probe to construct an Early Signature from internal diffusion states, assessing reuse validity through risk-aware compatibility decisions. The same evidence characterizes reuse scope by localizing target-specific computation and guiding joint reuse of historical latent trajectories and sparse attention connectivity. Across three text-to-video backbones, Carnator consistently achieves higher cache-hit end-to-end acceleration than the evaluated cross-request baselines despite more selective cache acceptance, reaching up to 2.17$\times$ speedup while maintaining competitive generation quality.

</details>


### [186] [MergeHEIR: Mitigating Multimodal Hallucinations as the Tax of Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32422)
*Jinyu Li,Hao Fang,Zhiming Zhang,Jiawei Kong,Bin Chen,Shu-Tao Xia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MergeHEIR is a post-merge adaptation framework that reduces hallucinations introduced by model merging while preserving task expertise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model merging allows combining several task-specialized models into a single one, but this consolidation comes with a “merging tax”: the merged model hallucinates more than the original experts, and naively applying hallucination-mitigation after merging can damage the inherited task capabilities. There is a need for a principled way to mitigate hallucinations in merged models without sacrificing the benefits of merging.

Method: After merging expert models, MergeHEIR collects task-specific activations on small calibration sets, performs SVD layer-wise to construct null-space projectors representing directions crucial for inherited expertise, and during post-merge adaptation periodically projects parameter updates onto these null spaces. This constrains learning to directions that minimally distort expert capabilities. The framework includes theoretical analysis of distortion, dimensionality, and the trade-off between adaptation and retention, including robustness to finite calibration data.

Result: Experiments on three multimodal LLM configurations and eight model-merging methods, covering 24 paired comparisons, show that MergeHEIR consistently lowers hallucination rates of merged checkpoints while largely maintaining the capabilities inherited from expert models, outperforming unconstrained post-merge adaptation in the hallucination–retention trade-off.

Conclusion: MergeHEIR provides a principled post-merge adaptation framework that addresses the hallucination “merging tax” in model merging. By constraining adaptation through null-space projection derived from expert-task activations, it reduces hallucinations and theoretically controls the adaptation–retention trade-off, yielding merged models that better preserve expert abilities while being more reliable.

Abstract: Model merging consolidates task-specialized experts into a single deployable model. However, we show that such capability consolidation incurs a merging tax of increased hallucination: across 8 model-merging methods, every merged checkpoint exhibits a higher hallucination rate than the average of its constituent experts. An intuitive approach is to adapt existing hallucination-mitigation methods to the post-merge model, yet this unconstrained adaptation disrupts inherited capabilities, creating a tension between hallucination mitigation and expertise retention. To tackle this challenge, we introduce MergeHEIR, a post-merge adaptation framework designed to reduce this merging tax while preserving expertise inherited from initial experts. Using small expert-task calibration sets, MergeHEIR constructs layer-wise null-space projectors via SVD from task-specific activations collected from the merged checkpoint, and periodically projects the accumulated post-merge displacement onto the resulting null spaces to preserve inherited expertise. Theoretically, we establish minimum-distortion and maximum-dimensionality guarantees, characterize the threshold-controlled adaptation-retention trade-off, and extend perturbation guarantees beyond finite calibration data. Across 24 paired comparisons spanning three MLLM configurations and 8 model-merging methods, MergeHEIR consistently mitigates hallucination while largely preserving inherited expertise, demonstrating a more favorable hallucination-retention trade-off.

</details>


### [187] [PluginRSI: Recursive Improvement of Agent Harnesses with Reusable Plugins](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32423)
*Yaorui Shi,Yuchun Miao,Yuxin Chen,Jiayuan Zhang,Yueqing Sun,Xierui Song,Xiang Wang,An Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces PluginRSI, a plugin-based framework for evolving and optimizing LLM harnesses, outperforming monolithic program search and transferring well across models and tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods optimize LLM agent harnesses by searching over entire programs, making it hard to isolate, reuse, or systematically improve individual mechanisms. This monolithic approach limits interpretability, transferability, and sample efficiency when adapting to new tasks or models. The authors aim to create a more modular, reusable, and scalable way to evolve agent harnesses so that improvements can accumulate over time and generalize better.

Method: They propose PluginRSI, which represents a harness as a composition of small, atomized plugins (modular mechanisms). The optimization process focuses on these plugins: (1) decompose the harness into plugins, (2) independently improve individual plugins and store them in a shared plugin library, and (3) periodically recombine plugins from this library to form new, complete harnesses. This evolution is iterated over multiple tasks and models, with the plugin library acting as a growing repository of reusable mechanisms. They evaluate this approach against existing harness optimization methods on software engineering, command-line interaction, and question-answering tasks, and also test transfer to different solver models and new tasks.

Result: PluginRSI outperforms prior harness optimization approaches across the evaluated domains (software engineering, CLI interaction, QA). Harnesses built from the evolved plugin library maintain their performance advantage when transferred to different underlying language models without additional tuning. Furthermore, as the plugin library grows, optimization on new tasks becomes both faster and more effective, achieving higher performance with fewer iterations from the same initial harness.

Conclusion: Decomposing LLM agent harnesses into reusable plugins and organizing optimization around these components enables more effective and scalable harness evolution than monolithic program search. The accumulated plugin library serves as a persistent memory of useful mechanisms, improving sample efficiency, facilitating transfer across models and tasks, and providing a strong foundation for continual improvement of language-model-based agents.

Abstract: The harness surrounding a language model is a central determinant of agent performance. Recent methods optimize harnesses by searching over complete programs, where individual mechanisms are difficult to isolate and reuse. We introduce PluginRSI, which represents a harness as a composition of atomized plugins and organizes harness evolution around these plugins. Individual plugins are improved independently and accumulated in a shared library, then recombined into new harnesses at each iteration. PluginRSI improves over existing harness optimization methods across software engineering, command-line interaction, and question-answering tasks. The resulting harnesses retain their advantage when transferred to other solver models without further optimization. The evolved plugin library accelerates subsequent optimization from the initial harness, which helps faster and higher convergence on unseen tasks. These results show that accumulating reusable mechanisms provides an effective basis for continued harness improvement.

</details>


### [188] [Authorization Closure Graph: Minimal Repair for LLM Agents with Evolving User Instructions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32428)
*Qingzhuo Wang,CaiYi Wang,Jinglu Meng,Ruiyang Qin,Kunyu Peng,Zhihua Wei,Wen Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Authorization-Closure-Graphs (ACG), a framework that models and updates user authorization for tool-using LLM agents so they can safely adapt to revised instructions without redundant re-authorization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tool-using LLM agents increasingly execute state-changing actions that must be authorized by users. When user instructions are revised, existing systems lack a principled way to determine which prior authorizations remain valid and which should be revoked or renewed, often leading to either unsafe reuse of stale permissions or overly conservative, repetitive authorization prompts. The paper aims to provide a structured mechanism for partial, fine-grained authorization updates in response to instruction changes.

Method: The authors propose an Authorization-Closure-Graph (ACG), which encodes authorizations, their dependencies, and their versions as a dynamic state graph. When instructions are revised, the ACG identifies graph regions affected by the change, selectively invalidates only the impacted authority, keeps unaffected portions intact, and then computes a minimal repair set—i.e., the minimal set of missing evidence or permissions needed to safely execute the updated plan. They implement this framework with LLM agents and evaluate it across multiple models on naturalistic tool-use tasks.

Result: Across two natural tasks and three advanced LLMs, using ACG leads to consistent improvements in both action safety rate (fewer unsafe or unauthorized actions) and task success rate (more tasks completed successfully) compared to baselines that do not use structured, incremental authorization updating.

Conclusion: Modeling authorization as a versioned, dependency-aware state via Authorization-Closure-Graphs enables LLM tool agents to adapt to changing user instructions in a principled, fine-grained manner. The approach selectively revokes and repairs only what is necessary, reducing stale permissions and redundant prompts, and empirically improves both safety and effectiveness of agent actions.

Abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents increasingly perform state-changing actions that require user authorization. Yet existing approaches do not provide a principled mechanism for selectively updating prior authorization when only part of an instruction changes. To this end, we propose an Authorization-Closure-Graph (ACG)-based framework that represents authorization and its dependencies as an evolving, versioned state. ACG selectively invalidates authority affected by a revision while preserving unaffected portions of the authorization state, and computes a minimal repair that identifies only the missing evidence or authority required for execution. This enables agents to adapt to revised instructions while avoiding stale authority and unnecessary authorization requests. We evaluate ACG across three advanced LLMs in two natural tasks, and ACG consistently improves action safety rate and task success rate. Code is available at https://github.com/weiliang822/ACG.

</details>


### [189] [PrismQuant: Optimal Null-Space Rotations for Grouped Quantizers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32429)
*Yanlong Chen,Yining Chen,Song Zhang,Amirhossein Habibian,Yawei Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PrismQuant introduces a rotation-based, quantizer-aware method that aligns activations with the structure of grouped INT4 quantizers, achieving state-of-the-art low-bit LLM performance and practical speed/memory gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing low-bit quantization methods often focus on reducing activation outliers but overlook whether activation energy is aligned with the quantizer’s representational subspace, especially for asymmetric grouped INT4. Misalignment leads to inefficient use of quantization levels, higher error, and degraded performance in large language models. The paper aims to systematically align activations with the quantizer to improve accuracy and efficiency under very low precision (e.g., W4A4KV4).

Method: The paper proposes PrismQuant, a quantizer-aware rotation framework. It learns orthogonal rotations that align the leading activation eigenspace with the constant group subspace inherent in asymmetric grouped INT4 quantization. This is formalized as a Ky Fan trace maximization problem, for which the authors derive a closed-form, provably optimal solution under their alignment objective. They implement these rotations using compact Householder transformations and the compact-WY representation, enabling gradient-free construction and efficient application both in offline (foldable) and runtime (online) settings. They also derive a predictive range law linking unaligned activation energy and group size to quantization-relevant variation, guiding design choices like group sizes. Experiments evaluate PrismQuant on multiple LLM families (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, including dense and MoE models) under W4A4KV4 settings.

Result: On Llama-3.2-3B, PrismQuant attains state-of-the-art performance among compared methods in both perplexity and accuracy under W4A4KV4. On Llama-3.1-70B, it achieves 3.85 perplexity and 72.46% average zero-shot accuracy, only 0.22 percentage points below full-precision performance. In a deployment study on Llama-3.1-8B, the optimized implementation yields 1.51× prefill and 1.22× CUDA Graph decode speedups over FP16 baselines, alongside 56.34% lower decode peak memory, with just 2.35% additional Graph decode latency compared to a Hadamard-based approach.

Conclusion: Aligning activation eigenspaces with the structural subspace of the quantizer is crucial for effective low-bit quantization and cannot be substituted by merely shrinking activation outliers. PrismQuant provides a theoretically grounded, closed-form rotation design that is efficient to implement and apply, enabling 4-bit weight/activation/key/value quantization with near–full-precision accuracy on large LLMs and demonstrable speed and memory benefits in deployment. This establishes alignment-aware rotations as a powerful tool for practical low-bit LLM quantization.

Abstract: Smaller activation outliers do not necessarily imply better low-bit quantization: their alignment with the quantizer matters. We introduce PrismQuant, a quantizer-aware rotation framework that aligns the leading activation eigenspace with the constant group subspace of asymmetric grouped INT4. The affine offsets represent the energy in this subspace without widening the range within the group. We formulate rotation design as a Ky Fan trace maximization and derive a closed-form solution that is provably optimal for this alignment objective. Compact Householder transformations and their compact-WY representation enable gradient-free construction and efficient application at both foldable and online sites. A predictive range law further connects unaligned activation energy and group size to quantization-relevant variation. Experiments on Llama, Qwen, and Mistral span dense models up to 70B parameters and a 30B mixture-of-experts model. Under W4A4KV4, PrismQuant sets the state of the art on Llama-3.2-3B among the compared methods in both perplexity and accuracy. On Llama-3.1-70B, it attains 3.85 perplexity and 72.46% average zero-shot accuracy, only 0.22 percentage points below full precision. In the deployment study on Llama-3.1-8B, our optimized implementation achieves 1.51x prefill and 1.22x CUDA Graph decode speedups over matched FP16 baselines, with 56.34% lower decode peak memory and only 2.35% additional Graph decode latency over Hadamard. Code is available at https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/PrismQuant.

</details>


### [190] [Multi-Agent System Search via Active Substructure-aware Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32430)
*Beicheng Xu,Bowen Fan,Weitong Qian,Lingching Tung,Bin Cui*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes ASPO, an RL framework that actively selects queries and assigns substructure-level rewards to automatically learn effective multi-agent LLM workflows, outperforming 12 baselines on 6 benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Designing multi-agent systems with LLMs currently requires manual specification of roles, prompts, and communication patterns, which is labor-intensive and requires expertise. Existing automatic methods use reinforcement learning but treat all queries equally and only provide rewards at the full-workflow level, ignoring that different queries have different learning value over time and that only certain parts of the workflow structure may be responsible for performance gains.

Method: Introduce Active Substructure-aware Policy Optimization (ASPO), a reinforcement learning framework for searching multi-agent LLM architectures at the query level. ASPO includes: (1) an Adaptive Query-Selection Mechanism (AQSM) that concentrates training on queries at the policy’s competence boundary—those solved inconsistently—to maximize learning signal; (2) a complementary discovery mechanism that expands the space of architectural variants for hard queries, separating issues of insufficient exploration from fundamental operator limitations; and (3) substructure-level reward assignment that computes quality improvements attributable to each action’s descendant subgraph, enabling policy gradient methods (like PPO) to directly reinforce beneficial architectural refinements and penalize redundant or harmful computations.

Result: Using ASPO to learn multi-agent LLM structures, the authors evaluate on six benchmarks covering math reasoning, QA, and code generation. ASPO achieves the top performance on every benchmark when compared to twelve state-of-the-art baselines, indicating superior effectiveness and generality of the learned MAS architectures.

Conclusion: Active, query-aware training and substructure-level credit assignment are crucial for efficiently learning high-quality multi-agent LLM workflows. By prioritizing queries near the current competence boundary and rewarding useful substructures rather than whole workflows, ASPO yields more effective and efficient MAS designs than existing approaches, with consistent state-of-the-art results across diverse benchmarks.

Abstract: LLMs enable multi-agent systems (MAS) to tackle complex tasks, but manually designing agent roles, prompts, and communication structures requires substantial expertise and effort. This motivates learning policies that construct query-specific MAS from execution reward. Existing approaches typically train these policies by repeatedly traversing a fixed set of training queries and assigning rewards at the workflow level. However, this overlooks differences in queries' evolving learning potential and obscures which substructures improve solution quality. In this paper, we propose Active Substructure-aware Policy Optimization (ASPO), a RL framework for query-level MAS search. ASPO introduces an Adaptive Query-Selection Mechanism (AQSM) that focuses training on queries at the policy's competence boundary: those it can solve but not yet reliably. A complementary discovery mechanism widens architectural exploration for hard queries, helping distinguish insufficient exploration from operator capability limits. Beyond query selection, ASPO introduces substructure-level rewards that measure output-quality gains within each action's descendant subgraph. These rewards guide proximal policy optimization to reinforce useful architectural refinements and discourage redundant or harmful computation. Together, these mechanisms prioritize learnable queries and provide fine-grained feedback for learning effective MASs. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, general question answering, and code generation, ASPO ranks first on every benchmark against twelve baselines.

</details>


### [191] [From Latents to Wires: Surgical Post-Editing on Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32434)
*Jiankai Jin,Xiangzheng Zhang,Zhao Liu,Wenzhuo Xu,Dongdong Yang,Deyue Zhang,Quanchen Zou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces L2W, a framework for surgically editing large language models to remove specific semantic behaviors (like identity claims or refusal policies) while preserving other capabilities, showing it can reliably locate and remove targeted behaviors and supporting post-editing as a complement to post-training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model owners may want to precisely remove or modify specific behaviors or properties (e.g., identity, embedded watermarks, refusals) in a trained LLM without retraining it, and to do so in a way that is targeted, reliable, and minimally disruptive. Existing approaches to interpretability or fine-tuning either lack this surgical precision or risk affecting broad capabilities. The authors therefore seek a method to locate and edit the exact model components responsible for a named semantic behavior and remove that behavior while preserving other functionality.

Method: The authors propose L2W (latents to wires), a two-stage framework for post-editing. First, they localize model components related to a named semantic target using Jacobian lens (J-lens) attribution, which scores components by how strongly they influence the target. Second, they perform a Counterexample-Guided Causal Cut (CGCC): they progressively close (disable) components whose activity contributes to the target, observe remaining occurrences of the target as counterexamples that reveal additional contributing components, and iteratively repeat this process until the target behavior disappears. Afterward, they selectively reopen some components to recover general capabilities, leaving only the unwanted target removed. This is applied to both LLMs and a text-to-image model.

Result: In a controlled test where a behavioral watermark is implanted in a model, L2W is able to both remove the watermark behavior and correctly localize to the region that had been modified. Across three model configurations, L2W successfully removes model-metadata self-claims (such as identity) in 9/9 runs and removes adult-content refusal behavior in 3/3 runs, with no residual expression of the targeted behaviors on held-out tests. On a text-to-image model, they successfully compose two edits: the first removes refusal to produce nudity, and the second removes the actual nude rendering exposed by the first edit, demonstrating that multiple post-edits can be combined.

Conclusion: The study concludes that L2W enables surgical post-editing of trained models: it can reliably locate and remove specified semantic targets from LLMs and other generative models while keeping other capabilities largely intact. This shows that post-editing can effectively complement post-training: post-training is used to install desired behaviors, and post-editing to selectively remove particular unwanted behaviors, offering model owners fine-grained control over model behavior after deployment.

Abstract: Given a large language model (LLM), can whoever holds the weights name a semantic target (e.g., the model's identity), locate the model components that produce it, and edit them so that the target no longer appears while other capability is preserved? We call such an edit on a trained model a post-edit. We present L2W (latents to wires), a framework that performs surgical post-edits for named semantic targets. For localization, L2W uses Jacobian lens (J-lens) attribution to score components against the semantic target. For surgical removal, because LLM mechanisms are redundant (i.e., a semantic target may have multiple components producing it), L2W runs Counterexample-Guided Causal Cut (CGCC) until the target no longer appears. CGCC first cumulatively closes model components, treating each surviving expression of the target as a counterexample that exposes the next components to close, and then reopens some of them to preserve capability. In a controlled experiment with an implanted behavioural watermark, L2W removes the watermark, and its localization lands on the model region the implant changed. Across three model configurations, L2W removes model-metadata (e.g., identity) self-claims in all nine runs, and adult-content refusal in all three, with no held-out target residual. L2W further composes two post-edits on a text-to-image model: one removes the refusal of requested nudity, and a second removes the nude rendering the first exposes. The results support post-editing as a complement to post-training: post-training installs preferred behaviours, and post-editing removes named unwanted ones.

</details>


### [192] [Controllable GNN Explanations via Multi-Metric Preference Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32436)
*Rachit Verma,Yashraj J. Deshmukh,Anirban Dasgupta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new method for explaining GNN predictions that jointly optimizes fidelity, sparsity, interpretability via motifs, and stability to perturbations, outperforming a strong baseline on several datasets and revealing trade-offs between explanation metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GNN explanation methods mostly focus on fidelity under sparsity constraints, neglecting two key properties needed for trustworthy explanations in high-stakes settings: interpretability (explanations formed from human-understandable motif patterns) and stability (robustness to minor changes in the graph). The authors want to design explanations that are not only accurate but also understandable and robust, and to provide explicit control over the trade-offs between these objectives.

Method: They introduce a novel explanation framework for GNNs that simultaneously optimizes multiple metrics: fidelity, sparsity, interpretability via a motif library, and stability under structural perturbations. The method treats the relative weights of these metrics as tunable controls. Given an input motif library tailored to the application domain, the approach searches for subgraphs that both explain the model’s prediction and can be decomposed into known motifs, while also enforcing robustness of the explanation when the input graph is slightly perturbed. They then analyze the tradeoff surface between the metrics, including how it varies with different motif libraries.

Result: On several real-world datasets (MUTAG, BA-2Motif, BAMultiShapes, and PROTEINS), the method achieves higher-fidelity explanations than a state-of-the-art baseline on MUTAG and PROTEINS for all explanation budgets and on BA-2Motif for larger budgets, while being faster for small explanation budgets. It can also quantify the relative importance of different motifs from the input library in forming explanations, and using this motif-importance information further improves explanation quality. The authors empirically characterize trade-off surfaces among fidelity, interpretability, sparsity, and stability and show their dependence on the chosen motif library.

Conclusion: Jointly optimizing fidelity, interpretability, sparsity, and stability leads to better and more trustworthy GNN explanations than optimizing fidelity alone. Exposing the weights between these metrics as user controls enables practitioners to navigate the trade-offs required in different domains. Motif libraries are a powerful tool both for constraining explanations to be more interpretable and for analyzing which structures are most important for the model’s decisions, suggesting a path toward more transparent and robust graph learning systems.

Abstract: Mechanisms for generating GNN explanations are crucial for building trust and mitigating biases in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), especially in high-stakes scenarios. Most current methods optimize only for fidelity under the sparsity constraint. However, this discounts the need for interpretable explanations (those that consist of familiar motif patterns) and stable explanations (those that remain unchanged under structural perturbations). We propose a novel approach that optimizes GNN explanations across these metrics, exposing their relative weighing as a control. Experiments on various real-world datasets, including MUTAG, BA-2Motif, BAMultiShapes, and PROTEINS, suggest that our method produces higher-fidelity explanations than a state-of-the-art baseline on MUTAG and PROTEINS across all evaluated budgets, and on BA-2Motif at larger budgets, while being faster in the regime of small explanation budgets. We also explore how, given an input motif library containing standard motifs for the corresponding domain, the method can be used to determine the relative importance of those motifs in generating the explanations, and how this information can be used to further improve the quality of the output explanations. We also examine the relationship between different metrics through their induced tradeoff surface, and explore its dependence on the nature of the motif library.

</details>


### [193] [ForkLeft: Entropy-First Rollouts for Prefix-Aligned Autoregressive-to-Diffusion Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32448)
*Junming Liu,Jicheng Wang,Yifeng He,Hao Chen,Jianzhong Qi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes ForkLeft, a distillation framework that transfers next-token prediction (NTP) style reasoning from autoregressive teachers to diffusion language models (DLMs) while preserving their parallel generation, achieving strong gains on multiple reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive NTP models have strong reasoning abilities but generate tokens sequentially, limiting parallelism. Diffusion Language Models allow flexible token orders and parallel decoding but lack NTP-like reasoning. There is a need to combine the reasoning strength of NTP models with the efficiency and flexibility of DLMs without discarding DLMs’ native generation process. Direct distillation from an autoregressive teacher to a DLM is fundamentally mismatched because teachers condition only on left prefixes while DLMs can condition on both left and right context, so a new method is needed to resolve this mismatch.

Method: The authors introduce ForkLeft, a distillation framework that decouples how the student DLM rolls out tokens from how it is supervised by an autoregressive NTP teacher. During training, the DLM student first performs entropy-first rollouts, committing to uncertain positions to reveal potential “forks” in the generation. This rollout defines a fixed student prefix. The autoregressive teacher is then run under this same context to provide supervision, with the correctness of the student’s answers determining whether to use teacher or student signals. At inference time, the DLM student reverts to its default confidence-first parallel decoding, retaining its native generation advantages while leveraging the distilled reasoning skills.

Result: Using Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base as the teacher, ForkLeft improves the Efficient-DLM-4B model across ten benchmarks, including boosting MATH500 accuracy from 72.60% to 79.60%, and consistently outperforms three alternative distillation designs. The performance gains grow with stronger teachers and transfer to another DLM, SDAR-4B, with only 500 training updates. At comparable parameter scales, the distilled 4B and 8B DLM students outperform published SDAR-Chat and OPDLM models on seven benchmarks.

Conclusion: ForkLeft demonstrates that diffusion language models can effectively acquire NTP-style reasoning capabilities through a tailored distillation process that respects their bidirectional and parallel generation nature. The method resolves the teacher–student context mismatch and yields DLMs that maintain native parallel decoding while achieving state-of-the-art or superior reasoning performance at similar scales. This suggests DLMs can be competitive reasoning models without adopting strictly autoregressive generation. The authors plan to release code and datasets upon acceptance.

Abstract: Autoregressive Next-Token Prediction (NTP) has enabled strong reasoning capabilities in language models, while Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) offer flexible token orders and parallel generation. We ask whether DLMs can acquire NTP-style reasoning through distillation without giving up their native generation process. Direct distillation, however, faces a fundamental mismatch: an autoregressive teacher predicts from a left prefix, whereas a DLM can condition on tokens on both sides. We introduce ForkLeft, a distillation framework that resolves this mismatch by separating the student's rollout from teacher supervision. During training, the student first performs entropy-first rollouts that commit uncertain positions and expose potential forks. We then fix the resulting student prefix and distill an NTP teacher under the same context, with answer correctness determining the supervision source. At inference, the student returns to its native confidence-first parallel decoding. With Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base, ForkLeft improves Efficient-DLM-4B on all ten benchmarks, raising MATH500 from 72.60% to 79.60% and consistently outperforming three alternative designs. The gains scale with teacher strength and generalize to SDAR-4B with only $500$ updates. At matched scale, the distilled 4B and 8B students exceed the published SDAR-Chat and OPDLM models on seven benchmarks, showing that DLMs can learn NTP-style reasoning without sacrificing native parallel generation. Code and datasets will be released upon acceptance.

</details>


### [194] [PULSE: Identifying Demonstration-Utility Features with Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32469)
*Chenduo Hao,Chuanbao Gao,Pinjun Zeng,Jingze Zhu,Chonghan Liu,Zidong Liu,Xu Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes PULSE, an SAE-based method that selects in-context learning demonstrations using model-internal feature activations instead of only external similarity, improving performance across several tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In-context learning performance depends heavily on which demonstrations are chosen, but current selection methods mostly rely on surface-level or embedding-based similarity between queries and candidate demonstrations. These similarity metrics can fail to capture how the specific target model internally represents and uses different demonstrations: two similar demonstrations by external metrics may trigger very different internal features and behaviors. The authors are motivated to directly exploit model-specific internal signals to identify which demonstrations are actually useful for a given task and query.

Method: The authors introduce PULSE (Paired Utility Localization over Sparse Encodings), which uses sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to connect model-internal features with demonstration utility. They first construct a small labeled discovery set and repeatedly sample candidate demonstration sets for that discovery data. For each candidate set, they measure its relative zero-shot utility (how much it helps compared to zero-shot performance) under the target model. Using an SAE fitted to model activations, they compute feature activations for these candidate sets and then score each SAE feature by how strongly changes in that feature’s activation correlate with changes in utility across sampled sets. The most positively and negatively correlated features are combined into a sparse “utility-localization” vector over SAE coordinates. This vector is then used in two ways: (1) as a signed score to rank complete demonstration sets in a controlled setting, and (2) as PULSE-Retriever, which converts the magnitude of the vector into a feature-relevance mask enabling scalable retrieval of individual demonstrations from a large pool.

Result: On classification, text generation, and reasoning benchmarks, PULSE-Retriever outperforms the strongest existing demonstration-selection baselines. The reported gains are about 2–3 percentage points in accuracy, 0.6–0.9 points in BLEU-4 for generation quality, and 3.2 points in exact match for reasoning tasks. Experiments using controlled ranking of full demonstration sets confirm that the learned features genuinely encode a predictive, set-level utility signal rather than merely overfitting. Qualitative feature inspection and cross-dataset tests indicate that the localized SAE features capture patterns that are both task-relevant and conditioned on the dataset while still retaining utility information that transfers partially to other datasets.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that model-internal features, uncovered via sparse autoencoders, can be effectively used to guide in-context demonstration selection, leading to consistent performance improvements across multiple NLP task types. PULSE provides a way to localize and exploit a sparse, interpretable representation of demonstration utility, validating that certain internal features correspond to useful, transferable patterns for in-context learning. This opens up a direction for using interpretability tools not just for analysis but also for practical control over model behavior in demonstration-based setups.

Abstract: In-context learning is highly sensitive to demonstration choice, yet most methods select demonstrations using external query-demonstration similarity. Such criteria can miss model-specific signals: Similar demonstrations may activate different internal features and downstream behaviors. We introduce PULSE (Paired Utility Localization over Sparse Encodings), an SAE-based framework for identifying model-internal features associated with demonstration utility and using them for demonstration selection. Using a small labeled discovery set, PULSE samples candidate demonstration sets, measures their zero-shot-relative utility under the target model, and scores SAE features by how their activation differences align with utility differences. The top positive and negative coordinates form a sparse utility-localization vector. We use this vector in two complementary ways: as a signed score for controlled complete-set ranking, and as PULSE-Retriever, which converts its magnitude into a feature-relevance mask for scalable pool-scale retrieval. Across classification, generation, and reasoning benchmarks, PULSE-Retriever improves over the strongest baseline by 2-3 accuracy points, 0.6-0.9 BLEU-4, and 3.2 exact-match points, respectively, while controlled ranking validates the identified features encode a predictive set-level utility signal. Feature inspection and cross-dataset experiments suggest that the identified features capture task-relevant, dataset-conditioned patterns, yet retain utility signals that partially transfer across datasets. Our code is available at https://github.com/aohenuo/PULSE.

</details>


### [195] [VPEvolve: A Self-Evolving Virtual Process Engineer for Computational Lithography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32473)
*Tianyi Li,Wenxuan Dong,Donger Luo,Nan Wang,Yanpeng Chen,Jiaqi Liu,Xinyun Zhang,Hao Geng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents a language-model-driven framework that automatically improves OPC recipes, significantly reducing edge placement error while keeping model weights fixed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: OPC recipes become increasingly complex as engineers manually add local rules over time to fix emerging lithography hotspots. These incremental patches can interact in unintended ways, and the knowledge gained from running commercial OPC tools is dispersed across scripts, logs, and code. This leads to suboptimal and difficult-to-maintain recipes. The authors aim to systematize and automate this process, capturing engineering expertise and experimental feedback in a reusable, data-driven form.

Method: The authors introduce a system that couples a frozen language model with a "Virtual Process Engineer" (VPE) harness and a Skill Bank of accumulated experience. The harness gives the LLM access to process manuals, layout analysis tools, recipe-editing capabilities, and the ability to invoke commercial OPC tool evaluations. The LLM acts as an agentic "actor" that proposes modifications to global recipe parameters, local targeted rules, or diagnostic experiments. After each evaluation by the commercial tool, an LLM-based reflector and curator analyze the measured outcomes, generate evidence-linked judgments, and store them in the Skill Bank. The actor retrieves and reuses this structured experience before issuing its next set of edits, iteratively refining the OPC recipe. Throughout, the LLM parameters remain frozen; only the recipe and the Skill Bank evolve.

Result: On a benchmark derived from FreePDK45, with ten commercial-tool evaluations allowed per test case, the system substantially improves OPC quality. It reduces the mean per-case maximum edge placement error from 18.294 nm to 5.361 nm for Poly layers and from 22.052 nm to 15.692 nm for Metal1 layers. Furthermore, all final recipes satisfy predefined quality constraints, and each case achieves at least a 0.1 nm improvement in maximum error.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that a frozen language model, when wrapped in a VPE harness and augmented with a structured Skill Bank of prior trials, can serve as an effective autonomous assistant for OPC recipe optimization. The system reliably improves edge placement error within a constrained number of commercial-tool evaluations and enforces quality constraints, demonstrating a practical pathway to capture, reuse, and operationalize human-like process engineering expertise for lithography OPC without retraining the model.

Abstract: Optical proximity correction (OPC) recipes grow as engineers add local rules to repair newly discovered lithography hotspots. Each correction can interact with existing rules, while lessons from commercial-tool trials remain scattered across code and logs. \system combines a Virtual Process Engineer (VPE) harness with a Skill Bank of measured engineering experience. The harness equips a frozen language model with process manuals, layout analysis, recipe editing, and commercial-tool evaluation. The actor proposes changes to the global parameters, local targeted rules, or diagnostic trials. After each evaluation, an LLM reflector and curator turn the measured response into evidence-linked judgments. The actor retrieves them before its next trial. Feasible improvements update the retained recipe; every measured trial informs the Skill Bank that guides the next edit. The model weights remain fixed. On a FreePDK45-derived benchmark with ten commercial-tool evaluations per case, \system reduces the mean per-case maximum edge placement error from 18.294 to 5.361 nm on Poly and from 22.052 to 15.692 nm on Metal1. Every final recipe satisfies the predefined quality constraints and improves the maximum error by at least 0.1 nm.

</details>


### [196] [From Outcomes to Strategies: Learning Strategy Utility for Mathematical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32482)
*Ruikang Zhang,Xiao An,Xuli Shen,Jiaxing Sun,Xiaoyi Yu,Jin Zeng,Jiang Wu,Tong Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces SURE, a framework that learns a reward model over high-level solution strategies (rather than just final correctness) to improve mathematical reasoning in RL, yielding consistent pass@1 gains and reduced compute versus standard GRPO baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing reinforcement learning approaches for mathematical reasoning mostly reward only terminal correctness and formatting, which fails to evaluate or guide the quality of high-level strategies like theorem choice or subgoal planning. As a result, models may stumble upon correct answers without learning generally useful strategies, and we lack a signal about which strategic plans are more likely to lead to success given a fixed executor. The paper aims to explicitly model and exploit the utility of strategies themselves so that training can favor plans that are more reliably solvable downstream, improving accuracy and efficiency.

Method: The authors define "strategy utility" as the probability that a given high-level strategy leads to a correct solution under a specified executor. They introduce SURE, which first disentangles high-level strategies from detailed reasoning traces. Using strategy-conditioned rollouts and teacher-generated contrasting strategies, they construct pairwise preferences over strategies. A Strategy Reward Model (SRM) is then trained to predict relative utility between strategies. In the subsequent reinforcement learning stage, this SRM is frozen and used as an additional reward signal that only reads the extracted strategy, independent of execution details. Its score is combined with correctness and format rewards within a sequence-level GRPO (a policy-gradient style) objective, so the policy is optimized both for final correctness and for choosing strategies that the SRM deems more useful.

Result: Across three different policy backbones, SURE yields consistent performance improvements over standard outcome-and-format GRPO baselines, improving average pass@1 by 1.87%, 2.64%, and 2.93%. Furthermore, when compared to stronger reward baselines that use richer or more expensive signals, SURE attains comparable or better accuracy while significantly reducing the computational cost during the GRPO training stage, indicating that modeling strategy utility is an efficient way to boost reasoning performance.

Conclusion: Modeling and rewarding high-level strategy quality, rather than only final correctness, leads to better mathematical reasoning in reinforcement learning systems. By learning a Strategy Reward Model from pairwise comparisons over strategy-conditioned executions and then using it as a frozen guide during GRPO, SURE can systematically prefer strategies that are more likely to succeed under a given executor. This approach produces consistent pass@1 gains across architectures and rivals stronger baselines at substantially lower compute cost, suggesting that explicit strategy-utility modeling is a promising direction for more scalable and efficient reasoning training frameworks.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has substantially improved mathematical reasoning. However, terminal correctness alone provides limited insight into the quality of high-level strategies, such as theorem selection and subgoal decomposition, when considered separately from their subsequent execution. This paper studies strategy utility, which is defined as the likelihood that a strategy supports a correct downstream solution under a given executor. We introduce SURE, a framework for learning and leveraging relative strategy utility. In this framework, high-level strategies are separated from their detailed reasoning. Based on the pairwise preferences constructed from strategy-conditioned rollouts and teacher-generated contrasts, a Strategy Reward Model is learned to estimate relative strategy utility. During reinforcement learning, the frozen reward model reads only the extracted strategy, whose score is combined with the correctness and format rewards in a sequence-level GRPO objective. Compared with outcome-and-format GRPO baselines, experiments show that SURE improves average pass@1 by 1.87%, 2.64%, and 2.93% across three policy backbones. Our method also achieves competitive or better accuracy than stronger reward baselines while requiring substantially lower GRPO-stage compute.

</details>


### [197] [Separating Diagnosis from Disease Representation: Dual-View EEG Learning with Neural-Dynamics-Guided Deformation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32483)
*Jiaying Wang,Shouqian Shi,Yutong Chen,Xu Yang,Jie Chen,Xingyu Pan,Lei Zhang,Sheng Zhong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a dual-view EEG framework that separates diagnosis from anatomical interpretation, using a fixed scalp classifier and a deformable source-space model that highlights disease-related changes across brain regions, frequencies, and timescales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Closed-loop EEG neuromodulation needs detailed, subject-specific brain states (which regions, which frequencies, which temporal lags are abnormal), not just a single disease probability. Existing approaches either lose anatomy (sensor space), lose predictive power (source space), or only add anatomy post hoc. The authors want a representation that is both predictive and anatomically interpretable, and consistent across EEG montages.

Method: They introduce DMD-EEG, a Dual-view Multiscale Deformation model. One branch is a fixed scalp spectral expert that performs diagnosis in sensor space. The second branch operates in source space: it starts from a healthy neural-dynamics prior over a 46-ROI × 5-frequency × 4-lag tensor and learns a low-rank, sparse, iterative deformation that captures disease-related deviations. The two branches are combined only at a decision (fusion) level so that the source representation remains architecturally separate and readable as ROI-frequency-lag saliency.

Result: On data from major depressive disorder (MDD), first-episode psychosis (FEP), and Parkinson’s disease (PD), the decision-level fusion matches the performance of the best single expert for MDD and FEP and outperforms the source-space branch for PD. For FEP, the source expert itself is the best-performing branch, indicating that the deformation-based source model adds substantial value. The resulting source-state attributions align with known disease circuits (fronto-limbic-temporal for MDD, motor cortex beta for PD), and the ranked MDD source pattern generalizes to an unseen cohort with a different EEG montage.

Conclusion: Separating sensor-space diagnosis from source-space anatomical representation via a deformable prior yields an interpretable, anatomically coordinated predictive state over ROIs, frequencies, and lags. This dual-view design preserves diagnostic strength while producing directly readable neural attributions that agree with known circuitry and show cross-montage transfer, making the approach suitable for hypothesis generation and potentially for closed-loop neuromodulation control states.

Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based closed-loop neuromodulation calls for a subject-specific structured state, as opposed to a single disease probability, specifying which brain regions are deviant, at which frequencies, and at which lags. Sensor-space models keep the strongest diagnostic evidence without anatomy, source-space models give anatomy at a loss of predictive signal, and post-hoc attributions stay outside the prediction. We separate the two instead of forcing them into one representation, and propose DMD-EEG (Dual-view Multiscale Deformation for EEG), which keeps a fixed scalp spectral expert for diagnosis and models the source-space disease-related representation as a low-rank, sparse, iterative deformation of a healthy neural-dynamics prior in a $46$-region-of-interest (ROI) $\times$ $5$-frequency $\times$ $4$-lag (autocorrelation-timescale) space. The two experts meet only at a fixed decision level, so the source state is architecturally separate from the scalp expert. Across major depressive disorder (MDD), first-episode psychosis (FEP), and Parkinson's disease (PD), decision-level fusion matches the strongest single expert on MDD and FEP and exceeds the source branch on PD. On FEP the source expert is the strongest branch, the task where the deformation contributes most. The source state is an explicit ROI-frequency-lag attribution defined in a shared source coordinate system across montages, which we treat as an anatomically-coordinated predictive representation whose coordinates are directly readable and hypothesis-generating. The highest-saliency coordinates align with established disease circuitry (fronto-limbic-temporal regions in MDD, motor-cortex beta in PD), and the MDD state transfers by rank to an unseen cohort recorded with a different montage.

</details>


### [198] [Towards Scalable Data Diversification for Language Model Pretraining via Leverage Score Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32484)
*Zailin Ma,Quzhe Huang,Yujun Li,Congyuan Rao,Yaodong Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Lev, a scalable leverage score-based data selection method for language model pretraining that improves diversity, efficiency, and downstream performance compared to existing quality- and diversity-based selectors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing quality-based data filtering for language model pretraining improves performance but causes diversity collapse, excluding important underrepresented domains (e.g., code in web data). Existing diversity-oriented methods either optimize coverage only indirectly or require expensive covariance recomputation, limiting scalability. There is a need for a data selection approach that is both diversity-aware and computationally efficient, and that can serve as an unsupervised alternative where quality labels or criteria are hard to define.

Method: The paper introduces Leverage Score Sampling (Lev), which operates on embedded representations of candidate data points and iteratively selects samples that maximally expand the determinantal volume of the dataset. It uses leverage scores as an efficient proxy for determinantal point process-style diversity, avoiding repeated covariance matrix recomputation. Lev is applied to web-scale corpora such as CommonCrawl and StarCoderData, and evaluated against strong baselines including DiSF and quality-filtering methods like DCLM-fastText.

Result: Lev achieves up to 72× speedup over the strong diversification baseline DiSF. It increases dataset diversity, as measured by the Vendi score, by 9.2% relative to DiSF. On CommonCrawl web data selection, Lev yields up to 1.31% accuracy improvement across seven downstream tasks compared with existing baselines. On StarCoderData for code, Lev-selected subsets reduce bits-per-byte by 3.08% over DiSF, indicating better modeling efficiency. The study also shows that quality-filtered CommonCrawl data using DCLM-fastText fails to preserve enough code content, leading to worse code performance than Lev-selected data.

Conclusion: Leverage Score Sampling offers an effective, scalable method for diversity-aware data selection in language model pretraining. It improves diversity and downstream task performance while being significantly faster than previous diversification approaches. The results highlight that pure quality-based filtering can cause harmful cross-domain diversity collapse, especially for domains like code, and that integrating diversity-aware criteria into data curation is crucial for building more robust language models.

Abstract: Data selection for language model pretraining faces a fundamental tension between quality and diversity. While quality filtering is empirically effective, it often induces diversity collapse: by favoring texts similar to high-quality reference corpora (e.g., educational or QA-style data), it systematically excludes valuable data from underrepresented domains. In contrast, diversified selection preserves domain balance and encourages robust downstream performance, yet existing methods either focus on coverage-oriented objectives that indirectly enhance diversity, or directly optimize for diversity via costly covariance matrix recomputation that limits scalability. To address these issues, we introduce \textbf{Leverage Score Sampling (Lev)}, which iteratively selects samples that maximally expand the determinantal volume of the embedded data via leverage scores, a computationally efficient criterion that eliminates matrix recomputation and enables scalable selection. Empirically, Lev delivers up to $72\times$ speedup and improves dataset diversity, measured by the Vendi score, by $9.2\%$ over the strong diversification baseline \textbf{DiSF}. On CommonCrawl (CC) web data selection, Lev improves accuracy across seven downstream tasks by up to $1.31\%$ over existing baselines. For domains where robust quality criteria are inherently difficult to define (e.g., code), Lev serves as an effective unsupervised curation alternative: on StarCoderData, the selected subset reduces bits-per-byte by $3.08\%$ over DiSF. Notably, we uncover a cross-domain collapse of quality filtering: CC data filtered by DCLM-fastText fail to retain sufficient code-related content, yielding inferior code performance relative to Lev-selected data. These findings advocate for integrating diversity-aware practices into quality filtering for more effective data curation in language model pretraining.

</details>


### [199] [When Helpful Text Hurts: Option-Redirecting Bias in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32489)
*Tam Le Thi Thanh,Hoang Tran Van,Hong-Hanh Nguyen-Le,Thanh Duc Ngo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how unreliable auxiliary text in tri-modal VQA harms model decisions and proposes a diagnostic protocol plus an inference-time mitigation method.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In tri-modal VQA, models use auxiliary text (e.g., captions, retrieved passages) alongside images and questions. This auxiliary text is often noisy or unreliable, and prior work only coarsely analyzes modality conflicts without distinguishing how specific reliability patterns of the text influence answer selection under the same image-question-option setup. The authors aim to understand which kinds of unreliable auxiliary text are most harmful and why, and to build tools and methods to diagnose and mitigate these effects.

Method: The authors systematically manipulate auxiliary text while keeping the image, question, and answer options fixed. They introduce the Textual Reliability Ladder, which decomposes auxiliary text along three orthogonal axes: (1) image consistency (whether the text agrees with the visual content), (2) question relevance (whether it is related to the user query), and (3) option support (which answer choice it implicitly or explicitly favors). Using this ladder, they construct controlled variants of auxiliary text that range from faithful to misleading, especially focusing on text that supports specific distractor options while contradicting the image. They then evaluate multiple vision-language models across several tri-modal VQA datasets (ScienceQA, VCR, A-OKVQA, Causal-VidQA), measuring accuracy and error concentration under different reliability conditions. To mitigate the adversarial effect, they design a training-free, inference-time intervention that leverages noise-stability steering (probing model robustness to perturbations) and dynamic grounding (adjusting reliance on text vs. image) to counteract the redirection towards distractor-supported options.

Result: Experiments show that auxiliary text which aligns with the question but contradicts the image while explicitly supporting a distractor is the most harmful type, even compared with more factually incorrect text that does not support a specific wrong option. This type of text causes large drops in accuracy, reported up to 53.1%, and systematically redirects predictions toward particular incorrect answers, concentrating errors instead of randomizing them. The proposed inference-time intervention substantially decreases these redirected errors and recovers robustness with minimal or no loss in performance when the auxiliary text is reliable. The findings are consistent across multiple datasets and modern vision-language models, indicating that the phenomenon is widespread and not model-specific.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that reliability of auxiliary text in tri-modal VQA must be assessed at the decision level, focusing on how it steers the model’s answer preferences, rather than treating reliability purely as factual correctness. Distractor-supporting, question-aligned but image-contradicting text is identified as a key failure mode because it systematically redirects model predictions. The Textual Reliability Ladder provides a fine-grained diagnostic framework to reveal such vulnerabilities, and the proposed training-free inference-time intervention demonstrates a practical means to mitigate them by dynamically rebalancing reliance on modalities. Overall, the work advances understanding of tri-modal reasoning failures and offers actionable tools for building more robust VQA systems that are less susceptible to misleading auxiliary text.

Abstract: In tri-modal visual question answering (VQA), auxiliary text is commonly used to complement visual and textual inputs, yet its reliability is often uncontrolled. While prior work studies modality conflicts in general, it remains unclear how different types of unreliable auxiliary text affect answer selection under fixed image-question-option contexts. In this work, we show that the most harmful auxiliary text is not necessarily the most factually incorrect, but the one that aligns with the question while contradicting the image and favoring a specific distractor, leading to systematic redirection of model predictions. To isolate this effect, we introduce the Textual Reliability Ladder, a controlled diagnostic protocol that decomposes auxiliary text along three axes: image consistency, question relevance, and option support. Across multiple datasets (ScienceQA, VCR, A-OKVQA, Causal-VidQA) and recent VLMs, we find that such distractor-supporting text induces the largest accuracy drops (up to 53.1%) and concentrates errors on specific incorrect options. To mitigate this failure mode, we propose a training-free inference-time intervention that explicitly counteracts this redirection effect via noise-stability steering and dynamic grounding, reducing redirected errors while largely preserving performance under faithful text. Our results highlight that auxiliary-text reliability must be understood at the decision level, rather than solely through factual correctness, and provide a practical pathway toward more robust tri-modal reasoning.

</details>


### [200] [RepoMAS: Solving Progressively Specified Tasks with Issue-Driven Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32490)
*Yuchen Song,Andong Chen,Wenxin Zhu,Muyun Yang,Tiejun Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces ProgSpec, a benchmark and RepoMAS, a multi-agent framework, to handle progressively specified tasks where requirements emerge during problem solving.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most current LLM-based multi-agent systems assume that task requirements are fully specified upfront, which is unrealistic because in real-world scenarios user requests are often incomplete and additional requirements surface only during reasoning, tool use, or execution. There is a need to systematically study and benchmark this progressive specification setting and to design MASs that can recognize, track, and adapt to newly discovered requirements.

Method: The authors define and formalize the problem of progressively specified tasks and introduce ProgSpec, a benchmark that evaluates systems against both initially explicit requirements and additional requirements inferred from task evidence. They then propose RepoMAS, an issue-driven multi-agent framework inspired by open-source repository management. RepoMAS maintains a structured repository of Issues that capture newly discovered requirements, conflicts, and failures during problem solving, and uses these Issues to iteratively revise the task specification and modify the execution plan and agent coordination.

Result: On ProgSpec and five existing benchmarks, RepoMAS outperforms alternative multi-agent baselines, achieving the best performance across evaluations. Ablation and further analyses indicate that the issue-driven revision process and repository maintenance mechanisms are key contributors to this performance gain.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling and updating task requirements during execution—rather than assuming they are fixed upfront—substantially improves the effectiveness of LLM-based MASs on complex, realistic tasks. Issue-driven mechanisms like those in RepoMAS, combined with benchmarks such as ProgSpec, provide a practical framework for building and evaluating systems capable of handling progressively specified tasks.

Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MASs) have shown strong potential for solving complex tasks, but most assume that task requirements are sufficiently specified before execution. In practice, user requests are often incomplete, and additional requirements may only become clear during reasoning, tool use, or execution. We refer to such problems as progressively specified tasks.
  To systematically study this setting, we introduce ProgSpec, a benchmark that evaluates final outputs against requirements explicitly stated in the initial request and additional requirements supported by the available task evidence. We further propose RepoMAS, an issue-driven multi-agent framework inspired by open-source project management. RepoMAS records newly discovered requirements, conflicts, and failures as structured Issues and uses them to revise the task specification and execution structure during problem solving.
  Across ProgSpec and five existing benchmarks, RepoMAS achieves the best performance. Further analyses show that its issue-driven revision and repository maintenance mechanisms consistently contribute to performance. These results highlight the importance of allowing MASs to revise not only how a task is solved, but also revise their explicit representation of task requirements during execution.

</details>


### [201] [Beyond Prompt or Skill? Attribution-Guided Optimization of Modular LLM Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32492)
*Haoran Shou,Haoyue Liu,Yu Huo,Kun Zeng,Xiaoying Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SPARO is a unified framework that jointly optimizes prompts, reusable skills, and routing rules for large language models, leading to better reasoning performance than prompt-only or skill-only optimization methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although large language models can handle diverse reasoning tasks, their success is highly sensitive to prompts, intermediate instructions, and how reusable skills are integrated. Existing optimization approaches treat these components separately—typically tuning a single prompt or independently training skills—so they lack a principled way to decide which component to adjust after an error and rarely optimize all components together. This fragmentation limits systematic improvement and reuse of task knowledge.

Method: The authors introduce SPARO (Skill, Prompt, And Routing Optimization), which represents a language program as three components: task-level instructions (prompt), skill blocks (reusable subprocedures), and routing rules (policies deciding when to call which skills). For each training example, SPARO performs controlled counterfactual evaluations to see how changes in each component would affect performance. It then turns these effects into a probabilistic responsibility distribution over the prompt, skills, and routing parts, samples one component according to that distribution, and applies a targeted mutation (edit/update) to that chosen component. Iterating this process jointly optimizes all three parts within a unified framework.

Result: On five benchmarks and across five different LLM worker models, SPARO consistently surpasses baselines that focus only on prompts or only on skills. This indicates that its joint optimization of prompts, skills, and routing leads to more effective and robust task performance.

Conclusion: Effective optimization of language-based programs requires not just discovering useful task knowledge but also deciding how to factor that knowledge into prompts, reusable skills, and routing policies, and when to activate each piece. By providing a unified framework that assigns responsibility for errors and selectively updates the most relevant component, SPARO advances beyond global prompt rewriting toward structured, reusable, and context-dependent task knowledge, yielding better performance across varied reasoning benchmarks.

Abstract: Large language models can solve increasingly diverse reasoning tasks, yet their performance remains highly sensitive to task prompts, intermediate instructions, and the way reusable problem-solving knowledge is incorporated. Existing optimization methods usually focus on only one part of this design space: they either optimize a monolithic prompt, or separately induce and refine skills from model traces. As a result, they lack a principled mechanism for deciding which component should be updated when failures occur, and they rarely optimize prompts, skills, and skill-use policies in a unified framework. We propose SPARO (Skill, Prompt, And Routing Optimization), a framework that jointly optimizes task instructions, reusable skill blocks, and routing rules. It performs controlled counterfactual evaluations, converts examples' effects into a probabilistic responsibility distribution over prompt, skill, and routing components, samples one component from that distribution, and applies the corresponding targeted mutation. This design moves language-program optimization beyond global prompt rewriting toward structured, reusable, and selectively activated task knowledge. Across five benchmarks and five worker models, SPARO consistently outperforms both prompt-centered and skill-centered optimization baselines. These results suggest that effective language-program optimization depends not only on discovering useful task knowledge, but also on deciding where that knowledge should be stored and when it should be activated.

</details>


### [202] [DAAF: From Failure Localization to Editable System Assets in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32498)
*Xiaoyang Yuan,Qi Liu,Yubin Ruan,Xinyi Mou,Zhuomeng Zhang,Wenjin Wang,Hanying Jiao,Di Wu,Mingye Xu,Yi Bin,Ke Feng,Zixun Sun*

Main category: cs.AI
