TL;DR: The paper introduces a framework (DAAF) to identify which persistent system asset in an LLM agent should be edited to fix failures, using learned, intervention-grounded attribution over component attributes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing failure-localization methods show where errors appear in an LLM agent’s execution trace, but not which editable system asset (like routing rules or knowledge snippets) should be changed to actually repair behavior. As LLM agents increasingly depend on many persistent, versioned components, there is a need to systematically connect observed failures to specific assets whose modification is likely to improve task outcomes without harming successful runs.

Method: The authors define component-attribute failure attribution, focusing diagnosis on versioned items (e.g., knowledge segments, prompts) rather than execution steps. They propose the Detection-Aware Attribution Framework (DAAF), which: (1) aggregates sparse, noisy failure signals to decide whether an intervention is needed; (2) learns the effects of attribute replacements from controlled replays of interactions, evaluated by executable task outcomes; (3) conditions effect learning on component types and shares supervision across requests with similar intervention responses. At deployment, DAAF uses only the actual execution trace, registered candidate assets, and available failure signals—without counterfactual replay or task rewards—to output either no_change, a specific asset to repair, or unresolved when evidence is insufficient.

Result: On held-out tau^2-bench Telecom tasks, DAAF attains 80.72% Hit@1 in identifying the correct attribute, recovers 62.65% of previously failed executions while causing only 3.23% regression on already successful tasks, and achieves 71.93% overall task success. These metrics suggest that DAAF effectively pinpoints repair targets with limited negative side effects.

Conclusion: Intervention-grounded attribution over component attributes can bridge the gap between traditional failure localization and actual, executable repair in LLM agent systems. By learning from controlled intervention data and using detection-aware aggregation of noisy signals, DAAF can reliably propose when and where to intervene in persistent system assets at deployment time, improving failure recovery while preserving performance on clean tasks.

Abstract: Deployed LLM agents increasingly rely on persistent, versioned system assets such as routing rules, knowledge segments, prompt instructions, and reusable skills. Failure-localization methods can identify where an error manifests in an agent or execution trace, but repair requires a different decision: which editable system asset should be changed, and is that change expected to improve the task outcome? We study this gap through component-attribute failure attribution, where diagnosis targets versioned, addressable items rather than execution locations. We propose the Detection-Aware Attribution Framework (DAAF), which learns the effects of valid attribute replacements and amortizes this intervention evidence into deployment-time diagnosis. DAAF combines sparse and noisy failure signals to decide whether intervention is warranted, learns component-type-conditioned replacement effects from controlled replays evaluated by executable task outcomes, and shares supervision across requests with compatible intervention responses. At diagnosis time, DAAF uses only the observed execution, registered candidates, and available failure signals; it requires neither counterfactual replay nor task reward and returns no_change, a repair target, or an unresolved decision when evidence is insufficient. On held-out tau^2-bench Telecom tasks, DAAF achieves 80.72% attribute Hit@1, recovers 62.65% of failed executions while limiting clean-task regression to 3.23%, and reaches 71.93% overall task success. These results show that intervention-grounded attribute attribution can connect failure localization to executable system repair.

</details>


### [203] [TreeRef-BFN: Equivariance-Free De Novo Molecule Generation based on 2D Topology and Internal 3D Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32502)
*Ruiqing Sun,Sen Yang,Dawei Feng,Bo Ding,Yijie Wang,Huaimin Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TreeRef-BFN is a new framework for de novo 3D molecular generation that jointly models molecular size, topology, and geometry using a tree-based representation and a Bayesian Flow Network, enabling flexible, variable-size, and structure-conditioned generation with strong validity and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3D molecular generation methods either pre-fix molecular size and use Cartesian coordinates, limiting variable-size conditional tasks and often requiring equivariant architectures, or rely on internal coordinates that need known graphs or autoregressive construction, which can accumulate errors. There is a need for a representation and model that can jointly and flexibly handle variable molecular sizes, topology, and 3D geometry without these constraints.

Method: The authors introduce TreeRef, a tree-based molecular representation where nodes encode both molecular topology and local 3D geometry, including special RingRef nodes for ring closures that preserve the tree structure and Null nodes that let molecular size emerge from node occupancy. On top of TreeRef, they build TreeRef-BFN, a Bayesian Flow Network with a standard Transformer backbone that globally couples discrete molecular variables and continuous local geometry, allowing joint generation. Masking within this pretrained model enables unconditional and variable-size, structure-conditioned 3D generation without retraining.

Result: TreeRef-BFN achieves high chemical validity, molecular stability, and diversity in generated molecules, reproduces accurate local geometric distributions, offers fast sampling, and provides competitive performance on property-conditioned generation tasks, showing strong empirical performance across several evaluation criteria.

Conclusion: TreeRef-BFN, based on the TreeRef representation, is an efficient and flexible framework for de novo 3D molecular generation that overcomes limitations of previous approaches, supporting unconditional and variable-size conditional generation in a single pretrained model while maintaining strong chemical and geometric quality.

Abstract: De novo 3D molecular generation jointly models molecular size, topology, and geometry. Most methods pre-sample molecular size and generate Cartesian coordinates, limiting variable-size conditional tasks such as fragment completion and scaffold decoration while often relying on equivariant architectures. Internal-coordinate methods avoid rigid-body redundancy but typically require a known molecular graph or autoregressive construction, which may accumulate errors. We propose TreeRef, a tree-based molecular representation that assigns molecular topology and topology-dependent local 3D geometry to a naturally variable-size tree. RingRef nodes encode ring closures while preserving the tree structure, while Null nodes allow molecular size to emerge directly from node occupancy. Based on TreeRef, we develop TreeRef-BFN, a Bayesian Flow Network with a standard Transformer backbone that globally couples these locally defined variables and jointly generates discrete molecular variables and continuous local geometry. A single pretrained TreeRef-BFN supports unconditional generation and variable-size structure-conditioned 3D generation through masking alone, without retraining. Empirical studies demonstrate strong chemical validity, molecular stability, and diversity, accurate local geometric distributions, fast sampling, and competitive property-conditioned generation, establishing TreeRef-BFN as an efficient and flexible framework for 3D molecular generation.

</details>


### [204] [Learning from Others, Acting for You: Cross-User Memory Sharing for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32511)
*Jinming Hu,Haodong Zhao,Qi Jia,Die Chen,Tianhang Zhao,Sufeng Duan,Gongshen Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ShareMem is a shared-memory architecture for LLM agents that lets them reuse cross-user experiences while still respecting each individual user’s preferences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Different users’ LLM agents often tackle similar or related tasks, so their accumulated experiences could benefit one another. However, naïvely pooling all memories causes preference mismatches and cross-user interference, where behaviors tuned to one user’s tastes or constraints are wrongly applied to another. The paper aims to design a memory system that can safely and effectively share task know‑how across users while still grounding decisions in each user’s distinct preferences.

Method: The authors propose ShareMem, a multi-user memory architecture with (1) a separation between reusable experience traces and user-specific preferences; (2) a two-stage consolidation pipeline that first refines new experiences locally, then selectively integrates accepted edits into a global shared pool; (3) scope-first retrieval that jointly chooses what to fetch from both local and shared memories under a single token budget; and (4) a user-bound preference channel that allows both initial and agent-initiated retrieval of the current user’s preferences. The system is tested with four different LLM backbones across three benchmarks: web navigation (Mind2Web), personalized dialogue tasks (VitaBench 2.0), and multi-session coding (MemoryCode). The authors also run ablations by disabling components such as two-stage consolidation and preference retrieval.

Result: Across all four backbone models and three benchmarks, ShareMem outperforms a strong baseline that only uses user-local memory. It yields higher step success in web navigation, higher average task success in personalized online interactions, and better dialogue-macro coding scores. Ablation studies show that two-stage consolidation yields smaller and more efficient shared memory pools, reduces induction token usage, and improves downstream task performance. The experiments further indicate that explicit experience guidance and active preference retrieval work complementarily. Additional analysis reveals that sharing is most beneficial when an agent has limited relevant local experience, while low-quality source memories and cross-user preference clashes reduce the gains from transfer.

Conclusion: ShareMem demonstrates that cross-user sharing of agent experiences can be made both effective and preference-safe by decoupling task know-how from user-specific values and by carefully controlling how memories are consolidated and retrieved. The architecture consistently improves performance over local-only memory, especially in data-sparse settings, but its benefits are sensitive to the quality of shared experiences and to how well user preference conflicts are managed.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents serving different users often solve related tasks, yet separate user histories can leave reusable experience inaccessible to other agents. Pooling memories expands access but risks transferring preferences that conflict with the receiving user's requirements. We introduce ShareMem, a memory architecture that shares reusable experience while grounding its application in the receiving user's own preferences. Shared experiences indicate how to act and which preferences to consult; the receiving user's memory supplies their concrete values. Two-stage consolidation refines experience locally before integrating accepted edits into a shared pool. During execution, scope-first retrieval jointly selects local and shared experiences under a common entry budget, while a user-bound channel supports initial and agent-initiated preference retrieval. We evaluate ShareMem across web navigation (Mind2Web), online personalized interaction (VitaBench~2.0), and multi-session coding (MemoryCode) with four backbone models. It improves step success, average task success, and dialogue-macro coding scores, respectively, over matched user-local memory across all four models. Ablations favor two-stage consolidation for smaller shared pools, lower induction token usage, and better downstream performance, and support complementarity between experience guidance and active preference retrieval. Further analyses show that sharing helps most when relevant local experience is scarce, while source quality and cross-user preference interference limit useful transfer.

</details>


### [205] [From Anomalies to Failures: Constructing Causal Error Graphs for Agentic Trace Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32514)
*Shu-Xun Yang,Yidong Wang,Zhuoer Feng,Bosi Wen,Jiayi Gui,Dayong Yang,Wenbo Yu,Haoke Zhang,Jie Tang,Cunxiang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces CEG-Agent, a causal-diagnosis framework for LLM-based agents, along with CEG-Bench, a benchmark with causally annotated traces, showing improved state-of-the-art performance in diagnosing why agent tasks fail.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM-driven agents are used in complex, multi-step tasks, their long execution traces make it hard to understand why and where failures occur. Existing diagnostic methods blur the distinctions between anomalies, errors, and actual task failures, and they lack a principled, causal model of how early errors propagate to final failure, leading to ambiguous and unreliable failure attribution. There is also no standard, high-quality benchmark with causal annotations to rigorously evaluate trace diagnosis methods.

Method: The authors design CEG-Agent, a tool-augmented framework that (1) defines a clear taxonomy separating anomalies, errors, and failures; and (2) builds Causal Error Graphs (CEGs), typed graphs that connect execution events, diagnostic nodes, and final outcomes through explicit causal relations. They also design an Adversarial Agentic Adjudication Protocol (AAAP) where multiple agents interact adversarially/cooperatively to generate, critique, and consolidate CEG annotations for agent traces, resulting in CEG-Bench, a benchmark with high-confidence, consensus-based causal error graphs. They validate these automatic annotations against an expert human gold set. They then run experiments on CEG-Bench comparing CEG-Agent to baselines under both relaxed semantic matching and exact structural matching criteria for the produced CEGs.

Result: The automatically generated CEG annotations produced using AAAP closely match an expert-curated gold standard, indicating that the protocol can reliably create high-quality causal labels. On CEG-Bench, CEG-Agent outperforms existing methods for trace diagnosis across multiple evaluation setups, including semantically tolerant metrics and stricter, structure-aware criteria, achieving state-of-the-art performance in causal failure attribution for agentic traces.

Conclusion: By introducing a clear taxonomy of anomalies, errors, and failures and modeling their causal relationships with Causal Error Graphs, CEG-Agent provides a principled framework for diagnosing LLM-agent failures. The CEG-Bench benchmark and AAAP protocol offer a scalable way to create reliable causal annotations and to evaluate causal diagnosis methods. Together, these contributions advance the state of the art in understanding and attributing failures in complex LLM-driven agent systems, enabling more reliable and interpretable agent deployment.

Abstract: LLM-driven agents are increasingly deployed in complex applications, where long agentic traces make failures difficult to diagnose. Existing trace diagnosis methods often conflate anomalies, errors, and failures, making diagnostic targets ambiguous; they also lack structured modeling of how causally relevant errors propagate and amplify into final task failures, resulting in unreliable failure attribution. To address these problems, we propose CEG-Agent, a tool-augmented agentic framework for causal diagnosis of agentic traces. Specifically, CEG-Agent introduces an explicit taxonomy of anomalies, errors, and failures, and constructs Causal Error Graphs (CEGs), a unified typed representation that links execution events, diagnostic nodes, and failure outcomes through causal relations. To evaluate causal trace diagnosis, we further construct CEG-Bench, a fully agent-annotated benchmark with high-confidence, consensus-derived CEG annotations obtained through an Adversarial Agentic Adjudication Protocol (AAAP). We validate the resulting annotations against an expert-curated human gold set, which shows close agreement with the automatic annotations. Experiments on CEG-Bench demonstrate that CEG-Agent achieves state-of-the-art performance under both semantically relaxed and structurally exact evaluation criteria. Our code is publicly available.

</details>


### [206] [LocalProp: Neuro-Localized Memory-Efficient Backpropagation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32517)
*Diana-Nicoleta Grigore,Iuliana Georgescu,Radu Tudor Ionescu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes LocalProp, a memory-efficient and biologically motivated local-training method that reduces backpropagation span while preserving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard deep learning relies on global end-to-end backpropagation for both pre-training and fine-tuning, which is biologically implausible and memory intensive. In contrast, biological learning appears highly localized, suggesting that deep networks might also be trained using local signals, potentially saving memory and enabling new scalability/efficiency regimes.

Method: The authors introduce LocalProp, a training procedure that updates model weights locally instead of backpropagating gradients through the entire network. The method follows a pre-training-then-fine-tuning pipeline: (1) pre-train the model with locally constrained weight updates using an I-JEPA-based objective, (2) apply a pruning step that removes parameters in a way that facilitates the flow of learning signals from higher to lower blocks, and (3) perform a short global fine-tuning phase. They vary the number of blocks that are jointly optimized to control how far gradients are allowed to propagate, effectively tuning the gradient-propagation span.

Result: Experiments on multiple datasets, including ImageNet, show that LocalProp achieves competitive performance compared to standard end-to-end backpropagation while using significantly less peak GPU memory. The study demonstrates that the number of jointly optimized blocks directly affects the accuracy–memory trade-off, providing empirical evidence that partial local training can preserve much of the accuracy with substantial memory savings.

Conclusion: LocalProp offers a practical alternative to fully end-to-end backpropagation by using neuro-localized, block-wise training with pruning and short global fine-tuning. It is more memory efficient, aligns better with biological learning assumptions, and introduces gradient-propagation span as a tunable handle to balance accuracy and memory usage in large-scale vision models.

Abstract: The current deep learning training paradigm employs end-to-end backpropagation, regardless of the training stage, i.e. pre-training or fine-tuning. However, backpropagating through the entire model is neither biologically plausible nor memory efficient, since learning inside the brain is highly localized. Therefore, we propose LocalProp, a training procedure that locally updates the weights of a model. Our neuro-localized weight updates follow the "pre-training then fine-tuning" paradigm, where the pre-training is based on I-JEPA. After locally updating the weights, a pruning operation is performed, followed by a short final fine-tuning phase. Pruning helps by sending the learning signal from higher blocks to lower blocks. We perform experiments on several datasets, including large-scale benchmarks such as ImageNet, and empirically show that LocalProp reaches good performance at a fraction of GPU peak memory. By varying the number of jointly optimized blocks, we identify gradient-propagation span as a practical control over the accuracy-memory trade-off.

</details>


### [207] [STR: Supervised Transcoder Replacement for Reducing Steering Side Effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32519)
*Haonan Yu,Junhao Liu,Zhenyu Yan,Haoran Lin,Xin Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Supervised Transcoder Replacement (STR), a way to reduce unwanted side effects when steering language models, by replacing a model’s MLP block at a steering layer with a supervised “transcoder” that preserves non-target behavior while still allowing effective steering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing model steering techniques can effectively enforce a target behavior (e.g., safety, corrigibility), but they often degrade other useful or benign behaviors because they directly manipulate internal directions without explicit protection objectives. Many already-deployed steering vectors were trained without mechanisms to preserve non-target capabilities. The authors want a method that can retrofit protection against side effects onto existing steering methods and vectors, without needing to retrain the whole model or discard current steering approaches.

Method: They introduce Supervised Transcoder Replacement (STR), which learns a replacement module for the MLP computation at a selected steering layer. This replacement (transcoder) is trained with three simultaneous objectives: (1) target control (enforce desired steering behavior), (2) non-target preservation (keep unrelated behaviors intact), and (3) fidelity to the original model when no steering is applied. After training the transcoder and freezing it, standard steering methods (including those originally trained without protection) are refit or applied on top of this replacement layer to obtain steering directions. Experiments are run on Gemma and Llama models, using Corrigibility preference data and safety datasets from SALAD-Bench (for training and in-distribution evaluation) and HarmBench, AdvBench, StrongREJECT (for out-of-distribution tests).

Result: STR significantly reduces negative side effects of steering while maintaining strong target control. On in-distribution SALAD-Bench evaluation splits, steering quality remains high but side-effect metrics improve. On out-of-distribution safety datasets (HarmBench, AdvBench, StrongREJECT), STR generalizes this protection: for target-only supervised steering vectors, the pooled attack success rate drops from 42.46% to 14.42% on Gemma-3-4B and from 34.97% to 12.91% on Gemma-3-12B, showing much lower vulnerability to harmful-request attacks compared to standard steering without STR.

Conclusion: Replacement training of an MLP block via STR can retrofit side-effect protection onto existing steering methods, including those not designed with protection objectives. By jointly optimizing for target control, preservation of non-target behavior, and unsteered fidelity, STR yields steering directions that are safer and more robust across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution safety evaluations, without sacrificing the effectiveness of target behavior enforcement.

Abstract: Model steering can strengthen a target behavior while degrading other useful behaviors. We introduce Supervised Transcoder Replacement (STR) to reduce these side effects for existing steering methods, including those fitted without a protection objective. STR learns a replacement for the multilayer perceptron (MLP) computation at the steering layer through supervision for target control, non-target preservation, and fidelity without steering. Selected steering methods then fit directions on the frozen replacement while retaining their own fitting objectives. We evaluate three steering methods across Gemma and Llama models using Corrigibility preferences and four harmful-request safety datasets. SALAD-Bench supplies protection training data and a separate in-distribution evaluation split; HarmBench, AdvBench, and StrongREJECT are reserved for out-of-distribution testing. STR substantially reduces steering side effects on the in-distribution evaluation and extends this protection to the unseen safety datasets while retaining effective target control. For target-only supervised steering vectors, pooled out-of-distribution attack success rate falls from 42.46% to 14.42% on Gemma-3-4B and from 34.97% to 12.91% on Gemma-3-12B. These results show that replacement training can benefit steering methods fitted without protection objectives.

</details>


### [208] [MemAgent: Learning to Manage Heterogeneous Memory Providers for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32521)
*Yongxian Wei,Yilin Zhao,Runxi Cheng,Xinrui Chen,Chun Yuan,Yaoru Wang,Jiahong Yan,Dian Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces MemAgent, a content-aware routing framework that dynamically selects among heterogeneous memory providers to improve long-horizon agent performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based agents are mostly stateless across tasks and depend on a single type of memory representation (e.g., trajectories, reflections, skills), which fails to generalize across diverse benchmarks. There is a need for a method that can flexibly and efficiently manage multiple heterogeneous memory sources to enable continual improvement and robust long-horizon behavior.

Method: The authors first systematically evaluate 13 different memory methods and show that none generalize well across tasks. They then frame agent memory as a routing problem, where a specialized memory agent decides: (1) which memory provider(s) to retrieve from, (2) whether to inject short-term memory, and (3) which providers should store new experience. They implement this as MemAgent, which has a content-aware routing architecture with three key components: (a) content-aware probing before retrieval, (b) short-term memory gating during execution, and (c) selective multi-provider storage. They also design a training-data synthesis pipeline that generates phase-specific supervision signals for learning effective routing policies.

Result: MemAgent improves average accuracy by 10.0% across three benchmarks (GAIA, WebWalkerQA, and xBench-DS), consistently outperforming every individual memory method on all benchmarks. It achieves these gains with minimal computational overhead (<0.3% routing cost) and even reduces average task steps by 12%, indicating improved sample efficiency and decision quality.

Conclusion: Heterogeneous memory management through learned routing is more effective than relying on any single memory representation. By treating memory as a routing problem and combining content-aware retrieval, short-term memory control, and selective storage, MemAgent yields substantial gains in performance and efficiency on long-horizon tasks, suggesting a promising direction for scalable agent memory systems.

Abstract: Current agents remain largely stateless across tasks, limiting their ability to continually improve from prior interactions and making memory essential for long-horizon agentic behavior. Existing memory methods seek to reuse past experience, but most rely on a single memory representation (e.g., trajectories, reflections, skills, structured knowledge) whose effectiveness varies across task distributions. Rethinking this design space, we evaluate 13 memory methods and find that no single method generalizes across benchmarks, revealing the potential of managing heterogeneous memory providers. We formulate agent memory as a routing problem in which a memory agent decides which memory provider to retrieve from, whether to inject short-term memory, and which providers should store the resulting experience. Based on this perspective, we propose MemAgent, featuring a content-aware routing architecture and a training-data synthesis pipeline. The routing architecture combines content-aware probing before retrieval, short-term memory gating during execution, and selective multi-provider storage, while the training pipeline synthesizes phase-specific supervision for routing decisions. Across GAIA, WebWalkerQA, and xBench-DS, MemAgent improves average accuracy by 10.0% and outperforms every individual memory method across all three benchmarks. These gains come with less than 0.3% routing overhead and a 12% reduction in average task steps.

</details>


### [209] [Beyond Dyadic Memory: Interaction-Aware Multimodal Memory with Adaptive Agentic Retrieval for Multi-Party Spoken Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32522)
*Wenxu Jia,Xize Cheng,Zihan Zhang,Dongjie Fu,Linjun Li,Wenshi Chen,Yangyang Wu,Tao Jin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces VoxPolyMem, a multimodal long-term memory framework for multi-party spoken conversations, and evaluates it on a new benchmark, VoxPolyBench, where it substantially outperforms prior memory systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most long-term memory research for AI agents focuses on dyadic (one-on-one) text or image-text interactions, neglecting multi-party spoken conversations. Such conversations are more complex: the system must track multiple speakers across sessions, remember who said what to whom, and integrate multimodal evidence over time to provide persistent, personalized assistance. There is also a lack of benchmarks that rigorously test these abilities in realistic multi-party spoken settings.

Method: The authors propose VoxPolyMem, an interaction-aware multimodal memory framework with: (1) incremental speaker identification to recognize and track participants across sessions; (2) a hierarchical memory structure with three layers—interaction memory (raw conversational context), fact memory (extracted structured information), and participant profiles (personalized, longer-term information per speaker); and (3) a retrieval process framed as sequential decision-making, where an agent iteratively rewrites queries, selects retrieval tools, and chooses memory layers based on accumulated evidence. They develop Evidence-Gain GRPO (EG-GRPO), a reinforcement learning strategy with round-wise credit assignment to encourage the agent to gather complementary evidence over multiple retrieval steps. They also build VoxPolyBench, a benchmark designed to test memory evolution, personalized QA, memory retrieval and reasoning, and interaction reasoning and attribution in multi-party spoken conversations. Additional evaluations are conducted on Mem-Gallery and H2HMem-Multi benchmarks.

Result: On the newly proposed VoxPolyBench benchmark, VoxPolyMem achieves an overall score of 85.0, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 23.6 points. On two existing benchmarks, Mem-Gallery and H2HMem-Multi, VoxPolyMem attains scores of 89.6 and 74.4, respectively, exceeding the strongest public memory baselines by more than 8 points on each. These results show consistent and substantial improvements across metrics related to long-term memory and reasoning in multi-party multimodal conversation settings.

Conclusion: VoxPolyMem provides a robust long-term memory framework for multi-party spoken interactions, effectively handling speaker identification, interaction structure, and hierarchical memory retrieval. Its sequential decision-making retrieval policy and EG-GRPO training lead to superior evidence collection and reasoning compared with prior approaches. The strong performance on VoxPolyBench and other benchmarks suggests that VoxPolyMem is a promising foundation for persistent, personalized AI assistants operating in complex, multi-party multimodal environments, and the released code and datasets support further research in this direction.

Abstract: Long-term memory enables agents to accumulate information and reason across sessions, yet existing research primarily focuses on dyadic text or image-text conversations, leaving long-term memory for multi-party spoken conversations underexplored. This setting requires preserving conversational content, identifying participants across sessions, and retaining who speaks to whom. To this end, we propose VoxPolyMem, an interaction-aware multimodal memory framework combining incremental speaker identification with a memory hierarchy comprising interaction memory, fact memory, and participant profiles. We formulate retrieval as sequential decision-making, where an agent rewrites queries and selects retrieval tools and memory layers based on accumulated evidence to address information gaps. We further introduce Evidence-Gain GRPO (EG-GRPO), which uses round-wise credit assignment to encourage complementary evidence acquisition. We also construct VoxPolyBench to evaluate memory evolution, personalized answering, memory retrieval and reasoning, and interaction reasoning and attribution in multi-party spoken conversations. VoxPolyMem achieves an overall score of 85.0 on VoxPolyBench, surpassing the strongest evaluated baseline by 23.6 points. On Mem-Gallery and H2HMem-Multi, it scores 89.6 and 74.4, respectively, exceeding the strongest evaluated public memory baselines by over 8 points each. These results highlight its potential for persistent, personalized assistance in multi-party multimodal interactions. Code and datasets are available at https://voxpolymem.github.io/VoxPolyBench/demo/

</details>


### [210] [AmbiModBench: Benchmarking Gene Perturbation Prediction Beyond Shared Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32527)
*Sikai Huang,Zhiwen Yang,Kai Yu,Jiayuan Chen,Stan Z. Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AmbiModBench is a new benchmarking framework that evaluates how well models predict gene-specific cellular responses to perturbations, separating true target-specific learning from background effects and accounting for coverage in representation space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing computational models for predicting cellular responses to genetic perturbations in single-cell genomics are judged with metrics that suffer from three problems: (1) they cannot disentangle target-specific prediction from generic background response, (2) they stay high even when gene identities are shuffled, so they don’t confirm gene-level correctness, and (3) they provide scores at one training size that say nothing about how broadly in representation space the model can generalize (coverage). These issues make it unclear what high benchmark scores really mean and may overstate model capabilities.

Method: The authors introduce AmbiModBench, a new benchmark that: (a) pairs every performance score with a baseline based on the training-set mean fitted on the exact same data split, making it possible to separate target-specific gains from shared background responses; (b) performs gene-coordinate permutation tests for each readout to assess whether metrics remain high when gene labels are shuffled, thus checking gene-level specificity; and (c) quantitatively links distances in learned representation space (embeddings) to variation in cellular response, thereby characterizing coverage and the extent to which nearby points in representation space share similar perturbation responses. They apply this protocol to multiple datasets (K562, RPE1, and Norman).

Result: When applied to K562, RPE1, and Norman datasets, AmbiModBench reveals that many models’ strong absolute performance scores are mainly due to learning shared background responses rather than correctly capturing target-specific effects of individual perturbations. Common readouts appear to align more with overall response magnitude distributions than with which genes are affected. Performance improvements tend to follow how well the training data cover the representation space, rather than simply the number of training examples. However, for the RPE1 dataset, the benchmark identifies a reproducible, genuinely target-specific performance gain across five additional data splits and three different gene subsets—something that traditional absolute metrics alone would not distinguish from background effects.

Conclusion: AmbiModBench provides a more informative, specificity-aware, gene-resolved, and coverage-aware way to evaluate models that predict cellular responses to genetic perturbations. It demonstrates that widely used absolute metrics can be misleading, as they often conflate background and target-specific signals and fail to verify gene-level accuracy or coverage. By referencing a training-mean baseline, employing gene-permutation screening, and explicitly relating embedding distances to response variation, the benchmark clarifies which parts of model performance reflect real, target-specific predictive power. This framework can guide the development and assessment of more truly informative perturbation prediction models in single-cell genomics.

Abstract: Predicting cellular responses to genetic perturbations helps prioritize experiments in single-cell genomics, where exhaustive measurement is infeasible. While computational models increasingly predict these responses, three evaluation deficiencies obscure what their scores demonstrate. First, absolute metrics cannot separate target-specific predictions from a shared background response. Second, common metrics remain high under gene shuffling, so gene-level accuracy is never verified. Third, a score at one training size says nothing about coverage, which depends on representation-space proximity and response-constraining power. We propose AmbiModBench, a specificity-aware, gene-resolved and coverage-aware benchmark. It pairs every score with a training-mean reference fitted on the same split, screens each readout by gene-coordinate permutation, and links embedding distance to response variation. Across K562, RPE1 and Norman, strong absolute scores largely reflect shared background rather than target-specific learning. Widely used readouts track response magnitude distributions rather than the affected genes. Detectable gain follows representation-space coverage rather than training-set size. Nonetheless, on RPE1 the protocol yields a reproducible target-specific gain across five additional splits and three gene selections, which absolute scores alone cannot distinguish from shared background.

</details>


### [211] [Fail Loudly: An Auditable Runtime for Agentic Data Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32528)
*Hanxu Yan,Langxuan Deng,Zhengle Wang,Yibo Wang,Chunwei Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RADAR is a runtime system for LLM-based data-science agents that makes their analytical choices explicit, auditable, and correctable, substantially reducing silent errors and improving benchmark performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-powered data-science agents can orchestrate multi-step analyses over heterogeneous data, but they frequently make subtle semantic errors—such as mis-choosing data sources, mis-scoping cohorts, or mis-defining statistical quantities—that do not crash the computation. These errors yield plausible but incorrect results that are hard to detect because current systems lack explicit tracking and validation of analytical decisions. The authors aim to create a mechanism that exposes these choices, ties them to concrete evidence, and catches inconsistencies early so agents can correct themselves.

Method: The authors design RADAR, an auditable runtime with three main components. (1) An evidence-preserving exploration module retrieves content relevant to the task while maintaining detailed provenance information, including source locations and coverage of observations. (2) A typed-operator execution layer records each analytical operation together with its declared inputs, arguments, and resulting observations, turning the workflow into a structured, inspectable trace. (3) A runtime validation mechanism checks intended operations against observed data and constraints; when inconsistencies or conflicts are detected, it rejects the operation or returns diagnostic feedback. This feedback loop allows an LLM agent to revise its plan or computations before incorrect results propagate, while the LLM still handles high-level semantic reasoning.

Result: On the KramaBench benchmark, RADAR attains scores of 0.723 when using full source retrieval and 0.747 when supplied with gold-standard sources, yielding relative improvements of 35.9% and 28.8% respectively over the strongest baseline systems. On two additional benchmarks representing different data-analysis workflows—DA-Code and DABStep—RADAR provides relative performance gains of 14.0% and 59.3%, indicating that the approach generalizes beyond a single task suite.

Conclusion: RADAR demonstrates that embedding LLM-based data-science agents within an auditable, evidence-aware runtime that uses typed operators and runtime validation can substantially reduce silent analytical errors. By enforcing that agents “fail loudly” and by providing structured diagnostic feedback tied to data provenance, RADAR improves reliability and performance across multiple benchmarks and data-analysis settings. This suggests that robust, inspectable execution environments are a key ingredient for trustworthy LLM-driven analytics.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled data-science agents to automate multi-step analyses over heterogeneous files. However, incorrect choices regarding data sources, scope, or statistical definitions often lead to silent errors: computations execute successfully but produce plausible yet incorrect outputs that fail to answer the intended question. To mitigate this, we present RADAR, an auditable runtime that makes an agent's analytical choices inspectable and supports their revision through execution feedback. RADAR operates through three core mechanisms. First, an evidence-preserving exploration module retrieves task-relevant content while retaining source locations and observation coverage. Next, the runtime uses typed operators to record the agent's declared inputs, operation arguments, and resulting observations. Finally, runtime validation checks proposed operations against these observations. When a conflict is detected, the runtime rejects the operation or provides diagnostic feedback, allowing the agent to revise its choices before errors propagate. This design enables agents to fail loudly while leaving semantic interpretation to the LLM. On KramaBench, RADAR achieves overall scores of 0.723 with full source retrieval and 0.747 with gold sources supplied, corresponding to relative gains of 35.9% and 28.8% over the strongest baselines. Beyond KramaBench, RADAR achieves relative performance gains of 14.0% on DA-Code and 59.3% on DABStep, demonstrating its applicability across diverse agentic data-analysis workflows.

</details>


### [212] [LLMAdBench: A Human Preference Benchmark for Advertising in LLM Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32533)
*Rui Ai,Yuqing Liu,Sitao Qiu,Yun Qiao,Yuhan Wang,Jessica Xiwen Wang,Yiqi Yang,Lihong Huang,Ruiyao Sun,Kaifeng Zhang,Shengze Ding,Jiaqi He,Xinman Wang,Tianhao Gao,Jimmy Qin,Jianghao Lin,Chonghuan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents LLMAdBench, a human-preference benchmark for evaluating where to place ads in LLM-generated responses and shows current LLMs are unreliable judges of ad placement preferences compared to humans, while fine-tuning on the benchmark yields significant improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As ads in LLM outputs become a new business model, there is no standardized way to evaluate how ad insertion—particularly ad placement—affects user and advertiser outcomes. Existing evaluations lack controlled, shared data on human preferences over where ads should appear in AI-generated content, and there is uncertainty about whether LLMs themselves can reliably serve as proxies for human evaluators in this domain.

Method: The authors construct LLMAdBench, a benchmark consisting of paired LLM responses that are identical except for the position of a single, matched advertisement. For each user conversation, base answer, and ad, they create such pairs under two disclosure conditions (explicitly labeled as sponsored vs. blended into the answer). Human annotators then compare each pair along six criteria capturing both advertiser-centric and user-centric objectives. They aggregate more than 18,000 such judgments and use the dataset to (1) test eight frontier LLMs in a judge role, analyzing consistency under order-swapping and agreement across models, and (2) train a Qwen3-8B model on these human preferences to assess learnability and generalization on held-out data.

Result: The evaluation shows that all eight tested frontier LLMs perform poorly as preference judges for ad placement: they reverse around 25% of their decisions when the order of options is swapped, demonstrate low agreement with each other, and exhibit systematic biases in placement preferences compared with human annotators. In contrast, a Qwen3-8B model fine-tuned on the LLMAdBench data substantially outperforms its base version and all evaluated zero-shot frontier models on predicting human preferences in the held-out set. Additionally, analysis of the benchmark reveals quantifiable trade-offs between advertiser and user objectives and highlights that explicit sponsorship disclosure leads to different user preferences over where ads should be placed.

Conclusion: LLMAdBench offers a controlled, large-scale human-preference benchmark for ad placement in LLM outputs, enabling rigorous study of how ads should be integrated into generated content. The findings indicate that off-the-shelf frontier LLMs are currently unreliable as substitutes for human judgment in this setting, but that human preferences over ad placement are learnable with targeted fine-tuning. The benchmark also provides quantitative evidence of advertiser–user trade-offs and shows that sponsorship disclosure materially shifts user preferences, underscoring the importance of transparency and data-driven design when deploying ad-supported LLM systems.

Abstract: Inserting advertisements (ads) into consumer-facing LLM output is emerging as a new business model, but there is little shared evidence on how such ad insertion should be evaluated or how it affects user preferences. We introduce LLMAdBench, a human-preference benchmark for studying advertising in LLM-generated content. The benchmark isolates a simple but practically important decision: given a user conversation, an LLM response, and a matched advertisement, where should the ad be placed? Our dataset compares pairs of responses that differ only in ad position while holding all other conditions fixed including the user query, base answer, advertisement, and disclosure condition. Human annotators evaluate each pair based on six criteria from both advertiser's and user's perspectives. The resulting benchmark contains more than 18000 human judgments across two disclosure conditions: explicitly labeling the ad as sponsored and merging it into the response without disclosure. We use LLMAdBench to evaluate eight frontier LLMs as preference judges and find that they are not reliable substitutes for human evaluation. Even the most stable models reverse roughly one quarter of their decisions when the presentation order is swapped, agreement across models is low, and their placement preferences differ systematically from those of human annotators. Moreover, LLMAdBench contains substantial learnable signal. In particular, a Qwen3-8B model fine-tuned on the human preferences improves substantially over its base model and outperforms all zero-shot frontier judges on the held-out prediction task. Beyond model evaluation, LLMAdBench provides quantitative evidence on the advertiser-user trade-off and shows that the sponsorship disclosure systematically changes users' preference over ad placement.

</details>


### [213] [Interpretable Physics Informed WiFi Indoor Localization: Learning an Effective Access Point Geometry and Using It to Prune](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32539)
*Arshia Eftekhari zadeh,Rezvan Nasiri,Hadi Moradi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a physics-informed, hierarchical deep learning model for WiFi fingerprint-based indoor localization that jointly estimates user positions and the underlying geometry of access points, improving accuracy and enabling effective access point selection without needing true AP coordinates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Indoor localization with WiFi fingerprints can be accurate using deep learning, but existing models are black boxes: they offer limited interpretability, cannot easily reuse learned spatial information, and typically assume access to surveyed AP positions. There is also a need to reduce the number of APs (features) without sacrificing localization quality, especially when AP coordinates are unavailable.

Method: The authors design a hierarchical deep learning framework where decoders are constrained by physical signal-propagation relationships. From RSSI fingerprints and labelled user locations, the network jointly predicts user position and infers a latent geometry of surrounding APs, approximating their spatial configuration without using ground-truth AP coordinates. The learned geometry is then used to rank APs via Fisher information and to prune less informative APs, enabling geometry-guided AP selection and feature reduction.

Result: On the UJIIndoorLoc benchmark, the chained physics-informed model attains a mean 3D localization error of 7.07 m, improving error by 26–36% compared to baseline deep models and outperforming previously reported methods on the same split by 10.6–31.0% relative error. Pruning 35–50% of APs causes only minor degradation in localization accuracy. On Tampere/TUT and UTSIndoorLoc datasets, AP selection driven by the inferred geometry achieves performance comparable to selectors trained directly on labelled data with known AP information.

Conclusion: Embedding physics-informed structure into deep models allows simultaneous learning of user locations and an interpretable AP geometry from RSSI data alone. This improves indoor localization accuracy and enables robust AP ranking and pruning, even without surveyed AP coordinates. The work demonstrates that adding physically meaningful interpretability can enhance performance while supporting efficient, data-driven feature selection in WiFi fingerprint-based indoor positioning systems.

Abstract: Deep learning models can achieve high accuracy for indoor localization, but their black-box nature limits interpretability and the reuse of learned information. We propose a hierarchical deep learning framework for WiFi fingerprint-based indoor localization that jointly predicts user location and learns an effective geometry of the surrounding access points (APs). Physics-informed decoders infer this geometry directly from RSSI measurements and labelled user positions, without requiring the true AP coordinates during training. The learned geometry is then used to rank and prune APs.
  On the UJIIndoorLoc dataset, the proposed chained model achieves a mean 3D localization error of 7.07 m, reducing error by 26% to 36% compared with baseline models. Previously published methods evaluated on the same official split report errors 10.6% to 31.0% higher. Pruning 35% or 50% of the APs causes only a small loss in localization accuracy. The inferred geometry also enables Fisher-information-based AP ranking even when fingerprint databases do not contain surveyed AP coordinates. Experiments on the Tampere/TUT and UTSIndoorLoc datasets show that geometry-guided AP selection performs comparably to selectors built directly from labelled data. These results show that physics-informed interpretability can improve indoor localization while also supporting effective feature selection.

</details>


### [214] [Porimon: An LLM-Based Pokémon Battle Agent Enhanced by Long/Short-Term Knowledge Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32544)
*Dongyin Zhuo,Fengjunjie Pan,Nenad Petrovic,Alois Knoll*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces an LLM-based Pokémon battle agent, Porimon, using a Long/Short-Term Knowledge Augmented Generation (LSTKAG) framework, shows strong performance gains over prior LLM and rule-based baselines via external tools and retrieval, but finds mixed evidence for benefits from long-term experience summaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents struggle with tasks requiring opponent-aware planning, especially when they must reason over long interaction histories and reuse knowledge from past similar tasks without task-specific fine-tuning. Pokémon Battles are a complex, strategic environment well-suited as a benchmark. The authors aim to understand how to systematically boost LLM agent performance using external information, past states, and reusable experience, while staying within a pure prompting / tool-using paradigm.

Method: They propose Long/Short-Term Knowledge Augmented Generation (LSTKAG), which augments an LLM with (1) short-term memory of past states within the current game and (2) retrieval of long-term experience summaries from similar previous battles, conditioned on the current state. Building on this, they design Porimon, an LLM-based Pokémon battle agent that uses LSTKAG plus an external API to obtain precise damage calculations and detailed game information. They run large-scale, tournament-style self-play and versus-baseline experiments—about 15,000 battles—for hyperparameter tuning, ablations (e.g., with/without extended information retrieval and long-term KAG), and performance comparison against PokéLLMon and a rule-based heuristic player.

Result: Porimon agents with tuned hyperparameters substantially outperform both PokéLLMon (a prior LLM-based Pokémon agent) and a rule-based heuristic opponent across 15,000 battle experiments. Ablation results show that variants with extended game information retrieval clearly outperform versions without that extension, confirming its positive effect. However, experiments do not provide conclusive evidence about the effectiveness of the long-term experience retrieval component (Long-Term KAG); its contribution remains uncertain given current data.

Conclusion: Porimon, built on the LSTKAG framework and enhanced with external game APIs, demonstrates that equipping LLM-based agents with rich external resources and structured short-term context can significantly improve performance on opponent-aware planning tasks. While long-term retrieval of experience summaries is a promising idea, its impact is not yet clearly validated. Overall, the study suggests that combining precise external tools, systematic access to recent task states, and potentially reusable prior-task experience is a viable path to making LLM agents more competitive in complex strategic environments such as Pokémon Battles.

Abstract: In this paper, we use Pokémon Battles as a case study to investigate how to improve the performance of LLM-based agents in tasks that require opponent-aware planning without additional fine-tuning. We propose Long/Short-Term Knowledge Augmented Generation (LSTKAG), a mechanism that enables LLM-based agents to leverage past states of the current task and retrieve experience summaries from similar previous task instances based on the current state. Based on LSTKAG, we design Porimon, an LLM-based agent structure for Pokémon Battles. For optimization, we introduce an external API for precise damage calculation and more detailed information about the game. We conduct tournament-like evaluation experiments comprising 15,000 battles for hyperparameter optimization, ablation studies, and performance evaluation. The results indicate that Porimon-based players with hyperparameter optimization significantly outperform players based on PokéLLMon, an LLM-based agent structure proposed in previous research, and the rule-based heuristic player. Furthermore, our ablation study shows that Porimon variants outperform the one without extension in game information retrieval, which shows the contribution of that extension. However, the current experiment results are inconclusive regarding the contribution of Long-Term KAG. These results suggest that introducing external resources, information from previous states of the current task, and experience summaries from similar previous task instances could elevate the performance of LLM-based agents designed for tasks requiring opponent-aware planning.

</details>


### [215] [Are Vision-Language-Action Models Robust to One-Step Observation Perturbations?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32550)
*Shojiro Yamabe,Jun Sakuma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies a new safety risk for vision-language-action (VLA) models: brief, one-step observation corruptions, and proposes CARE, a method that adaptively adjusts action execution length to improve robustness without hurting normal performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most prior safety work on VLA models focuses on persistent, continuous perturbations to the agent’s observations across an entire episode. In the real world, however, sensors or perception can be corrupted only momentarily (e.g., a brief occlusion or glitch), which might still cause serious failures. This type of one-step, transient perturbation and its interaction with how long an agent commits to an action sequence are underexplored, so the paper aims to understand and mitigate this specific safety threat.

Method: The authors systematically test robustness of VLA models to one-step perturbations that occur at a single time step within each episode. They vary the action chunk execution length—how many steps the agent commits to before re-observing and re-planning—to see how it affects vulnerability. Building on these insights, they introduce CARE, a mechanism that dynamically chooses the execution length at each decision point. CARE compares the current predicted action chunk with the previously predicted one and, when inconsistency is detected (suggesting a perturbation), it switches to shorter execution lengths; otherwise, it maintains longer chunks to keep efficiency and performance under clean observations.

Result: Experiments show that one-step perturbations can significantly degrade VLA task performance, and that the extent of degradation depends strongly on the chosen action chunk length. Longer execution lengths tend to amplify the negative impact of a single corrupted observation. With CARE, the system becomes notably more robust to such momentary perturbations, while incurring only small computational overhead. Importantly, CARE preserves high performance in unperturbed (clean) settings by only shortening execution lengths when perturbations are suspected.

Conclusion: Momentary, one-step observation corruptions are a serious and previously underappreciated safety risk for VLA models, especially when they commit to long action chunks. The proposed CARE mechanism, which adaptively adjusts execution length based on action consistency, effectively mitigates this risk, improving robustness with minimal cost and without harming clean performance. This suggests that dynamic control over action commitment is a practical direction for safer deployment of VLA systems in the physical world.

Abstract: Understanding the safety risks of vision-language-action (VLA) models is essential for their deployment in the physical world. Existing safety research has mainly considered persistent perturbations that are applied continuously to observations throughout an episode. However, momentary observation corruption, in which observations are severely perturbed only briefly within an episode, remains an underexplored safety threat. To address this gap, this work investigates robustness to one-step perturbations applied at a single time step per episode. Our experiments reveal that these perturbations substantially degrade VLA performance and that their impact depends on the action chunk execution length. Based on them, we propose CARE, which dynamically selects the execution length based on consistency with the previously predicted action chunk. CARE improves robustness with low computational overhead while preserving clean performance by selecting shorter execution lengths only under perturbations.

</details>


### [216] [Artificial intelligences and human scientists exhibit complementary strengths in theory building](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32562)
*Ke Li,Spyros I. Zoumpoulis,Phanish Puranam,Philip Parker,Matthew Eshbaugh-Soha,Izzy Gainsburg,Michael Gilead,Igor Grossmann,Britt Hadar,Yoel Inbar,Almog Simchon,Robb Willer,Rui Ai,Ruicheng Ao,Gavin J. Bala,Matthew Bidwell,Shuang Cai,Kai Chang,Skyler Y. Chen,Cory J. Clark,Irmak Dai,Abhinandan Dalal,Connor Douglas,Alexis Du,Zhehang Du,Leyun Feng,Isabel Fernandez-Mateo,Linnea Gandhi,Cyrille Grumbach,Anmol Gupta,Vansh Gupta,Maria Hademer,Jay H. Hardy,Chen Kai Huang,Jacob Xiangyu Jin,Ufuk Keskin,Na Hyun Kim,Mert Kobaş,Byounghoon Koh,Gabrielle Lamont-Dobbin,Gregory Lanzalotto,Sun Young Lee,Dingzhe Leng,Chenjun Li,Weiyuan Li,Zeyuan Li,Zhongyuan Liang,Ning Liu,Peihong Liu,Yuhan Liu,Jiuyao Lu,Wanteng Ma,Nicolas Martinet,Natnael Mulat,Christina A. Nguyen,Khai Nguyen,Quang Minh Nguyen,Naja Pape,Chanwoo Park,Stefanos Poulidis,Jeffrey Sanchez-Burks,Michael Schaerer,Isabelle Solal,Yanbo Song,Junghyo Sun,Qingyao Sun,Rui Sun,Roderick Swaab,Kevin Tan,Dequn Teng,Michelle A. Vaccaro,Robin Vigerbaeck,Xiaomeng Wang,Randol H. Yao,Duygu Yilmaz,Shun Yiu,Ecem Yucesoy,Allen Zang,Ruijia Zhang,Xilan Zhang,Yichi Zhang,Zhanhao Zhang,Eric Luis Uhlmann*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper compares LLMs with human social scientists on high-level theory-related tasks about inequality, finding that AIs often outperform individuals but humans provide more diverse and efficiently predictive theories, making both complementary for collective scientific work.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether and how large language models can match or exceed human social scientists in complex cognitive tasks like theory building, prediction, and theory updating within a concrete, contentious research domain (gender and race inequality), and to clarify what unique strengths and weaknesses each brings to scientific inquiry.

Method: The authors evaluated 25 large language models against 13 senior researchers and 60 doctoral scholars on tasks including formulating theories about gender and race inequality, predicting novel empirical results, and revising theories when presented with new evidence. They compared performance on predictive accuracy, theory quality (as rated by independent blind raters), theory complexity, diversity of ideas, and responsiveness to new data.

Result: LLMs outperformed most individual human participants on most tasks, producing more elaborated and highly rated theories, and they were more willing to revise theories to accommodate new evidence. However, their added complexity often did not improve predictive accuracy. Human theories, though simpler, achieved better predictive efficiency and showed greater diversity and larger gains in accuracy when aggregated across individuals.

Conclusion: AI systems, especially LLMs, appear well-suited to handling complex theoretical elaboration and rapid belief updating, but humans contribute crucial diversity and parsimony that enhance collective prediction and creativity. The paper suggests a complementary division of labor in which AI augments but does not replace human scientists, particularly in domains like social science theory-building about inequality.

Abstract: We investigate the effectiveness of artificial intelligences (AI)-specifically large language models (LLMs)-relative to human scientists at high-level cognitive tasks in social science such as theory formulation, predictions of novel empirical results, and theory revision in response to new evidence. The research domain was academic discourse regarding gender and race inequality. Our findings, comparing 25 LLMs with 13 senior researchers and 60 doctoral scholars, reveal that the AIs outperformed most humans individually on most of the present tasks, while human theories were more diverse and exhibited greater gains in predictive accuracy from aggregation. AI-generated theories were more extensively elaborated, involving additional theoretical paths and latent variables, and were rated as higher quality than human theories by independent raters blinded to source. However, this theoretical complexity was in part ornamental, in that it was not associated with more accurate predictions about empirical patterns in data; in contrast, human scientists achieved greater predictive efficiency with simpler theories. The AIs were significantly more likely than human scientists to revise their theories to incorporate new evidence; human scientists updated their beliefs in a selective way that is sensitive to prior prediction errors. We speculate that the superior processing capacity of artificial intelligences makes them especially well-suited to tasks requiring grappling with complexity, but that the greater diversity of human ideas is essential to wise crowds and collective creativity.

</details>


### [217] [ProTTT: Learning to Learn Semantic User Memory with Test-Time Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32564)
*Sejun Park,Hyoungjo Bhang,Hyein Jeong,Yohan Jo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes ProTTT, a profile-supervised meta-learning method that builds a compact, evolving user memory for language model personalization, outperforming history-based and parametric baselines while reducing inference cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing personalization methods for language models either use long, ever-growing user histories at inference time—which is expensive and requires separate retrieval/summarization—or rely on parametric user representations that must be repeatedly reconstructed as new data arrives. Moreover, test-time training on user history alone may not reliably extract the semantic user knowledge needed for effective personalization. There is a need for a method that can continuously incorporate new user data into a compact representation that captures high-level user preferences and knowledge, while remaining efficient and robust to varying history sizes.

Method: The authors introduce ProTTT, a profile-supervised meta-learning framework that learns a semantic user memory. They start from a shared memory initialization (a set of parameters common to all users) and adapt it for each user through test-time training on that user’s history, enabling continuous evolution as new interactions appear. To ensure this memory encodes semantic user knowledge rather than just overfitting to history, they meta-train the shared initialization using textual user profiles as supervision, so that subsequent test-time updates from history naturally move the memory toward meaningful user-specific semantics. This yields a lightweight, parameterized user memory that stands in for the full history at inference time.

Result: Across diverse personalization benchmarks, ProTTT outperforms in-context learning with full user history as well as all compared parametric personalization baselines. It achieves these gains while significantly reducing inference costs by compressing long user histories into compact parameterized memories. Empirical analyses further show that using profile supervision leads to better capture of semantic user knowledge, that the learned memories can track and retain evolving user preferences over time, and that the method is robust across varying amounts of history.

Conclusion: ProTTT effectively leverages test-time training and profile-supervised meta-learning to build continuously evolving, semantic user memories for language model personalization. The approach offers better personalization quality than both history-based ICL and existing parametric methods, while being more efficient at inference by replacing long histories with compact memories. The study positions ProTTT as a strong baseline for future work on adaptive, user-specific memory mechanisms in language models.

Abstract: Personalization requires language models to capture user-specific knowledge from a growing user history. Existing context-based approaches incur increasing inference costs as user history accumulates and rely on separate retrieval or summarization stages, while parametric-based approaches often require reconstructing user representations when new user data is added. We introduce ProTTT, a profile-supervised meta-learning framework for learning semantic user memory. The memory construction starts from a shared initialization and is updated for each user through test-time training on user history, allowing it to evolve continuously as the history grows. However, since test-time training alone does not explicitly encourage the memory to capture semantic user knowledge necessary for personalization, we learn this shared initialization using textual user profiles as supervision, so that test-time training on user history captures semantic knowledge more effectively. ProTTT consistently outperforms both full history ICL and all parametric baselines across diverse benchmarks, while substantially reducing inference cost by compressing user history into a lightweight parameterized memory. Our analysis also shows that profile supervision is a reliable objective for learning semantic user knowledge and that the resulting memory can track and retain evolving user preferences, while remaining robust across different history sizes. Overall, we demonstrate the effectiveness of test-time training for personalization and establish ProTTT as a baseline for continuously evolving user memory.

</details>


### [218] [CUE-Mem: Benchmarking Long-Term User Memory via Implicit Cues in Multimodal Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32574)
*Yulin Hu,Yanyan Zhao,Zimo Long,Xing Fu,Mengtong Ji,Weixiang Zhao,Yutai Hou,Qianchao Wang,Dandan Tu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents CUE-Mem, a benchmark for testing how multimodal agents build and use long-term user memory from subtle, implicit cues across text, images, and audio.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most existing memory benchmarks focus on text-only inputs or explicit multimodal facts, overlooking user information that appears only as subtle, recurring cues in images or audio. This gap makes it hard to evaluate whether agents can form realistic long-term memories in multimodal, conversational settings.

Method: The authors construct CUE-Mem, a benchmark with 2,674 questions spanning explicit and implicit evidence scenarios over text, images, and audio. The benchmark includes four tasks—Entity Recall, Long Pattern, Personalized Recommendation, and Answer Refusal—to probe different aspects of long-term user memory. They evaluate memory systems that store textualized representations versus those with native multimodal access, compare performance against oracle evidence, and analyze the impact of more detailed captions and different backbone models, as well as retrieval noise from multimodal indexing.

Result: They find that performance on questions requiring implicit cues is much worse than when oracle evidence is directly provided, indicating that the main difficulty lies in preserving and retrieving subtle multimodal cues, not in answering questions per se. Adding more detailed captions recovers some evidence but yields uneven improvements and rapidly increases token usage. Native multimodal access can help but does not consistently solve the problem: results vary considerably by backbone model and are degraded by retrieval noise in multimodal indexing.

Conclusion: CUE-Mem exposes a fundamental bottleneck in current multimodal memory systems: capturing and reusing subtle, implicit cues spread across images, audio, and text. The benchmark offers a targeted testbed for developing memory mechanisms that can selectively retain, retrieve, and effectively exploit such cues, highlighting the need for more efficient and robust multimodal memory representations and retrieval methods.

Abstract: Long-term memory is essential for multimodal agents that interact with users across sustained conversations. However, user memories are not always explicitly stated: they may also be implied by recurring background objects in images, ambient sounds in audio, or other peripheral multimodal cues. Existing benchmarks largely focus on text-only memory or explicit multimodal evidence, leaving implicit multimodal cues underexplored. We introduce CUE-Mem, a text-image-audio benchmark for evaluating long-term user memory from implicit cues. CUE-Mem contains 2,674 questions across explicit and implicit evidence settings and covers four tasks: Entity Recall, Long Pattern, Personalized Recommendation, and Answer Refusal. Across textualized memory systems, implicit performance remains far below oracle evidence, locating the main bottleneck in preserving and retrieving subtle cues rather than question answerability. Increasing caption detail recovers more of this evidence, but brings uneven gains and rapidly growing token costs, motivating native multimodal access. Yet native access does not uniformly resolve the bottleneck: evidence use depends strongly on the backbone, while multimodal indexing introduces substantial retrieval noise. CUE-Mem provides a testbed for memory systems that selectively retain, retrieve, and use subtle multimodal evidence.

</details>


### [219] [EMIR$^2$: Evolution-Aware Memory with Intent-Guided Multi-Round Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32584)
*Jinlan Liu,Hongliang Sun,Yong Wang,Bolin Zhang,Dinabo Sui,Dianhui Chu,Zhiying Tu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces EMIR^2, a framework that gives LLM agents better long-term memory by modeling how knowledge evolves over time and retrieving evidence through multiple intent-guided rounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-term memory systems for LLM agents treat memory as static and use single-shot retrieval, which makes them poor at handling changing facts, conflicting information, and evidence scattered across long interactions. The authors aim to build a memory system that can track the evolution of knowledge and flexibly gather distributed evidence for complex tasks.

Method: The authors design EMIR^2, which has two key components: (1) a State-Evolving Memory Graph (SEMG) that represents memory as evolving knowledge states built from temporal event trajectories and evidential links, and updates these states semantically based on new evidence; and (2) an intent-guided multi-round retrieval mechanism that iteratively identifies what evidence is missing for the current task and expands retrieval in multiple rounds using accumulated context and inferred intent.

Result: On two benchmarks, LoCoMo and MemConflict, EMIR^2 yields better performance in utilizing long-term memory, managing both dynamic and static conflicts, and handling complex retrieval tasks, with more than 12% relative improvement in some evaluation categories compared to baselines.

Conclusion: Jointly modeling memory evolution and adaptive, multi-round evidence acquisition significantly enhances LLM agents’ ability to use long-term interaction history, particularly in scenarios with evolving facts, conflicts, and distributed evidence.

Abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to leverage historical interactions for future tasks. However, existing memory systems struggle to utilize continuously evolving historical information, as they often rely on static memory representations and single-round retrieval strategies, failing to track factual changes or integrate distributed evidence across long-term interactions. To address these challenges, we propose \textsc{EMIR}$^{2}$, an \textbf{E}volution-Aware \textbf{M}emory framework with \textbf{I}ntent-Guided Multi-\textbf{R}ound \textbf{R}etrieval, enabling LLM agents to maintain evolving historical knowledge and adaptively retrieve relevant evidence. Specifically, \textsc{EMIR}$^{2}$ constructs a State-Evolving Memory Graph (SEMG) that represents long-term memory as evolving knowledge states supported by temporal event trajectories and evidential associations. By maintaining semantic states through evidence-based updates, SEMG preserves historical evolution and enables evidence tracing under complex and conflicting scenarios. Building upon this, we introduce an intent-guided multi-round retrieval mechanism that iteratively identifies missing evidence and expands retrieval based on accumulated information. Experiments on LoCoMo and MemConflict demonstrate that \textsc{EMIR}$^{2}$ improves long-term memory utilization, dynamic and static conflict handling, and complex retrieval performance, achieving relative improvements of more than 12\% in certain categories. These results highlight the effectiveness of jointly modeling memory evolution and adaptive evidence acquisition for long-term agent interactions.

</details>


### [220] [MA-FPPO: Multi-Agent Flow-Pretrained Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32594)
*Guowei Zou,Haonan Chen,Haitao Wang,Beiwen Zhang,Na Yan,Hejun Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce MA-FPPO, a method that fine-tunes multi-agent flow-based policies online to improve cooperation beyond what offline data supports.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline-trained multi-agent flow policies work well only within the distribution of their training data and fail to generalize to novel situations that require both adaptation to environment changes and improved coordination among agents.

Method: Pretrain multi-agent policies using flow matching on offline data, then convert the pretrained model into policies with explicit action likelihoods for both discrete and continuous actions and fine-tune them online with a policy-optimization style update that uses shared team advantages as the learning signal to enhance coordination.

Result: Across a wide benchmark, MA-FPPO yields an average 52.8% relative improvement over the best offline baselines in 30 settings and a 29.8% improvement over purely online learning methods under matched interaction budgets and evaluation protocols.

Conclusion: Combining offline flow-based pretraining with online advantage-based fine-tuning produces multi-agent policies that generalize better and coordinate more effectively than either offline-only or online-only approaches.

Abstract: Multi-agent flow policies learn cooperative behavior from fixed offline datasets, but often struggle to complete tasks in situations not covered by the offline data. In these situations, agents must both adapt to changes in the environment and coordinate with one another, yet action patterns learned offline are often insufficient for effective adaptation and coordination. To address this problem, we propose Multi-Agent Flow-Pretrained Policy Optimization (MA-FPPO), which uses online fine-tuning to improve the cooperative behavior of models pretrained with flow matching through new interactions with the environment.
